summary: The Food Inspector took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found in exhibit PW 1/C that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the Lal mirchi seed was adulterated. The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a samples of lal Er mirchi Powder from the shop of respondent. The Public Analyst found in the sample only nine living meals worm and he has neither stated that it is insect infested nor that it was unfit for human consumption on account of the presence of the meal wyorms nor that the same is otherwise unfit for animal consumption on the account of its presence. The respondent filed a Criminal Revision before the High Court which dismissed the criminal revision in limine. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that in the case where food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting, decomposed or insectable, it would be deemed to be unfit for ' human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section 2(1)(f). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The true meaning of Section 2(ia) (f) has been brought out in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal, ; , and the conclusion that 'it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfitfor human consumption ' is a correct statement of the law. [473B] 1.1 The true interpretation of Section2(ia)(f) had been brought into the Municipal Corporation Delhi vs Tek Chand Bhatia, ; and Municipal Corporation, Delhi vsKacherooMal, ; ; , referred to. 1.2 In the instant case, the Public analyst has found in his sample only 9 living meal Worms and he had neither stated nor that there was it insect in infested or infested form or that on account Of any other cause. The certificate of the Public Examiner does not support the case. [474C D] 1:3 In the present sample, however worm was found to be present and that in our view does not satisfy the requirements of the definition "adulterated article" under Section 2 (1)(a) of the Act. [475E] Municipal Corporation Of Delhi vs M/s. Narkeklange Roller Flour Mills & Anr., ; , followed. 1:4 The true effect of the sub clause is that all the adjectives used earlier refer to the quality of the articles being unfit for Human consumption. But the presumption may not be conclusive in a cases, irrespective of the character of the Article, and the nature and extent of the vice afflicting it. [476E] 1 :5 The word "otherwise" in sub clause (f)(1) does suggest that all adjec ttives used previously refer to its quality. Nor is it necessary for me to do so having regard to the facts of this case. Even if the nine wormss found by the public Analyst in the samples are considered to be insects, the certificate of Public Analyst does not supported the case as of the Prosecution that the lal mirla powder was either worm. infested Or insect or infestation or that On account of presence of meal womorms the sample was unfit.

The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. He appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas, Dumka and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that he was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. HELD : The appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. [901 D] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , followed. In the present case the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Indeed no adequate reasons were given for rejecting the testimony of witnesses. The Magistrate rejected the testimony on the ground that he had been in fact carrying on agricultural operations. [1001 E F] Manipur administration vs M Nila Chander Singh, , followed and approved. The appellant cannot be regarded as doing business as a dealer unless a series of transactions by him of sale were proved against him.

The respondent executed a registered Kabuliyat in favour of the Receiver, by which he purported to take settlement of the land in suit for a period of 10 years at a rental of Rs. There was a covenant in the lease that on the expiry of the term if the lessor did not require the land for his own purposes and decided to re settle it, the lessee would be entitled to fresh settlement on enhanced rent and on such terms as might be then agreed upon between the parties. The claim was based substantially on the terms of the Kabuli tyat executed by the respondent on 24th December, 1924, and the suit was in fact one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the leased lease. It was contended that the defendant was at no point of time a monthly tenant under the plaintiff or his predecessor, and there might have been, according to the terms thereof, two tenancies for one year each for successive periods, but on the termination of the second annual lease which happened on 7th December 1926, the defendant ceased to be a tenant and no fresh tenancy was created by holding over as is contemplated by section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. Held, that the relationship of landlord and tenant between the par ties came to an end on the ques tion of section 106 of the . The question whether payment of rent to the Receiver amounted to payment to payment of the plaintiff himself was one from month to month since its inception in 1924. The tenancy thus created would be a tenancy from monthto month under section 116, Transfer of property Act. The relationship of the landlord and the tenant between them came to a end on tho expiration of that one year 's lease.

A gift by the husband to his minor wife to be valid must be accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of her property under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say, by the father or his executor or by the grand father or by his executor. The law is satisfied without an apparent change of possession and will presume that the subsequent holding of the property was on behalf of the minor wife. In the present case there was a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammotty and as the gift was by a registered deed no question in this behalf could arise. In so far as Mammatty was concerned there was delivery of possession, and the deed also records this fact. Possession was not delivered to Seinaba but to her mother, the first appellant, and she accepted the gift on behalf Of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living; His gift included immovable properties and it was accepted by the mother who took over possession on behalf 'of her minor daughter. A gift to a minor is completed ordinarily by the acceptance of the guardian of the Property of the Minor Wilayat ul Mal. A mother can exercise guardianship of the person of a minor daughter (Hizanat) till the girl attains puberties after which the guardianship of his person is that of the father if the girl is un 36 2 S.C. The mother was thus not the guardian or the de facto guardian or 'quasi guardian ' provided there was real and bona fide intention on the donor 's part to transfer the ownership of the subject matter of the gift to the donee, and that even a change in the mode of enjoyment is sufficient evidence of such an intention. The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's mother when the gift is from the husband or his guardian and when the minor 's father and father 's brothers are not alive and there is no executor of the one or the other. In such cases the benefit to the minor and the completion of the gifts for his benefit is the sole consideration. In this case there is a declaration, and a tendered by the donee Mammottty and in as the gifted property was by A registered deed No question in that behalf can arise. The trial Judge and the first Appellate Court did not accept it. After the death of Seinabai, the present suit was brought by Kunhamu an eider brother of Mammothty for partition and possession of a 6/16 share of the properties which he claimed as an heir under Muhammadan law, challenging the gift as invalid. To the suit he joined his two sisters as defendants who she submitted were entitled to a 3/16 shares each. He also submitted that the first three defendants (the appellants) were entitled only to the remaining 4/16th share as heirs of Seinsaba. The first three respondents (the appellant) were not entitled to the other 4/4 share as there was no issue and the remaining 3/4 was divisible between 552 Kunhamo and his two daughters, Kunhamuku getting twice as much as each sister, These shares according to him were unaffected by the invalid gift in faVour of SeInaba and accepted on their behalf by her mother. This contention has been accepted and it has been held in this case that when a document embodying the intention of the donor was delivered to the minors possessing discretion and accepted by her it amounted to acceptance of gift.

The respondents who were trustees of the Venkataramana Temple at Mulki, District South Kanara, moved a petition in the High Court for an order restraining the Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments from enforcing the provisions of the Amending Act 27 of 1954. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 63 to 69 and 89 as amended by Act 27 Of 1954 were invalid : Held, that the rules under the Act had to be general; they did not contemplate separate rules to be made in respect of each religious institution likely to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which the contribution is to be levied. The concession by the Advocate General at the hearing in Devraja Shenoy 's case does not oblige the State to frame separate rules in respect Of each religious Institution likely to obtaining the benefit. The rules under Act had no application to each religious math likely to get the benefit Of services rendered for which they were to be rendered. The Commissioner had to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts of the religious endowment. The percentage of income levied as audit fee must of necessity be based on an estimate, and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. The Court had proceeded upon the ground of ab sence of determination by the Commissioner which was never pleaded, and it was not the case of the respondents in their petition that the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 76(2).

The appellant, a contemner under section 19(1) of the , was prosecuted for committing con tempt of the High Court. The notice was issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the Act to show cause against the appellant 's alleged liability to be punished under section 15. A preliminary objection was raised by the respondents that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section19. In the meantime, there may be many interlocutory orders passed in the said proceeding by the High court. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal to this court as a matters of right from each and every such order made by the 'High Court in the proceeding for contempt. The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Courts affecting their right, the mere order issuing the notice is not appealable. The matter has to be decided either finally or may be. even at an earlier stage an order is made, which does decide a contention raised by 'the alleged contemner asking the High, Court to drop the proceeding on one ground or the other. But unless and until there is some order or decision of the ' High Court adjudicating upon any matter raised before it by the parties affecting their rights, the Mere order issuing notice is no appealable. [512 H] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, ; , referred to. Baradkanta Mishra v Justice Gogatikrunna Mishra; , distinguished.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The Magistrate convicted him and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In an application filed for special leave, it was contended that (i) section 6 (1 A), which was repealed by the 1952 Act, did not save the previous Act, and (ii) if section 6 was not on the statute book there could be justification for this view as the words wireless telegraphy apparatus " in section 6 of the 1952 'Act were comprehensive enough to take in wireless telegraphic transmitter. Held:(i) The word " text " is comprehensive enough so to take within its ambit all wireless telegraphs and wireless telegraphies, in practice it was found that the detection of unlicenced apparatus and the successful prosecution of offenders were difficult with the result that the State was losing revenue. (ii)(a) Section 6 (I A) inserted in the Act of 1933 did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the amending Act of 1949, but only gave power to control the establishment, maintenance and working of wireless apparatus, in practices it was held that section 6 had no application to a case of repeal of an earlier Act which had been applied, incorporated or referred to. (b) Section 20 of the Indian Wireless Telegraphy (Amendment) Act, 1949 did not indicate any intention different from that envisaged by the said section. (c) The words " unless a different intention appears" in the section do not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. As the Act only gave powers to control, the establishment and working Of wireless apparatus in practice, it could not be said that section 4 of the 1951 Act continued to be on the Statute book even after the amending Acts of 1949 was repealed. (d) Section 4 of 1952 Act had no applicability to a ease of repeal by the Amending Act of 1948, because, under that section the repeal of the earlier Act did not effect the continuance or continuation of the original Act.

The appellant, who was the managing Shebait of a deities from 1926 to 1930 and as Shebait, executed a Hatchita in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty some time in April 1928 on the basis of which he received advances of money from time to time from the latter. The properties described in Schedules Ka, Kha and Ga were put up for sale and they were purchased ostensibly by the two decreeholders. On the 28th August, 1941, the deities represented by some of the Shebaits filed two applications under section 36(6)(a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned above and the passing of new instalment decrees in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The principal opposite parties to these proceedings were the original decreeholders, Oramba Sundari Dasi, who figures as the appellant in the appeals before the High Court and who, it may be noted, was the wife of Aghore Nath Roy, a son of Adwaita, the former managing Shebaits of the debutter estate. The main allegation in the applications was that the Chakrabortys were mere benamidars for Aghpur Nath Roy who was a real lender and the real decreeholder in both these suits. It was alleged that Aghoy Kumar Roy purchased these properties in benami of the decreeholders in two out of the three execution proceedings and in the benami of his wife Orambba Sundri Dasi, he executed a fictitious conveyance made in favour by Aghigore Nath Ray on July 26, 1940, on the strength of which she received advances from time and that the said properties were knocked down to Srimati Oramma Sundari. The decreeholders claimed that they were entitled to have the two decrees reopened and on the passing thereof fresh instalments decrees should be passed in their places in accordance therewith. Held, that the High Courts had rightly held that Orambe Sundari did not bona fide acquire any right which could be protected under clause (b) of section 36 of theBengal Money Lender Act. It is true that the object of restoring possession of the properties sold in execution of the decrees to the judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the sale itself is not annulled and in case of default in payment of any of the instalments, the properties are returned to the decreeholder purchaser. The object of restoration of possession of these properties sold by both the courts below should be kept in view and the Court has not only the right but is under a duty to make an enquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale, or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decree holder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (a) of sub section (1) of that section. The drafting of section36 is obscure and somewhat clumsy but it cannot be disputed that the court shebaitserate a decree under section36(2) only for the purpose and so far as it is necessary to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act, namely, to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the Indian Contract Act. Clause (a), of section 35(2), empowers the court to pass a new decree in accordance 'with the provisions Of the Act and one of the powers which is mentioned in clause (c) of subsection (1), is to reopen any transaction and take an account between the parties.

The appellant, who was the assignee of a decree obtained by the respondent company in respect of certain transactions in gold and silver effected by the firm as pucca adatias in bullion and cotton at Bombay under the name and style of Habib & Sons, filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 7,113 7 0 with interest at 6 per cent. annum on the ground that the decree was not in existence at the date of the document it operated as an agreement to transfer the decree when it would be passed. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal by certificate, Held: (i) Order XXI, r. 16 contemplates the actual transfer by an assignment in writing of a 'decree after it is passed and that while a transfer of or an agreement of transfer a decree that may be passed in future may, in equity, entitle the intending transferee to claim the beneficial interest in the decree after it was passed, such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transferee of the decree by assignment in his writing within the meaning of Order XXI rule 16. (ii) The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of actual decree holder and that the language of Order 21, r . 16 contemplates actual transfer of the original decree by an assignee in writing or by operation of law and enables such transferee to apply for execution of the same to the Court which passed it. But if he fails to establish his title as a transferee by assignment within the terms of Order XXII, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure there is nothing in the provisions of Order XX, r., 16 which prohibits him from availing himself of section 146 if the provisions Of that section can be availed of by him. The respondent cannot claim to be a transferee or of the judgment debtor, which was subsequently obtained by Habib & sons, by an assign in writing within tho meaning of order XXI, rule 1(2)(j) and therefore there was no proper application for execution before the Court and the same was liable to be dismissed.

The respondent carried on the business of fabricating and selling window and door leaves. The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fixing "S.H. Windows" and "Composite Window" of certain sizes "in accordance with the specifications, designs, drawing and instructions". The tender was accepted and the respondent carried out the contract. The Sales Tax Officer included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract, the price received under it, and held that the contract with the Executive Engi neer was one of sale of goods and the amount received by the respondent was not taxable. The Board of Revenue exercising revisional power confirmed the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner observing that the contracts undertaken by the respond ent were not a contract of service. The High Court in appeal held that from the acceptance of the tender two contracts resulted : one for providing doors and windows and another for "fixing" those doors and window leaves and sashes etc. and entered into a contract for sale of its manufactured goods undertook to fix the windows without demanding any charge for that service, and that the price of the supplied but not the charge for service, was taxable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the terms of the contract were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the con tract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and (ii) the High Court was in error in holding that the transaction of the assesses with their customers was not a pure works contract but a combination of two distinct and separate contracts. HELD : (i)(a) The object of the Respondent was to enter into a works contract. [505 D] (b) The primary undertaking of the respond ant was not merely to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows. The service is not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves. [511 E F] (c) The High Courts were in error holding that it was only upon the "fixation" of the window leaves, and when the window left had become a part of the building construction that the property in the goods passed under the terms Of the contract; and the predominant idea underlying the contract was the bestowing of special skill and labour by the experienced engineers and mechanics of the assessees. [500 G] (d) The test in each case is whether the object of party sought to be taxed is that the chattel as chattel passes to the other party and the services rendered in connection with the installation are under a distinct contract or are incidental to execution of the works for sale by tho person who supply window leaves.[511 E] (e) The tests in each ease are whether the objects of the party soughtto be taxed are that the party seeking to be deter mined is that he has agreed to and did supply "motor bus being one for sale" of chattels, they were liable to pay sales tax. [51 G H] (f) The question in each particular case is: whether the contract is in substance one for work and labour or one for the sale of a chattel. If it is of the first category, it is a composite contract for work, but where it is for the second category, that it is, of the second class, it was a composite con tract for work & sale of ' goods; and where it was of the third category, there is no sale of any goods.

The appellant was a broker of foreign machinery parts went to Ram Avtar Prasad complainant and told him that he (Shanker Lal) could arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The complainant agreed to the proposal and wanted to see the seller of the foreign goods in question. On November 15, 1967 Shankar Lal handed over the formal order to Ram L. A day after that Shanker Lal brought one Saheb Jaman Khan along with him to Ram Pal and introduced Saheb Jamen Khan as agent of M/s Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. Ram Avtar then agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plates at the rate of Rs. 38/ per piece. Formal order, it was then agreed that this transaction would fetch him a profit of Rs 3200/ . On November 16, 1967 Shanker Lal handed back the formal letter to Ram and stated that the goods would be supplied on the following day. Ram L lodged a report with the police against Shankar Lal after his suspicion had been aroused. Later on that day Shanker Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla came to the shop of Ram Avtar with a view to cheat and cheat the complainant, and introduced him Saheb Jamban Khan as an agent of R. The appellant was discharged by the Magistrate. On appeal by the State, the High Court allowed the revision petition filed by the appellant. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwalla respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report; and (ii) the High court had wrongly quashed the charges framed against him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i). The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along with Shankar Lal when the latter brought washer plate in a taxi and demanded the price of the goods. It would hardly warrant an inference that Raj kumar respondent too was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. [279E] (ii). The report which has been lodged by R. P.S. is not a part of the same kind as that made no reference of the names of Raj k Kumar Agarwalli respondent because the case was of the complainant itself that he appeared on scene only later to the filing of the complaint.

The petitioner, an allopathic doctor by profession had himself drafted and filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the reports of the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees appointed by the Railway Administration. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 (Act ' for short) has prescribed several safety measures; based upon experience, the Railway Board through which apex body the administration is run and controlled has also prescribed rules and issued instructions which are not properly implemented. The Union Government had appointed three high powered Committees in the post independence period, namely, the Kunozru, Shah and Sikri Committee to investigate into the affairs of the Railways with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unmanned level crossings, increasing human error as a contributing factor to accidents, non allocation of adequate funds for improvements, improper utilisation of the assets and facilities, inefficiency in the administration at different levels, prevalence and increase of indiscipline, frequency of thefts, robberies and murders of passengers, ineffective checking and supervisory system, want of replacement equipment and repairs to bridges as also non provision of adequate facilities to passengers. Initially it used to be the obligation of the respective State Governments to provide for such level crosses at their cost in view of the accepted position that at a level crossing the right of way is of the train in preference to traffic on the road. As that arrangement was not working well, with effect from April 1, 1966, a Railway Safety Work Fund has been set up and expenses are being met out of it. From 1978 potentially hazardous unmanning level crossing with a volume of traffic of more than 6000 train units or poor approach visibility is being manned in a phased manner at the cost of the Railway and control at the gate is also improved. As on June 1, 1982 there were as many as 27233 unmaned level cross remarks on the Railways and if all of them are to be manned, a capital expenditure of 330 crore rupees would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs.44 crores will have to be met. Relying on the Sikri Committee Report of 1978, it has been submitted that the State Governments appeared to be aware of their responsibilities in this matter and about 2/3 of the funds of the Safety Works had been utilised by March 31, 1982. While admitting that in the initial period utilisation of funds was poor and finalisation of schemes for over bridges and under bridges was slow, the situation is claimed to have improved and in 1982 83 as manyas 15 works in different States involving an expenditure of RS.22 crores have been cleared. Every accident, it had been averred, is thoroughly inquired into to fix the responsibility for it and to visit the delinquent with proper punishment. Adverting to robberies & dacoities in the running trains, it was pointed out that they are problems of law and order, maintenance of which is an obligation of The State Governments. It is said that the total life of 80 years for steel work and 100 years for masonry part of the bridges stipulated in the Railway Code is for the purpose of provision in the Depreciation Reserve Fund. The Petitioner has filed a rejoinder pointing out that the counter affidavit clearly indicated a negative approach on the part of respondents to the entire matter. According to the petitioner assistance of 500 crores of rupees was to come during the year ending March 31 1983 and from out of such funds pressing improvements like manning the unManned level Crossings could be undertaken.

The appellants applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953. The claim was rejected by the Jagir Tribunal on the ground that the applications were time barred. The appeals filed before the Revenue Tribunal were dismissed for non prosecution on account of non appearance of the advocate of the appellants. Against the dismissal of the appeals for non Prosecution the appellants filed applications for restoration before the Tribunal on May 6, 1961. The Tribunal held that the application for restoration should have been made within 30 days from the date of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoring the appeals were made in time under Regulation 21 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals are received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the restitution applications filed on May 5, 1961 were within 30 day of the receipt of the Order of dismissal, and hence they were timebarred under Regulation 19(1) of the Saurashtra Revenue Tribunal Regulations. HELD: The language of Regulation 20 applies not only to a case where the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a cases where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing, the Tribu nal may dismiss the appeal and decide it on merits. [143 E] The words "decide it on merit" are used not only in the language or context of Regulation 19 but also in the context of section 20 and in view of the express language of section 17(1). Therefore, the Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all the four appeals.

The appellants, descendants of Dinanath Sao brought a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for removal of the respondent Kamal Narayan, another descendant of Dinnath Sao from the office of trustee of the God Shri Ramchandraji Swamy for the village of Telibandha and for accounts. The appellant 's case was that Telihambi was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandraaswami as early as 1857 by Dinanath, Sao himself and later in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinnath, Saooo but also dedicated the village Telivancorebandha to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The Trial Court held that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village and it was a public religious trust, as Shri Ramchandra temple for which the trust was created, was a Public institution. The High Court agreed with the trial court that the dedication had been made by one Dinanath but held that the suit was not maintainable because the evidence showed that there was no trust either express or constructive, created at any time by any one in respect Of Telihoobandha village ; that neither he nor his father was trustee in respect thereof and there was also no breach of trust by him. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the use of words " Kul haq" in paragraph 2 of the Panch Faisala that by this Award Teli Oriya village was dedicated absolutely to the deity of Shri Ramachandra Swamy temple either by Dinath Sao or later on by his descendants, and (ii) that there were no breach Of trust by the respondent. Held: (i)(a) The use of the words "Khoorna" in para 2 of a Panch Faish Milkiyat" in the opening clause of paragraph 2 was merely a presumption which can well be displaced by what follows in the same document as regards this very property. The fact, therefore, that Ramsaran Lal used to credit the income from Teli psychology to the Gharu Khata which was maintained for the general expenses of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property cannot change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication. (b) The document (the Panch Fausala Award of 1896) clearly and unambiguously showed anabsolute dedication of the Village to Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple, it could not be said that the words 'Khotena ' in para. 2 were intended to be used and that supports the presumption arising from the use by the word " Kul hq samet milkiyat". (c) The fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion, the award suffered from any infirmity. On the contrary, the document (he Panch Fairsala) clearly showed an ababsolute and unequivocal dedication of this village to Shri Ramachandra Swami temple, which was upheld by the High Court. (d) The words " Khoorana" in Para 2 of that Panch Fahisla raises a presumption that absolute interest was given thereby to Ramsarhan Lal absolutely with only a charge on it for the temple.

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Ayodhya Bar Association. There were three charges against them. It was not necessary to refer in detail to the same. The gist of the charge against the appellants was that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. The text of the resolution was this "The Action Committee is of the opinion that the chief Justice is acting in the dis charge of administrative power under clause 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a highly partisan manner". It was also stated that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associating with the passing of the Resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Judge and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of 'Criminal Contempt '. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the language used by them was unfortunate; (2) that they were not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The language used in the resolution clearly showed that the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. [605C] (b) It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. It is said that lawyers are the custodians of civilisation. Lawyers have to discharge their duties with dignity, decorum and discipline. In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the foregoing observations. [ 603D] (c) The High court confused 'criminal contempt ' with 'contu macious conduct '.

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother respondent No. 1 were entered into a deed of agreement between the four brothers, being the appellants Nos., 1 to 3 and their younger brother, respondent No 1 was entered into regarding partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators; namely, three appellants Nos 5, 6 and 7 herein. On or about 2nd July, 1977 the same agreement was re written on a fresh stamp paper and the said registered by which the abovenamed arbitrators were given the option to take assistance of one, two or more persons. The dispute related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah the district of Hooghly in the State of West Bengal. The three arbitrators took the assistance of appellant No. 8 and he functioned and acted as one of the arbitrators. On November 28, 1977, the arbitrators explained their award to the parties and made and signed the award. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting the same for registration. The High Court quashed the registration under Article 227 of the Constitution holding that the award had been presented for registration beyond time and directed the Sub Judge to return back the Award to the arbitrators holding that it was the Registrar and not the Sub judge who could determine the question of limitation for the purpose of registration of the award, and that the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending was to say, from 28th January, 1978 to 24th November, 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down under Section 15 of the . On behalf, it was submitted that the order made by the court directing the arbitrators ' application dated 14th August, 1978 should be kept pending and be heard when injunction order was vacated. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The limitation period for registration is four months from the date of its execution. [123D] 2.1 In the instant case admittedly during the period from 26th July, 1978 till 20th December, 1982 there was subsisting injunction preventing the arbitrators from taking any steps. Furthermore, as noted before the award was in the custody of the court, that is to say 28th of January,1978 till the return of the Award, the Arbitrators or the parties could not have presented the award during that time. The award as we have noted before was made on 28th November of November, 1977 and before the expiry of the four months ' from 28st November,1977, the award is filed in the court pursuant to the order of the Court. It was therefore manifest from the order in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1977 that the arbitrators had tried to obtain the custody and of the awarded award which the court declined to give to them. The principles enunciated by this Court in Nityananda M. Joshi and others vs Life Insurance Corporation of India and others; , would have no application to the facts of this case. [124E F] 2:2 In the aforesaid view of this matter, the judgment and order of High Court cannot be sustained and are set aside. The order of Sub Registrar, Arambagh dated 24th of June, 1985 is restored.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The terms of the lease were contained in a document dated June 7,1948 which is a letter in Marathi written by the respondent to the appellant and contains the following terms: " In the shops in the old chawl which are with you have kept sub tenants. The submission of the appellant was that the word 'sub tenant ' should be in the plural but whether it is in the singular or plural it does not make any difference to the principal argument advanced in this Court. On January 3, 1949, the respondent gave notice to the respondent terminating the tenancy and asked him to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The appellant denied that under the terms of a lease he had the right to sub let the premises. The trial court held that section 15 of the Act completely prohibited sub letting and under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rent Act, the landlord bad the right of eviction on account of sub letting. Held, that the appellant could not be permitted to assert in a Court of justice any right founded upon or growing out of an illegal transaction. The respondent was only seeking to enforce his rights under the statute and the appellant cannot be permitted by the court to assert his right based on such contract. The suit for ejectment was not brought for the enforcement of the agreement which recognised sub letting but he asked the Court to enforce the right which flows directly from an infraction of a provision of the statute.

The appellant, a student of the respondent Board, was found tampering with the subjects in which the marks were found tampered with. The marks initially obtained and the marks increased due to tampering, and also indicated the proposed punishment, if in the enquiry it would be found that marks were tampered with the knowledge or connivance or at the instance of the candidates or parents or guardians. The first question was whether the Standing Committee of the concerned Divisional Board had power under the Act and Regulations to enquire into the use of unfair means committed at the final examination conducted under the . The State Board was also empowered to make regulations to conduct examinations and also to deal with the use, of unfair methods at the preliminary examination conducted by the Board. The Divisional Board is also empowered under the Rules to deal With the use or use offair means at the stage of final examination. It is not disputed that all the students admitted, the factum of fabrication and it was to his or her advantage and that the subject/subjects in which fabrication was committed belong to him or her. The respondents contended that the fabrication in the moderators ' mark sheets in the subject or subjects and the mark were increased to their advantage. The Board also did not apply its mind to the facts, nor recorded reasons in support of its conclusions that the examinees/parents/guardians were parties to the fabrication and the fabrication was done at their behest. The learned Judges of the High Court were justified in reaching the conclusion that the Board had not established that the fabricated was done by either the candidate or the parents or guardian or guardians or were parties parties to fabrication and whether their complicity was established from record and whether the evidence was sufficient to support such conclusion reached by the Standing committee or the Enquiry Officer. The High Court, however, held that the Standing Committees had no power to take the impugned decision, etc. without approval of the Divisional Board. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notification is vitiated for the reasons that the Committee itself did not record any reason in support thereof and that it was the duty of the Examination Committee, etc., to maintain purity of examination and if examinee is found to have used unfair means at his examination, it is the duty to take action against the erring examinees to maintain the educational standard. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The finding of the learned Judge Sugla, J. that the resolution passed by the authorities that the inves tion of the examinee/parents and the parents/ guardians were parties is clearly illegal and cannot be sustained. [798C] 1.2 In the light of the fair attitude adopted by the counsel for the Board it is not necessary to go into the question of quantum of punishment. [781D] 1:3 The essential question, therefore, is whether the conclusions reached by them can be fairly supported by the evidence on record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [789E] Shanti Prasad Jain vs The Director of Enforcement, ; , referred to. 1.4 In the instant case, the findings of the Committee were based on no evidence and the conclusions were reached on the basis of the admission made by the respondents. It depended on the type and gravity and nature of the offence to be proceeded against by the Disciplinary Authority. [788E] 2:1 The High Courts were justified while reaching the conclusions that they had not been established that fabrication was carried out at their instance or the parent or guardian is amply borne out from the record. They also admitted that the forging in the toilets ' mark sheet in the subjects and marks were increased, to their benefit.

The first appellant was a partner in the firm of Kundan Lal Raja Ram of Saharanpur. The second appellant, a partner of the firm, was a proprietor in the Firm of Kundanlal Raja Ram. He was a munim of a firm called Lekh Raj Shambhu Nath. Some of the Saharanpur merchants including the three firms were suspected of exporting potatoes at concessional rates on false declarations or certificates that they were seed potatoes. Police investigation was proceeding in this connection at Saharanpur in October, 1951. Madan Lal refused to have anything to do with such a proposal but as the accused persisted in their offer it was ultimately decided that a trap should be laid for them at Delhi in Madan Lal 's house. The three accused and Labhu Ram were at Delhi on the morning of the 29th December and an increased sum of Rs. 5,000 was paid in the shape of currency notes to Madan Lal by Ram Kishan while two police officers and a Magistrate were hearing the conversation from an adjoining room and saw the payment through a hole in the door. The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 to be committed by Madan Lal one of the prosecution witnesses. They also stood charged with an offence under the same section read with section 116 of the Evidence Act for abetting the commission of criminal offence by the said Madan Lal in offering false declarations and certificates that were seed coldoes. The trial court convicted Madan Lal but on appeal the High Court reduced the sentence to one already undergone and a fine of Rs 5, 000 was offered as a bribe and not as compensation money in settlement of the amounts legitimately due to the Railway. In appeal by special leave: Held, that before it can be made applicable there must be proof, it was said, that the public servant adopted corrupt or illegal means and thereby obtained for himself or for any other person any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. To force a bribe out of an unwilling person is different from the acceptance of a bribe from a voluntary giver and that before a charge under section5(1), sub clause (d) could be sustained, there must he threat or inducement proceeding from the public servants or duress or extortion practised by him to obtain the pecuniary advantage advantage. The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receiver. One may accept money that is offered or solicit payment of a gratification, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case he obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public servant. It is enough if by abusing the position as public servant a man obtains for himself any pecuniary advantage, entirely irrespective of motive or reward for showing favour or disfavour. But to go further and contend that the offence as defined in clause (c) does not come with. in the meaning of bribery is to place too narrow a construction on the sub clause. A speedy disposal of corruption cases by special courts, the benefit of in vestigation by higher police authorities are some of the provisions intended for the protection of public 189 servants prosecuted under the Act while they are subjected also to increased disabilities, namely, a longer term of imprisonment as punishment and the application of the presumption referred to in sub clause(3).

The appellant Bank of Saurashtra (the Bank) had mortgaged the goods pledged by it to the Bank. The Bank was to be responsible for safe custody and keeping of the pledged goods. It was also contended that the principal debtor would provide such quantity of goods as would provide full cover to the outstanding balance in cash credit account and the Bank was liable to be discharged from his liability under the guarantee. On behalf of the respondent it was contended that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter of guarantee Ext.31 and the bond executed by the principal creditor in favour of the Bank, all on September 16, 1957 constituted one composite transaction and they evidence that the Principal debtor had offered two securities, one the pledge of goods and the other the personal guarantee of the surety. The respondent surety contended that though the goods were to be kept in the godown in the compound of Vijay Oil Mills Pvt. it was not discharged from its liability under a guarantee. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security from the principal debtors at the time when the contract of suretyship is entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the Principal employer, if the creditor loses or without the consent of the sureties parts with the other security the surety would be discharged to the extent of the value of the security. In the instant case as found by the High Court and not controverted, the principal borrower had offered 5 securities, (i) the pledge Of goods, (ii) personal guarantee on the specific understanding that the main debtor was offering another security, namely, pledge of good goods. 31 executed by him and the surety bond Ext. 83 executed by it at one sitting on September16, 1957, evidence one composite transactions, it is an inescapable conclusion that the respondent became surety upon the faith of there being some real and substantial security pledged as well as his own credit, to the plaintiff, and he was entitled, therefore, to benefit of that real and reasonable security in the event of his being called on to fulfil his duty as a surety, and to pay the debt for which he had so become surety. [924F G] 1.2 In order that attract section 138 it must also be shown, that the debtor had taken less than onesecurity from the Principal creditor at the relevant time when he entered into the composition with the principal employer and that the surety gave personal guarantee to the satisfaction of the Court that the security was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank. [936C] 1:3 In order, to attract Section 141 it should be shown by the creditor that the defendant had taken greater than one surety on the basis of which advance was made and the sureties gave personal guarantees on the good faith of other security being offered by him which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of the securities. [946E] 1 :4 In order under section 141, it must he shown that a creditor had took more than two security from tho principal debtor at the date when the Contract of Guarantee was entered into, and irrespective Of the fact, whether the defendant knew of the existence of such security offered or not, even though they were given after the contract OF guarantee was entered. [948F] 1;5 In order ' to attract s 141 it is shown that creditor had take more than a one security on the ground that the pledge was lost and, therefore the surety was discharged to that extent.

The appellant was the holder of a "patelki inam" lands situate in what was previously known as the ceded area of Berar. The appellant was a member of the family and was entitled to hold the "p Patelki inam". He was also entitled to his share in the emoluments of the patel 's office. The grant was recognised by the British Government, and he was granted a sanad by the Ruler of the State. In 1922, the jagir of Nawabag was abolished and the appellant was given certain lands as emoluments of his office to the working patel. On August 28, 1922, Government excluded the " patelki Inam" lands from the resumption proceedings relating to the jagir on the footing that they were separate from and independent of the jagir which was a class III inam. The order of Government in 1922, however, made it clear that the "Patelki inams " were treated on the same basis in the resumption proceeding of 1917, and by the order dated August 28.1922, Government deleted the " Patelki Inams " lands from resumption proceedings pertaining to the Jagir on the ground that they did not belong to a branch in which the right to officiation resided, his claim could not be considered. The High Court substantially held that (1) the lands in suit were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for 91 services to be rendered by the p Patel and the grant was recognition as a service inam by the Government; (2) it was open to the revenue authorities to resume and regrant the lands, in accordance with the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 in force in Berar and section 190 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, in force at the time when the Jagir was abolished, and (3) it had been assumed as if these were interests carved out of the lands granted. Held, that the grant made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag did not confer any new right nor did they deprive anybody of any subsisting right in respect of the "patatelki" inam lands and regarrant the same to respondent No. 1. The fact that the patels had alienated "pateki inam " lands and the " patwaris" lands were treated as a homogenous unit by the orders passed on August 28 and 1922, did not establish that they belonged to a separate branch in whose favour the right was created.

The respondents claimed that they were governed by the Hindu Law of inheritance and succession, that as there was only one solitary decision of the High Court of Madras which limited the application of Hindu law to matters of succession and inheritance only. His case was that despite their conversion, the Cutchi Memons retained a large part of Hindu Law as their customary law including its concept& of joint family property, the right of a son by birth in such pro perty and its devolution by survivorship constituted the customary law of Cutchi memons governed matters of inheritance only and that therefore when a Cutchi was Memon widow dies issueless her property would be governed by Hindu Law. The respondents claimed to have settled down first in Madras and then in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930, as a large portion of the State was situate in Madras, he should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. The Deputy Controller held that neither the said evidence nor the fact of their having paid succession duty on one third of the said estate only concluded the issue before him, viz., whether the rules of Hindu laws were consistently acquiesced in and applied to their family and the other Cutchi could not be said to be in possession of any usage which was otherwise valid as a legal custom and which did not conflict with any express law of the English government. The High Court held that the Khojas who had settled down in Madras had regulated their affairs, since they had settled it, but had retained on their conversion the Hindu law as to inheritance and inheritance as it would (1) Bom. In appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The question whether a particular rule of Hindu statute is applicable to a particular case must depend upon its own facts and circumstances. [234 D] (ii) A line of demarcation between ancestral property as against self accquired property and that the rule of succession has no application in the present case. [235 E] (iii) The conclusion which we arrive at on consideration of the decisions referred to above is that 'he Cutchi ' Memons who had entered into a customary law with Hindus, was governed by that rule. [236 F] (iv) A distinction between ancestral properties as against joint family properties and their devolution by inheritance has no relevance in the matter of succession or inheritance but it depends upon the facts and circumstance of each case. The conclusion is that the accountable persons, having been born lone before 1948, had already acquired a right by birth to the property held by their father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act. [237 G] (v) A comparison of the two decisions shows that barring one or two stray deci sions, the general trend of judicial opinion in Bombay was that both the Khoias and the Cutch Memons had retained, despite their converted portion of their personal law and that they discarded the rules as to coparcenary and the son 's interest in the property of his grandfather. Since there were no reported decisions on the position of the Cut Cochin Memons which had settled up amongst Hindus, Hindu surroundings and traditions there regulated their conduct as regards their property, succession and succession according to the Hindu laws which they had retained while in Cutch and to which they were already accustomed. [238 G H] (vi) The contention that the Cuttala Memons in Madras bad regulated their practice, since it had regulated succession and devolution by virtue of survivorship, was not correct.

The appellants manufactured fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. The yarn so obtained is further processed in an integrated process in the said composite mill of the appellant No. 1 for weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not disputes their liability in respect of yarn which is also removed from the Factory. It is the contention of the appellants that no duty of excise can be levied and collected in respect thereof of yarn, which is sought to be subjected to an integrated processing process for the manufacture of different fabrics. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 have been given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force, that is, February 28, 1944, the appellants and others similarly situated may be called upon to pay enormous amounts of duty in respect for intermediate goods which have come into existence and again consumed in the integrated process of manufacture of another commodity. It was further contended that if at one stage a commodity known to the market is produced and is transferred, within the factory for the purpose of production of another product, there is removal within the meaning of rules9 and 49. 709 Apart from the above two views, there are a third view which has A also been expressed by the Delhi High Court, namely, that if an intermediate product is obtained in an integral process of manufacturing a commodity, there was no removal and, therefore, such intermediate product although known to market and comes under a particular tariff item yet, as there is no removal, there will be no question of payment of duty on such intermediate products. It has been further contended on behalf of appellants that the Explanation to rule 9 and rule 49 are ultra vires the provision of clause (b) of sub section (4) of section 4 of the Act inasmuch as "place of removal" as defined therein, does not contemplate any deemed removal but a physical and actual removal of the goods from a factory or any other place or premises of production or manufacture or a warehouse etc. The Explanation to Rule 9 and Rule 49 do not contain any definition of "place" but provide that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place or Premises at an intermediary stage and consumed or utilised for the manufacturing of another article in a continuous process, shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or property as mentioned in sub rule (1) of rule 9. 709 The Explanation provides that excisable good goods made in a factory and consumed/or utilised for manufacture of any other commodity whether in a continuously process or otherwise, in such factory or place or any premises appurtenant thereto, specified by the Collector under sub rule(1), shall be so deemed to be have been issued out of, or removed from, such factory, place, premises, store room or other place of storage approved by the proper officer under sub Rule (1). The Explanation further provides that "place where the goods are to be manufactured by a manufacturer, that was to say, the site of the factory cannot be specified by him. In other words, if the place of removal is not the place where the excisable goods are produced, cured or manufactured, but any premises ancillary thereto, mentioned by the collector under subrule (1), the provision Of deemed removal as contained in the Explanation shall be construed and regarded as removed". It has also been contended that so long as such specification is not made by the Collect of the place manufacture or production of the excisable commodity, it will be a case of removal for the purposes of payment. of excise duties are, in our opinion, correct.

The petitioner, the holder of a permit issued under Chapter IV of the U.P. State Road Transport Corporation Act, 1948 to ply stage carriage on Bulandshahr Siana Garh Bugrasi Brijghat Bhasi Pradarsindpur route in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner filed his objections to the said scheme along with several others. After a number of adjournments the Hearing Authority empowered under section 68 C of the Act was able to conclude the proceedings by April 26, 1979 and it is alleged that the Authority in the course of hearing ob served that it would finalise and approve the scheme by 21.5.1979. Before the hearing authority could give its approval to the scheme under section68 D of the . The petitioner also filed a revision petition before the Additional District Judge, Bulandshahr. That revision petition was dismissed. Against the order of the Civil Judge, the petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court which was also dismissed. In this special leave petition it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the suit was not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by him; (ii) during the pendency of the suit the petitioner 's application before the Civil Court for staying the hearing of the case till the disposal of a special leave Petition before this Court since the question relating to the maintainability of suits of similar nature was involved in the said special leave petitions, and (iii) the petition was not filed within 30 days from the date of its publication. Dismissing the special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the civil courts is impliedly barred from entertaining suits of the present nature. [545C] 2.1 In cases of the instant nature where invariably reliance is placed by the private operators on Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution a writ Petition lies before the High court. In such cases a suit is hardly the remedy which can be availed by them. If suits of this nature are allowed to be entertained, the very object of the several provisions of Chapter IVA of the Uttar Pradesh Act can be frustrated by interested parties by resorting to a civil court with the sole object of delaying the implementation of a scheme. Such attempts should be curbed at the earliest opportunity. The learned Civil Judge was right in declining to stay the further proceedings in the suit. [544D E] H. C. Narayanappa and Ors. vs The State of Mysore and Ors., ; at page 753, referred to.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellant had used to live in 1962 with her father at Fazilka. She developed illicit connection with her mother 's husband. On August 29, 1963 the child was handed over to Roshan Lal who was employed as a sister in the Ambala Air Force Hospital and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. The appellant asked Russel Niel to bring to him the daughter of his sister 's father. The girl told the appellant that if they wanted to save themselves they should make some settlement with him and demanded a bribe of Rs. 1,000/ . But the appellant did not pay anything whereupon the appellant removed a golden ring from his finger. On September 4, 1963 RusselNathaniel handed over currency notes to Roshanlal and his wife in police uniform and accused Russel was asked to come to the house of N. K. Lal. The daughter of the appellant went to Ambala to her maternal uncle 's place where she was employed. At that time the appellant asked the girl to pay something to him. On the same night the appellant contacted the girl, Miss Eylene and his friend expressed their reluctance to send Miss EHygi with the appellant to the police station and therefore the appellant interrogated the girl at the resi dence of N ' K. The statement of Russel P.W. 2 was recorded by the Special Judge who accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 161, Indian Penal code and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 6(2). The High Court maintained the conviction of the appel lant under section 165(1)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act and section 5 (2) on the ground that all the relevant papers and materials were not placed before the D.I.G., Police, Mr. M. P. Singh who was the sanctioning authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal Act or any other criminal statute and if the appellant obtained money from Russel ' Nathaniel, it cannot be said that the appella nant had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act, or for showing or forbearing to show in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any son. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. When a public servant is charged under s 161 Indian penal Code and it is alleged that the illegal grati fication was taken by him for doing an official act he is not necessary for the Court to consider whether or not the accused public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act. [187 D] 2. When the public servant charged under S. 161, I.P.C., and it was alleged that illegal gra tation was taken for doing something or forbearance to show, in the course of his duties as public servant, it is not neces sary for the court to consider Whether or not he accused public servants was capable ously doing or likely to do an official acts. [188 E] 3.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 by a Special judge who sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. No separate sentence was passed under section 6(1)(c). The charge framed against the appellant related to the same transaction stated that on or about May 12, 1952 he had accepted Rs. 100 as illegal gratification from V. section Doraiswamy as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions favour to whomsoever in seeing that a speedy and favourable settlement of the claim cases preferred by him against the Bengal Nagpur Railway was subsequently the Eastern Railway. The charge under section 161 I.P.C. was proved by both the courts below and the appellant was sentenced as stated above. The only question canvassed before this Court was whether there had been a valid sanction given under section6 of the Act without which no court could take cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the appellant. Held, that the sanction accorded in this case was a valid one. The sanction accorded was a validly granted and it was not for the Chief Commercial Superintendent to judge the truth of the allegations made against the accused. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1924) L.R. 70 I.A. 222, relied on. Gokul Chand Dwarkadash Morarsa vs The Queen, , distinguished. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 6 of the . it was necessary to decide whether the sanction had been accorded by the Chief commercial Superintendent or not.

The respondent landlord filed a petition under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for eviction of the tenants from two different tenancies. The tenant contended that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises in question and that it was inherent in such a life estate that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1) (b) as grounds for eviction were: (i) that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction; (ii) that since the interest of the remainder man may be prejudiced, the landlord with a lifeinterest in the property cannot evict the tenants on these grounds. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of tenants. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the tenant against the orders of eviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant tenant that (i ) the landlord has only a limited life interest, in the building and that the tenant is raising it in seeking to support the earlier order of the appellate authority; (2) the landlord having only a lifetime interest in his premises cannot evict tenants on those grounds; and (3) the tenant was raising it with regard to the terms of the Deed of Settlement. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainderman with regard regard to both the terms and conditions of the deed of settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings, if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. [276E] 2. When the objection on the score of the landlord being a holder of life interest and hence incapable of invoking section 14 is not maintainable, it must be decreed. It was strenuously submitted by Mr. Natesan that a tenant with a Life interest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se, be not bona fide. [277F] 3. The right between section Manicka Chettyar and the rest man with regard thereto to the term of the Settlement win has to be work out in proper proceedings, If necessary and general law will govern the field if any, occasion arises, [277G H] 4. In the result the appeals are allowed and the order of eviction is restored. The order of tho Controller allowing eviction of tenant stands restored. [278C D] 5. It is clear that when the objection about the landlord ' being a tenant of life Interest and hence capable of invoking Section 14 ( 1) (a) fails, the suit must be dismissed. [279F G] M/s Raval & Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others, ; , referred to.

The respondent decree holder filed execution proceedings in the executing court against the appellant, who was the judgment debtor. The executing Court dismissed the execution application holding that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, no more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of Act which says "intermediary grove means grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such". Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The contention must fail. [10 D] (2) The principle is well settled that trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'land '. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are parts of groves, and grove land. [11 F G] (3) The proposition is well established that trees before they were cut, formed parts of the 'land" and an "interrimediary 's groves are equated and groves were on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncut standing trees are deemed to be parts of land. Section 18(1)(a) of U. P. Zamindari Act provides that an "Intermediary"s grove is bhumidhari property. Rights in it are part of bhumidhari rights.

The appellants were charged with an offence under Section 302, 324, 323, 341, 148, 149 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC. The prosecution case was sought to be proved by the ocular testimony of PW4 Biju and PW5 Anil both aged about 13 years at the time of occurrence and the other evidence. At the trial however four eye witnesses, PWs 6 and 7 salesman and his assistant in the arrack shop and PW8 Unni @ Velayudhan turned hostile and did not support the prosecution case. The Trial Court convicted accused 2 to 6 under Section 326/149 IPC with the aid of Section 149 I.P.C. and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. On an appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence recorded against them by the learned Sessions Judge was set aside. In view of the limited notice issued by this Court, it is directed that issue notice limited to the question as to the nature of offence and the quantum of sentence. The appellants were put on trial and the prosecution sought to establish its case by examining as many as six eye witnesses besides other evidence, documentary and oral. At trial however, four eye witness, PW3 Devassenutty, PWs6 and 7 saleman and their assistant in arrack shops and PW 8 Unni @ Vayudan turned hostile. The trial court convicted accused 1 to 4 under Section 324 I. P.C., and sentenced him to suffer imprisonment for seven years each. On appeal before High Court the conviction of accused 2 was set down aside. The High Court did not hold that beside the four accused convicted by it, there were some other known or unknown accused who had also been a party to the commission of the crime. In the appeal before this Court on behalf of the appellants it was contended: (1) The medical evidence is clear on this aspect of the case and it is not possible to say that the injuries inflicted by the first appellant with the chopper were inflicted with the intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause such death; (2) The injuries attributed to him were not sufficient in ordinary course to cause the death of the deceased; and (3) The evidence on record shows that none of the accused persons individually had been charged for the substantive offence of murder under Section 307 I.C.; and therefore, in defending himself he can not be said to have been called upon to meet that charge and he could very well have considered it unnecessary to concentrate on that part of the prosecution 's case during the cross examination of the Prosecution witnesses. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The intention to causing murder of a person is not an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 and cannot, therefore, form the basis for conviction for an offence with the help of Section 34 I.p.C.[94D] 1.2 In the instant case none of these accused persons collectively had been charges sheeted for the offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 148 and 149 I P. C. The participation of the 6th accused and the role assigned to him by the prosecution was doubted by the Judges of the High court and he was given the benefit of doubt and acquitted. While setting aside the conviction, and sentence of the said two accused, the High Courts did not held that beside four accused, convicted by them, there had been some other unknown or unknown persons who had further been a Party to the prosecution. Thus only four accused could be saidto have been the members of the unlawful assembly but such an assembly which comprises of less than five members is not unlawful assembly.[94E F] 1:3 The intention of causing murder by accused No. 2 and 3, was with a torch, iron rod and a cycle chain.

The assessee, Standard Triumph Motor Co. Ltd., is a non resident company having its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. The assessee was maintaining its accounts on cash basis and not on mercantile basis, that no part of the royalty amount has been received by it and, therefore, nothing is taxable. For the assessment years 1969 70 and 1970 71, however, the assessee did not actually receive the amount nor did it take credit for the said amounts in its books at Coptry. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the method of accounting was mercantile, that for the A.Y. 1967 68, the assesseee did never contest its liability to be taxed on the amounts disclosed and further that it was not open to it to change the method Of accounting to suit its convenience without the approval of the Income Tax officer.
