The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessment orders for the past years relating to the assessee reveal that the system of accounting regularly adopted by an assessee is binding upon the department; on that basis, it was argued that if the assessee was proved to have maintained its accounts with respect to royalty amount on cash income basis then there is no receipt until it is received in U.K., the assessee has not received the income and, consequently, nothing was taxable. The Tribunal held that the question of method of assessment adopted by the assessee must be examined afresh and for that purpose allowed the appeals and remanded the matters to the Income tax Officer. It directed further that if it is found that the assessee is maintaining its account with respect respect to the royalty amounts on cash receipt basis, then there was no receipt till it is so remitted to and received in the U. K., the appellant has not actually received any royalty income from the Indian Company, but had taken credit for it. In these appeals by the asses see against the judgment of the Madras High Court answering the reference made at the instance of the Revenue, the questions that arose for consideration were: (1) Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that royalty amounts should be assessed on cash grounds for 1967 68. 1968 69 and 1969 70 assessment if the books and balance sheets of such receipts were found to be maintained on cash bases and directing fresh assessment on such basis; (2) Whether the assessee can be said to have received the royalty money only when it receives the same in U .K., in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own Books at Costry. Since it is maintaining the accounts with regard to the said royalty on cash per basis, receipt means receipt in UK. Section 145 was relied upon by the Revenue to say that the methods of accounting generally adopted by a assessee are binding upon him; on this basis, the question whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between section 5(2) and section 145 of the Act nor is it necessary to express ourselves on the view expressed by the High Court that in the case of a nonresident assessee like the petitioner clause (a) of sub section (2), of Section 5 has no application whatsoever and that section 5 (2)(b) governs it irrespective of the fact whether it maintains its accounts or mercantile basis. The question referred did not really arise in the facts & circumstances of this case and need not have been answered. In view of the above, it must be held that in these circumstances of a case, it is immaterial whether the assessee, is keeping his accounts in regard to a particular income regularly on the cash basis. " In the instant case, there was an agreement between the assessee and the Indian company which was not aware of the true state of affairs relating to its assessee 's accounts.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The third accused was acquitted and the fourth accused was convicted. On appeal by the High Court, it was found that there should be corroboration of the approver in material particulars and qua each accused. 834 Held, that the conviction of the appellant is unsustainable. In coming to the above conclusion the law has been correctly laid down by this Court in Bhuboni Sahu vs The King, (1949) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308, Bhubani Sahu vs State, ; , and Bhubnoni Sahu v The King (1924) L . R. 76 1. A. 1. R. vs Baskerville, (1878) L L. R 76 I A. C. Mad., 308, referred to. Bhubnioni Sahu 's evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction Of the first accused upon which we express no opinion but so far as the appellant was concerned it is clear that there was no corroboration of his story and it was not sufficient that there is evidence to corroborate the participation of the second accused in the murder. Bhsubnoni Naik vs The Queen, (1918) L I. R., 76 I .A. 1, referred. Bhoboni Sahu V. King, A.I.R., , distinguished. Bhunni Sahu vs King, ; and Bhurboni Sahu, A B.I., Mad. 309, approved. Bhumoni Sahu & Anr. vs The State of Orissa, [1924] L.L.R 76 I Q.B.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961, the Electrical Executive Engineer accompanied by his Head Clerk, the appellant paid a visit to Janta Oil Mills situated at Fatuhas. Ramprit Singh, P.W. 2 in the mill premises and told him that the outer seal of the meter, technically called the body seal, was tampered with. The Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.,W. 16, accompanied by the Head Clerk met P. W. 2 and he paid a visits to Janta oil Mills situated near Fatuhahas. He also accompanied by two Head Clerks, one in the Mill premises and the other in the mills premises. On July 8. 1961, a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent, PW. 17, the Deputy superintendent of Police met P W. 1 in the Mills premises and informed him that he had the outer sealed seal of meter, properly called the outer lock of the body, seal, and that the inner seal of it, technically marked the body seals, was not tampered but on a threat by the Executive Engineer, P W 2 was compelled to give a written statement that 684 the outer outer seal was tampered. The appellant was convicted under section 161 Indian Penal code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the sanction of the Government was required under section 197 because taking of a bribe was not acting or purporting to act in the discharge of the official duty of a public servant; (ii) the word 'officer ' used in section 21, Indian Penal. Code as it stood after the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1964, meant some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances a delegated function of Government was not an officer within the meaning of el. (12) of section 21; (iii) the appellant could not be deemed to be a public servants within the expression "public servant" within the contemplation of section 2(2), because he was not a "public Servant" within that clause and therefore, he could not have been convicted under that clause in view of the language of section 81 of the . HELD: (i). The appellant cannot be deemed as a public officer within section 21 of the because he is not acting ' or purporting ' to act ' in pursuance of any of the provisions of that Act. [684 B] (ii). The word "officer" used in the section means some person who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. In the present case, the very designation "Head Clerk" denotes that there are other Clerks attached to the office who occupy subordinate positions in relation to the Head clerk and the duties of the Head Clerks from the nature of things are bound to be immediately auxiliary to the head of the office. [687 C] (iii). The words "public servants" include every officer in the service or pay of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of any Government company as defined in section 617 of the '. It is not disputed that the appellant was in the Service of the State Electricity Board which falls within the language Of el. 12 of section 1, and therefore a "Public servant" under the meaning Of that section. [688 E F] (iv) The word 'Officer ' used by the Legislature in the context of the section is not an expression of any definition but of any other description.

The appellant was prosecuted and convicted under r. 125(9) Defence of India Rules, 1962 for contravening cl. 4(b) of the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase and Sale Control of Movement) Order, 1964. The Magistrate ordered confiscation to the Government. The appellant appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge but failed. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Restriction on Purchase 'and Sale Control Order, 1965. In appeal by special leave it was contended that r. 141(2) of Defence of india Rules 1962 is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to. the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the seized stock of juar set aside and the rest of the order of tho High Court maintained. [273 D] Rule 141(1) is within the powers conferred by section 3(1). Section 3 gives very wide powers. It seems to us that r, 141( 2) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the Defence of Indian Rules. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [272 E F] In the result the appeal partly allowed, the order maintaining the forfeited stock of the juar seized from the house of the appellant is maintained.

The appellant and the deceased were tried by the Sessions Judge, Farrukhabad in connection with the murder of one Kunwar Singh. The prosecution case was that on October 20, 1970, when the deceased and his companions were hiding behind a Shisham tree came out and confronted Kunwar Singh and his associates, Sia Ram fired a shot from his gun as a result of which Kunwar Singh fell down. The other lawyer, Om Prakash Dubey, contacted the District Magistrate and the Superintendent of Police vainly attempting to have the dying declaration of Kunwar Singh recorded. A person called Soney Lal, also alleged to be an eye witness lodged the First Information Report at the police station at about 5 p.m. on October 21, 1970. The Sessions Judge acquitted Sia 's evidence and convicted Sia as well as Ram Chandra. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia and Ram Violet. It dismissed the appeal filed by the State Government except in regard to Shri Ram whom it convicted under section 302 read with section 109. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A person may for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the murder Of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission of the murder, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not enough that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happens to facilitate commission of crime. Intentional aiding and therefore active complicity is the gist of the offence of abetment under the third paragraph of section 107. Apart from the words attributed to Violets, there is nothing at all to show that she was aware of the nefarious design of Sian Ram and his associate. Vioadlet had not given intimation of the arrival of the advocate, the persons concealing themselves behind the SHISH tree may not have noticed the arrival or the arrival thereof in time to assault him. In case the accused were not assisted by Smt. ViOlet, they would have to sit in such a manner that they could watch persons moving about on the road. Viaslet was real and valuable. [626 H; 627 A B] (2) The High court erred in holding that Sia had played an important role in the murder and that it was unsafe to convict him.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that the appeal was against an order of acquittal. In regard to accused 2, they held that he was one of the participants in the assault and there was no basis for his plea of private defence. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that when three of the four named accused were acquitted, the court could not convict only one of them on the basis of constructive liability. Held: (i) The judgment of the High Court cannot stand. [684 B] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed. (ii) In the present case, the conviction of accused 2 was clearly wrong. In the first illustration the court certainly can convict two or more of the named accused if it accepts the evidence that they acted conjointly in committing the offence. Can it hold, in the absence of a charge as well as evidence 'that though the three accused are acquitted, some other unidentified persons acted conjointaneously with one of their named persons ? There must be some foundation in the evidence to show that persons other than those named have taken part in the commission of the offence and if there is such a basis the case will be covered by the third illustration. In support of the contention that a Court even in the first instance can acquit two or several of the accused, if it accept the evidence which may disclose the existence of named or unnamed persons, other than the acquitted accused, in respect of the charge under section 149 because along with the two or three persons convicted were others who composed the unlawful assembly but who have not been identified and so have not be named. In such cases, either the trial court or even the High court in appeal may be able to come to the conclusion that the acquittal of some of the persons named in the charge and tried will not necessarily displace the charge Under section 149, because along alongwith the two accused or more are acquitted leaving before the Court less than five persons to be tried, then section 149 cannot be invoked. [686 C D] Mohan singh vs State, A.I.R. 1959 S.C. 971, followed.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of MSCR defective sheets or coils, imported certain goods from the customs authorities. The goods arrived at Bombay Port on 12th June, 1984 and the clearing agent of the petitioner filed bills of entry on 30th July, 1984 for warehousing under section 59 of the . 1962 (the Act '). The petitioner asserted that he was ever ready and willing, rather was anxious to get the material on payment of the then prevailing customs duty. However, due to circumstances beyond the control of the peti tioner, that it to say, by the order of the Income Tax Authorities the goods could not be released. This factor was not of the Petitioner 's making, according to the petitioner. On 4th April, 1988, the petitioner 's agent contacted the customs authority for clearance of the goods. The demand, according ly, was arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional. The instant writ petition was filed under Article 32 of the Constitution on 16th April 1988 and on 22nd April, 1989 this Court passed the following order: "Pending notice, there will be limited stay to the extent that the goods name, "MSCR defective Sheets/coils" which have arrived at the Bombay Port per S.S. It is contended on behalf of the respondents that for the payment of duty, the liability of the petitioners to pay the duty was the duty at the time of clearance of goods. This circumstance was not relevant in view of the language used in section 15(1)(b) of the Act. On behalf of it was contended that for payment of duties, the liabili ty of the assessee to pay, the duty is the duty of the customs Authorities and the Central Govern ment were right in taking the view that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse. Disposing of the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. If there is breach of the fundamental rights, the Petitioner can certainly have recourse to Article 32 Of the Constitution provided other conditions are satisfied. [626C D] Smt. 842 of the report as under: "In my opinion, the correct answer to the two questions which have been referred to this larger Bench must be in the negative. An order of assessment made by an authority under a taxing statute which is intra vires and in the undoubted exercise of its jurisdiction cannot be challenged on the sole ground that it is passed on a misconstruction of a provision of the act or of a notification issued thereunder. Nor can the validity of such an order be questioned in a petition under Article 226 of the constitution. [625E F] Smt, 842 of this report as contemplated by section 15 (1)(a) clearly requires that the rates of duty and tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the dates on which goods are actually removedfrom the ware house. Under section 49 and importer may apply to the Assistant Collector of Customs for permission to store the imported good under a licence pending their clearance and he may be permitted to do so; and section 68 provides that an importer of any warehoused goods may clear them if the import duty leviable on them has been paid. In that case, it was found that as the goods were removed from warehouse after the amending Ordinance had come into force, the customs authori ty and the central Govern ment are right in take ing the view, that the levy of duty is not unreasonable or arbitrary. [ 625E F; 626A B] Smt Shanti Devi vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Bihar & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants were the managing director of a bank. The respondent Bank was the auction purchaser of the bungalow and in execution of this payment order a bungalow belonging to the appellants was attached by the Collector under the Bombay Land Revenue Code on July 27, 1942. Notice for sale was issued on November 24, 1942, and the proclamation on December 24, 1943, was published in the Gazette. The sale was fixed for February 2, 1943. On January 16, 1943 M. B. Jakati, defendant No. 1 of the Bungalow was not binding on the joint family as it was not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of the respondent Bank which were characterised as misfeasance " Held, that the liability of the sons to discharge the debts of the father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the appellants to see that their father 's debts are paid, prevents the sons from asserting that the family estate so far as their interest is concerned is not liable. The liability of a father who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration, incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyavaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals ". The liability to pay the debts does not become any different merely because the sale is held under section 155 of the Bombay Act rather than the Code of Civil Procedure. The obligation of a son to discharge his debts is ended by the partition, but as he has no right to challenge the sale on showing the immoral or illegal purpose of the debt and partition cannot relieve the sons of their pious obligation or their shares of their liability to be sell or be a means of reducing the efficacy of the attachment or impair the rights of the creditor. The consequence is that as between the sons ' right to take a vested interest jointly with their father in their ancestral estate and the remedy of the son 's creditor to seize the whole of the estate for payment of his debt not contracted for immoral or unlawful purpose, the latter will prevail and the sons are precluded from setting tip their right and this will apply even to the divided property which, under the doctrine of pious obligation continues to be liable.

The petitioners, who were both guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends, filed affidavits before the Committee and other peculiar features of the case. The Committee recommended the transfer of the petitioners in these cases, namely, Ms. Kiran Bedi, D.C.P. (North) and Jinder Singh S.I. Incharge Police Post Tis Hazari and S.H.O., P.S. Tis, Hazari and Badli. Section 8B of the Act provides that if at any stage of the inquiry, the Commission considers it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person, or (b) is of opinion that the reputation of any persons is likely to be prejudicial affected by the inquiry. The petitioners filed affidavits in support of their respective cases. The question whether a party has the right of cross examination or not shall be decided by the Committee in accordance with section 8 C of the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1973. PG NO 521 PG NO 520 PG NO 522 Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners Ms. Kanta Bedi and Jandinder Singh are persons who fall under section 8 B of the . They have to be dealt with accordingly. According to the Committee 's own opinion formed in the light of the facts and circumstances of the cases, all those persons to whom notices under section8 B of Act are issued have to he examined at the end of the enquiry. This is obvious from the order of the Committee passed on 29.6.88 after it was asked by this Court by its order dated June 2, 1988 to reconsider the whole question relating to the order in which the witnesses had to be examined in the case, and to produce evidence in his defence. [521D E] 1.2 The action of the committee in asking them to be cross examined at that end appears to us is discriminatory. Mere non issue of notices to them under section 9B ought not to make any difference if they otherwise satisfied the conditions mentioned in section 8B. The issue of such a notice is not contemplated under section 10 of the Commission of Inquiry Rules, 1972. It is enough if at some stage the Commission consider it necessary for inquire into into the behaviour of any particular person. Such person would thereafter be governed by section 8C of the , before asking them, to get into the witness box for being cross examined till the end or the inquiry [522D E; 523A B] 1:3 The issue that such a notification is not required under section 6 of the commission of Inquiry and is governed by Section 8 B. It was enough if it at any time stage the commission considers it appropriate to inquire in the conduct or of any other person. [525G H] 1 :4 The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by s.8B of Act before asking him to get in the witness examined till that end of inquiry, and if the Committee had found that the petitioners are covered under section.8 B then perhaps they would not have been asked to get them into the witnesses box for getting cross examined until the end is of the Inquiry.

The petitioners who were seven in number, challenged the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, and a notification issued under R. 8 of the Act on the ground that it was invalid as it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the tax is for purposes of State and falls upon passengers and goods carried by motor vehicles within the State. There is no tax on fares and freights attributable to routes outside the State except in one instance which is contemplated by the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 of the , and the imposition of the tax was justified on the assumption that there may be vacant periods when no passengers or goods are transported but the tax, is payable, is of any force, because there may arise days when the business done might result in tax in excess of the lump sum payable. The word "shall" used both in r. 8 and section 9A of the General Clauses Act, 1897, means a person who can elect to pay tax calculated on actual fares and fares and therefore the imposition is justified on that assumption. All operators using the better kind of roads have to pay the heavier tax, and there is no discrimination between them as a class. It is the cost of construction and maintenance which makes the difference in the tax and no case of discrimination can be said to be made out. The last contention was that the proviso was extra territorial in nature because it makes the tax payable on fares or freights related to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan.

The appellant, a private limited company having set up an industrial unit in engineering industry, served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week and the mounting loss. The Tin Workers ' Union, Ghaziabad, espoused the cause of such retrenched workmen and ultimately the Government of Uttar Pradesh by its notification dated 9th October 1974 issued in exercise of the power conferred by section 4 K of the U.P. lndustrial Disputes Act 1947 referred the industrial dispute arising out of retrenchment of 43 workmen between the parties for adjudication to the Labour Court. E 2, viz., heavy loss caused by non availability of tin plates, persistent power curbs and mounting cost of production were not the real reasons for affecting retrenchment but the real reason was the annoyance felt by the management consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April 1974 and, therefore, the retrenchment was illegal. The Labour Court by its award directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st August 1974 with full back wages permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The appellant challenged the Award in this appeal. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that for the limited purpose of arriving at a just decision on the question whether the workmen should be awarded full back backwages, it should look into the compelling necessity for m retrenchment of the workman. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The relief of reinstatement with continuity of service can be granted where termination of service is found to be invalid. It would mean that the employer has taken away illegally the right to the work of the worker contrary to the relevant law or in breach of contract and simultaneously deprived deprived workman of his earnings. If after such a protracted time and energy consuming litigation during which period the workman just sustains himself, ultimately he is to be told that though he will be reinstated, he will he denied the back wages which would be due to him, the workman would be subjected to a sort of penalty for no fault of his and it is wholly undeserved. If the normal rule in a case like this is to award full back Wages, the burden will be on the appellant employer (l) [1959] Suppl. 569 thus the employer is found in the wrong as a result of which the workman is directed to be reinstated. The Award shall stand modified to the effect that the retrenched workmen who are now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back rent after deducting the amount paid to them as wages when recalled for work since the date of retrenchment and adjustment of the retrenchment compensation towards the amount found due and pay able. [567F G] 2. The award shall stand accordingly modified to that effect that all retrenched workmen shall not charge any fee for the services rendered as Director, no dividend shall be payable to equity shareholders, and the Managing Director shall not be paid any overriding commission, if there be any, on the turnover of the company since this will account for the pragmatic approach of common sacrifice in the interest of the industry. [568C] 3. The workmen concerned did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated and, accordingly, reinstatement was held to be the appropriate relief and Act aside the order of the Tribunal. [569D E] 4. It is no more open to debate that in the field of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of services is bad and the workman continues to be in service. The question in controversy which fairly often is raised in this Court is whether even where reinstatement is found, to be an appro priate relief, what should be the guiding considerations for awarding full back rent.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 Indian Penal Code for committing murder of his wife Churl. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the material on record was not sufficient to justify the conviction of the accused. According to the prosecution case, the injuries found on the body of the deceased were caused by the accused; in order to bring the charge home to the accused, the prosecution has relied upon the confessional statement PH of the said accused recorded by him as well as the other circumstances of the case. HELD: (i) The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of Churi deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house of the brother of the complainant and with which the injuries on the bodies of the de ceased, according to Dr. Besides that it is established by the evidence of Girju PW 2 that the accused along with his wife were illtreating Churi. The discovery of the dead bodies from the house was hardly consistent with his innocence. [434 D] (ii) It is not a fit case in which the extreme penalty need be exacted from the accused.[435 F] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Singhara Singh and Others, ; , referred to. (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the record of such a confession could not be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act.

The plaintiff 's father Tarak Lall and Tarak Nath were the mortgagors. The mortgage was exe cuted on the 12th June 1936 in favour of one Mst. Gyarsi for a consideration of Rs. 80,000. For convenience I will call this suit the mortgage executed by three brothers,Tarak Kedar and Naku. The mortgagee sued in 1938 and obtained a preliminary decree for sale on the 17th February 1939 for a sum of Rs, 181. This was done and 20 Round Tank Lane was conveyed by the present plaintiff to the Hooghly Flour Mills on the 18th March 1943. Out of the consideration a sum Of Rs. 1,19,116 11 0 in satisfaction of the mortgage debt was paid out of the amount due and payable by the two defendants. The Mills executed a reconveyance of the rest of the properties to the mortgagors in release of the mort gage on the same day. The plaintiff claimed that he was entitled to receive the balance of Rs 79,744 7 from the two respondents and that each of them was liable for a half of that sum namely, Rs. 15,000 and C 's to Rs. 5,000 which came to Rs, 2,500. The defendants denied that they were shut out from relying on section 82 because that was not their case and the question was never raised by them in the High Court. Held, that the whole law of mortgage in India including the law of contribution arising out of a transaction of mort gages is now statutory and is embodied in the Transfer of Property Act read with the Civil Procedure Code. The whole law relating to contribution arising from a mortgage is now statutorily statutory and it is embodied In the Transfer Of Property Act, read with section 82 of the Transferof Property Act. It confers rights on the mortgagor who redeems and directs that in the absence of a contract to the contrary, he (1) (1922) 49 I.A. 129, A.I.R. , but reading the two reliefs together, I am of opinion that though the claim is inartistically worded the plaintiff has in substance asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs., Therefore, though he has not used the word "subrogation" he has asked in substance for the relief to which a subrogee would be entitled under the Transfer.

The appellant No. 1 is a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction getting 69.96% marks in the qualifying examination, thus in all 450 Civil Engineers and 110 Mechanical Engineers. Both the appellants applied for the posts of their choice in Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. Appellant No. 2 secured 29.50 marks out of 50 marks in interview and 69.95 marks in his qualifying examination thus in both the appellant were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 were excessive and in violation of the decision of this Court. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by special leave. It was not necessary to examine the matter in detail inasmuch as the question whether 50 marks for interview out of 150 are clearly in violation in the judgment of this court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R., 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State o Punjab & Ors, J.T. and Mohinder Singh Gill Garg vs The State of Punjab & ors., J. T.N. Sinha & Ors.; , J.J.T., ; was decided on 4th September, 1991. In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [439C D] Ashok Kumar Gupta & Ors vs State Of Haryana & Anr., ; , JT.R. [1988], Sup. C.R.] 657 and M/s. B.B.S. Oil Mills Ltd. & Anr. vs Union of India & Ors; , Jt.T, Jt., Jt,T.J.,T. & K.S., Oil Mills & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. vs The Union of lndia & Ors ; , ; Mohinder Sain Jain vs State and Ors., ; ; Mohinder Singh Sain Garg v State of Delhi & Ors,, J. & Ors . ; J.S, Oil Mills and Natural Gas Commission vs The Stale of Haryana and Ors. , ; referred to.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court, in appeal, confirmed their conviction and sentence. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appel lants that (1) the prosecution evidence on record should be rejected as when on 10th July, 1982 Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector 's murder on 11th April, 1983; (2) the evidence of 14 witnesses who were examined to show that Yadav was very close to Sadanand and (3) the recovery of the bomb exploded with a loud noise and as a result of the burst Mahesh Prasad fell rolling on the ground and part of his body was blown off. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As this court pointed out in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; the confes sion of a convict staying in the said jail stated that his wife had an interview with him in the jail by paying bribe of Rs.2 or Rs.3 on 11.4.1983. While he was talking to his wife, he saw accused Yadav talking to Sadananand and P.W.4 has admitted that he has been convicted in three cases of murder and several dacoities. His wife who was a material witness has not been examined in the case. Obviously, as the jail records did not show that P.Ws. 4 had an ac cused 's presence on that day. Adverse inference for not examining the wife has to be drawn against the prosecution. It is true as argued by Mr. Jai Narain for the State that it is difficult to support the charge of conspiracy with direct evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to he established and the chain has to been completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [434E F] Kashmira singh vs State Of Madhya Pradesh; , ; Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs State o/s. State of Bihar, ; ; Hari Shanker Kurmi & Ors. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, , ; and Hari Charan Debi & Anr., vs State, ; referred to. In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. [414G H] 2. The prosecution has also led evidence to show, turned into a den of criminals. The deceased, Mahesh Prasad, who was Collector of Gopalganj made an order under the Crime Control Act detain ing Sadanand in jail. On 14th July 1982 the Commissioner dismissed the appeal filed on behalf othe Ashram and on 15th July1982 the entire structure of the Ashram was demolished under the direct supervision of the Collector. It was not disputed that from July,1982 Sadanand has continuously been detention in jail until the Collector"s murder. Yadav was staying with 412 Sadanand. The Prosecution had further led evidence about the recovery and he had also confessed to his guilt but gave out that he had committed the ghastly murder at the behest of appellant Tripathi. [413C E] 3. In view of this fact, the prosecution has established by circumstantial evidence the complicity of Sadanand is in the conspiracy to kill the Collector through Yadav. [411D] 4. The conviction and sentences awarded by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court are set aside.

The appellants were the workmen of the first appellant company and its main activity was to invest money in manufacturing concerns. The last three companies were controlled by the first company, namely Greaves Cotton and Co., in one way or the other and that is how the main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance was dealt with together by the tribunal. It may also be stated that there was noserious dispute before the Tribunal as to the financial capacity of the companies and further as the first Company controls the other three companies, the wages and Dearness allowance are the same so far as the clerical and subordinate staff are concerned. The main attack of the appellants on the wage fixed for these six categories is that in doing so, the Tribunal completely overlooked the wages prevalent for these categories in concerns which it had considered comparable. It was also urged that the Tribunal has not properly considered what would be the total wage packet including basic wages and other dearness allowance and that has made the total wages (i.e. basic wage) and dearness allowances fixed by the Tribunal much higher in the case of the appellant 's workmen than in comparable concerns which is not comparable. Held, that the wage scales fixed for factory workmen must be set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal to fix the same rates of dearness allowance for factory workers as for clerical staff; but in doing it the Tribunal must when making comparisons take into account the total Wage packet (i) the dearness allowance fixed is more or less on the same lines, i.e., less than 371 the highest but more than the lowest in other comparable concerns.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Annappa and against whom the present appeal is directed, had executed a usufructuary mortgage (Ex. D 51) in favour of Lalchand Bhavanchand Gujar and Tuljaram Bhavanchand Bharal Teli (the original plaintiff). The mortgagees by a Kabuliyat for Rs. 1,300 made up of Rs. 1000 due under a previous mortgage and Rs. 200 presently advanced in cash. 600 in favour Of the same mortgagees. On March 22, 1900, before the simple mortgage deed was presented for registration, Shiddappa gave a Rajinama under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code recording his desire to submit an unconditional surrender of the above mentioned khata of R. Section No. 301 which is Devasthan Inam Lands burdened with the obligation to supply oil for Nand Deep, i.e., keeping a lamp always burning before Shri Tholaba Deity in the village of Nipani. The mortgagees, defendants 1 to 4, filed suits against the mortgagees for accounts to be taken under the Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act. Thereafter, in 1911, annappa died and his son Mallappa Tukaram became the original plaintiff No. 1. After having made and published his last will and testament bequeathing his interest in the mortgaged properties to one Krishna Kallappa, that Krishna Kalirappa applied for Letters of Administration in respect of Annaappa 's estate and that in spite of the opposition of the first plaintiff, letters of administration with a copy of the will annexed was granted to Krishna Kalrappa. The trial court held that by the Rajinada, Shudappa intended to convey the title in the suit land to the mortgagees and hence he could not claim redemption of Shiddhaappa ' share by adverse possession. In appeal, the District Court held that the Raj inama had not the effect of transferring the interest of Ananappa to the mortgagors and that inasmuch as the mortgages were subsisting, the defendants could not acquire title by adverse Possession. The High Court also rejected the appellants ' claim for redemption of one half share of the mortgaged property on payment of one of the amounts due under the two mortgages. In second appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that under section 73 of the Code of Civil Procedure as Shiddana was the registered occupant, the Rajnama passed by Shiddppa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgage property and that the plaintiffs were not the heirs of the deceased Annappappa. Held: (i) The Rajinree passed by Shri Thiddappa did not affect the right of annappor to get the mortgaged land registered in his name on behalf or of an unregistered occupant as laid down in the Code but did not take away the rights of other occupants. In Lalchand Sakharam Marwadi vs Khendu Kedu Ughade, , this case was clearly out of the way, learned advocate for the appellants urged that under the section, where there are more occupants than one, the notice of relinquishment must be given by the registered occupancy occupant; and the person, if any, in whose favour an occupancy is relinquished or, if such 700 occupancy is relinquish in favour, of more persons than one. That their right as occupants remains clearly recognised by the opening paragraph of section 74 which gives an occupant a right to relinquish his occupancy either absolutely or in favour or of a specified person. It is true that no specific reference was made in the judgment to section 74 but the actual decision in that case, the facts of which are very similar to those of the instant case quite clearly indicates the court 's understanding of the law applicable to those facts and that law was nothing but the provisions of section 73.

The respondent company was assessed to sales tax at the point and at the rate specified in the Schedule to the Notification. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10% was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. Hence this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of the denomination of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [839C] Attorney General vs Winstanley ; , referred to. In popular parlance, the word "paper" is understood as meaning a sub stance which is used for bearing, writing or printing, or for packing, orfor drawing on, or on for decorating, or cover ing the walls. Now carbon paper which is manu (1) [1831] 2 Dow & Clark 302=(1901) ; (2) at 248. 840 factured by coating the tissue paper with a thermo setting ink (made to a liquid consistency) based mainly on wax, non drying oils, pigments and dyes by means Of suitable coat ing roller and equalising rod and then passing it through chilled rolls cannot be used for the aforesaid purposes but is used. according to 'the Randon House Dictionary of the English Language between two sheets of plain paper in order to reproduce on the lower sheet that which is written or typed on the upper sheet i.e. making replicas or carbon copies cannot properly be described as paper. It will be well at this stage to refer to a few deci sions which confirm our view. In Kilburn & Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of Sales Tax U.P., Lucknow, ; , relied on.

The respondents were employed by the appellant Mills at the Sugar Mills at Amroha. In 1951, the partners of the appellant mills purchased the building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at Kiccha in the district of Nainital. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed in the appellant 's factory at the time when they were not proprietors of the Sugar Mill at Bulandshahr. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager served a notice on the respondents 1, to 4 stating that they had disobeyed his orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. 920 of the U.P. Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The respondent raised an industrial dispute which was referred by the State Industrial Tribunal for adjudication to the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that both the concerns i.e., the mills at Amroha and the mills formed one unit, the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) of the Act. It further held that the management had no right to transfer the respondents I to 4 to the new factory and therefore the order dismissing them was illegal. The management appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The appellant 'had no such right. Further, it was not a condition of service of employment of the respondents either express or implied that the employer had the inherent right to the transfer them to a new concern stared by him subsequent to the date of their employment. The question whether in the circumstances of each case the transfer from one concern to another was valid or amounted to victimization must be considered in relation to the said facts. (ii) In the present case, as the two factories were distinct entities, situated at different places and, to import a term conferring a right on the employer to transfer respondents I, to4 to a different concern is really to make a new contract between them. As he refused to comply with the order of transfer, he was dismissed. (iii) The question raised was one of law, namely, whether the appellant had the right to transferred the respondents from one ' concern to other. A substantial question of law involved between the parties and that raised also an important principle governing the right of an employer to transferred his employees from one company to another of his in the circum stances of this case.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the . The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in case of sickness, maternity and employment injury and to make provision for certain other matters in relation thereto. The Act extended to the whole of India and came into force on such date or dates as the Central Government may appoint, different dates being permissible for different provisions of the Act and other necessary provisions have been made in this Chapter. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter VA by filing a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat under article 226 of the Constitution. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court on September 7, 1971. The present appeal has been filed pursuant to a certificate granted by the Supreme Court under Article 132(1) and 133(1)(c) of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of Chapter VI A of Part V A is analogous to a deferred insurance policy which parents often take out on the lives of their children, but which are to be effective only from a future date after the children attain a certain age, though premium is liable to be paid right from the start. [1091C] 2. The object of the scheme is that the benefits which it provides should become available to the employees in all factories through out India as soon as circumstances make it practicable. When the whole Act is brought into force in the whole country, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter.[1092D E] Basant Kumar vs Eagle Rolling Mil/s(l) where it was stated that the benefit clauses are not extended must also make their contributions though at a lesser rate. The payment of contribution by an employer towards the premium (what else is it ?) of an employee 's compulsory insurance under the falls directly within entries 23 and 24 of List II and it is wholly unnecessary to seek justification for it by recourse to Entry 97 of List I or Entry 47 of List III in any circumlocutous fashion. Even if the charge is to be construed as a fee as the High Courts have done, it appears to be justifiable on that basis too. It is not capable of any controversy that services and benefits are indeed meant to be and are bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer, in due course, when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. For a start the scheme was confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they be, in the case of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is higher while in the cases of employers, who straightaway receives the benefits under the insurance schemes, their rates of contribution are lower. So far as the latter are concerned, the scheme being analogous to deferred insurance policies which parents usually take out from the life time of their child attain a specified age, although premium is not liable to he paid right for right from start. In fact it may often happen that the rendering of a service or the conferment of a benefit may only follow after the consolidation of a fund from the fee levied. The question of how soon a return may be expected or ought to be given must necessarily depend on the nature of the services required to be performed and benefits required to he conferred. This contribution goes to a fund known as the Employees ' State insurance Fund which is to he utilised for the benefits to be granted to the employee under the Act. The cost of these benefits will` not be met from the general revenues of the state, but will be borne entirely from the aforesaid fund only.

The petitioners, who were working as regular workers in the respondent management, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging their regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The High Court rejected the petitioners ' claim and came to the conclusion that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners and that for quite some time they have been continued on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work for them, and that the accumulated loss to the establishment as on 31st March 1988 is Rs. 10,29,40,583. A copy of the balance sheet has also been enclosed with the counter affidavit. It was stated therein that a Voluntary Retirement Scheme offering considerable amount to these daily rated workmen has been framed which is Annexure R V to the counter affi davit. This document shows the amount of retrenchment com pensation and the ex gratia payment offered to the 63 daily rated workers under this scheme. The 54 petitioners are included therein. It is stated at the hearing before this Court that 9 out of these 63 daily wages mentioned in Annexure RV have accepted this Scheme of Voluntary Retirement and respondent No. 2 is prepared to give benefit of the same even to those who may not have agitated their claim. On behalf of respondent No 2 it was contended that a voluntary retirement scheme offering considerable amounts to them for the daily rated employees has been issued which is annexure R V thereto, which is annexed to the Counter affi tavit and that there is no vacancy in the Establishment to absorb the petitioners immediately as regular workmen. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily wage rated workman is doing the same work as the ordinary workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same Work is taken from him. On the clear findings in this case, this is not the position. This petition must fail. [638C D] 2. The principles of regularisation are of a Daily rated workman & payment ' to him of his the pay equivalent to that he of a regularly paid workman arises Only when the regular workman is do the same job as the normal workman and therefore there being an vacancy available in him, the he is neither absorbed against nor paid the senior equal pay. [438E] 3.

The appellants were the lessees of a tea estate. The original lease granted in 1928 was for a period of 99 years and the lease was renewed from time to time. In 1931, the appellants purchased the entire 16 as interest in the property at a Court sale in pursuance of a decree obtained by them against Kazi Mohammed Ismail, the eldest son of Azam Ali. The appellants contended that the lease granted by the original lease in 1928 in favour of the 1st defendant was his sole and individual pro perty and even if for any reason the other heirs of Azam had an interest in it, they did not have any such interest in tile property covered by the fresh lease. Held, that the plaintiffs were precluded from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by him under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that the sale in execution passed the entire 17 as share to the purchaser. The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12(i) were held to be real, the plaintiffs would be entitled in addition to the 8 pies share decreed to them by the High Court. The order to remit would be remitted to the Trial Court for recording evidence as regards truth of the transaction on the basis of the evidence adduced and to decide whether it was real or intended to pass title to the full 16 as. share belonging to the 1 st defendant, the sale being not held to have been real to no more than what the High court has decreed in favour Of the plaintiffs by the judgment now under appeal.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge of Karimnagar in what used to be the State of Hyderabad (now part of the State) under section 302, Indian Penal Code for the murder of his brother Baga Rao and sentenced to death. The conviction and sentence were affirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the provisions of sections 173(4), 207A and other sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied with, and (ii) the omission had the effect of vitiating the entire proceedings ending in the trial of the accused persons, and that therefore, ipso facto a fresh trial became necessary irrespective of whether or not the accused had shown any prejudice. Held:(i) The provisions of section 173(1), Cr. P.C., have not been observed. It is not clear as to whether all the documents contemplated by section 173 (4) were furnished to the accused or documents other than the statements of witnesses had not actually been so supplied. There was no doubt that those provisions have been introduced by the amending Act of 1955 in order to simplify the procedure in respect of inquiries leading upto a Sessions trial, and at the same time to safeguard the interests of accused persons by enjoining upon police officers concerned and magistrates before whom such proceedings are brought to see that all the information for the proper conduct of their defence, are furnished. It has rightly been contended on behalf of the appellant that it was the duty of the magistrate to see whether the provisions aforesaid had been fully complied with. The word "shall" occurring both in sub section (4), Cr., P. C., and section 207A(3) is not mandatory but only directory, because an omission by a police officer, to fully comply with the provisions Of section 173, should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. Gurbachan Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; , followed. (ii). It is well settled that in cases exclusively triable by a Court of Sessions, it is the duty and duty of a magistrate while holding a preliminary inquiry, to satisfy himself that the documents referred to in section 173 have been furnished to him and if he found that the police officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf, the magistrate should see to it that is done. The words "shall " shall be used in the context of these provisions only mean "shall". In cases exclusively governed by a court of Sessions it is its duty to see to them that they are not handicapped in their defence by any omission on the part of police officers. The expression "shall ' occurring both under sub section 4 and sub section 5 of section 207 A is not directory but only mandatory, because the omission by the police Officer to fully complied therewith the provisions contained therein have been complied. [294 H] Gurbachan singh vs The state of Punjab ; , applied. (iii) It was not clear from what has been said above that those sections had been introduced in order that they were intended to safeguard their interests by enjiting upon police officials concerned and in other cases before whom the committal proceedings had fended, had caused prejudice to the appellant in the interest of justice. The provisions contained in section 207(4) Cr.P.C. have not, therefore, been introduced for the first time in order, to simplulate the procedure to safeguard interests of the ' accused persons and by enjerting upon police Officers concerned and other magistrates, before whom they are brought, to see see that the accused person is not handicapped or prejudiced in their prosecution by any omissions on the parts of police officer.

The respondent Municipality was carrying on the business of chemical works in the State of Saurashtra. The appellant 's chemical works discharged effluent in very large quantities containing calcium, sodium and other salts through Katcha Channels thereby corrupting potable water of wells in the surrounding area by percolation. The respondent Municipality accordingly after having obtained the approval of the Government issued a notice to the appellant under section 153A (1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 as adapted and applied to the State for discharge of the effluent through a covered pucca drainage and for pumping it over a distance of about 8 miles in Ran ' area of Cutch near Kuda. The notice was served on the appellant by the Municipality on the 14th June 1956. The appellants replied that the Special Officer had unduly restricted the scope of enquiry by taking an erroneous view as to the scope or scope of the enquiry before him and thus had refused to exercise jurisdiction which was vested in him under the Act. The question for decision was whether the discharge of effluent through the covered pucca drain and adversely affected the fertility of soil was one for the subjective satisfaction of the respondent Municipality and beyond the scope Of his enquiry before an officer of the rank of a District Judge. Held, that the requisition under section 295A (I) of Bombay District Municipalities Act, 1925 is to leave it to the subjective opinion of the Municipality as to whether a nuisance existed or not. The provisions of section 153 A of the Act are to leave the subjective satis faction of the municipality as to existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to the party concerned. These provisions make it clear that the Legislature intended, where there was an absolute objection to the notice and the requisition contained therein as in the present case, that tho dispute between the Municipality and the party concern would be enquired into by a judicial officer of that rank of District Judge, then it would not require a judicial Officer of the ranks of a Special Judicial officer to enquire and report only as to when a nuisance of the kind alleged by the respondent municipality existed. The Legislature intended that the party to whom the notice had been issued should not be the victim of exercise of any power vested in the Municipality in a capricious manner. It is plain that before the appellant could be called upon to comply with the requisition of the Respondent Municipality involving several lakhs of rupees as expenditure the Special officer ought to decide and report whether a proper nuisance existed.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which by definition of section 2 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution case was that the appellant failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods. On the strength of some information received on 28th July 1964 that some stolen railway property was being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a Sub Inspector attached to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspector of Police searched the premises of the motor transport company at Lucknow the same night and found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years. The appellant put a remark either "O" or "N", 'O" signifying old goods and "N" meaning new ones. The report was accepted by the Magistrate who convicted the appellant under section 3 of the Act. On appeal, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles belonged to any particular railway administration but they were used or intended to be used for the construction or operation of a railway. HELD: The evidence in the case did not establish that goods belong to any of the railways in India. [188E] (i) In order to prove the existence of the incriminating articles belonging to a particular railway, it is necessary to establish that they had been manufactured for such a large number of articles which are 'the property of a Railway administration but which has been discarded or rejected for further use would be outside the definition of railway Stores. Evidence to the effect that the goods conformed to the specifications of the Indian Railway Standards were held that they belonged to some of the Railways in India, and their further evidence that they were "brand new" is also sufficient to show that they are intended to he used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a ' railway. [189F] (ii) The mere description of the articles as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 3(b). Some evidence will have to be led to the conclusion that the said goods were being actually used by a railway administration and that the same were in a serviceable condition. In the case of goods which had not been put to use evidence would have to he led to establish the effect, that they conformed with the Railway Standards they held that the items were 'old ' and 'N ' meaning new one. [190G] (iii) The prosecution must also prove that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. It is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his Possession of the same. He may, for instance, show that he had purchased the property in open market where goods of this kind are usually sold or that he has bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the facts.

The appellants had leased out the demised premises to the respondent landlord. The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. She died in September 1966. The demised premises were governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 for short the 'Act '). Section 13(1)(a) provides that "notwithstanding anything contained in any law or a contract, no court shall pass any decree or make any order in favour of the landlord whether in execution of a decree or otherwise evicting the tenant so long as he is ready and willing to pay rent thereof to the full extent allowable by the Act" unless the landlord proves to the satisfaction of the Court any one of the grounds enumerated in Clauses 'a ' to 'k ' thereof. The action for ejectment was initiated by the respondent on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised shop. The appel lant filed a suit for ejectment of the appellants from the demised Shop. The Trial Court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The tenancy came to a terminus with its determination by issuance of notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of property Act and the legal representatives of the deceased tenant did not acquire heritable interest in the commercial tenancy under that Act. It is a personal right to the tenant. A reading of the amendment to the definition of 'tenant ' in section 3(vii) makes the legislative intent manifest that from the date of the Amendment Act came into force, on the demise of the tenants, his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with personal law as applica ble to him, who had been, in the case of premises leased out for residential purposes, ordinarily residing and in the ease of premises let out for commercial or business purposes, normally carried on business with him/her in such premises as members of his/her family upto his death. The contractual tenant has an estate or property in the lease hold interest of the tenancy and hisitability is an incidence of the ' tenancy. The word 'tenant" had been defined under section 2(1) of that Act, thus: "a person by whom or on whose account or behalf the rent of any accommodation is, or, but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any accommodation and includes any person continuing in possession after the termination of a tenancy whether before or after the commencement of this Act; but shall not include any person against whom any order or decree for eviction has been made" he definition is the same as in the present case on hand under Clause (a) of Section 2(i) of the Act, therefore, it was held that they succeeded as legal representatives to the lease holding interest of th e commercial premises. The tenancy rights are heritable and the heirs of the lord tenant are entitled to enjoy the protection of the Rent Act. [108E F] 1.2 In case of commercial premises the heirs Of the deceased tenants not only succeed to the tenancy rights in the premises but they succeed to their business as a whole. If it be held that commercial tenancies after the determination of the contractual tenancy of thetenant are not heritable on the date, the heirs and legal representatives are not entitled to enjoying the protection under the Act. an irrepara surmise mischief which the Legislature would never have intended was likely to be caused. [109G H] 1:3 The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest In the lease held by the tenant Smt.

The appellant Board, which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum, claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The Industrial Tribunal accepted this contention and held that if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the appellant Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the State Government is the financier of the Electricity Board which charges Interest now at 6.26 per cent and that the services of the workers are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they were deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal had dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [44E] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, ; , referred to. 2.1 In the instant case the decision might very often depend on a close analysis of the financial condition of the board. The various sums payable under the provisions of section 67 have to be deducted before the profits could be ascertained. Even with regard to the depreciation reserve the provisions Of section 68 may have to he taken into account. If it is not it would have to been met by loans on which interest will have tobe paid and deduction of interest so paid will have, to be taken into consideration in calculating the profits. [45F G] Gramphone Co., vs Its workmen, ; referred to In the present case the Tribunal did not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on the Board under various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the Boards to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident fund or other amenities the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question. [46G] Gram phone Co operative vs Its Workers, ; and Gramophinone Co Co. Ltd.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate rejected the application holding that as he was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligation, she could not persuade herself to live with him and thus inflict on himself a life of perpetual torture. On appeal by the respondent wife, the High Court held that the husband having been found to be impotable, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live alongwith her husband. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that it is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the husband to refuse live with her husband and hence the wife is not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live With the husband merely because her husband had been impotently. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The decision in Arunachala Anandayammal vs Khimji Cooverji, ; relied on by the High Courts taking a contrary view must be held to be no longer good law and are accordingly overruled. [799G] 1.2 In the instant case, the facts of the case show that the grounds on which the wife refuses to live were impotenceable. The High Court was right in holding that the marriage having been proved to be bona fide one should not be a valid ground for refusing to live and hence she was entitled to the grant of the maintenance. [700C] 1:3 In the circumstances, it follows that the decisions referred to above in the judgment taking a contra view must not be held good law. [699D] 2.1 It is now too well settled that impetency is not good ground for refusal to live separately from her husband when it seems to us that the ground of impotability which had been held by a number of authorities under the civil law to be a good ground not only for restitution of conjugal rights but also for divorce. Indeed, if this could be a ground for divorce or for an action for restitution or restitution of matrimonial rights, could it be said with any show of force that it would not be just ground within the meaning of the second proviso so as to make the refusal of the wife 's refusal to living with her. [899E] 2:2 In view of our decision in this case, it is clear that the decision in the instant cases taking a similar view must also be held not to be good law for the purpose of deciding the question whether the husband was impetent and was able to discharge marital obligations, which would undoubtedly be a reasonable ground as contemplated by the aforesaid proviso for the respondent 's refusing to reside with her deceased husband. [900G] 2 :3 In view Of our decision that where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a husband is impotant and is unable to discharging his matrimonial obligations, this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would certainly be a proper ground as envisaged by the proviso for her wife ' s refusal to reside separately from such a husband. The said alteration gives a wider discretion to the Court, which means that in passing such an order it is legitimate for it to take into account the relations between the husband and the wife, and the husband 's conduct towards her. This decision, given as far back as 1907, while construing the proviso appears to be both prophetic and pragmatic in its approach, is rather unfortunate that subsequent decisions have not noticed this important principle of law decided by the Bombay High Court.

The plaintiff respondent Municipality filed a suit for declaration of its title and for possession of the suit property described in the schedule to the plaint. The defendants pleaded that by virtue of these orders, the entire suit lands mentioned in the plaint had vested in the plaintiff the land of the Parade Ground or the lands and buildings known as Rasala Lines and that consequent upon the Bhavnagar State acceding to the Indian Union and consequent on the Federal Financial Integrity of States, accommodation, lands and building in the use or occupation of the Ex state forces were transferred to the Government o[ India and became its property. The plaintiff also pleaded that the Parade ground was used by the Ex Bhavna gar state forces and that barracks and other military build ings used for accommodation of the ex Bhavnagar state forces known as Lancer 's Lines were in existence for a long time prior to 1948 in the suit land known as Namala Lines. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit lands and that they were in possession in the Suit property till 7th July, 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Government of India to the State Public Works Department of the State of Saurashtra. However, on the ground that in respect of Rasala Line the plaintiff have admitted that they did not own the buildings thereon, they were not entitled to recover possession of lands covered by the Survey numbers de scribed in the second part of the schedule. The High Court allowed the appeal of the Union of India in the view that even assuming that by the Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1948 the title to Parade Ground had come to be vested in tho Municipality, there was nothing on record to show that the Municipality was formally handed over the land in question, that its right over the suit premises was never recognised by the Union or the State Government and that the various documents filed in this case would go to show: that as early as July 1950 these lands and other properties which were in occupation of erstwhile erstwhile state military had been taken over and remained under the control of the Defence Ministry of the union of India and that possession was handed back by the Government to the Saurashtra Government on 7th7 1952 for use. The appellant contended that the High Court should have given a finding on title as Article 65 of the is applicable to this case since the suit was filed on 3rd March, 1964, and that on the finding of the Trial Court in favour of the plaintiff on the question of title in respect 'Parade Ground ' and in the absence of specific plea of adverse possession in tile writ ten statement, the Trial court 's decree should have been confirmed. The respondents contended that even if by virtue Of the Resolution dated 19nd January,1948 the title of the Receiver had cometo be vested In the Municipality there was no nothing on the record to indicate that the municipality was formally handing over the lands in question and that its rights over the property were never recognised. It is also not open to the appellant to rely on the principle that possession follows title. In this case, it is not open for the appellant now to rely upon the principle of that possession follow title. The suit itself is for possession based on title and the plaintiff has not proved title. Therefore, since the Suit itself is liable to be dismissed as barred by limitation, and since the plaintiff 's claim is based on the title and tile defendants had denied title, of the plaintiffs it is necessary for the Court to give a finding thereon on title of t he plaintiff even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse possesion.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He accepted from one Nanak Singh currency notes of the value of Rs. 150 as illegal gratification as a motive for securing a job for one Kallu. The prosecution case was that on the day of occurrence, the appellant and his two companions had accepted a sum of Rs 150 as a bribe from Nanak Singh to deliver it to him currency notes. The appellant was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code with having induced the said Nanak Singh by corrupt or illegal means pecuniary advantage in the shape of Rs, 150 from the said R. On appeal by the State, Held, that the appellant was an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) and therefore a public servant within the definition of a public ' under section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. Ram Krishan vs Delhi State, A.I.R. 1954 Cal. 1, approved. The word "officer" in section 21 of the Indian Penal code is not used in the sense of an office which is defined by section 21 (9) of the Act and therefore it was a rule that where one man 's work to do with another 's affairs against his will, and without his leave, that this is an office, and he who is in it is an officer. The true test, therefore, in order to determine whether a person is an Officer of the Government, is: (1) whether he is in the service or pay of the government, and (2) whether, he is entrusted with the performance of any public duty.
