The Respondent along with one Gora Lal and Sat Pal, had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69. The licences paid a sum of Rs. 86,450 leaving the balance unpaid in spite of repeated reminders. Ultimately recovery proceedings under the said Act were started by the department and the Collector. Excise and Taxation Department, Patiala issued a proclamation prohibiting the transfer or creation of a charge by the Respondent of his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga with a building constructed thereon. The auction in respect of the said share was notified for June 14, 1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the auction sale the Respondent filed a suit against the State and the collector cum Deputy Excise andTaxation Commissioner, Patiala Division, for a permanent injunction restraining the State from auctioning his said half share. The contention of the respondent was that a part of the building standing on the plot of the land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and therefore his halfshare was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (l) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Trial Court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. The Respondent then filed a second appeal before the District Judge, Patiala being Civil Appeal No. 554 of 5.9.79. The Additional District Judge dismissed it with costs but the Division Bench allowed the Second Appeal holding that the portion of the property used for residence was exempt under clause(ccc)(c) and that the part of it used for residential purpose was exemptfrom attachment and sale under clause.(ccc). Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The opening words of sub section 2 of Section 59 are "The following property is liable to attachment and sales in execution of a decree". On a plain reading of the aforesaid section 60, it is clear that section has no application to attachment or sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said provisions are concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment levied on, and the auction sales notified in respect thereof were not in execution. [848B C] 2. Section 60 has no applicability to an attachment and Sale under any other of her statutes made expressly or applicable thereto; So far the said section is concerned, the provisions of Section 61 of the Civil Procedure Code do not apply to an attached and sale in any proceedings other than in execution thereof.

The lands in question were acquired by the Government under the Land Acquisition Act. The Special Deputy Collector of Land Acquisition awarded a total compensation of Rs. 20,000. This compensation was received by Rashid himself during his lifetime. In making this assessment also the respondent as well as the High Court had proceeded on the wrong assumption that the acquired lands formed part of the estate of the deceased and passed on his death for, it was on such basis that the High court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands such property (meaning lands) had been undervalued in the original assessment and as such it had escaped assessment to duty. According to him the lands no longer formed part or of the Estate of the appellant at the date of his death, namely, May 7, 1965, inasmuch as long prior thereto they had vested in the Government, and therefore, it had merely the right to receive compensation which, if at all, could constitute property passing on the death of the said deceased but he contended that during the lifetime of the lands in ques tion had not merely been acquired but even the compensation as determined under the awards made by the Special Deputy Commissioner was paid to and received by the deceased. The High Court held that the right which the deceased had was the right, to receive the compensation at market value on the dates of the relevant notifications accrued to the deceased which was property and it would be such property that would pass on the 'future ' of the acquired land. In these appeals by certificate, it is contended for the appellant that the lands were no longer forming part of estate of deceased on May 7 1965 inasmuch as the lands had vested to the Government long prior to his death but they had been acquired by two separate awards both made on January 31, 1963 and January 18, 1962 under the land Acquisition Act; that the notices issued by the respondent on the basis that it was case of change of opinion as regards the valuation of lands acquired and not a case of mistake apparent from the record and as Such the impugned notice had not been issued on the ground that such right to compensation had been valued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as on 328 the date when the death, but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law inasmuch as it had issued a notice purporting to act under section 61 of the Act on the grounds that the estate had been value determined by the special Deputy Collector in his award and the accountable person had no objection to this course and therefore the respondent himself did not estimate the market value of the land on the date. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that assigning the right of compensation survived and it was that right which was being prosecuted by the heirs of Rashid in Civil Court, the impugned notices had not be issued on tho ground that the said right to claim compensation had already merged in those awards and the only right which he had was to agitate against the correctness of the awards and nothing more and this right to seek further compensation was a precarious right, being merely a right to litigate a chancy and dicey right, which could not be elevated to the status of any asset or property and as a such there was no question of any property having escaped assessment. On the other hand it was submitted that assigning that the rights to receive compensa tion at market values on the years of the respective dates of relevant notifications had beenvalued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the civil court, and the High 's decision upholding the issuance of such notice on wrong basis was liable to be set aside.

The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the Bank from the Brehmapuri Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. His election was not called in question according to the procedure prescribed by the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Act to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors as per the provisions of section 73FF and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 11 678 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The notice stated that the appellant had borrowed a loan of Rs. 10,000 (Rs. 7,000) from the Bank and he kept the loan constant in arrears till 21.10.1986, and being elected as Director of the bank on 18 8.86. Till then he was working as the Director of respondent Bank. The appellant 's election was challenged by him before the Cooperative Court which dismissed his writ petition holding that section 73F(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act 1960 came into force on 12.5.1986 and the appellant could be treated as a defaulter under that section; and the mere making of payment on 21. 10.86 did not mean that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 8.1986 to 21.11.1986 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. The Cooperative Court further held that section 78F(2) became applicable from 6.8 1986 as per Government Notification issued on 18 4.86, and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21 10.1986 when he was nominated as Director, he was defaulter under section 73 FFF(1). The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the above order of the Cooperative court contending that section 74F(I)(b), became applicable only from 6 8.6.86 as per government Notification issued by the Government on 18 April 1986 and that since he had received all the debts on 21st October, 1986, he could not be "absolved of the disqualification" on the day he contested the election; and that the question of giving retrospective effect to section did not arise because the appellant 'was a defaulter when he contested his election and though he paid all the debt on 21th October,1986 yet he could have been "absected of the disqualifications on the date he contested election". The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 78F (2) of Bombay State Co Operative Societies Act provides that a person shall be disqualified for being elected or to continue as Director or Executive Committee Member of the Executive Committee of a Cooperative Society and his seat shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant. This section was inserted by Maharashtra Act XX of 1986 with effect from 12.686. If the impugned order is found to have been passed by way of setting aside the election of the appellant, the order would be bad as the appellant`s election had not been called in ques tion in accordance with the procedure provid ed by the Act. No doubt there is reference to the Appellant 's having been a defaulter and disqualified for becoming elected but it has been addressed to the appel lant as Director.

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. After his retirement, the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent 's representation to the State Government was rejected by the State Govt. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. A Division Bench of that Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's orders dated December 4, 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from Service. Relying on a decision of this Court in B.J. Shelet vs State of Gujarat & Ors., ; the High court held that the initiation of disciplinary enquiry and the order of punishment was unauthorised and illegal. The State Government preferred this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 184 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was In service or after the completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government servant depend upon the good conduct of the government servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 expressly confers powers on the State to withhold, or withdraw from any part, of it, if the pensioners be convicted of serious crime or be found to have been guilty of serious misconduct while in service provided that before any order to this effect is issued, the procedure referred to in Note I to Rule 33 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules shall be followed. [189D E] 1.2 The State Govt 's power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government Servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. 35 The validity of these Rules was not challenged either before the Supreme Court or before this Court. In this view, the reduction of pension by 50 per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the Respondent. [190F] 1:3 The reduction of 50 per percent was too severe and disproportionate. The reduction was too low. The reduced pension was too high. The reducing pension was more than the amount of pension payable to the respondent. The High Court committed serious error in holding that the respondent had retired from services and the reduction was only due to the charges proved against him.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents from their shop premises. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court in revision set aside the order passed by the trial court and restored that of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 3(4) does not expressly exclude the jurisdiction of civil courts to entertain the question about the correctness, propriety or legality of the order made by the Commissioner in the present case whereby he granted permission to the appellants to bring the present suit. [56 F] (ii) The words "any other questions in relation to the grant or refusal of the said permission have to be decided by the appropriate authorities constituted under the Act" indicate that the jurisdiction is intended to be excluded, appears to be inescapable. [58 C D] (iii) Section 16 of the Act does not specifically exclude the jurisdic tion of civil Courts. The bar created by the relevant provisions of the , excluding the jurisdiction Of the civil courts cannot operate in cases where the plea raised before the civil court goes to the root of the matter and would, if upheld, lead to the conclusion that the impugned order is a nullity. If it is shown by a party impeaching the validity of the orders in a civil court that the order was passed by a person who was not a District Magistrate, the order in law would be a nullity, and such a plea cannot be ruled out on the ground of exclusion of the jurisdiction.

The President of India, Shri Saini, Member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was removed from his office by an order dated May 5, 1983. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that he had been involved in a false incident since the Chief Minister of Punjab, Shri Darbara Singh, was not happy with his appointment as a Member of Punjab Public Services Commission. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the case of Shri Saini is that he has been involved for the offence of assault because he had incurred the wrath of the Chief Ministers of Punjab and the hostility of the posted Member of that Public Service Commissions; (2) the incident of slapping took place as alleged and not on any other matter; and (3) the allegation that Shri Saini had been implicated into the charge of assault was false, inspired and motivated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The President has made the Reference. The material is of a kind and nature enough to justify the President 's opinion that a prima facie case exists for an inquiry and report by this Court. [639C D] 2. Article 317(1) provides that subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the Supreme Court may, from time to time, with the approval of the President make rules regulating the practice and procedure of the court. Rule 2, which is in point, provides that while making an inquiry into the matter referred to it by the President, this Court is entitled to summon and examine witnesses, but nothing contained therein can be read to mean that after deciding which witnesses should be summoned and examined, evidence must be recorded by this court itself. [643E F] 3. The inquiry contemplated by the Article is into the facts themselves and facts also so as to enable this Court to pronounce upon the question whether the allegations made against the Chairman or member are proved at all. The purpose of article 317( 1) is to ensure independence of members of the Public Service Com mission and to give them protection in the matter of their tenure. Any allegation of misbehaviour made against them has to be examined by the Supreme court on merits unlike the allegations contained in those others whose interests are directly affected by these proceedings, that is to say the Chairperson Smt. Sanghi who appears for the Member that evidence should be allowed to be led only on the question as to whether the charge against him is false, motivated and motivated.[642E F; 647A B] 4. The enquiry contemplated by article is into facts themselves. The object of Article 317 is to secure independence of the members of Public Service Commissioners and to provide them protection. Any allegations of misbehaviour against them have to be scrutinised by the High Courts on merits particularly when they are not in a position to decide the reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. [ 647C D; 647E] 5. The power of the Court to summon witnesses, is not subject to any condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that the Chairman may summon such witnesses as it considers necessary. This rule shows that while exercising its powers under article 317 (1), this Court has to examine the evidence in a regular trial. It is only fair that an opportunity should be given to Shri Saini to prove his case that the charge is false inspired and actuated. [625E F, 647A] 6. The proceedings will normally be held in Delhi. The mere fact that the evidence of any particular witness is recorded by the learned Judge will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act 4 of 1939), for setting aside the order dated 4 8 1950 of the respondent defendant by which the temple of the appellants was declared to be a public temple and a trust and the endowment was held to be of a public nature and, therefore, was to be governed by the Act. The Subordinate Judge decreed the appellants plaintiffs suit holding that the deity installed in the temple was a family deity of the Pani family and the Endowment being of a private nature, the Act had no application and the order passed by the respondent regarding the management was set aside. The respondent defendant preferred an appeal before the High Court against the decision of the Subordinate Judge which was heard by the Division Bench referred to above. The High Court reversed the decision and held that the temple and the deity install therein being a public endowment fell within the four corners of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that under the Hindu law, however, it is not only permissible but also very common to have private endowments which though are meant for charitable purposes yet the dominant intention of the founder is to instal a family idol in the Temple and worship the same in order to effectuate the spiritual benefit to the family of the founders and his descendants and to perpetuate the memory of the Chairman. [830G] 1.2 The mere fact that members of the public are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members of a particular community which also shows that even if the family was to become extinct, the private nature of the endowment could not be changed. [861C D] 1:3 In the peculiar circumstances of this case, the appellants will be entitled to costs of the appeal in this Court quantified at Rs. Appeal allowed.

The appellant Bank originally agreed to finance the contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. For the purpose of carrying out this arrangement, Malhotra executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The power of Attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into certain contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat Bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorneys have agreed to advance moneys against his bill for supplies. . . . The appellant was also authorised to sue for, recover and receive the monies due in connection with the contracts with the approval of MaLhotra, to conduct and defend proceedings in consultation with him and to take steps in his name and on his behalf. Malhotra promised and declared that "all powers hereby granted are and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorney 's against us whether for principle, interest, costs or charges or otherwise remain outstanding and unpaid." Intimation of the power of the Attorney was given by the appellant to the military authorities for payment. Before the appellant received the payment, the amount due under the bill was attached by Takhatmal in execution of a money decree obtained by him against Malhotra. The appel lant filed objections in the execution proceedings. On September 11, 1952, the objections were dismissed. On December 12, 1952 the appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhat Mal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhatal had no right to attach it. The trial Court held that the appelLlant was the assignee of that bill and decreed the suit. On appeal by the plaintiff, the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit holding that the power attorney dated July 13. 1946 coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 amounted to an equitable assignment of the monies payable under the bills in favour to the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the powerof attorney dated 7.7.1948 did not amount to an ordinary assignment of future debts, see Tailby vs Official Receiver, ; and (ii) the document was brought into existence in connection With a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that there was no equitable assignment. [705 B] Palmer vs Carey, , referred to.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and received out of this provident fund an 439 amount of Rs. 27,948/ which represented the interest on the amount of his own contribution to the fund. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but on further appeal to the tribunal, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income tax Act, 1961. The High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) The meaning of section 17(3)(ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. [445E] (2) The expression "salary" in section 2(24) means "profits in lieu of or in addition to any salary or wages". [446F] (3) In defining the expression "Profits in lieu ' of salary", the legislature excluded from the scope of that expression any payments received by the assessee from a provident fund his own contributions to the Fund or any interest on such contributions. From that it follows that the receipts of Rs 27,949/ by the appellant in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income.

The Bihar Act, in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of buffaloes, male and female, is constitutionally valid. The Bihar Act makes no distinction between she buffaloes, bulls and bullocks (cattle and buffalo) which are useful as milch or breeding or working animals and strike down the ban on the slaughter Of her buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (dattle and buffaloes) without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness. The impugned Acts put a total ban on slaughter of all animals belonging to the species of bovine cattle which includes buffaloes (male or female adult or calves) but it is still possible for the butchers of Bihar to slaughter goats and sheep and sell goat ' meat and mutton for food. The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned Acts on two grounds, namely, (i) that a total prohibition against the slaughter was not in the interests of the general public; (ii) that the impugned Act violated articles 19(1)(g), 31(2), 39(3), 40(4), 41(5), 42(6), 43(7), 44(8), 45, 46 and 47 of the Constitution. The contentions were : (i ) that a large ban on her slaughter was imposed on the slaughtering of buffaloes and she buffaloes; (iii) that it violated articles 14, 19(2)(g) and 31(1); (iv) that section 40(5) of the Act offended article 19(6) of Constitution. HELD: The Bihar Legislature has made no distinction in regard to her cattle which are not useful as a milch and breeding or Working animals and strikes down the restrictions on the said slaughter of she buffaloes. [655 C] (i)(a) The impugned Act is constitutionally invalid in so much as it purports to completely prohibit the slaughter, of all animal except those which are useless. It is not possible to apply the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban upon the slaughter. [660 D] (b) The Bihar Acts make no distinction on the ground that she buffaloes were useful as rap and breeding and working animals without prescribing a test or require as to its age or utility, it offends against article 19 (1)(f). It is true that in some of the States total ban has been imposed on slaughter by cattle, many of the states have not conidered it necessary to impose such blanket ban. The entire provision banning the slaughter is reasonable but of those which were useless is not valid. [666 F] (ii)(a). The impugned legislation is constitutionally void in so insofar as it completely prohibits the slaughtering and working of buffaloes without prescribing no test or condi tion as to her age or good usefulness, it infringes the rights of the petitioners under article 19 of the Consti tution.

The respondent was a typist in the Nagpur Electric Light and Power Co. Ltd., a public limited company having its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh, its Manager and Assistant Manager. The respondent was appointed Deputy Head Clerk in 1947 in the grade of Rs. 120 10 225. Since 1952 he had been receiving a basic salary of Rs,. 245 per month. On November 28, 1955, an explanation was called for from him with regard to the issue of certain bills to consumers of electricity called "high tension consumers ", without having certain notes for the information of consumers " printed at the back of the bills. The Respondent submitted his explanation on the next day, marking a copy thereof to one of the directors of the Company. On December 2,1955, he was again asked to explain why he marked a copy of his explanation to one Of the directors. The preliminary objections taken were these: (1) that the service of the respondent was terminated in accordance with the Standing Orders of the company approved by the relevant authorities under the provisions of the (XX of 1946), and (2) that as the termination of the service was without statutory authority, it must be vacated. Held, that the Standing Order No. 2(a) should apply to the respondent and his service had been terminated in compliance with Standing Orders No. 18, which provided for penalties for misconduct, and submitted that the provisions thereof have not been complied with by the appellants. The words " whose names and ticket numbers are included in the depart. mental musters " occurring in Standing Order 2(b) should be read as " whose name and ticket number, if any, are included In the depart, and mental musterers " in Standing Orders.

The appellant, an undertaking owned controlled and managed by a Government Company, was started in the year 1961 and it went into production in 1964 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year 1967 68. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect Of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into manufacture. The Tribunal held that alloy steel Project could not be treated as a new establishment for purposes of section 16 of the Act. On appeal by the appellant company to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that simply because Alloy steel project was owned, controlled and run managed by Hindustan Steel Ltd., it had to be treated to be a separate Establishment. [630 D] (ii) The proviso to sub section (2) of section16 also does not stand in the way of this claim, because there is no evidence at all that in any year, after Alloy iron Project was set up bonus was paid to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. [643 E] (iii) The provisions of sub section(1) are to apply even to new departments, undertakings or branches set up by existing establishments. Consequently, even if Alloy is treated as an establishment newly set up for purposes Of section 16(1), the exemption claimed would be fully justified.

The appellant State of Haryana has enacted the Central Act for the prevention and control of water pollution. There are also certain provisions relating to constitution of joint boards, the details of which need not detain us. The Cess Act is an enactment imposing li ability for cess. The levy and collection of cess provided under the Cess Act are on water consumed by persons carrying on certain industries specified in the Schedule. The cess is payable by every person who carries on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed, by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in corresponding entry in column II thereof as the Central Govern ment may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. "Specified industry" is defined in the Act as meaning any industry specified in Schedule I. The Punjab and Haryana High Court and the Allahabad High Court have taken the view that sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 of the Sched ule I as processing vegetable products industry. On the other hand, the Andhra Pradesh State Board for Prevention and Control of Water Pollution vs Andhra Pradesh Rayons Ltd. and others; , The question for consideration was whether the industries manufacturing sugar were covered by Entry 15 that is "processing of vegetable product industry". From the point of view 'vegetable ' may include any plant but in common parlance it is understood as refer ring to edible plants or parts of edible plants. In the World Book it is defined as: "A plant used or cultivated for food man or domestic animals, as the cabbage, turnip, potato bean, dandelion, etc., also the edible part of such a plant, as prepared for market or the table." The word vegetable in the context does not attract the botanic meaning. The sugar manufacturing industry do not, therefore, come within Item 15 of Schedule I of the Cess act. 814 of 1990) the appellant is Haryana Distillery who purchases molasses which is a by product of the manufacture of sugar and manufactures alcohol. Manufacture of alchohol was held by the High Court to come within entry 15 of Sched underle I. It was held that sugar industry is one of the main source of causing water pollu tion and since the object of the Pollution Act and the Cess Acts were intended to control water pollution, it would be covered by the Act. The appellant is directed to pay the cess on the amount of cess payable by the respondents. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that sugar manufactured by them would come under Entry 15 as "process ing vegetable products" and not under Entry 14 of Schedule 1. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'vetable ' in Item 15 is generally understood to mean as bringing into existence a new substance and does not mean 'merely ' to produce some change in a sub stance, however minor in consequence, the change may be. [514C D] 2. Unless we give the bottanical meaning to the word ' 'veholdg etable ' it is not possible to conclude sugar cane as vegetable. Construction of words and the meaning to be given for such words shall normally depend on the nature, scope and purpose of the statute in which it is occurring and to the fitness of the matter to the statute. In order to bring an industry within any of these entries in Schedule 1 it has to be seen what is the end product produced by that industry. Sugar cane is not a vegetable though it may be an agricultural product.

The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The respondent contended that Section 10(3)(a)(iii) used the expression 'business ' only and not the expression "profession". The Rent Controller rejected the contention of the respondent holding that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of section 10( 3)(a) (iii). The Appellate Authority confirmed the order. Before the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that Section 9(3) (a) used expression 'profession ' only, and not to the expression `profession. ' Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The word 'business" in section 10 (3)(b)(iii), is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the purpose of livlihood or profit '. It is obvious that the meaning must be gleaned from the context in which it is used. Reference to the provisions of the Constitution or other statutes where the expression is used cannot be of any assistance in determining its meaning in section 2(a)(ii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1960. [14 F G] 1.2 The word must be interpreted in the context of the statute in which the term has been understood in the several statutes does not necessarily throw any light on the manner in which a term should be understood generally. On the other hand it is a (1) A.I.R. 1950 Mad. 891, referred to. 1.3 The word "business" must be construed in the sense of the context In which it occurs and not in the background of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context. [15 F G; 16A] 1:4 The expression business occurring in section 9(1) (b)(ii), is given a wide meaning so as not to include any profession. It would be anamolous to hold that all the provisions Of the Act including section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and section 10 which bars the eviction of tenants apply to nonresidential buildings owned by an Advocate but not section 10, which bars eviction of tenant apply to Non residential buildings owned under an advocate but not Section 10 (1)(a), (iii) only. In our view the expression business ' occurring in Section 10 must take their colour from the content in which they appear. [16 B C] 1 :5 The word business ' is used, in a broad sense so that to include everything that occupies tho time attentionand labour of man for the purposes of lvlihood or profits '. [17 F G].

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant contended that Article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 was the relevant Article because if was a case of money deposited under an agreement that it was payable on demand and therefore the limitation would commence from the date of demand and the suit was filed within three years from the demand. Held: (i) The High Court was wrong in decreeing the suit. (ii) The letter exhibit A 5 bears the date 29 September, 1942 and is contemporaneous with the entire transaction between the appellant and the respondent. (iii) The evidence on record showed that there were advances which were in the nature of deposit and were not covered by the award. It was not a case where the respondent gave loan to the appellant. (iv)The relationship between the parties was that the amount was deposited with the appellant, and the appellant had to be put on a footing of financial stability by giving the appellant the use of the sum. The transaction was between the respondent and the Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills. (v)There was no demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 because Padampat Singhania said that there was demand in the month of October, 1943 and therefore limitation would start from that date. (vi)The appellant 's contention that the background of the transaction was mercantile loan would be more a conjecture than a conclusion to be arrived at. It would be most consistent to hold that by allowing India Supplies a deposit of Rs 4,00,000 India Supplies would be relieved of the situation of repaying the money immediately. (vii)The respondent 's partner Padampat Singh Gupta gave oral evidence and substantiated the terms of the letter and the respond ent 's case.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue on February 28, 1986 made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The petitioner challenged the said order before this Court. It was contended that the period of parole had expired on February 20, 1987 and since the order of detention was liable to be quashed, it should have been added to the period from 15th May, 1986 till February 22, 1987, and that the order had lapsed and the detenu became entitled to be freed from the impugned order of deten tion. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is in jail for at the most one day does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining author ity was aware of the fact that he was already in custody and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his order of his detention became necessary. [845F G] 2. The facts that the petitioner is al ready in detention does not taken away the juris diction of the Detaining Authority in making the order preventive detention, are not relevant for deciding whether giving up the other pleas raised in the writ peti tion amounted to breach of professional duty on the part of the counsel not to raise those points against the validity of the detention order on which the Court had prima facie issued notice. [ 843C D] Ramesh war Shaw vs District Magistrate Burdwan, ; and Vijay Kumar vs State of Jammu & Kashmir, ; , referred to.

The petitioners, who were working as 'Daily Rated Casual Labour ' in the Posts and Telegraphs Department, challenged the orders of the Director General, Posts and telegraphs Department bearing No. 28 II/77 SR dated 15 5.5.1980 on the ground that they are being paid wages far less than the minimum pay payable under the pay scales applicable to regular employees belonging to corresponding cadres. The respondents contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are not being regularly employed, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. It was further contended that even though some of them have been working for the last ten years as casual labourers, the wages paid to them are very low and far less as the salary and allowances paid to regular workers of the Posts & Telegraphs department belonging to each of the categories referred to above and secondly no scheme has been prepared by the Union of India to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits, such as increments, pension facilities etc. which are enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. The petitioners also alleged that even although many of them had been working continuously for more than a year in the Department and some of their juniors have been employed continuously for nearly ten years, the pay paid to him is very low. It may be that the casual labourer has agreed to work on such low wages. The Union of india has also filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order dated 5.2.1986 passed by the Director, General Posts and Telecommunication Department bearing no. 28 11/77 PG NO 8 PG NO 9 directing the Union to pay to the petitioners same salary and allowance and other benefits as are being given to regular and permanent employees of the Union Government in the corresponding cadres and to direct the Union Public Service Commission to regularise the service of the casual labour who had been in continuous service for more over six months. The allegation made in the petitions to the effect that the petitioners are being denied the benefit, suchas increments, gratuity etc., which are enjoying by those working on regular basis, was not tenable. It is further contended by the respondents that since they belong to category of Casual Labour and are also not being regular employed, their case is not covered by the decision of this Court in State of Haryana & Ors. vs Ram Kumar & Ors., ; , and that the State cannot deny at least the minimum wages in the pay scale of regularly employed workmen even though the Government may not be compelled to extend all the benefits enjoyed by regularly recruited employees. It would also be against this background that the respondents have not been regularly recruited but many of their they have already been working continuous continuously for a year and some others have been engaged as casual labourer for nearly 10 years. Clause (2) of Article 38 of the Constitution of India which contains one of the Directive Principles of State Policy provides that "the State shall, in particular, strive to minimise the inequalities in income, and endeavour to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vacations." Even though the above Directive Principle may not have been enforceable as such by virtue of Article 37 of the constitution of India, it may be relied upon by the petitioners to show that in the instant case they have not be regularly recruited and many of the them have were engaged as Casual labourers for nearly five years. The Respondents contended that the Government agencies in particular should not allow 610 workers to remain as casual labour or temporary employees for an unreasonably long period of time, where is any justification to keep persons as casual Labour for years as is being done in the Postal and Telegraph Department Department.

The assessee, a partner of a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1945 46. The Income tax Officer did not act on this return but on February 27, 1950 issued a notice purporting to be under section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act calling upon the assessee to submit his return. 59,026 could not and should not have been included in his income, that the amended section 34 had no retrospective effect, and that the assessment completed on February 26, 1951 was invalid inasmuch as it was completed four years after the end of the relevant assessment year. The assessee contended that since he had submitted a return under section 22(3) of the Act on January 5, 1950, the assessment if any had to be completed before March 31, 1950 as required by section 34(3), and with a voluntary return before the Income tax officer there was no scope for the issuance of a notice under section 24(2). Held, that in answer to a notice issued under section 23(2) of that Act (corresponding to section 22)(1) of Act) the best judgment assessment was not bad. The only question is whether in such an event the Income Tax Officer was precluded from issuing a notice tinder section 34 after a return was already made before it, and the benefit of the extended period of limitation for assessment available under the first proviso to sub section (3) Of section 34 was not available in this case. If the return filed on January May 5,1950 was a return of income, there was nothing to show that he had any assessable income. The notice did not mention that the assessee might file the 'voluntary ' return on the last day showing income less than the taxable limit. The assessment completed by February 26 was valid and could not be treated as such a return filed under section24(1) or a return called for under that section but filed under that provision.

The petitioners, who are principal office bearers of the first petitioner and are officers of different nationalised banks, challenged Circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi, whereby it was purported to have been issued in terms of sub clause (c) of Clause 3 of the Nationalised Banks (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970. The petitioners contend that the circular is contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Ac quisi tion & Transfer of Undertaking) Act 1970 read with the Scheme insofar as it cuts at the root of the representative form of selection for appointment to the Board of Directors as contemplated by the statute. It further contended that Clause 3(c) in terms whereof the circular was purported tO have been issu ed is ultra vires Section 9 of the Act unless the said clause is so read as to be in harmony with the Section, and when so read, the said cl does not justify or support the circu lar. The respondents contend that Clause (3) of the Scheme in terms thereof which the circular has been issued is ultra legis lative and contrary to it and the scheme insofar as they cuts at root of its representative character in consonance and harmony with extremely delicate, vital and significant role of the banking industry in the context of the national policy and objectives. The Respondents contend that clause 3(b) of Scheme in con sideration is ultra viola tive and contrary ly to the letter and spirit of the scheme inasmuch as it sets at naught the root and objective of the representatives form of Selection for appointment of Directors, as contemplated under the statute, and that interpretation is wrong. The Respondent State contended that the Act postulates both election and nomination of members of the Board and the choice between the two modes of appointment is left to the Central Government; and that the notification in question is ultra rites Section 9(1) of Act provides for the constitution of the board of Directors so as to include representatives of the employees and other speci fied categories. The respondent State contended: (1) Clause 3 does not support the impugned circu ary, (2) Clause (c), which is a self contained provision, is vaguely drafted and when read without regard to the legislative intent, as disclosed by the Act, is capable of a contrary interpretation, as is now sought to be put upon it by the Central Govern ment, and (3)(a) so as not to restrict the choice of appointment to three persons specified on the panel furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen as the case may be. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of the legislature is to give the Board a truly representative character so as To reflect the genuine interests of the various persons manning or dealing with the bank as an industry and a commercial enterprise. The mode of election or nomination must, therefore, be such as would be ideally suitable and appropriate to the banking Industry and the indi cate choice of the mode is generally a matter for decision by the central Government. [857C D] 1.2 The Central Govern ments under stood sub clause(c), of Clause (b) regarding non workmen employees to warrant the same type of representation as in the case of workmen mentioned under sub clause.(b)of Clause 3. The field of choice was thus understood by the Government to be limited to the panel of names furnished by representatives of workmen and Association of Non workmen as tho case may he, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election.

The respondent was imposed penalties in respect of the assessment years 1954 55, 1960 61 and 1961 62. The penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act for concealment of particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of penalties imposed. The Tribunal declined to grant any such a prayer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the proceedings as also the collection of the penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that in the absence of any express provision in sections 254 and 255 of the Act relating to stay of recovery during the pendency of an appeal it must be held that no such power can be exercised by the Tribunal, suffers from a fundamental infirmity inasmuch as it assumes and proceeds on the premise that the statute confers such a power on the Income Tax Officer who can give the necessary relief to an assessee. HELD: (i) The Appellate Tribunal must be deemed to have the power of stay as incidental or ancillary to the appellate jurisdiction of the Tribunal. This is particularly so when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the powerof doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. [69 H] (ii) The Tribunal 's powers in dealing with appeals are of the widest amplitude and have in some cases been held similar to and identical with the powers of an appellate court under the Civil Procedure Code. In Polini vs Grey, , followed. Dharmadas vs State Transport Appellate Tribunal, , referred to. (iii) The power of staying by the tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It wilt only be when a strong prima facie case is made out that the tribunal will consider whether to stay recovery proceedings and on what conditions and the stay will be granted in most deserving and appropriate cases where the Tribunal is satisfied that the entire purpose of the appeal will be frustrated or rendered nugatory by allowing the recovery proceedings to continue during the disposal of appeals by the Appellate Tribunals. [70 H] Dharmadhas vs State of Mysore, ; , referred.

The respondent was appointed a constable in U. P. Police Force on December 1, 1945, he was promoted to the rank of Head Constable and posted as officer incharge of Police Station Intiathok, District Gonda. Complaints were received by the District Magistrate, Gonda, to the effect that the respondent was receiving bribes in the discharge of his duties. On February 17, 1953, the Superintendent of Police made an endorsement in his character roll that a strong officer with plenty of push in him and met with a strong opposition in this new charge. The respondent submitted his explanation on November 29, 1952, but the Superintendent Of Police dismissed the respondent from service with effect from the said date. The appeal preferred by the respondent to the Deputy Inspector General of Police was dismissed by his order dated June 2, 1954. Thereafter the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereto the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage and therefore it fell within the express terms of para 489(2). Held, that the departmental trial was validly held. The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect the question, if substantially the subject matter of the mag ministerial inquiry and the departmental enquiry is the same. In this case the departmental proceedings were held subsequent to the completion of the Magisterial inquiry and therefore the departmental Trial was validly upheld.

The appellant, a highly qualified ophthalmic surgeon feeling aggrieved by the promotion of respondents 4 to 24 though convinced that even if the Court were to accede to his request he was in no way likely to be benefited by this bizarre exercise. The Union of India has framed Central Government Health Scheme and in implementation thereof has set up various institutions for medical relief and medical education. A Central Health Service became a necessity for effectively implementing the scheme. With a view to constituting the Service, Central Health Services Rules 1963 were framed and brought into operation on May 15, 1963. The Rules envisaged categorisation of personnel manning the Service into five different categories, to wit, category 'A ' supertime scale Rs. 1600 2000, category `B ' super time scale Rs., 1600 2000 category 'C senior scale Rs, 1300, category D ' junior scale Rs,. 425 950 and category 'E ' class II scale Rs . 325 800. The appellant contended that as these 28 posts were in Specialists ' grade and the strength of Specialists Grade posts was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 vacancies added to supertime grade II was required to be filled in, it can only be filled by promotion from amongst those originally belonging to specialists ' Grade I. The Central Government converted one post from amongst unspecified Specialists and appointed the appellant as and by way of promotion. The contention of the appellant that all 28 posts which were deducted from the strength were in specialists grade and added to Supertime gradeII must on that account alone be filled is not correct. It was also contended that the service to be rendered for the qualifying period must be in the category and, therefore, a general duty Officer Grade I can only become eligible for promotion after he renders 10 years of service in that category which came into existence on September 9, 1966. The High Court rejected these contentions. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. When a post from among unspecified specialists is converted to a specified post it can be filled In either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. [50E] 2.1 The appellant was not qualified for being promoted to super time grade II in February 1971 from which date he claims as being eligible for promo tion to super Time grade II because he had not put in 8 years of ' service in the Category of specialists " grade officers formed on September, 9 1966. Was it ever intended that a Specialists " Grade officer belonging to category "C" under 1963 Rules who had put in more than 8 years ' of service but who was not promoted prior to September 9 1966, the date of initial constitution of Service some of the officers belonging to categories "D" and "E" who were absorbed in categories II and III respectively may have been put on probation but for qualifying service for upward promotion service rendered as probationer is not to be ignored. It is equally possible that on September9, 1966 i.e. the date when a post in supertime Grade II was created at Willingdon Hospital from amongst unpecified Specialised specialists" posts they were promoted as being found qualified for the same and for the post to which each one of them was promoted appellant was neither qualified nor, therefore he must be considered eligible for promotions to superfire grade II.
