The Haryana Government enacted the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 whereby ceiling on land ownership was set; surplus lands were taken over for settling ejected tenants and others and peasant proprietorship created. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientific, though its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time, has made for ambiguity obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. If, however, he has lands beyond the permissible area, he becomes a large land owner and has to cough up the excess. This creation of a surplus pool or reservoir is vital to the success of the statutory project since, by distribution of such lands, rehabilitation of ejected tenants, and landless persons is to be "accomplished". Even if a person is small holder, it is quite on the cards that, by inheritance or other operation of law, or by voluntary transfer he may acquire lands in excess of the permissible limit. In short, the legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible Area and the surplus in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of Law will go to feed the surplus pool. To explore the import and ambit of these two provisions, particularly the former with a view to see whether it strikes at a gift made by the respondent in favour of his sons whereby he sought to stow away some of his lands, shed some of their excess lands and look slim on as a small holder before the law Language permiting, the Court as interpretor must fulfil, not frustrate the legislative mission. So much so, on the date when the Act came into force, he was the owner of about 178 bighas which, admittedly fell safely short of the permitted area of 30 standard acres [vide section 2(3)]. The unhappy consequence was that his holding expanded to 363 odd bighas far in excess Of the permissible permissible area as set out in section 2 (3). The unhppy consequence is that his holdings continued to be a small land owner. This invited legislative attention and an amendment of the Punjab Act, 1962 which brought in certain significant restrictions on alienations and acquisitions of large land holders starting off in the statement of objects thus: "Some of the recent judicial pronouncements have the effect of defeating the objectives with which the Punjab Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1961 was enacted and amended from timeto time. It was intended that the surplus area of every land owner recorded as such in the revenue records should be made utilisable for the settlement of ejected tenant. " The Court held that to accept the construction which has appealed to the learned Judges is to frustrate the agrarian reform scheme of tho Act and the alternative reading gives life to the law, teeth to its provisions and fulfilment to its soul. After the commencement of the Amendment Act he inherited nearly 30 ordinary acres and thus he held well the permissible surplus area and ceased to be small land owners. This invite legislative attention, and an amend ment of the Land Reforms Act was made viz., section 10A whereby decrees and orders of courts were to be ignored in dealing with surplus lands. The statutory remedies did not see the first respondent (writ petitioner) safe ashore and so he sought harbourage by moving the High Court under article 26 where he urged that the land inherited by him and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10 A and section 19B of the , He succeded in the Court in view of a certain strict construction adopted by the Court and the State has come up in appeal challenging the soundness of the High court 's approach.

The appellants, who were the descendants of a Zamindar, instituted an action in the Court of the Additional District Judge Chanda for a decree for possession of property immovable (including the Zamindari of Dhanora) and movable specified in the Schedules annexed to the plaint. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court on the ground that the right to receive compensation arose upon the death of Amarshah upon Pratapshah and Zamindari devolved upon the first plaintiff. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) the order of the Governor recognising Dayaram as Zamindar was not binding and conclusive; (ii) the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951 had become binding and conclusively against the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof; and (iii) the decree of the High court was not correct. HELD: The order of compensation Officer under sub section (1) shall not be subject to any appeal or revision but any party may, within two month from the day of such order institute a suit in the civil court to have the order set aside, and the decision Of such Court shall be binding on the Compensation officer, but subject to the result of such suit, if any, the compensation Officer shall be final and conclusive. Section 14 was enacted with a view to put an end to disputes with regard to the claims to proprietary rights which by virtue of the notification issued under section 3 are extinguished. It is not intended by an Order under section 14 to determine complicated questions of title by the adjudication of a revenue officer in a summary inquiry without even a right of appeal and to make his adjudication conclusive unless a suit be filed within two yea from the time of the order. That is also clear from the terms of section 35(7) of Act 1 1951 which provides "The payment of compensation under this Act to the creditors of a proprietor or to the proprietor in accordance with the prescribed manner shall be a full discharge of the State Government from all liability to pay compensation for the divesting of proprietary rights, but shall not prejudice any rights in respect of the said rights to which any other person may be entitled by due process of law to enforce against the person to whom compensation has been paid as aforesaid".

The Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 was enacted to provide for the passing of a decree for eviction against tenants on certain grounds. The Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1948 came into force on April 1, 1948. Section 12(3)(a) provides that where there is a dispute as to the amount of standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2), he makes an application to the Court under sub section(3) of section 11 and thereafter pays or tenders the amount specified in the order made by the court. The appellant tenant contended that the dispute concerning standard rent was one which must have been raised before service of the notice and since there was admittedly no dispute regarding standard rent, he could raise a dispute within the meaning of section 12( 3)(a). The High Court rejected the revision application holding that the tenant can raise a disputed as to standard rent. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant tenant that the suit was governed by the provisions contained in section 12 (3) (b) of the Act and that the provisions of section 13(3), (a) and (b), of the Bombay Rents Hotel and House RatesControl Act,1947 would apply. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Gujarat High Court in Ambalal 's case held that the effect of sections 11 and 12 of the said Act is to give the tenant a right to dispute the standard rent in the event of a suit and if the tenant raises a dispute in answer to a suit for recovery of rent it would be a dispute under the meaning section 12.(3) [632C] 2. The High Courts were wrong in holding that there was no dispute about standard rent nor did they decide whether the question as to how standard rent should be raised was one raised subsequently in a written statement with a view to avoiding the operation of section12(3). [633D E] 3. The provisions contained therein are as follows: "Where at any stage of a proceeding for recovery or without a claim for possession of the premises, the Court is satisfied that the tenants is withholding the rent on the ground that the rent is excessive and standard rent shall be fixed, the court Shall and in any other case if it appears to the court that it is just and proper to make such an order the Court may make an order directing the tenant to deposit in Court forthwith such amount of the rent as the Court considers to be reasonably due to the landlord or at the option of the tenant an order directs him to pay to the landlords such amount thereof as the court may specify. " [634E] 4. The notice was received by the respondent on 21 April, 1955, The suit for ejectment was filed on 15 March, 1956 on the grounds that the defendant was in arrears of payment of rent and permitted increases and as such not entitled to the protection of the provisions Of the Act. This Court found in Chhaganlal 's Case that the appellant landlord made no payment within the period prescribed by section 11(3); but this was not sufficient to oust the operation Of section 12. [635F G] 5. The contention that the disputed standard rent is one which should have been raise before service was of the notices and since the notice was served on the tenant on 21st April, 1956, the suit for eviction was filed in May, 1955 on the basis that the respondent was in arrear of payment within a period of six months from the date of service of notice under section 12 of Act. [643C] 6.

The respondent company was a company incorporated in what was then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600 divided into 360,000 shares of Rs 10 each. The Aluminium Limited, a company registered under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, held 359,790 shares in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1939 and December 31,, 1941, December 31 and 1943, and December31, 1942 and December 30, 1943, respectively and December 1, 1943 and December 32, 1943. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the Company. Two of these directors eventually retired and only one, namely Mr. L. G. Bash and the other directors had between them during the chargeable period ending on Dec 31, 1941, 12 months and December 28, 1943 only 210 shares and in the said chargeable accounting period ending December 31. 1942, December31 and January 31, 1943 respectively and January 30, 1948, i.e., December 31st, 1943 & December 31 1, 1944, and January 10, 1948 respectively. In exercising the powers conferred by article 90 of the Articles of association the respondent Company appointed three persons on the Board of directors. Two directors eventually resigned and only a third one, viz., Mr.L. G Bash and Mr. Bash was appointed to vote and/or from time to time appoint a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Limited. The respondent company thereupon appealed to the Incometax Appellate Tribunal which reversed the decision of the Excess Profits Tax Officer. The High Court held that in computing the standard profits the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per cent. per annum and not at 8 per cent per annum, and not 9% per annum. In appeal by certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution it was contended on behalf Of the appellant company that the directors who held the majority of shares as trustees they, so far as the respondent is concerned, were the registered shareholders and the right to vote is vested in them, although as between them and their beneficiaries the beneficial interest is vested In them, though as between themselves and their beneficiary the beneficial interests are vested in the latter. Held: (i) The decision of this Court of Appeal in Commissioners of Inland Revenue vs Jamed Hodgkinson ([Salford) Ltd., ([1946] 14 I.T.R. (Suppl.) 29; , 194 to. (ii) The analogy is inapt, for the principle of that decision can have no application to the case before this Court. In the present case the facts found are entirely different from the facts of the case and that decision has no manner of application to it. It is, therefore unnecessary for us to discuss or express any opinion as to whether the observations to be found in the judgment in that case are or are not well founded. For reasons stated above, this appeal must be dismissed.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Hyd erabad. On 1st October, 1957, the Mysore State Electricity Board was constituted under the Indian Electricity (Supply) Act. An option was given to the respondent to continue in the Government service or to opt to the Board. On 2nd November, 1972, the respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. In 1960, the Board framed Recruitment and Promo tions Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Act. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December 1966. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination. On 30th December, 1966, some persons junior to the respond ent were promoted on their being promoted on having passed the S .A. S. Examination while promotion was denied to the Respondent as he had not passed the examination. The respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970 and 21st November 1972. On 21st 11 1972,the respondent 's representations were rejected. The Respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court on 13th February 1973. The learned Single Judge who heard the petition dismissed it and the respondent preferred an appeal to a Bench of the Karnataka High Court which was dismissed. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January 1970, it could not be said that the writ petition ought to be dis missed on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the grounds that in the view of this later resolution it was no longer open to the resolu tion to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May 1969. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court found that the later resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the plea that the subsequent Resolution did not make any reference to the earlier Resolution and that there is no reference to tho allottees at all. [502C] 2.1 In the circumstances of the case, the relief to the re spondent should not be denied on the view that the respondent was exempted from passing the S,.A.s examination before qualifying for the promotion. Before referring to the two Resolutions of the board, namely, 19th and 5th Janu ar 1970, the relevant provisions of the law and Regulations made thereunder may be referred to. The Elec tricity (Supply ) Act, 1948 by section 79 empowers the Board to make regulations not inconsistent with the Act and the rules made thereunder to provide for all or any of the matters referred to in clauses (a) to (k) of section, Sub clause (c) empowers the board to make Regulations not inconsistentwith the Act, and the Rules made thereunder. By virtue of the powers conferred by the statute, it framed Mysore State Board Recruitment and Promotion of Employees of the . Board Regulation 1960. The method of recruitment prescribed for promotion to Accounts Superin tendents is prescribed in Chapter V of Annexure 2. The mode of recruitment is by promotion from the cadre of I Grade Clerks on tho basis of merit cum merit. The minimum qualification prescribed is that the candidate ought to have passed S.S examination Part I & Part II. This provision which was enacted in 1960 continued to be in force during the relevant time. If this Regulation is applicable, the respon dent 's plea has to fail on the question whether the Regulations framed under section79(c), specifi cally prescribe the passing of the examination and Kannada language test. These G.O.s do not apply in the present case as the Regulations made by the Board under section 80(c).

The petitioner, a police constable, was taken in police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, under Police Station Bisra, Distt. Sundergarh in connection with the investigation of an offence of theft and detained at the Police Outpost. At about 2 p.m., the next day on 2.12 .1987, the petitioner came to know that the dead body of her son was found on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraikela railway station. There were multiple injuries on the body of the deceased, when it was found and obviously his death was unnatural, caused by those injuries. The allegation made is that it was a case of custodial death since Suman Behera died as a result of the multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police possession. The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determination of compensation to the petitioner, the mother of the petitioner for contravention of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the constitution. The defence of the respondents is that Suman Behra managed to escape from police custody at about 3 a.m. on the night between 1st and 2nd December, 1987 from the Police outpost under Police station Bisra. There was multiple injuries sustained by him while his dead body was thrown on the Railway track near the Police Station. The alleged allegation made in the petition is that the petitioner was taken to police custody in connection With the investigation in connection therewith of an incident of theft, and detained in police Outpost, where he was detained and guarded by Police Constable Chhabil Kujur; he could not be apprehended thereafter in spite of a search; and the dead bodies were thrown on railway track. The respondents contended that Suman behera managed to escaped from police detention at about 4 p.M. on 1st December,1987, and that it is a case where custodial death was caused by injuries sustained to him whilst he was still in police detention. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, on the finding reached, it is clear case for award of compensation under Article 30 by this court or by the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitu tion, and is no defence to the constitutional remedy under Articles 32 and 226 of Constitution which enables award of monetary compensation in appropriate cases, where that is the only mode of redress available. [509C D] 1.2 The decision of this Court in Kasturilal upholding the State 's plea of sovereign immunity for tortious acts of its servants is confined to the sphere of liability in tort, which is distinct from the State liability for contravention under fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immune does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in private law in an action based on tort. [609E] 1:3 The Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution, which enable the award of money compensation in suitable cases, wherever that is, the only practicable mode of remedy available. The above discussion indicates the principles on which the Court 's power under Articles32 and 226 is exercised to award monetary compensation for contravention Of a fundamental fundamental right. [599E] In the present case, the mode of relief which commends appropriate is to make an order of monetary amend in favour of the Petitioner for the custodial death of her deceased son by ordering payment of compensation by way of exemplary damages.

The petitioner, a prisoner under the sentence of death, sought to be interviewed on the ground that she was under a sentence of imprisonment for life. The petition was dismissed by the Chief Reporter of the Hindustan Times, but the High Court allowed her petitions and directed the Superintendent of Jail to allow her to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who are under a sentenced sentence of life. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) There is no reason why newspapermen who can broadly and we suppose without great fear of contradiction be termed as friends of the society be denied the right of an interview under clause (4) of rule 549. Rule 559A also provides that all reasonable indulgence should be allowed to a condemned prisoner in the matter of interviews with relatives, friends, legal advisers and approved religious ministers. Surprisingly, but we do not propose to dwell on that issue, this rule provides for a search of the person who wants to interview a prisoner. If it is thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview an prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. There is a provision in the rules that if a person whom desires to interviewed a prisoner is a female she can be searched only by a matron or a female warden. Taking an overall view of the matter, we do no see any reason why the petitioner should not be allowed interview the two convicts billa andanga. [1186C D] (2) The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President of India rejected the petitions filed by the prisoners for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment for Life.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s Das Bank Ltd. On January 19, 1950, the Bank applied for the appointment of a Receiver. The District Judge directed that the Bank should nominate a Receiver in terms of clause 12 of the mortgage deed first. The appellant filed an appeal against that order but it was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner on June 29, 1970. In the meantime the respondent moved an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for damages from the Receiver and the appellant prayed that execution do issue against the appellant as directed by the Court. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he allowed the respondent 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. He also ordered that the Receiver should pay the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs. 50,000. Civil Miscellaneous First Appeal No. 22 of 1956 filed by the Receiver against that judgment was dismissed for default by the judicial Commissioner on December 18, 1959. The respondent ' thereupon filed a revision petition before the Judicial Commis sioner and the Judicial Commission which dismissed it on June 30, 1970 holding that the surety bond could be enforced only by or at the instance of the presiding officer of the Court and not by either of these, it was incompetent for him to enforce the surety bonds. The Judicial Commissioner allowed the revision petition and enhanced damages to the extent of Rs 32,525 and enhanced it to Rs 4,500. On October 4, 1961 respondent filed an application before the judicial Commisisoner praying that execution be made against the Receiver as directed in the bond. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that under the terms of the surety 's bond the appellant was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) Under section 150 of the C.P.C., save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. [359 D] (2) The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District Judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the court of the Subordinate Judge. Thus by virtue of section 150, the Subordinate judge was entitled to exercise the same power in the matter of the enforcement of the bond as the District judge himself.

The appellants who were dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U .P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants rejecting the contention raised by them that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. In appeal the Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the Act and therefore the sales made to the State Government under the provisions were sales within the 'sale ' under section 2(h) of the . The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales tax. The High Court held that despatches of sugar pursuant to the directions of the Controller were not made in pursuance of any contract of sale and therefore no tax was exigible on such transactions. In appeals to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the supplies of sugar did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax because steel products were supplied pursuant to directions issued under a Con trol Order may be regarded as a sale. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The High Courts have rightly held that there was nothing to justify the view that even if the liberty of contract in relation to the fundamentals of the transaction is completely excluded a transaction of supply of goods pursuant to direction issued under an Conciliator Order may not be regarded 'sale" even if it is the person supplying goods is declared entitled to the value of goods, which is determined or determinable in the manner prescribed. Assuming that between the licensed dealer and the Controller, there may be some arrangements about the place and manner of delivery of wheat, and the payment of " controlled price", the operation of cl. 5 of the Order takes no account of the volition of the licensed dealers and until the State Govern ment directs otherwise of the controller or the authorised officer. The State Government has also no option but to purchase fifty per cent of the wheat held in stock by the dealer at the commencement of the levy order. [459 B C] Indian Steel & Wire Products Ltd. vs State of Madras, ; , followed. (2) The expression "sale of goods" in section 2 (h) is defined in section 3(h). It is true that a licensed dealer is obliged to sell to the state Government fifty per% of the ' wheat held by him at the beginning of the order and thereafter 50% of it, but the price at which the wheat is sold is the maxi mum price fixed in the Wheat (Uttar Pradesh) Price Control Order 1959 as notified by the Government of India. Delivery of the goods has to be given by the dealers to the regional Food Controller or a person authorised by him in that behalf. The dealer has no option, but to sell the specified percentage of wheat to the occupier of the factory; if the cane grower made an offer, the occupier was bound to accept it and the agreement resulting therefrom was recorded in writing and was signed by the parties. [460 D E] Ram Bilas Ram Gopal vs State Of Bihar, ; and Indian Steel and Wire Products Limited vs State o/s. State of Bihar, , distinguished. (3) The State of U. P. treated the transaction as a 'sale and levied tax thereon under the (1 ) [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 32, followed.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was acquitted on May 26, 1986. Though acquitted, he was not straightaway released from prison. The reasons are not clear to us from the record. Presumably he was required in connection with some other case. He had been due for release from prison on June 23, 1986 when an order for his detention was made under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The mandate of article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are or have been qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. Section 10 stipulates that in every case where a detention order has been made under section 11, the State Government shall within three weeks from the date of detention of the person under the order place before the Advisory Board the grounds on which the order has be made, the representation, if any, made by the detenu and the report, ifany, of the authorised offi cer. What is important for the purposes of this case is that on the date when the detention order was made there was no Advisory Board in existence to which a reference could be made under sec. 11 of the Act and whose report of its opinion regarding suffi cient cause for the detention was required to be obtained within three months of the detention under article 22 (4) thereof. The period of 3 weeks stipulated by section 11 expired on July 14, 1986 and the appellant was entitled to be released on July 19, 1986 as no reference had been made to the Advisory Boards within the period statutorily prescribed by section II of the Bombay Prevention of anti Social Activities ' Act,1985. But he was still not so released. This state of affairs continued till August 7, 1986, when the order of detention dated June 23. 1986 was revoked and a fresh order of deten tion was made on the same facts on the earlier day. In the meanwhile, the order for detention had been challenged by filing a writ petition in the High Court. Consequent upon the revocation of that order, the appellant has been detained under the provi sions of the Gujrat Prevention of Social Proce dure Act, 1986 against which this appeal arises, was filed questioning the second order of his detention dated August 7. 1986. The Advisory Board was constituted on August 18, 1986 but it did not make any reference to the Board within the time stipulated by sec. II of section 11 of that Act. On September 26,1986, the Advisory board made its report on September 26. 1986 and it would be seen that the report of the Advisory Committee was more than three weeks after the detention which commenced on the making of the order. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that there has been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22 of the Constitu tion and therefore, the appel lant is entitled to he set at liberty. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. If a reference to an Advisory board is to be made within three days, it is no answer to say that the reference though not made within 3 months, was made before the hearing of the case. If the report is to he obtained within 3 weeks, it was no answer. [209E] 2. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The procedure is, there fore, to be strictly complied with if any value is tobe attached to the liberty of the subject and the constitution rights guaranteed to him in that regard.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, filed an application for setting aside the award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act '). The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation. The High Court dismissed the civil revision application. In the special leave petition it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties to refer the disputes to arbitration and that the respondent had agreed to such entrustment. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there were an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed agreed to refer both the disputes in writing to the arbitrator. This agreement was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award, and secondly by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter dated 14th August, 1978 (Exhibit 40). In that view of the matter, it is clear that the conduct of parties that the proceedings under the Act have become highly technical accompanied by unending prolixity, at every stage providing a legal trap to the unwary. With respect, we could not agree more in the facts and circumstances of this case. [537C D] 2. The petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award. The Civil Court had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the Award under sections 14 and 17 of Act. This question had come up for consideration before the Judicial Committee in Chowdhri Murtaza Hossein vs Mst. Bibi Bechunnissa, ; , referred to.

The respondent instituted a suit against the appellants for partition of the Searsole Raj Estate. The suit was decreed by the Subordi nate Judge on March 30, 1937 and the decree was confirmed in appeal by the High Court. In execution case No. 1 of 1941 the said receiver with the permission mortgaged certain properties to the said firm as security for the due repayment of the loan advanced by that firm. The appellants contended before the executing court that under section 36(1) of the Act the Court could not reopen or otherwise affect a decree of a Court unless such decree was one which was passed in a suit to which this Act applied and that the attachment had been continued by a special order. Held, that the words "any suit or pro ceeding in execution" used in section 36 (5) make it plain that an assignee of a mortgage debt is within the sub section since section 28(1)(a) is concerned only with assignment of debts" and not with assignment thereof to the sub mortgagee and that he had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section (1). The words "all the rights of any assignee or holder for value" in section 2(22) make the it plain clear that an assignees of a mort gage debt is not within the meaning of sub s.(5) since section 29(2)(b) is applicable only with the assignment of the debt due under the original mortgage debt and of "the entire interest" of the original mortgagee. The words and that they have not received notice referred in clause(a) to section 28 make it clear that the assignee of the mortgage debt must, in that context, be understood with reference to the sufficiency of the right assigned to enable the sub mortgagor to sue the original mortgagor in his own right, so as to bring the relevant provisions of the .

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. By two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds dated April 15, 1946, (Exbts. A 1 and A 2), he transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1 & A 2 there was a disruption of the joint Hindu family and a severance of the Joint status between Venkatacharyulu and his sons. In 1954 his widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 14, 1946 were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court dis missed O. S. No 62/54 and decreed O.s. 63/54. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfers were by way of gifts and not in consideration of past cohabitation, and that Venkatachallulu was competent to alienate for value his undivided interest in the coparcenary properties. HELD: (i) The past cohabitations were the motive and not the consideration for the transfer under exhibit A1 and A2. [719 C] (ii) The transfers were without consideration and were by gift. The gifts were not hit by section 6(h). But the properties gifted under exhibit B 1 & 2 were coparcenary properties, and under the Madras school of Mitakshara law by which Venkatac hodulu was governed, he had no power to make a gift of his own property to his concurbine. [771 D] (iii) The gifts under Exs. Al 'and A 2 were not invalid because they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubines for her past services. In Balo vs Parbati, I.L.R. , 217, referred to.

The appellant was the Chief Justice of a High Court. He had filed an appeal against the order of the Election Tribunal under section 116 A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, to the High Court of Madhya Pradesh. The appeal was dismissed by the High court on the ground that it was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the right of appeal in the case before this Court was conferred by section 116A of the Act and it was by virtue thereof that the appeal was filed by the respondent to the Supreme Court, it was still an appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure; and (ii) the provisions of section 12(2) of the Limitation Act would be attracted. HELD: (i)(a) The right of appeals in the present case was conferred on the appellant to the high Court. It was by way of abundant caution that the question should be considered as one under the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. [143 H] (b) The words "where any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application" occurring in section 29(2)(a), are wide enough to include a suit, appeals or applications under a particular local or special law. [144 C D] (c) The first limb of sub section (2) is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under special or general law for which a period of limitation is provided in the First Schedule. Therefore what has to be seen is whether a suit appeal or an application under a certain local or Special law is of a kind similar to one for which no period of Limitation is prescribed in the first schedule. [145 E] (d) The second limb of section 29 is concerned with proceedings under a special or special local law for Which a period Of limitation is prescribed. Therefore, what has been seen is that whether a Suit, appeal, application or an appeal thereunder is of the kind which a suit or an ap pellate suit.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, challenged the validity of the Order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate declaring the old bus stand of T.A. Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage and booking at this very stand and to pay standcommission to T.T.A., Section 68 which is in Chapter VI dealing with 'control of traffic ' confers the power on the State Government to make rules regarding the maintenance and management of parking places and stands and the fees, if any, which may be charged for their use. The appellant challenged the said order by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magis trate to fix the places for the bus stand orhalting places ' and that the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses was only a halting place and hence the order made under section 76 was unassailable. It further observed that since the impugned order did not specifically state that the bus operators could allow the passengers to get up and pick up the passengers, it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as a Bus stand. The Court also held that since tho impugned order does not specifically mention that the Bus operators could permit the passengers who were asked lo stop their bus stand at the bus stands/Halting place for purposes of taking up or setting down passengers was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a specif ic provision in section 68(2)(r) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for that pur pose. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The District Magistra trate had passed the impugned Order in question with the object of establishing a bus stands in the area in question. That appears to be so from the order passed by District Magistrate and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of Town Area Committee, Baldev to the President of the Union requiring the bus operator to stop his buses at the Bus stand and for booking at such very stand or halting places and requiring the driver of a stage carriage to stop and remain stationary for a reasonable time when so required by a passenger desiring to board or alight from the vehicle at a notified halting place. Parking places and halting stations The State Government or any authority authorised in this behalf by the State Govern ment may, in consultation with the local authority having jurisdiction in the areas concerned determine places at which motor vehicles may stand either indefinitely or for a specified period of time, and may determine the places at Which public service vehicles may stop for a longer time than is necessary for the taking up and setting down of passengers. [717C D] 2. The power to regulate or prohib it the use of municipal land as a haltingplace of vehicles could not therefore be used to compel people to use such land as halting place.[718D E] 3. The order passed under section 68 (2)(c) of Madhya Pradesh Municipal Act, 1922 which authorises the District Commis sioner to specify places within the limits of any municipality notified area, town area or cantonment or within such other limits as he may define where alone public service vehicle or any specified class or classes of public services vehicles and/or goods vehicles may stands indefinite ly or for such period as may be specified or public service Vehicles may stop at a time than was necessary for taking up. [750E F] 4.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the , and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. The High Court dismissed their revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export; (2) there had been an attempt on their part to commit export paddy to Delhi, and so there was an attempt to commit an offence of exported; and (3) there could be no attempt to export the paddy. HELD: (i) The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. On the other hand an attempt is to commit a crime, he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit that offence and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. [666 D] (ii) The appellants should not have been convicted under sections 7 and 8 of the . For these reasons there was nothing in section 8 of Act which makes a preparation to commit any offence punishable. It follows therefore that the appellants should be acquitted under section, 7 of Act. [665 E F] (iii) There is no provision in the Act which made a preparation for committing an offence punishable, and it follows therefore, that the appellant should not be convicted under s.7 of the Act. For these reason there was also no provision to commit such an offence. [667 G] (iv) The conviction and sentence of fine imposed upon each of them must be set aside.

The Sassoons had not earned any part of the Managing Agency commission which had been paid by the Companies to the transferees and were not liable to tax in respect of the same. The Income tax Officer, however, held that the Sassoon became entitled on the very date of the respective assignments to a proportionate share of the year 's remuneration for the managing agency, and that accordingly the share accrued to the Sassoonons as their taxable income, then and there, and did not cease to be such notwithstanding the assignment thereof. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal in reference under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, held against the Sas Soons, but on a reference made by the High Court, the High court answered the question in favour of the Sasifons as well as the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Managing Agent remuneration for a particular year accrued as a matter of law to the assignee and was his sole income, on the ground that the agency was the source of income and whatever income could be attributed to those services was earned by the Sasiverons; (ii) the managing Agency commission was payable in respect Of services for an entire calendar year and not for a portion thereof and therefore no commission became due to the assessee to the company during the chargeable accounting period, though it had been ascertained and paid to the transferee together; and (iii) the assignment operated to transfer the assignor 's share of income on its accrual. HELD : (i)(a) The managing Agency remuneration for an assessment year is a remuneration on the completion of a whole year ' 's work, which is the source or source of the income. It is not necessary that the remuneration for that year should be the same as that for the entire year is the income of the assignee. [372 E] (b) The true legal position, therefore, is that what was assigned was an income bearing asset, viz., the Managing agency which was the basis of the assessee 's claim to receive all the remuneration from the company and it is the profits and gains of the business carried on by the assignee, when as a fact he stepped into the position of the managing Agent only on some date in the course of the assessment year. [373 E] Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal & Son, Ltd. vs The Government of Hyderabad, ; , followed. (ii)(a). Though the right of the holder to receive the entire remuneration did not depend on any specific term between the assigner and the assignee but on the fact that what is transferred is an income which carried with it a right to the entire income that falls due after the date of assignment. It may be mentioned in this context that clause 10 of the agreement in Agarwals case has been relied on by counsel for Agarwals to show that while, it may be, that in the normal run of events the contract for remuneration under the Managing Agents Agreement is an indivisible contract for a whole Year 's salary, on tho completion of the whole year, 's worked, this clause necessarily implied divisibility of contract and of the remuneration in the year of assignment since the assignment necessarily took place with the consent of the principal Mill Company. [375 G H] (c) The right of assignee to receive a entire remuneration does not depend upon any specific terms between the assigningor and the transferee, but upon the fact of that what been transferred is the an income having bearing asset which carried With it a liability to the estate or estate of the deceased, such a right may arise by virtue of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferor, either as part of tile deed of transfer or independent thereof.

The appellant was a resident of the Lucknow. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker. The deceased and his wife were living with their father. It is said that Sunderpatti developed illicit intimacy with Sahoo; but there were incessant quarrels between them. On August 12, 1963, at about 6 p.m. the appellant brought her to home in the morning of August 13, 1963 when Sunderpatti was found with serious injuries in the room of the house where she was sleeping and the appellant was not in the house. Sunderpatti died on August 26, 1963 at 3 p. m. The only other inmate of the family was the appellant 's second son, Kirpa Shankar, a lad of about 8 years. On the morning day of August, 1963 the deceased was found in the company of the accused for the fast time when she was alive and the accused was not there. Sunder promptly lodged the F.I.R. at 5 p.M. on that day. The appellant 'S second son Kirpa Narain was sent up for trial before the Court of Sessions, Gonda, on a charge under section 302 I.P.C. The Sessions Judge convicted the appellant under section 307 I. P.C., and sentenced him to death. On appeal, a Division Bench confirmed both the conviction and sentence. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) A confession is a species of that genus. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. Generally they are mutterings of a confused mind. Before such evidence can be accepted it must be established by cogent evidence what were the exact words used by the accused. Even if so much was established, prudence and justice demand that such evidence cannot be made the sole ground of conviction. It might be used only as a corroborative piece of evidence. The circumstances found by the High Court lead to the only conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder. No other reasonable hypothesis was or could be suggested. [90 D F] (2) A confessional soliloquy is a direct piece ofevidence. It can be an offence, but there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional Soliloqury is a primary piece of Evidence. It cannot be said that one cannot confess to himself: he can only confess to another. [91 G H] (3) The word "statement" in section 157 meant only "something that is stated" and the element of communication was not necessary before "s something that is mentioned" and that the element or communication was no necessary ingredient of the concept of "confession". [90 F G] (4) A retracted confession is an expression which may be a statement made by an accused admitting his guilt. What does the expression "statement ' mean? The dictionary meaning of the word does not warrant any such extension; nor the reason of the rule underlying the doctrine of admission or confession demands it. Admissions and confessions are exceptions to the hearsay rule. [92 F G]. (5) A statement, whether communicated or not admitting guilt is a confession of guilt. But there is no clear distinction in principle in the case of an oral statement. Both must stand on the same footing. This aspect of the doctrine doctrine of confession received some treatment from wellknown authors on evidence like Taylor, Best and Phipson.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi, the general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. The appellant was kept under suspension from August 9, 1973 pending investigation into the embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973 in response thereto the appellant submitted his reply on December 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The appel lant challenged it in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a learned Single Judge on November 11, 1983 and was confirmed by the Division Bench in Letter Patent Appeal No.351/1984 dated April 23, 1984. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that Rule 5 is ultra vires of Article 14 of the Constitution; that whereas Rule 9 in D.T.C. 's case Rule 5 provides guidelines, the Board of Directors have to take a decision, whether the need to continue the employee 's service subsists which would be based on the relevant material. Thereby there would be objective consideration before taking a decision not only regarding the need for continuance of the post but also the services of the officer or the employee. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Board of Management did not abolish the post and put an end to the service of the appel late employee. Obviously due to loss of confidence as his honesty and integrity became suspicious and his continuance in service was felt inexpedient and not in the interest of the business of the respondents. But Rule 8 was available for taking action for misconduct but was not availed. Therefore, the impugned order terminating the services is illegal. [226B] 1.2 The Board did not abolishing the post, but put an rest to the serv ice of the employee, and that the appellant could not be said to have been appointed by tendering one month 's salary in lieu thereof. It was not necessary to go into the grounds taken in the High Court assailing the invalidity of the termination order as they were not pressed before this Court. [227C D] 1:3 The Board had no power to abolish the posts but put a end to it. [228G H] 2.1 Rule 5 does not become arbitrary. unreasonable or void offending Article 14. [229B] D. T.C., 's Case has no application. Rule 9 of the rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation gives naked power to terminate the services by giving one month notice or pay in lieu of notice or salary in addition thereof. The rule does not provide for prior notice, post decisional opportunity would be read into the rule. If so read, the rule is not ultra vires Article 14 [229C] D R.T.,C. vs D.C Mazdoor Congress & Ors., 225 Judgment today, referred to.

The appellants were licensees to sell intoxicating liquors and were selling liquor. The State Government issued a fresh order under the provisions of the amended section 29(2) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915 for re auctioning the shops and declared that rule 103(1) of Board 's Excise Rules was ultra vires the Act. The Collector issued a notice to the appellants calling upon them to submit their tenders in accordance with the order. The appellants submitted their tender. The appellant submitted his tender. But the Collector did not issue the licence for an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sellliquor. The High Court quashed the direction of the State Government dated April 15, 1970 for reauctioning the license and declared rule 103 (1) as ultra vires. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that section 6(a) of Amending Act of 1970 was not made retrospective in operation, the effect of section 6 was that thereby the Legis lature had directed the State to disregard the decision given by this Court in Ajodhya Pra sad 's case. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred on the State under section 29 (1 ) is "to regulate the conditions and conditions of licence". It is not a privilege of a citizen of the state, and it is not an privilege of citizens of the Union, and therefore the State has the exclusive right or privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor." [822D] 2. The question whether section 6 (a) was ultra rites or not is a matter for consideration in this Court. It would be permissible for the State Govern ment to accept payment of a sum in "conSideration" of the exclusive privilege under section 22(1). [823F G] 3. Section 29(1), however, provides that the State Govt. may grant to any person on such conditions and for such periods as it may think fit, the exclusive privileges".

The appellant was charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with an approver. The prosecution case against him was that he had entered into criminal conspiracy with the approver for committing murder of a person who was not in charge of the crime and that the murder came to be committed in furtherance of common intention of all the accused. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellant but reduced the sentence of death passed against the appellant. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that there was corroboration of the actual participation in the crime, and secondly that the appellant had not been corroborated because it was put to Dinkar in cross examination that it was Dinkar alone who killed Narendra. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The evidence of the tailor was that accused No. 2 gave him some pieces from silver idols and other silver articles and wanted money by disposing of the same. He had also been a piece of hand writing with the signature of accused No 2 at the foot of it and that was the list of the articles sold to Gadekar. The evidence showed that there were civil and criminal proceedings between him and Dr. Nanavati. [621 E] (2) The appellant washerman and he had been living in a house which was near the rear portion of bungalow No. 3. He washermen also said that Dinkar and accused No, 2 gave them some pieces of silver idents and other metal articles and asked money by disposed of the property so as to frighten Narendra to vacate the bungalow. The appellant had with him a boy who was of fair skin and wore khaki shorts and a white shirt, Mohan Lal Boob, an agriculturist gave evidence that on 27 December 1967 he was watering the crops. 2 and 3 were known to him by face and the third was a boy of 14 or 15 years of age, wearing khakoi short 's and shirt. The shirt and the chain were identified by Dr. Lilavati and his wife to belong to Narendra. The presence of accused Nos. 2, 3 and 4 at the scene of occurrence would not corroborate the evidence of PW 1 and the recovery of the chain which Narendra wore was seen alive in the company of accused NO. 2. [625 G H] (3) The prosecution had failed to prove that there had been any corroboration of actual participation by the appellant in the murder and secondly, that accused Nos., 3, 4 and 5 were guilty of the offence. [ 625 C D] Lachi Ram vs State of Punjab ; , followed.

The appellant was the Karta of a Hindu undivided family. The Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq. and not Rs. 50 per sq ft. On appeal, the Town Planning officer awarded compensation at the rates of Rs 2. 40 p. on the basis of the market value of the land at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme with all the buildings and works thereon at that rate. Not satisfied with the decision of the Town planning Officer the appellant preferred an appeal before the State Government which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the State government. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that enactment of a rule determining payment or adjustment of price of land of which the owner was deprived by the scheme estimated on the marketvalue on the date on which the declaration of the intention to makes a scheme amounted to specification of a principle of compensation within the meaning of article 31(2). In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Town Development Officer 's decision in the appellant 's case was appealable either under clause (viii) or clause (xiii) of section 32(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating the compensation payable to an owner of land who has not been given a reconstituted plot. [92C] 2. Under section 65 increment means the amount by which at the time of the declaration or of the date 'of a notification under sub section (1) of Section 24 without reference to improvements contemplated in the scheme. The expression 'person interested ' as defined in section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act is the generally accepted meaning of that expression and we find nothing in the Act concerned in this case that suggests that it should be construed differently. It was then argued that if neither clause (ix) nor clause (xiv) was applicable, then there was no clause in section 32 (1). [92D] Shantilal 's Case at page 357 of the report: "It is true that under the Act the market price of a final plot calculated on the principle as if the improvements contemplated therein had stood completed on that date exceeds the market Value of the same plot when taken into account without the improvement. Under clause (xi) the Town Improvement Officer is required to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner of any property or right injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme in accordance with the provisions contained in section 69. Section 69 states that the owner 'of any property ' or right which is injuriously affecting by the passing of a Town Planning Scheme shall be entitled to obtain compensation from the local authority or from any person benefited or partly from the Local Authority and partly from such person as the Town Planner may in each case determine". The expression "person interested" as defined under section 3(1) (f) is the commonly accepted meaning. [93E F] Shandas vs State of Gujarat, ; , followed. Shantilal vs State, ; and Shantilal & Ors. vs Municipal Corporation, Delhi & Anr., ; referred to.

The testator appointed his brother as the guardian of his minor daughters as well as of his foster son. He left the management of his properties to his brother and provided that as soon as his minor daughter attained majority he should give to them per head one veli of nanja land and one vehi of punja land in vattam No. 149 in village Nagampadi 976 and further provided that the said Seetharama should pay to the minor daughters the income from the properties devised to them after the death of the testator. The appellant was prepared for a partition of land according to quality but was not prepared to accept the right of selection claimed by the daughters. It was contended on his behalf that in any case on the construction of the will it was for Seetharams or in the legatees, that the testator intended his daughter to select and that as his brother had died without making the selection, the lands devised to the daughters must now be partitioned in the ordinary course. Held, that where it is not possible to say on the interpretation of a will that the legatee himself indicated the selection or appointed a third person to make the selection but still intended to make a gift which could be made certain by selection made by the legatee, the English rule of construction that in such cases the testator meant the legatee to select should be applied in India also and the decision in Narayanasami Gramani 's case was correct. The words " he shall deliver possession" in section 89 of the Indian Succession Act are different in the case of daughters as compared to the words used in the present case. In those circumstances it was held that the will was void for uncertainty, for there was no way by which the will could be passed certain.

The appellant 's brother was the widow of one Syed Laek Husain and defendants No. 1 and 2 were her husband 's cousins. The plaintiff 's case was that she was living with her sons at Lucknow and her husband and their cousins were looking after the lands which consisted of agricultural lands and groves, she was given her share by her cousins from time to time. It was also alleged that she went to the village from time and got her share. In her statement before the trial court she had clearly stated that the defendants, Mohd. Bashir and Mohd. Rasheed used to manage the properties which were joint and used to give her share and assured her that her share would be properly looked after and protected by them. Thus having gained the confidence of the plaintiff the first and second defendants went on managing the properties and off and on gave her share so that she may not suspect their evil intentions. The appellant ' s brother filed a suit for joint possession over the share. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court but on appeal, the District Judge decreed the suit for partition in respect of Chakbandi plot Nos. 201 and 274 only. 93, 94 and 106. The dismissal of the appellant 'S brother was upheld by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondents were in separate occupation of the land or plots in dispute and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them; that although at some time before the lands in dispute were joint but during the consolidation proceedings the plots in possession of the respondent were occupied by Adhivasi who having acquired the rights of a Sirdar under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the appellant lost her title by operation of law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The possession of defendants, apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of plaintiff. Apart from this, the fact remains that the District judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the Consolidation operation either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights were sought to be extinguished. In this connection, the learned District Judge found as follows: "This shows that a planned fraud was made to drop the appellant"s name from the revenue records and full advantage was taken of the consolidation operations in the village by the respondents. In para 20 of the written statement, paper 31A it was pleaded by the respondent that they acquired the suit plot through litigation and the appellant right extinguished during the settlement proceedings. There is no evidence before me to show that there was any litigation with the sub tenants and the defendants acquired the plots exclusively. Even if no share was given to the plaintiff by the defendant, as the defendants were co shares, unless a clear ouster was pleaded or proved the possession was of the respondents as co sharers would be deemed in law to be the possession. [868C D] 2. The High Court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act. Thus, the grounds on which the High court reversed the decision of the District Court regarding fraud having been committed in the consolidation operation either either by defendants or through somebody else, as a consequence of which, the rights and liabilities of the parties were sought could be extinguished.[868E F] 3. The plea of bar of the civil courts ' jurisdiction to investigate and adjudicate upon the title to the land and sonship of the plaintiffs has no substance. [889F G] 4.

The petitioner was appointed as Deputy Prime Minister of India. He was then working as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him. The oath register was by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Prime Minister, while being sworn into office, he describes himself as Prime minister and this practice is in vogue eversince 1950. The petitioner challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 on the ground that the oath administered to it as Deputy Ministers was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution; and (ii) that he was still functioning as the chief Minister of the Haryana when oath of Office of his old assignment was administering to him, and that the practice is being in vogue since 1950. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The essential requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India.[3H; 4A] 2.1 In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Cabinet Minister but the description of him as Deputy Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Minister along with his other submis sions, it is the first contention raised by the petitioner. [4B C] 2:2 The requirement of article 173 read alongwith Form VIIA was that he person taking oath or make the affirmation will bear true honestly and allegiance tto the Constitution.

On 1st November, 1948, the management of the Mills had expressed its inability to comply with the request of the workers to declare the forenoon of the 1st Nov., 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. On the 3rd November, the strike ended completely and the apparent cause for the strike was that the management had decided that the workers who had participated in the said strike would not be entitled to holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act. The management put up a notice that the stoppage of work on 1st 11th November,1948 amounted to an illegal strike and a break in service within the meaning of the factory was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike. The workmen 's appeal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union that the decision of the management was varied to this extent, that there was no break in the continuity of their service by the stoppage or that the non permitted absence as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day amounted to a strike and consequently an interruption of service of a workman for the purpose of section 49B. Held, that the conclusion reached by the adjudicator was clearly right and the conclusion could not be avoided that the workmen 'were acting in concert. That being so, the action of the workmen on the night of 1st11th November was clearly within the definition of the expression "strike" in section 2(q) of .

The appellant, a producer of cinematograph films, filed a complaint against the respondent alleging that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and beguiled into degeneracy. The Magistrate after examining some witnesses took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused. Thereupon the producer moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. on the score that the criminal proceeding was an abuse of the judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case, the film having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censors. The High Court dismissed the petition, ignoring the contention that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censor and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 79 I.P.C., is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and the certificate issued thereunder. [517 F] (2) The prosecution has failed to establish that the offence under section 292 I. P C. was justified by law in exhibiting the film. The prosecution case is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory, when read alongwith section 5 A of the Penal Code and the Certificate issued thereunder, it is right for the court to discharge the accused as the charge is groundless. [511 E] (3) Section 80 I.p.C.; does not apply to a case where the offending act is actually justified by Law or is bona fide believed by mistake of fact to be so justified. If, as here, the Board, after examining certain witnesses, took cognizance, of the offences and issued notices to the respondent, the producer and connected agencies do enter the statutory harbour and are protected because section 80 exonerates them at least in view of their bona fide belief that the certificate is justificatory. [51 E F] K. Maybe, art cannot be imprisoned by the bureaucrat and aesthetics can be robbed of the glory and grace and free expression of the human spirit if governmental palate is to prescribe the permit for exhibition of artistic production in any department, more so in cinema pictures. So it is that a special legislation viz. the Act of 1952 sets up a Board of Civilensors of high calibre and expertise, provides hearings, appeals and ultimate judicial review, pre censorship and conditional exhibitions and wealth of other policing strategies. [50 C] (4) The apparent conflict between section 292 Cr.P.,C. and Part II of the , relating to certification of films is that the cinema is one of the major mass media with millions of viewers and many millions in investment. The sole point for decision is the legal effect of the combined operation of section 5(A) of the . [516 D] (5) Section 5A has to consider, before certification, all the points section 292 Crl. P.,C., prescribes. Indeed neither the Penal code nor the can go beyond sections the restrictions sanctioned by of the Constitution and once the special law polices the area it is pro tanto out of bounds for the general law. At least as a matter of interpretation, section 79 I P. C. resolves the apparent conflict both between section 293 Cr.p., and Part 11 of the 'Act relating to certificate of films. If the Board blunders, the Act provides remedies.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as an Advocate in the Patna District, authorised to represent 'Government in all civil cases. During the currency of his term a plurality of nine Assistant Government Pleaders was appointed and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. Thereafter, the petitioner challenged the power of Government, like any other litigant, to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. He went to the extent of writing to the Government: "I am, therefore unable to comply with your instruction in allowing any Assistant Government Pleader to work in this case. Chagrined by this loss of income and mayhem to his monopoly he rushed to the High Court for the universal panacea of a writ. Sans substantial question of law of public importance which deserves to be decided by the Supreme Court or at least flaw in law which is fraught with manifest injustice, there is no other open sea for this House of Justice. That password has not been uttered here despite exercise in professional martyrdom the petitioner claims to have suffered and so he was unable to complying with his instruction in permitting any Assistant Govt Pleader to worked in this ease. ChaGrined by the High Courts, a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. The State of Bihar, like many other States in the country, has an enormous volume of litigation. It is lamentable that despite a national litigation policy for the States having been evolved at an all India Law Ministers ' Conference way back in 1957 and despite the recommendations of the Central Law Commission to promote settlement of disputes where Government is a party, what we find in actual practice is a proliferation of government cases in courts uninformed by any such policy. Indeed, in this country where Government litigation constitutes a sizeable bulk of the total volume, it is important that the State should be a model litigant with accent on settlement. The Central Law commission, recalling a Kerala decision, emphasised this aspect in 1973 and went to its extent of recommending a new provision to be read as Order 27 Rule 5B. It was also observed that there should be some provision emphasising the need for positive efforts at settlement, in suits to which the Government is an party. With the above end in view, it recommended the insertion of the following rule: "5 B(1) In every suit or proceeding to which Government is A party or a public officer acting in his official capacity is a Party, it shall be the duty of the Court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible to do so consistently with the nature of the circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. (2) If in any such suit or proceedings, at any stage it appears to the court that there is a reasonable possibility of a settlement between the parties, the Court may adjourn the proceeding for such period as it thinks fit, to enable attempts to be made to effect such a settlement. (3) The power conferred by sub rule (2), is in addition to any other power of the court to adjourn the proceedings. " The relevance of these wider observations is that avoidable litigation holds out money by way of fees and more fees if they are contested 763 cases and this lures a lawyer, like an any other homo economics, to calculate income on a speculative basis, as this Government Pleader has done in hoping for a lakh of rupees. The time has come for State Governments to have a second economic look not only at litigation policy but lawyer 's fees rules (like rule 115 in the Bihar instance) especially in mass litigation involving ad valorem enormity and mechanical professionalism.

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Navjivan Mills Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. Between the years 1943 47, the Mills purchased 5,000 shares of a Bank of India Ltd. At an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Bank of lndia held on May 6, 1948 a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the bank and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by the shareholders. The appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesinghbai Investment Co. Ltd., which was the holder of 5,00 ordinary shares. The Mills as the holder had to pay Rs. 100 for each new share. The mills as the holders of 5000 shares became entitled to receive 1,6662 shares of that Bank at the rate of Rs. 50 per share. On receiving the circular letter, the Directors of the Mills passed the following resolution: "Resolved that the company having a holding of 5.,000 ordinary shares in the capital of lstia Ltd. having now received an intimation from the said Bank that this company is entitled to get 1,6762 shares more ordinary shares on payment of Rs 50 as capital and Rs.50 as premium per each share and it is considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said bank.
