IT IS HEREBY RESOLVED that the funds of this company may be invested in the 66 shares out of 1,666 shares offered by 'the Bank of I, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the distribution of the right to apply for and obtain two shares of tho Bank of Indian Company (at half half their market value) for each share held by its shareholders amounted to distribution of dividend. [588 D] The High court was right In holding that distribution of a right to applied for and obtained two shares by the Mills amounted to "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A), it was still dividend within the ordinary meaning of that expression and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. Dividend need not be distributed in money; it may be distributed by delivery of property or right having monetary value. The resolution, it is true, did not purport to distribute the right amongst the shareholders as dividend. It did not also take the form of a resolution for distribution of dividends; it took the form for distribution and distribution of shares of 1.67 shares of I.T.C., but by the form, of the resolution sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the Resolution could not be altered.

The appellant, who was declared elected to the Haryana Legislative Assembly from Jind Legislative Assembly constituency filed an election petition under section 81 of the Representation of People Act 1951 for setting aside the election of the 1st respondent. The returned candidate challenged the election on the ground that the names of witnesses whom he desired to produce were already mentioned in the appropriate paragraphs of the election petition and that the appellant could not be permitted to examine more witnesses whose names had not been mentioned in his list of witnesses submitted in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the rules framed by the High Court. The High Court rejected the objection raised by the returned candidate that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered was not mentioned in 'the list and therefore, the election petitioner could not he permitted to examined more witnesses who had not already been mentioned. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the requirement of sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance of the court is t necessary; and (ii) the provision of the (1 ) of Order XVI. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The obligation to supply the list as well as the gist of the evidence of each witness whose name is entered in the list has to be carried out in respect thereof. [531D] (b) If mere omission to mention the name of a witness in the List envisaged by sub rule(1)of Rule 1 o order XVI would enable the Court to decline to examine such witness, Rule 1A would not have omitted to mention that only those witnesses kept present could be examined whose names are mentioned in that list. [525E] (c) The marginal note of Rule lA clearly negatives this suggestion. Marginal note of rule 1A clearly supports this suggestion and Marginal Note of Rule IA clearly denies this suggestion.[532C D] Marginal notes of Rule1A clearly negative the suggestion. [540D] Margina note of Rules 1A, 1A of order XVIII clearly negatives the suggestion that Marginal Notes of Rule '1A ' clearly negatives This suggestion. Roadinal note is in regard to witnesses to procuring whose presence assistance of Court is t requisite.

The appellant, a double M.A., and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran dated May 18, 1980 for the post of Principal. Pursuant to this decision of the Selection Committee, the Manager of the College issued an appointment order dated April 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of Management had suspended or withdrawn its power. The appellant presented himself at the college on May 1, 1981 and requested the Manager to hand over charge to him. On receipt of this letter, the appellant wrote to the Manager that as permitted by him he has assumed charge of the post and has started functioning. It appears that the State Government was contemplating to bring about a radical change in the mode method and power of appointment of teaching staff in non government aided schools and accordingly Secretary to the Government of U.P. there is some dispute between the parties as to whether this copy of radiogram was received by the Management of the college but there is a letter dated May 1 1981 addressed by the District Inspector of Schools, Ballia to the manager of the Institution. The Manager wrote to him that as directed by him, he has ceased charge of his post of principal at 7.30 A.M. and has been functioning. He requested the manager to hand back charge to the Appellant. On the same day, the Management sent a letter to the District Superintendent of Schools stating that as per the radiograms dated April 7, 1981, the Institution had received the order that the power of appoint of Principal had been withdrawn or suspended and that the appointment of the appellant was not valid. The District Superintendent dismissed the appellant 's appeal against this order. In a writ petition filed by the appellant, the High Court held that the radiagram dated April July 7,1981 contained an order of the State Govt in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointing teaching staff including Principal and therefore the Committee had no power to make any appointment and therefore, the appointment was not invalid. The High Court also held that since the radiugram had suspended the appellant could not be invalidated. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appointment was otherwise valid though ineffective and if appellant under the orders of the High court functioned as Principal, discharged his duties and was paid, no question of recovery of amount paid to him could arise and neither the Government nor the Committee would be entitled to recover any salary paid to the appellants. [975D] 1.2 The appointment of appellant could be invalidated, and therefore it may be declared that the appellant continues to hold the post as Principal of the institution. [980E F] 2.1 In the instant case, the letter dated 5th May 1981 which has been extracted hereinbefore clearly shows that on April 8, 1981 the Institution received the orders that the powers of appointment including the appointment were withdrawn or suspension. If the order was valid and power to making appointment was withdrawn or suspend it would not be open to the Selection committee to make and select appellant nor the Manager on behalf of the Committee Of Management can issue appointment order on April 27. 1981 to appellant and the appointment would be by a body not authorised to make the appointment and hence ineffective though it may not be invalid. [981F] 2:2 The State Government could be said to have rescinded that A regulation conferring power of appointments including the appoint ment of Principal and teachers.

The petitioners, manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as cloth is woven on looms. The petitioners state that the manufacturers of goods to whom they manufactured 'a textile" and also that it serves as part of raw material for what ultimately also goes into the manufacture of a fabric. After indicating the manner in which and the substance out of which "rayon tyre cord fabric" is made and its composition, the petition sets out item 22 of the first schedule of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1941 as the applicable entry covering the goods manufactured by the petitioners. This item reads as follows: "19. All cotton fabrics, rayon or artificial silk fabrics, woollen fabrics, sugar and tobacco, as defined in the Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act, 1957". Section 2(C) of the Additional duties of Excise and Salt (Goods Of Special Importation) Act 1957 lays down that "2(C), the words and expressions 'sugar ', tobacco ', 'cotton fabrics ', shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in Items Nos. 1, 4, 19, 21 and 22 of First Schedule to the Central Excise and salt Act, 1944". The petitioners asserted that from years 1966 to 1969, the respondent Commercial Tax officer was not subjecting the goods of this description to sales tax and accepted the case of the petitioners that they were exempt from taxation. The reasoning of the Commercial Tax Officer in exempting these goods is also mentioned. It is then stated that as some questions were put in the Rajasthan State Legislative Assembly on or about 20th April 1971, asking for the reason why this particular type of goods of the petitioner were exempted from Sales tax, the Commissioner of Commercial Tax issued a letter to the Commercial Taxes Officer to levy Sales tax on the "ray on cord fabric". Thereafter notices under the proviso to section 12(1) of Act were issued for the years 1965 69 and 1969 70 made by the Commercial tax officer. The view of the respondent was that the goods now sought to be taxed are not the "end product" but the "tyre cord fabric fabric" manufactured by it is woollen cloth on loom. The High Court did not find any error "apparent upon the face of the record" and dismissed the petitioners ' writ petitions against the assessment order dated 26th March 1971 for the year 1968 69 and1969 70 made in favour of the appellants. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended that: (1) the goods were now sought for taxed are neither the "first product" nor "theelon tyre mass fabric" but they were merely a piece of cloth which is a textile; (2) the tyres are not covered by item 19 in the Schedule to Central Excise Tariff Act, and therefore, they fall under entry 18 of the Schedule of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954; and (3) the High Court was wrong in holding that there was no error apparent on the face Of the record. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1(a) The word "fabric" has a wide meaning. The first example of such a product is: "An edifice, a building". The fourth example of the First meaning is: 'A woven fabric; any kind of cloth". Presumably it is not just the skeleton of a textile. But, against pushing this point of view too far it may be urged that in the technical and commercial parlance, there was nothing to show that the taxing authorities should be left to determine whether the "Textile" is more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or as merely cordending to pass off as ar textile fabric.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was accordingly dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred under Section 10(1)(c) of the Act to Labour Court Dhanbad for adjudication. The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court, Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is transferred to Labour court Patna. That application was made without intimation to the management. The Government howev er, has acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to the Management transferred the case to Labour Courts, Patna. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for the transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view the difficulties expressed by him to attending the labour court, Dhanbad regu larly due to his residence at Hajapur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before Labour Court. The High Court did not agree and summarily dismissed the writ petition with an observation: "Since no prejudice is being caused to the petitioner and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, we are not inclined to interfere with the order under challenge. This application is dismissed" The management in the appeal challenges the Government notification withdrawing and transferring the pending case from the Labour court Dhanbad to Labour Cour t Court Patna. Power to transfer certain proceedings: (1 ) The appropriate Government may, by order in writing and for reasons to be stated therein withdraw any proceeding under this Act pending before a Labour Court Tribunal or National Tribunal and transfer it for disposal to another labour court or Tribunal. (2) The expression 'may ' in sub section(1) Of Section 33B only makes it discretionary in so far as the appropriate Government taking a decision as to whether the power conferred thereunder has to be exercised or not. The authority is under legal obligation to record reasons in support of its decision. In the instant case, the key question for consideration is whether the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workman and transferring it from Labour Court to Labour courts Dhanbad should have given an opportunity to management? The validity of the reasons given by the Govern ment for transferring the case was another question to be considered. The Punjab High Court in Workman of Punjab Worsted Spinning Mills Chheharta vs State of Punjab & Ors., [1965] II LLJ 2 18 has expressed the view that the power to transfer pending case under Section 33 is not a mere administrative but quasi judicial power and the appropriate Govern ment cannot transfer a case on the basis of allegations of one party without giving reasonable opportunity to other party to represent its point of view. It was explained by the Madras High Court that the reasons gave by a party who moved for transfer may not be valid or relevant or may not he true at all. In Jay Engineering Works Ltd. vs Fourth Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, [1977] ( Lab) 1C 1739 at 1750 the Calcutta High Court has observed that it will be difficult to appreciate how under such circumstances, the Government could be called upon to give a notice to tile parties before making an order under Section33 B. It is also pointed out by the Labour Commissioner that the workman is having his residence in Hajipur, and it will he inconvenient for him not to attend to the Labour Ci nt Court regularly at Dhanbad.

The appellant, the manager of a hotel, was dismissed from service by an industrial dispute. The management filed a writ application in the High Court challenging the order of reference on the grounds (1) that the reference was incompetent inasmuch as it did not specify how many of the 480 workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute; and (2) that, the reference in this form was incompetent. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. The fact that in the order Of reference the quoted words were added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not make the reference incompetent. The word "as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi Chandni Chowk, Delhi, was merely for the purpose of convenience so that the tribunal may know to whom it should give notice when proceeding to deal with the reference. That however did not preclude the workmen if they wanted to be represented by any other union to apply to the Tribunal for such representation or even to apply for being made parties individually. The words "as representing by the hotel Workers ' union, Katra Shah Shahan ShahanShahanshaya, Chandni chowk, Delhi " were merely for their convenience so as to mention the names of the workmen concerned. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy, [1953] S.C.R. 334, followed. The dispute was with respect to the terms of employment and conditions of labour of the employees. The addition of the words " as represented by" in section 10(1) of the Act which gave power to the appropriate government where it was of opinion that an industrial disputes existed or was apprehended to refer the dispute to a tribunal for adjudication, did not exclude any officer of the trade union but mentions the union itself. This in our opinion is a technicality upon technicality and for the union not being a living person can only be served through some officer, such as its president or secretary and it is that officer who will really represent the workmen before the tribunal, The fact therefore that in this case the dispute was also about workmen to whom notice of dismissal had been given and in that connection the names Of the workmen were mentioned in the reference, did no make the refer incompetent.

The appellant, a bushings and bearings imported by the appellant, was assessed to duty under the Customs Tariff Act. The appellant claimed that the goods were classifiable under Heading 84.06 of the . The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of exemption under the Notification No. 281 Cus/76 granting part exemption from payment of customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by it, and held that the bushments and bear ingings were the same and as the bearings come under the Heading No. 84.63 and not under Heading No 84.6. The Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the Revenue. According to the Appellate Tribunal, the busi cials and bearions are the same, and as bearings came under the heading No.84.06 they are not entitled to claim any exemption for the bushes, even if they are parts of such engines. The Notification grants exemption in part from payment Of the Customs duty in regard to articles specified in column (2) of the Table annexed thereto and falling under Heading Nos. 8406. The Tribunal dismissed appeal of Revenue. Hence this appeal by the Revenue under Section 130E of the , Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Notification No 281 C.us/ 76 granting exemption in parts from payment to the Customs Duty in respect thereof is not applicable to the parts, will be to amend the Notification, which the Court will not do. [226F] 1.2 In the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption will be granted in respect Of parts of the engines, which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, we are unable to uphold the contention that they are included under a Heading other than Heading No . 84.05. [227G H] 1:3 The Notification does not only intends to grant exemption to internal combustion piston engines but also to 'parts thereof '. When, therefore, the intention is clear and manifest, it will be unreasonable to take a narrow view of the Notification and not to extend its benefit to the part of the engine referred to in Heading No, 84.07. [228H] 1 :4 The Notification has been inartistically drafted. It is, however, clear that the Notification not only intended to grant exemptions to internalviation pistons but also specifically mentions the parts 'part ' thereof ', that is to say, parts of those engines. [229B C] 2.5 In the instant case, there is no material or evidence nor is there any finding of the Appellate Authority or the Customs authorities that the bushes which have been imported by appellant are parts 'of the internal combustion Piston engine falling under heading No 8406, but they are distinct and separate. [230E] 2:6 The Notification exempts also parts of engines mentioned in paragraph 2 of column (1) of Table annexed to the Notification which is relevant for our purpose not only refers to internal fire pistan engines but further mentions the 'part "s thereof". In the context of the notification, it includes the parts of engine.

The appellants filed a suit for declara tion that they were entitled to be in enjoyment and pos session of Saint Syed Moosa Shah Khadiri Dargah in Madras for a period of 27 days in all in the months of February, March, June, July, October & November each year and to restrain the defendants from interfering with the plaintiffs ' right and management in the Dargah. The suit was contested by the plain tiffs on the ground that Fathima Bee had no right or claim of share in the Mujawarship and that he was receiving offerings by right of inheritence. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that if really the rights of Fathimma had become barred by her not exercising the rights, the plaintiffs themselves can have no independent right to claim. It also held that there was no evidence whatsoever to show at any point of time till her death in 1957 that Fafima Bee ever made a demand or asked for share of the Hundial collections as such it should be held that her rights had become extinguished by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were claiming through Fathiman Bee had lost their right by ouster. The High Court also held in favour of the plaintif fants. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the judgment and decree were res judicata or binding on Fathilima Bee, but his submission was that it should have been taken as a circumstance in proving ouster of Fafimma from the right or liabili ty of the Dargah or any claim in the offerings. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The only controversy now left to be determined is whether the High Court was right in holding that the rights had became barred by ouster or as such she were entitled ted to any right of management or posses sion in a Dargah and on that account they were pleading an ouster of Eathima Sai Bee from the fight or management of the Wakf. [529C D] 1.2 There is no controversy now as regards the period of 28 days falling to the share of plaintiffs and on the question whether females are entitled to any rights or management in a Ahmeddeen or the present plaintiffs. The only dispute now left is whether females were entitled under any right or management or possession of the offerings in the Wakf Dargah. [525D] 1:3 There is nothing in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the Court that any stand was taken that the right of Fatima Bee or plaintiffs was specifically denied on any particular occa sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of their defendants would be adverse to the inter est or rights of the plaintiffs of Ftathima Sura Bee. The defendants were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not entitled to claim any right in the management or offerings of Dargah. It is an admitted case of the parties that Fatna Bee was living and was being looked after by her broth ers and she was in fact being paid portions of the income from the Dargah and On that account she was satisfied in allowing the brothers to enjoy the office of Mujawar on her behalf also. 1 has admitted that Ftafima pair was living, and was getting a portion of the Income from the Wakf and on this account she had been satisfied in permitting the brothers who were enjoying the office as such there wasno question of any knowledge to Fathna Bee that she was being ousted from her right or share in Dargah. Thus it is clear that neither in the plaint nor in the reply to notice of t he plain tesss any stand has been taken that they had asserted hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoy ment to the knowledge of FfathimaE.

The first respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. The 1st respondent, who originally used to be known as the G.I.P., Rly., was allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance. The appellant 's claim for house rent allowances was rejected by the Authority on the ground that the house rent was not "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. On appeal, the Authority held that the House Rent Allowance claimed by the 1st Respondent came within the purview of the definition of "wages " contained in the Act and therefore the claim was inadmissible on the grounds that there had been no illegal deduction from the respondent 's wages inasmuch as the respondent had been allotted railway quarter of a specified type and that he had declined to occupy the quarters offered by the Government, but that even so, the appellant was not entitle under the Rules to any House rent allowance; in other words, it was contended on behalf of the 1 st respondent that the employee 's right to the allowance accrues as soon as he has fulfilled the terms of the contract of employment including regular attendance, good work or conduct and his other behaviour in terms of section 7(2)(b) and section 11 of the , and that in any event, if rule 3(i) aforesaid were to be considered as a part of the terms Of the contract between the employer and the employee, there was no absolute right in the employee to the house Rent allowance. Held: (1) The rules which must be included in the terms 'of the contract ' between the parties include the rule quoted above and that therefore the position in law is that there is no absolute rights in the employees at all places wherever he may be posted and in all circumstances irrespective of whether or not he has been offered Government quarters. (2) The house rent Allowance which may in certain circumstances be included In 'wages ' is not the same thing as the value of any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee; otherwise it would not be a legally permissible deduction from wages. It Is equally clear that house rent is admissible only so long as an employee is stationed at one of the specified places and has not been offered government quarters. Once an employee of the description given above has been offer suitable house accommodation and he has refused it, he ceases to be entitled to the House rent Allowance and that allowance thus ceases to become "wages".

The detenu, who was one of the detenus in Writ Petition 435 of 1980, was one Indru 's Ramchand Bharvani; while in Writ petition 435 of 1979, the detenu was carrying on business in diamonds and precious stones in partnership under the style of "M/s. Gems Impex Corporation". 35, New Marine Lines, Bombay, since 1971. On November 16, 1979, Customs Officers at Bombay raided the residential premises of the son Indru"s, and seized two cameras and three wrist watches worth about Rs. 55 lakhs and also some jewellery and Rs. 1,40,000 in Indian currency and two gold sovereign coins. On February 18, 1980, the Customs Officers intercepted the residential premise of the detenu and seized certain jewellery and cash articles worth about rupees 55 lakhs. The detenus were arrested on November 23, 1979 and interrogated. During interrogation, the detenus claimed that they had purchased the gems and other articles from whom these gems had been acquired. On March 25, 1980 an order of detention was passed purporting to have been made under section 3(1) of the (for short COFEPOSA) by the State Government on February 16, 1980 purporting to be made under Section 3(2) of COFEPOSA by the Central Government was served on the detenus. The grounds of detention were also served on them alongwith the order of Detention on February 18. On April 3, 1980 copies were received by the detenus on March 25. On the direction of the Central Govt., the detenu also made a representation to the State Govt. which, according to the information furnished at the Bar by Mr. Ram Jethmalani, appearing for the detenus, challenges the detention mainly on these grounds: (1) The order of deten tion, purporting to had been signed by Mr Salvi, Secretary in the Home Department to the Government of Maharashtra, is void because the concerned Minister of the State of Maharashtra never, in fact, passed any such order and under the rules of business framed by the Governor under Article 166 of the Constitution, Shri Salvi had no authority to pass the order; (2) The detaining authority never applied its mind to the earlier statements of four persons from whom the detenus alleged to have acquired the gem in question, and in which they had on the basis of documentary evidence supported the contention of the petitioners that the latter had acquired the Gems in question from those persons. On these facts furnishing of copies of statements and documents relied upon in the grounds for detaining the aforesaid accused at this stage would not be in public interest. The delay of more than a month, in supplying the copies to the detenus has vitiated the detention. [350D E] Khudiram vs State of Bombay ; , referred to.

The Gujarat High Court in its order referred to SS 258, 410 and 423 of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. The Division Bench of the High Court also recorded the main judgment only in Criminal Appeal No. 60 of 1965. The High Court, however, held that r. 6 did not prohibit a joint appeals by the state against more than one accused persons. On the view that it was wrong in holding the joint appeal not to be maintainable and summarily rejecting the same. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) A joint appeal is in compliance with this rule must be sustained. The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High court by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C. and r.6 does not seem to be inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code. Holding this rule to be valid, in agreement with the decision of the Full Bench, the competency of a Joint appeal by several accused person convicted at one trial must be upheld. [882 H] (ii) The High court was wrong, in holding that the joint appeals not to he maintainable and in summarily rejecting it. [884 A B] (iii) The view taken by the High Courts on the construction of this section is clearly unacceptable. Section 417 which provides for an appeal in a case of acquittal empowers the State Government to direct the public prosecutor in any case to present an appeal from an order of acquittal. This section also does not suggest any bar or prohibition against presentation of a combined appeal against several accused Persons acquitted in a cases. On this reasoning a joint 'appeal by the appellant against several accuses must be held not to suffer from any serious legal infirmity. And then the matter being one of mere form it calls for a liberal approach requiring the appeal to be heard on merits. To hold it to be unmaintainable on this ground would defeat the larger cause of justice.

The appellant was a firm registered under section 26(A) of the Income tax Act, 1922. Prior to the constitution of the firm, the partners were members of a Hindu undivided family. The family which consisted of Meyyappa Chettiar and his two brothers carried on money lending business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States and it was assessed under the Indian Income tax (1918) Act. There was a disruption of the joint family status on June 2, 1938 and thereafter the members of the family continued the business as partners. In the course of assessment for the year 1939 40 it was claimed by Meyappa Chettiar, one of the members, that having regard to the severance of joint family nature, the income from April 13, 1938 to June 2nd, 1938 was not liable to be taxed by reason of the provisions of section 25(3) and (4). The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business of the assessee could not be deemed to have been charged under the 1918 Act. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that in view of the fact that the entire income of the foreign business was remitted to the assessee and tax imposed on that income under the 1922 Act, it cannot be said that the foreign income of M/s. O.RM.SP Firm could not therefore be deemed liable to tax under the provisions Of section 25 (3) of 1922 Act. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeals holding that when a Hindu Undivided Family carrying on a business which was taxed under the 1920 Act became disrupted and the members continued the firm there after as partners, there could be no discontinuance but only succession by the firm of the business. On reference the High Court held that when the Indian undivided family carrying on business which is taxed under 1918 Act became entitled to relief under section 25.(3) Of the 1922 act, it was not assessed under section 3 of the 1918 act and accordingly answered both the questions in favour of the Department. The Revenue appealed to this Court by certificate. HELD: (i) The assessee was entitled to both parts of relief contemplated under section 2(1)(a) of that Act in respect of the Indian foreign business at Penang, lpoh and Kambar. [912 D] (ii) The exemption under section 5(3), is general. It is manifest that by section 3 Of the 1918 Income tax was charged upon the assessee in respect for his activity styled,foreign business ' and in relation to it and it must hence be taken upon the facts found by the appellate Tribunal in this case, that the Foreign business of M the assessee was charged under section 4 of the 1922 Income tax. [801 G] (iii) The income derived by the assessee from business is in relation tto a business and therefore the assessment of the income must be treated as an assessment of that business. No doubt, under the provision of the Act, the tax is payable by an assessee but the assessment is on the basis of various heads of income derived from the assessee one of which is business. It cannot, therefore, be said to be that because tax was payable by the assesee on the profits rec eived from a business in a foreign territory such assessment is an assessment Of the business and it can, therefore be said, that because Tax was payable on the income received by the assesses on the profit rec eved from a 'business in a Foreign territory such assess ment is an assess of the tax. No question of law arose in this appeal.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for the construction of the Capital Project, Ghandhinagar. Large quantities of bricks were manufactured and supplied under the contract and the applicant received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. The assessee made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales lax Act, 1959 on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax to determine the question whether the said supplies of bricks by the respondent to the Public works Department were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supply of bricks was sales. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department for the manufacture and sale of kiln burning brickbats to the aforesaid department and the supply thereof in terms of their running Bill No. 1 dated September 6 1965 for the purpose of construction of Capital Project; whether on the findings that the supplies of brick were sales, the transaction contemplated by the said contract entered in by the assessee with the respondent was a works contract." The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue holding that the transaction was a Works Contract. In coming to this conclusion the High court held as follows: "In view of certain distinguishing features of the contract with which we are concerned, the decision of the Supreme Court in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs The State of orissa and others, came to the conclusion that the contracts envisaged by it were not inconsistent in a contract of sale. " In coming, to that conclusion the Supreme court held that as per the special features and characteristics of the Contract with which the appellant is concerned, it would be difficult to hold in the light of the special feature and characteristics and characteristics, of the contracts with which this Court are concerned. The decision of this Court in Chander Bhan Gosai 's case will govern the present case where terms and conditions are almost identical so far as relating to the relevant subject matter. All the above terms relate to a stage in the process of proper and efficient manufacturing of bricks and are not inconsistent with a contract for sale of the bricks manufactured. All these terms relate not to a contract or works contracts depends upon the true construction of all the terms and condi tions of the document when there is one. A contract of Sale is, therefore, whose main object is the transfer of the property in and the delivery of the possession of a chattel as a chatte to the buyer. (Halsbury 's Laws of England Third Edition Volume 34 page 6.) The contract withwhich we are dealing here in this appeal is found in a tender for the supply Of materials containing a memorandum of the conditions. The question will depend upon the facts of this case. Chandra Bhan Bas Gosain`s case (supra). According to him the common features are the following: The land was given free for manufacture of bricks in both the cases. The materials shall remain at the contractor`s risk till the date of final delivery. In Chandra Bhan Saha Gosain 's Case, this Court observed as follows; "lt may be presumed that it was understood that in quoting his rate for the bricks, the appellant would take into account the free supply of earth for making the bricks.

The petitioner, who was a member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President of India on 26.6.1975 under Article 352 of the Constitution on the ground that it had ceased to be in operation on 4.2.1972; (2) The proclamation of Emergency dated 3rd December 1971 had ceased as in operation by the time the House of People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 was passed by Parliament both the Proclamations of Emergency and the two Proclomations of emergency dated 3.12.1971 and 25th June 1975 were either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased not to be In operation on 26th August, 1975; (3) The House of the People ( Extension of duration) Act 1976 was ultra vires Article 14 of the constitution inasmuch as it had continued to be operative by virtue of the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament approving the said Proclimations of Proclams of Emergency as required by clause (2); and (4) The Finance Act,1976 was ultra rites. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 Article 352 does not prescribe that a Proclamation of emergency should be published in the official Gazette. The petitioner 's contention that the resolutions of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha approving the two resolutions had been duly published in their official reports of the two Houses of the Parliament cannot be questioned. [447C] 1.2 The resolution passed by the Houses of Legislatures approving the second resolutions have been duly approved by the resolutions which were issued by both the Houses. Since the two proclamions of Emergency were in force when the House was passed its validity cannot be challenged. [441D E] 1:3 The production of Lok Sabha Debates and Rajya Assembly Debates containing the proceedings of the both Houses has been duly notified in the Official Gazette. [442G] 1 :4 The production, of the Rajya Sabha Debates containing proceedings of two Houses relating to the period between the time when the resolutions were passed in each of the Houses is adequate publication of the Resolutions of Parliament as there is no rule which requires that the resolution should be publish in the office Gazette. There is no Rule which requires the resolutions should be printed in the offices of the House. The production and the Lok Assembly Debates of the said two Houses has not been duly authenticated by the two Members who have signed the resolutions. [443C] 2:5 The production or the Rajya assembly of the Vidhan Sabha and the Rajya Committee Reports containing the proceeding of the meeting relating to period between time when resolutions were moved in each House of Parliament and the time, when the resolution were duly adopted amounts to proof of the aforesaid resolutions. There are no rules which require that the Resolutions should be publication published in a official Gazette.[442D] 2.6 The production in Lok Sabha Reports and Rajya Sabhas approving the resolutions have not been properly authenticated by two Members of Parliament. [444E] 2 :7 The production is of theLok Sabha Debates though after some short delay is adequate circulation of the resolution of Parliament, as there was no rule that required that the Resolution should be made published in an official Gazette, it cannot be said that the said resolutions had ceased or ceased to operate before the expiration of two months from the issue thereof. [44D] 3:1 The production by Lok Sabha debates and Rajya Committee containing the Proceedings of the Two Houses of parliament relating to periods between the date when the Resolutions were passed is adequate Publication of the speeches of Parliament in the year 1977. Since both Procluations of Proclamation of Pro Climations were kept in force by virtue Of the resolutions made by the House, the two provisions of Article 352 have been rightly held to be valid.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The application was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the High Court. He was therefore entitled to leave under article 133(1)(a) and (b). The respondents contended that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property of the family and that it was alienable property and therefore capable of a valid transfer. HELD: (i) The appellant 's case was accepted by the Trial Court but was rejected by the High court and the High Courts were right in holding that the property in question was the property of a public temple. [157 D] (ii) The suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application, being O.P. No. 37 of 1950 under section 84(2) of Madras Act 11 of 1927. Under that Act only a fixed court fee was payable. That being so, the appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. The refusal of the appellant to grant leave was based on the observation that whether the property was a private or a public religious temple could have no market value and therefore was incapable of valuation. [158 D] 157 (iii) The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that the suit property was the personal property of 'the family capable of alienation, the High 'Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to the respondents the property had been inalienable and was a public Temple.

The appellant, a subordinate staff of the respondent company, was employed as clerks and 131 belong to the subordinate staff. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of tiffin arrangements at present made by them. The Tribunal granted the first claim and directed that the clerical staff should be paid As. /8/ per day and the subordinate Staff as also in regard to the lowest grade clerks, the Tribunal thought it unnecessary to make any such direction. That is how the latter claim has been partially allowed. It was against this award that the appellant has come to this Court by special leave. The total number of employees in the employment of the appellant is about 453. 36 of them are officers; 90 are junior grade Assistants, while 196 are clerks and 132 belong to subordinate staff, and it is in regard of the last two categories of the employees 's employees that the two items of dispute have reference in the present proceedings. It appears that in 1956 there was an industrial dispute between the parties, one of which being the claim made by the respondents in respect of tafiffin on working days. In those proceedings, however, the said claim was not pressed and the matter was left to the discretion of the appel lant. After the award was published, the parties entered into direct negotiations in respect thereof. The appellant agreed to consider the claim sympathetically and make a suitable provision in that behalf That is why the prevailing arrangements for tiff in the region were not based solely on humanitarian grounds. When it appeared to the appellent 's counsel that some employees who had retired found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the appellant sympathetically and generously considered their request for re employment and that was, the basis on which some of the re employments have been made. The dispute was taken up for final negotiations between the con tentionants and the State Government, and the problem did not call for any consideration at that stage. Thereafter, the respondents represented to the State Govern ment that though the company gave assurances to its employees that re employment would not be resorted to on a liberal scale, those assurances were disregarded and the practice was being followed in many cases and that posed a serious problem to the respondents. Besides, it did appear that when the appellant had raised a dispute on this point in 1960, the State Gov ernment refused to make a reference on the ground that only 4 cases of reemployment had been brought to its notice, and so, the problem does not call any consideration for consideration at this stage. The question posed by the respond ents ' demand must be considered. Held, that the Tribunal has overlooked the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appellant can have no material bearing in dealing with the point; in the very nature of things, the same re employed person are bound to support the appellant. The result is, the appeal fails and is dismissed with cost.

The respondent, an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne addressed a letter to the Chief Accounts Officer communicating the sanction of the General Manager for payment of special contribution to provident fund to Browne in sterling in terms of r. 1410(1) of the Railway Establishment Code. Another communication was received from Browne (who had apparently by then migrated to the United Kingdom) on February 22, 1956 by which he requested that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident fund account be remitted to him by Bank Draft on the District Bank Water Street, Liverpool. After Browne retired from service, the Deputy General Manager, Eastern Railway, wrote a letter on July 27, 1955 to the respondent intimating the sanction for payment and the payment was required either under the first intimation at Liver by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the bankers of 'Browne at Birmingham. The respondent then drew two cheques in the name of Browne and sent them to the Reserve Bank for conversion of the amount in sterling, and to transmit the fund in sterling to the Bank for converted into sterling and to remit it to Brownee. The Railway Administration then drew three cheques in favour of the Reserve bank with instructions to convert amounts covered by the cheques into sterling, to transmit it to the credit in sterling and send them to Brownders. The Reserve Bank was the only authority which could permit such conversion in view of the 31 currency restrictions imposed by the Government of India. For purpose of conversion and transmission of the money to Brown grade, the Reserve Government of india was the agent of the railway Administration. Until the money was converted into Indian sterling and was transmitted by the Reserve Banks to Browner, the money remained at the disposal of the Railways Administration. The railway administration was in respect of the Provident Funds money in the position of a trustee for Browne, and it had undertaken to discharge its obligation by arranging to have the amount converted into French and to remitted it to Whitee. Under section 60(1)(k) of ' the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 read with section 3 of the , the compulsory deposit in any recognised Provident Fund Account is exempt from attachment in execution of a decree of a civil court. Section 3( 1 ) provides that "A compulsory deposit shall not in any way be capable of being assigned or charged and shall not be liable to attachment under any decree or order of any Civil, Revenue or Criminal Court in respect thereof". The respondent filed an application for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The executing court overruled the objection observing that the attached amount represented provident Fund money which by section 3 Of the , was immunefrom attachment under law. The Union of India then applied to the High Court for a review of the order passed by the executing court. The High Court confirmed the order of the executing Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High court was in error in holding that the moneys in the hands of the respondent had ceased to be provident fund and was liable to be attached. [31 E] (ii) The Union Government was a trustee of the 'Railway Administration for conversion and transfer of the amounts into sterling. The order of attachment of the said amount into which the two cheques drawn by the Railway Administration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3(1).

The appellant, a Regional Manager, was dismissed from service by the management on the ground that no dismissal was involved. The management 's appeal to this Court was allowed and the termination of his services was set aside. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The order of discharge is one of termination simpliciter under the provisions of the Standing Orders. [490C] (2) The employer must disclose to the court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. In the instant case this has not been done. There is only the ipse dixit of the employer that he was suspecting since 1968 that the appellant was divulging secrets relating to his business. Further after 1968, the appellant had been given two extra increments in addition to his normal increments as stated earlier. The Labour Court found that it was not a camouflage to cover up what really was an order (1 ) 496 of dismissal. This Court, in appeal, as a rule of practice, is loath to interfere with a finding of fact recorded by the trial court. But if such a finding is based on no evidence, or is the result of a misreading of the material evidence, and is so unreasonable or grossly unjust that no reasonable person would judicially arrive at that conclusion, it is the duty of this Court to interfere and set matters fight. [495E F] (3) The management has the power land, indeed, the duty to X ray the order and discover its true nature, if,he object and effect, if the attendant circumstances and the ulterior purpose be to dismiss the employee because he is an evil to be eliminated. The Court is concerned with the latter and not with the former, although circumstances may exist which justify a genuine exercise of the power of simple termination. There, a termination simpliciter may be bow fide, not colourable, and loss of confidence may be evidentiary of good faith of the employers. [493C D] (4) In the present case this Court has the powers land, undoubtedly, the duties to X liy the orders and discover their true nature if, they arehe object or effect, If the attendant circumstance and the oblique purpose beto dismiss the employees because he was an evil, to be avoided. The court is concerned only with the later and notwith the former although circumstances might exist which justified a genuine order of termination. [49E F; G] (5) In order to find out whether the order of retrenchment is one Of termination simpliciter or under the provision of standing orders, the Tribunal has ample jurisdiction to go into all the circumstances which led to the termination simpliciter. The power of the Court to go behind the form of the order, look at the substance and set aside what may masquerade as termination simpliciter, if in reality it cloaked a dismissal for misconduct 'as a colourable exercise of power by the Management. [48G H] (6) In this case, the management had the power to terminate the services of its employee without reasons but with notice pay only, the colourable exercise Of that power invalidated it and the (1)[1972] 3 section C. R. 822 followed.

The petitioners, who were the victims of this medical mishap, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the action of the State Government in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. The High Court directed the Indian Medical Council and the Union of India to be impleaded as parties to the proceedings. The petitioners contended that the victims were acting pursuant to and under the authority of the Government and that on the doctrine of State action, the activity must be reckoned as that of the state itself which must, accordingly be held vicariously liable. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines prescribed by the Union Government on 9.2.1988 arrived at after a careful study of all aspects of the problem are quite comprehensive. However, it is venture to suggest that some points made in the Report and Recommendation of the expert sub committee of the Indian medical Council may be consid ered by the union Government for incorporation in their Revised Guidelines dated 9.02.1988. The prescriptions re ferred to by the said sub committee are these: "Staff: The operations in the camp should only be performed by qualified, experienced Oph thalmic Surgeons registered with Medical Council of India or any State Medical Council. It is preferable to have a Dentist to check the teeth for sepsis and a Physician for general medical check up." [256E F] 1.2 The prescriptions prescribed by Union Government are sufficiently comprehensive to ensure the protection of the patients who are generally drawn from the poorer and less affluent sec tion of society or whether any further guide lines would require to be evolved. After the institution of these proceedings, Central Government, in the wake of reports of mishaps in 'Eye Camps ' constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of the Union Health Minister with six State Health Ministers and four experts as members to re examine and update the existing guidelines or evolve fresh ones. As a result of the deliberations of the said Committee and pursuant to its recommendations, the guidelines for conduct of eye camps earlier issued have been updated and revised. The Committee deliberated on the issue and its recommendations in regard to the norms for the conduct and management of eye camp have been filed before this Court. [256F H] 1:3 In the instant case, the factual foundations laid before the Court and the limited scope of the proceedings no appeal could be made to the doctrine Of State action. Shri Yogeshwar Prasad, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh submitted that the State would approach the matter not with the spirit of a litigant in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to the victims. He further contended that on humanitarian consideration, the victims should be afforded some monitary relief by the State Govern ment. [257E F; 257A] 1 :4 The victims entitled to receive the additional payment shall be the same as those who had the benefit of the interim relief of Rs.5,000. The amount shall be deposit ed, as was done in the matter of distribution of interim relief, with the District Judge who shall arrange to dis tribute the same in accordance with the procedure adopted at the time of administration of the Interim relief.

The petitioner No. 3,00,000 was elected as the President of a Society under the Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act 1984. The term of each body is 5 years from the date of holding of their first meeting. According to the Bidhan of the Samiti as it stood in 1982, the Chief Minister of Assam was the Ex officio President of the Society but as at the time of holding the first meeting the State of Assam had under President 's rule, consequently the office of Adhyaksha remained vacant as then there was no Chief Minister from Assam. But in the meantime the Samiti in its meeting of the Byabasthapika Sabha held on 17.7.83 passed a resolution for 167 amendment of the provisions of the Bidan in the following manner: "That the words contained in section 16 at page 21 of the bidhan to the effect that the Chief Ministers of Assam shall be the Ex Offi cio Adhyaksha of the Samitis be deleted. It is further alleged by the petitioner that as this amendment was passed on 17th July, 1983 from this date the Chief Minis tary of Assam ceased to be the ex officio President and since then according to the petitioner he had nothing to do with the Samiti. When the matter was pending in the Court for considera tion of the question of temporary injunction the Governor of Assam purported to act under Clause 1 of Article 230 of the Constitution of India promulgated an Ordinance called the Asam Rashtra bhasha Samchar Samiti, (Taking Over of Management & Control) Ordinance 1984 and Section 1 sub clause (ii) of this Ordinance provided that the Ordinance shall extend to all areas over which the Asop Rashtraba sambha shachar Samiti had its jurisdiction immediately before the commence ment of the Ordinance by a Notification No. EPG 57/34/75 dated 1.10.84 by which the Rashtradhasha prachar Board was consti tuted with respondents 11, 12 and 13 as members and by this order all persons except respondent No. 2 were substituted by Board appointed by the Government and all the functions, properties and affairs of the samba samiti Samiti were taken over by this Board and it is this action taken under the Ordinance and the Act and ultimately the Act which is the subject matter of challenge in this Writ Petition. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner in the writ petition that even after the new elections and a new Government comes into power in Assam the Act, which as its title disclosed was a temporary measure continued at perpetuity, and the Samiti is being run by nominated members and the rights of the members of the Board under Article 19 has not only been restricted but has been taken away. It has also been contended that even assuming that the new Government came into power under the Constitution itself it could have provided for the restoration of the elected body in due course. The question is whether the Act was enacted to meet a temporary con tention for taking over of the management temporarily it could be said that except that constitution was amended and the Chief Secretary was dropped from the place which he used to enjoy before the amendment of Constitution carried out under the Act. Allowing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellants were the sons of one Ram Kishori Lal Sao, a resident of Asansol in Bengal. They had no concern with the negotiation and it was alleged that Sumitra Devi made a gift of four houses at Asanshol on behalf of Kamala Devi. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that a deed of gift dated March 10, 1940, executed by Sumitra Devi in favour of her daughter Kamala Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on them. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the proper finding should have been that Sumitra ' made a "sankalpa" of the gift at Deoghar and the acceptance of such a gift by Nand Lal father in law of Kamala, was for spiritual benefit of Ram Kishori Lai; (ii) there was no reliable evidence that Sumitra had made a sankalna ' of the gifts when the bride was given in marriage and the question of confirming such a gifts at the Gowna ceremony did not arise; and (iii) even accepting the findings of the final Court of fact as correct, the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of Ram. Kishori Lal, the father in Law of Kamala 's case was for the spiritual benefit to her deceased husband irrespective of the consideration whether she made a ' sank or not. Held: (i)(a) The proper finding to the contrary should have be that Sumitra died made a Sankaltpa ' of ' the gift of the four houses in question after the Sampradan ceremony on the occasion of the marriage of Kamala and that the acceptance by Nand Lai father in fact was for his spiritual benefit. (b) The findings of final Court were that there was antenuptial agreement by Sumitra ' that she would give four houses to Asansi as her share on partition; (c) the gift was not made at the time of the settlement of the marriages of Kamala. (ii)(a). It is open to Sumitra Devi to fulfil that promise as a religious act which conferred spiritual benefit upon her deceased father, irrespective of whether she had made any " sank" at the date of the contract or not; and the gift made long after the marriage may be supported upon the ground that the gift when made fulfils that moral or religious obligation. The finding of the preliminary Court of facts was correct in law. (iii)(a), the gift is binding on the reversioners. (iv) There is no consideration, nor any discussion of the texts bearing on the question, and the learned Judge did not consider the alienation from the point of view that the marriage was a religious duty and the promise to make a gift to the daughter as her marriage portion created a moral or legal obligation in fulfilment of which it was competent for the father to execute a deed.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Baghapurana Constituency (District Faridkot) filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices detailed in the petition. The petition was dismissed by the High Court holding that the allegations of corrupt practice indulged in by Tej Singh have been clearly proved and that the appellant had not indulged in any corrupt practice as alleged by Avtar Singh. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of section Tej Singh will have gone to the appellant cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [419D] 1.2 In view Of the very wide margin of vote (123), between Tej singh and Avtar singh, a great presumption and possibilities that the vote polled in favor of section R/o the candidate will have went to the appel lant cannot be held out and the appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters. [420B] 1:3 In view, the very limited margin of voters (123). between Tejinder Singh and R/O is a strong proof and possibility of that the voters would have gone t0 to the appellants, the appellant is entitled to succeed on the ground of corrupt practices (referred to above) as contemplated by section 123(2) of the Act having been adopted by the first respondent.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was personally keen on giving him an office of profit. In order to achieve this objective, Bhajan Lal got an Ordinance being Ordinance No. 44 of 1982 promulgated by the Governor. The ordinance inter alia provided that the constitution of a Forest Development Board would be constituted with a view to appointing the said Devinder Sharma as its Chairman. It was further alleged by the appellant that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means, the respondent, Bhajan lal called him to his official residence on July 26, 1983 through the Acting Chief Conservator of Forests and criminally intimidated him to withdraw the writ petition and pursuant thereto, eleven officers withdrew from the petition. It is alleged by him that after failure to threaten & demoralize the appellant, through indirect ways the respondent Bhajan Lal called him again to his office residence on August 26,1983 through the acting Chief Conservator. The further allegation of the appellant was that after knowing fully well that the writ petitioner through indirect methods the respondent had called him at his official residential residence on September 27, 1983 by the Acting chief Conservator of Forest Forests and Penalally intimidating him to withdrawing the writ peti tion, called him as "the Chief Minister of the State". The further alleged allegation of mala fide against the respondent was that he threatened and demolishes the appellant. Thereafter, the appellant filed an application for contempt against the Respondent, in the High Court complaining of interference by the Respondent with due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the same by filing an affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the Appellant. The Single Judge of the High court after considering the application, affidavits and the submissions made on behalf of the parties took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the Court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In that view of the matter, the learned Judge dismissed the application and discharged the rule niisi. It also held that there was no contempt as defined in section 2(c) of the Act and the appeal is incompetent. The appellant filed this appeal by special leave against the order of the Single Judge discharging the rule on the ground that the authority concerned had erroneously exercised its jurisdiction by not granting exemption to the petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 An appeal will lie under section 19(1) of ' the Act only when the High Courts makes an order or decision in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. It does not, however, mean that when the Supreme Court does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the High 892 Court does no exercise its power or power to punishfor contempt under Article 215 of the Constitution. [893F] 1.2 In considering a question whether the alleged contemner is guilty of contempt or not, the court hears the parties and considers the materials produced before it and, if necessary, examines witnesses and thereafter, passes an order either acquitting or punishing him for contempt.[894H; 892A] 2.1 The High Court has derives its jurisdiction jurisdiction to dismiss for contempt under article 215 of 'the Constitution.

The respondents, who were the daughter and grand sons of the original plaintiff, filed a suit for possession of land on the forfeiture of a lease. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the amendment made in 1929 to section 111(g) of the Act embodies a principle of justice equity and good conscience and notwithstanding section 2 of the , that principle was applicable in this case and there could be no forfeiture unless notice in writing to the lessee of his intention to determine the lease by the lessor bad been given. Held, that the rule laid down in section 111 (g) is not based on any principle of equity or good conscience but is merely a procedural recognition of a principle by justice, equity and justice. The provision with regard to giving of notice before a right of re entry accrues to the landlord is expressly excluded by sub section (11) in cases of re entries on forfeiture for non payment of rent. It cannot therefore be said that what has been enacted in sub section(g ) of section 111 of the Transfer of Pro perty Act, 1929 is a matter which even today in English law is considered as a matter of justice, Equity and good justice. But as it is left to the lessor 's option to take advantage of it or not, the (1) L.R. [1923] A.C. 1021, referred to. The lessor has to simply express an intention that he is going to avail of the forfeiture and that can be done by the filing of a suit as in English Law, in all cases not governed by the . , or to leases executed prior to 1st April 1930. The lessee has to merely express an implied intention that it is going on to avail himself of the forfeited forfeiture and he cannot always be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and to plead relief against forfeiture on every occasion particularly when he was warned by the court of appeal on a previous occasion. In exercising the discretion, each case must be judged by itself, the delay, the conduct of the parties and the difficulties to which the landlord has been put should be weighed against the tenant, This was the view taken by the Madras High Court in Appaya Shetty vs Mohammad Beari, (1923) L I.R., Bom. 1022, approved.
