Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 provides that certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in section 52 or any other provision of the , or any law, or in any contract, custom or usage, or In any judgment, decree or order of court, any person in occupation at the commencement of the Act, shall be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation of such land for non less than two years within a period of twelve years immediately preceding the 11th day of April, 1967. The appellant 's plea before the Courts below was that he was himself the owner of the area having acquired title to it by adverse possession. The High Court held that the benefit of the section would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurveyed lands had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believing to be competent to grant such leases or had come into possession with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to those persons whose posses sion had a subsisting origin in that sense. [113D] 2.1 In the instant case the finding of fact entered by the High Court is that the appellant had come in possession of the lands by trespass. His plea before courts below was not that he himself the owners of the areas having acquired the title to them by adverse posses tion. The finding of facts recorded by the Courts is that he had come to possession of those lands by entering into agreements with persons whom he bona fide believe to be entitled to grant leases or has come into posses tions with the object of atten dating to the unlawful owners or upon the basis o f arrangements likevaram etc., which were merely in the form of licences. [114E F] 2:2 The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 7D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". In the present case the findings of fact recorded by both the High Courts are that the appel lant had come within possession of lands by trespasser. His claim before the courts below is that appellant was himself a owner of land having acquired right to it, by adverse Possession. [116F] 2 :3 The expression 'in occupation ' occurring in Section 7D should be construed in as meaning 'in lawful poses.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. He was prosecuted under section 135(b)(ii) of the , and (b) of . The goods were also confiscated. On 21 4 67, 1968, the police officers searched room No. 10 at 56 Sheriff Deoji Street, Bombay. The appellant and three other persons were found to contain cigarette lighters of "Imco Triplex Junior" brand "Made in Austria". Each of them contained fifty sealed tins of flints for cigarettelighters which bore the following writing: "Tego Lighter Flints of Superior Quality Made in Germany". On opening them, six of them were found in a room. The five boxes containing lighters were found written "Dubai" and "Male" in Austrian. Each of the six boxes contained fifty open tins with jute cloth and secured by iron strips were found there. On opening they were found containing cigarette Lighters of 'Imco triplex junior '. The remaining five boxes contained 50 sealed tinches of flintles for cigarepellants which bore a following writing. "Tejit Lighterlateral Flints Of Superior Quality Assurance Made in France" inscribed on them. A panchnama was prepared before Panchas. A rent receipt in the name of the appellant in respect of room No 10, in this house, of which a portion was occupied by the appellant, and a bill for consumption of electricity were also seized from the custody of the Appellant together with the Godrej lock and the keys produced by the Appellant. Subsequently, the seized articles were made over to the Inspector of Central Excise and Customs, Marine and Prevention Division, Bombay on 24 4 67 under section 110 of the . The value of 7200 cigarette was stated as Rs. 14,400/ and of 250 tins respectively of flask as Rs 15,840/ and Rs 10,500/ respectively on which Customs duty of Rs. 15, 840/ was alleged to be payable. In the complaint filed on 30 10 1968 by the Assistant Collector of Central excise, Marine & Prevention Division Bombay, it was alleged that the cigaretteLighters and flints were imported into India without an import licence and in contravention of provisions of Government of India, Ministry of Commerce & Industry, Import Control order No. 17/55 dated 7 12 1955 (as amended) issued under section 3(2) of Imports & Export (Control) Act 1947 which was to be deemed to be an order passed under section 11 of the Act. The goods in respect thereof were also as a necessary consequence, said to be liable to confiscation under section 111(d) of ' the Act and the appellant had denied being in possession on 214 1967. The production of the key which according to the prosecution evidence, was sought to be proved by the prosecution witnesses. The defence plea that the accused having been concerned in a fraudulent evasion of payment of Rs 26,340/ as customs duty to the Government had committed offences punishable under section 131(a) and (c) of , was rejected by the trial court. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the presumption contained in section 123 of the Customs Act, 1962, corresponding to section 128(A) of, could not place the onus of proving innocent possession of these goods upon the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution had failed to prove that the goods were legally brought into India. [541C] 2.1 Section 123 of 'the Act only lay down a procedural rule, they could be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided it on 15 7 1969. Indeed, the complaint itself was filed on 20 10 1968. It is immaterial that the appellant was in possession with full knowledge of what the goods actually were.

The appellants were the President of a registered Association formed for carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because it was not registered as a company under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The Association at Budhar consisted of 25 members who made contributions to the initial 771 capital of the association which was one lac of rupees. 1 Nagar Mal raised various points by way of defence, his main defence being that none of the members of the Association were entitled to any share in the profits on the sales of 284 bales of Gwalior cloth and inasmuch as Nagar Mal had rendered accounts with regard to all other transactions, the suit for accounts must fail. The District Judge who dealt with the suit in the first instance passed a preliminary decree in favour of the appellants. The decree directed Nagar Mal to render accounts of the Cloth Association at the close of April 1946 to June 26, 1946 and it further directed that leaving out 106 bales of the Gwalior cloth which Nagar Mal gave to the Association an option of taking over the consignment, if the Association did not exercise the option, the consignment would be taken over by Nagar Mal. The appellants appealed to the Judicial Commissioner who reversed the finding of the District Judge and came to the conclusion that the other members of their Association were not entitled to participate in the profit made on the sale of 284 bags of Gwalior cotton cloth and that the suit was maintainable for recovery of contributions made by the appellants and also for accounts. The preliminary objection taken at the time of hearing was founded on the provisions of section 4(2) of the Rewa state Companies Act 1935, which provided that no company, association or partnership consisting of more than twenty persons shall be formed for the purpose of carrying on any other business that has for its objects the acquisition Of gain by it, association, or partnership or by the individuals members thereof unless it is registered as an a company. Held, that the provisions in section 4 (2) were not applicable to the case and section 4 was not applicable. The suit before the High Court was not one for accounts of a dissolved firm but for accounts for an illegal association which had been in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked.

The respondents along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. On 25.6.1986 the Range Officer of Forest lodged a written complaint with the Judicial Magistrate alleging offences against respondents under Section 51 of the Wild Life Protection Act 1972 and that the matter was under investigation by the police. The Police filed a charge sheet against the respondents under Sections 447, 429 and 379 IPC read with section 54 and 39 of the wild Life Protection act 1972. The Magistrate took cognizance of an offence under Section 9(1) read with Section 51. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the Respondents. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. When the High Court is to exercise its jurisdiction to quash a proceeding at the stage of the Magistrate taking cognizance of the offence the High court is guided by the allegations, whether those allegations set out in the complaints or the charge sheet do not in law constitute or spell out any offence and that resort to criminal proceedings would, in the circumstances, amount to an abuse of the process of the Court or not. [463C] 2. When a Magistrate takes cognisance of an offi cation instituted otherwise than on a police report and an investigation by it is in progress in relation to same offence, the two cases do not lose their separate indentity. But, where as here cognisance can be taken only in one way and that on the complaint of a particular statutory functionary there is no scope or occasion for taking cognisance more than once and, accordingly, section 210 has no role to play. [462D] 3. When an act or omission constitutes an offence u/s 2(3) of the Contempts of Courts Act, 1953, then the offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be liable for punishment twice for the same offence. In order that the prohibition is attracted the same act must constitute an offence Under more than one Act. This Court said: "The offence of a conspiracy to commit a crime is a different offence from the crime that is the object of the conspiracy because the conspiracy precedes the commission of the crime and is complete before the crime is attempted or completed, equally the crime attempted or com pensation does not require the element of conspiracy as one of its ingredients. [461G H; 462A] 4. The expression "any act or intentionally which constitutes an offen cation under this Act" in section 56 of the Act merely imports the idea tat the same acts or omission might constitute an offences under another law and could be tried under such other law or laws also. Provision as to offences punishable under two or more enactments: Where an act Or omission constitutes a offence udder two or several enactments, then, the offender shah be liable under either of those Acts but shallnot be liable twice for twice for that offence. [ 462C D] In the instant case, the ingredients of the two offences and see whether their identity is made out. Though section 26 in its opening words refer to "the act or omissions constituting an offence" u/S.2(3), the emphasis is not on the facts alleged in the two complaints but rather on the ingredients which constitute the two offence with which a person is charged. This is made clear by the concluding portion of the section which refers to "shall not be liability to be punished twice for tho same offence". [462E F] Bathina Ramakrishna Reddy vs State of Madras, ; , referred to.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, Greater Bombay. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to one of life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (1) the power of the Supreme Court to enlarge a person during the pendency of a Special Leave Petition or of an appeal is very wide, as order 21 Rule 27 of the High Court Rules discloses; (2) if the court decides to grant bail with sureties, what criteria should guide it in quantifying the amount of bail and (3) Is it within the power Of the court to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State ? Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The power of this Court to enlarged a person on his own bond without sureties may not strictly arise. Moreover, an accused in judicial custody, actual or potential, may be released by the court, to further the ends of justice and nothing in section 441(2) and (4) use the word ' bail ' generically because the expression is intended to cover bond with or without sureties. [346E F] 2. The legal literature, Indian and Anglo American, on bail jurisprudence lends countenance to the contention that bait loosely used, is comprehensive enough to cover release on ones own bond with and without sureties; and the definition of bail as given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary: "The process by which a person is released from custody. " [346G H] 3. The law in its majestic equality, forbids the rich as well as the poor to sleep under bridges, to beg in the streets and to steal bread, lampooned Anatole France. The reality of this caricature of equal justice under the law, whereby the poor are priced out of their liberty in the market is the grievance of the petitioners. His criminal appeal pends in this Court and he has obtained an order for bail in his favour "to the satisfaction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate". [346H; 347A] 4. The practice which is now being followed in the United States is that the accused should ordinarily be released on order to appear or on his behalf before the court in criminal cases are so poor that they would and it difficult to furnish bail even in a small amount. [347B C] 5. There is already a direction for grant of bail by this Court in favour of the Petitioner and so the merits of that matter do not have to be examined now. The Supreme Court, therefore, directed release the petitioner on his executing bond in a sum of Rs. An after word We leave it to Parliament to consider whether in our socialist republic, with social justice as its hallmark, monetary superstition, not other relevant considerations like family ties, roots in the community, membership of stable organizations should prevail for bail bonds to ensure that the 'bailee ' does not flee justice. [349E F; 349A] 6. The remedy of the accused is a speedy remedy and he cannot be denied bail on the ground that he has been convicted under section 3(1) of the . [349G H; 347B] 7. The discretion of the court is to be exercised judicially, not capriciously or arbitrarily but in a manner which will lead to miscarriage of justice. It is only when it is found that there is substantial risk it is appearance or there are circumstances justifying imposition of conditions on release.

The assessee, a registered firm, had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 to another concern, the Bombay Fine Worsted Manufacturers ' Castle Mills. In the assessment year 1951 52, the assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in the undertaking. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to 'Castle ' in the computation of capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15 C. An application submitted under section 66(1) of the Act to the Tribunal to refer a question which it was contended by the Commissioner arose out of the order of the Tribunal was rejected and the petition of the Commissioner under section66(2) for an order directing the Tribunal, to state the case and refer it to the High Court was also dismissed. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) Under the Income tax law it is for the Tribunalto decide all questions of fact; the High court has the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of an order of a Tribunal. Such a question may arise out of a finding of the tribunal and also if the Tribunal has misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding. It must however appear that the Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at a conclusion. If the conclusion of the High Tribunal is based upon some evidence ignoring other essential matters, it cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the income of 'Ctastle in the assessment of the assessee may have been a relevant circumstance, but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had relied. Moreover, reliance placed by the Tribunal upon the single circumstance on which its decision was founded had proceeded on an assumption that in the previous year to the year of assessment 1951 52 'C ' had carried on business and had earned income. The observations made by the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner about 431 'Cantle ' being separately assessed at Bombay in the status of a registered Firm apparently refer to assessment of that business in subsequent years and not in the year o assessment of 1951 52.

The Minister concerned, in charge of Irrigation Department, was impleaded as a party to the writ petition filed by him challenging the notification dated January 29, 1974 fixing the seniority of the engineers ner. The High Court directed that the Minister be impleaded as party respondent. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The direction for impleading of the Minister as a Party was given by the High Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, it does not feel persuaded to interfere with the order of the High court adding the Minister. [97 F] 2. The Court is essentially for the Minister concerned to decide in the light of the allegation made in petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. It is essentially on the Minister alone to decide whether he or should file an affidavits. [98 C D] 3. Taking into consideration the totality and circumstances, it cannot be said that the direction for the impleading of Minister as party was given with a direction to apprise him of the alleged allegations made by the petition. [99 E F] 4. The order whereby the Minister was directed to file his personal affidavit is set aside. [100 C D]. 5. The appeal shall stand disposed of accordingly. [The parties in the circumstances shall bear their own costs. M.R. Appeal partly allowed.] 6.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala, on January 7, 1960 for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 259 of the Act on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of movable property of the Respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereupon the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge contending that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to realise the arrears of rents due under a lease 343 under section259 of the . The Sessions Judge accepted the view of the Magistrate and held that rent under a leases could not be recovered under section 260 of the , and made a reference to the High Court under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court, however, allowed the revision petition holding that the arrears due under the lease could not he recovered under s 259 of Act and made the reference to it under section 435 of the code of Criminal procedure. In appeal to this Court by special leave: HELD : (i) The words "rent on land and buildings" which appear between the words "any tax" and "any other money" must equally be governed by the words 'recoverable b a Board or a Military Estate Officer under the Act or the rules framed thereunder. Therefore, the action for recovery can be taken under section 258 with respect to rent on land & buildings provided such rent is claimable by a Board under the . [346 C D] (ii) The right of the Board to claim the rent on lands and buildings does not arise from these provisions under the , or the Property Rules or the Land Administration Rules but under the lessee 's rights to take action for recover it is ultimately traceable to the Act inasmuch as this liability has arisen by reason of the exercise of a power exercised or performance of duty by the Board under express provision of the statute and the Rules. [346 E] (iii) The section does not bar the right of a Board as an owner or holder of land and building to take proceedings for recovery of rent thereof by suit under the general law of the land. Further, by providing for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board 's to recover rent of its land and premises by suit for such rents are entirely outside the section and the right to recover it was ultimately traceable lo the Act so far as this liable is concerned. [347 C] (iv) The word "rent" in section 259 means a sum recoverable under an ordinary contract between the Cantonment Authority and others and that section 259 will apply. It is not intended to be included in that expression in section 260. Apart from section 257 no other provision has come to our notice which can support the view that the Legislature could never have meant that even a suit for recovery would be maintainable at the instance of the board only if it was for the purpose of recovery of ' rent from a tenant who was liable under an express provision Of the Act and the rules to pay rent to the Board. Therefore though strictly speaking, the 350 rent due from the tenant cannot be said to be payable under any express provision in the Act, the tenant 's liability to pay and the Board "s right to recovery it is finally traceable to that Act inasmuchas this liability had arisen by virtue of the exercising of a powers conferred or performance by the board under express provisions of the. Act and Rules.

The appellant was employed as a section salesman in the respondent company. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appellant was employ ed for canvassing and selling the product of the company in his area. The Tribunal also found and in fact it has referred to as an admitted case of both the parties that the respondent Company sells its product i.e cigarettes manu factured by it directly through their wholesalers who in turn sell the product to various dealers appointed by the company. Neither the section salesmen nor the local salesmen or local travelling salesmen were employed in the shop of the wholesaler or any retail dealer to sell the products of the Company and to collect the amount of sale. The section sales men and the local Salesmen and local salesman were employed by the Company in order to canvass and promote the sales of the companies. From 475 perusal of the records produced before it, the Tribunal further observed that the appel lant is required to send reports about the publicity and advertisement of placing posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. Some of the documents relate to matters of publicity in melas, some relate to the existing position of the stock of the goods of the respondent in the area and the action taken to ameliorate stocks. It was not the duty of the appellant to procure orders for the company and none of the salesmen was employed to sell them. The Labour Court further held that the termination of the services of the appe lant by the respondent was legal and justified and if not to what relief he was entitled to. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. [474B] Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah Oil Storage & Distribution Co. ; , D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J. Dechane Distributor vs State 476 of Kerala and others; , ; D. S. Nagaraj vs Labour officer, Kamal & Ors., 1973 FLR (42), P. 441, J J.Decane Distributor vs state 476 of Karnataka and others ; , referred to. 1.2 The appellant is required under the employment to do the work of one of the types of work referred to in the section i. e. manual, skilled and/or clerical in nature. The supervising work of other local sales men was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the areas of his operation. Such a person cannot be termed as a workman is also the ratio of the decision of this Court in Burmah Commissione Shell Oil storage and Distribution Co vs Burmahs Management & Staff; , D S.S Nagraj v Labour Officer Kamal and Ors., ; , J.C. The appellant company entered into a contract of lease with the Gwalior State Government (Sanitary Engineering Department) for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Sampatram. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed Suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. Issue No. 1(1) in that suit was in the following words: "Whether the plaintiff in accordance with paras 5 & 6 of the Plaint was a `gair Maurusi tenant ' and now by virtue of the Revenue Administration and Ryotwari Land Revenue and Tenancy Act of Samwat 2007 has become a `Pakka Tenant '. If so, what is its effect on the suit?" That issue was answered in the negative. The Court held that the Company was not a `pakka ' tenant ' under section 185 of the Code as it had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under Act No. 66 of 1950 and was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182. The High Court also observed that the land held by the Company under the lease was neither Zamindari nor ryotwari land. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 182 of the code is attracted. That section reads as "182. Government Lessees (1) Every person who holds land from the State Government or to whom a right to occupy land is granted by the State Govern ment or Collector and who is not entitled to hold land as a Bhumiswami shall be called a Government lessee in respect of such land". [179E] 2. The term `Phakka ' included Istmurardar tenants, Malikana Haq holder tenants, Hakkiyat Mutafarrikat Sharahyana and Sakitul Mikiyat tenants. An `ordinary tenant ' is defined by Act No 66 of 1951 as "a person holding land from State Government under section 181", Section 181 of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue Code 1959 as " a tenant other than a Pakka tenant and shall not include a sub tenant". The position, therefore was that in terms Of Act No 67 of 1950, the company was not 'a pakka tenant, as found by the High Court in the earlier proceeding. [179G H] 3. Section 183 of the M.P. Land Revenue code is applicable to the land as it has been held by this Court when that came into force. The finding of the Additional Collector is a finding of fact based on evidence and is not liable t be questioned in these proceedings. His finding shows that large amounts are due and payable by the company as rent and that the rents have remained unpaid for a long period far in excess of three months from the dates on which they became due. In the circumstances, the Additional collector was well justified in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 182 of Act. [180B C] 4. The findings of the High court to the contrary were totally unjustified and opposed to law. [181C D] 5. Section 184 of the C.P., Land Revenue Act, Samvat 2007 (Act 66 of1950) is attracted because section 182 provides that the Additional District Collector made his order for eviction of the Company.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such dates or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. By a notification issued on September 25, 1968 certain provisions of Ch. IV were brought into force. By another notification dated December 9, 1965 certain provisions Of the principal act other than those contained in Ch. III and IV were amended. By the Amending Act 15 of 1965 certain sections of the Principal Act were brought in force. The Orissa Land Reform (Amendment) Act 15 Of 1965 was brought into operation by section 1 (3) on the date appointed by the State Government by notification. By virtue of section 37 it was clearly enacted that under any law which provides for the acquisition of any land in an estate under the personal cultivation of the holder, compensation shall not be less than the market value of the land if such land be within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any laws for the time being in force or any building or structure standing thereon or appurtenant thereto unless the law relating to the acquisition was in force at the date of acquisition. The appellant contended that when the principal enactment was enacted it became law in force and the ceiling limits prescribed thereby became effective even though Ch.IV was not extended by a notification under section 1.(3) and since the subsequent legislation seeks to restrict the ceiling area and vest the surplus land in the Government under section 45 as amended, there is compulsory acquisition of land which may be laid only if the law provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the marketvalue of that part of the surplus Land which is within the Ceiling limit applicable under the principal. Held: (i) The expression "law in force" must be "construed only in the constitutional sense and not in the sense of its actual operativeness". (ii)The expression " law in operation" must mean "concluded only" in the Constitutional sense and cannot be said to be in force unless it is brought into existence by legislative enactment or by the exercise of authority by a delegate empowered to bring it into operation. The expression 'law in section 1 means "conveyor". (iii)The word "law" must have been used in the context of the provisions of article 31 A and not the context in which it is used. (iv)The words "in force" in section 2(3), are not intended to be construed as meaning "an Act in a narrow sense but they are merely descriptive of the word 'law". The expression has been used with reference to the constitutional scheme of the Constitution and the amending Act 13 of 1965 were both Acts enacted for ensuring agrarian reform, and the lands held by the appellants were "estates" within the meaning of article 3 A. (v)The definition of "law ' in section 3(3)(b) is not a narrow or pedantic definition but a broad and liberal construction must be given to the word "providing law". The words "law " in force " must be construed in their widest sense and they are not confined to the legislative scheme. (vi)The two Acts are not exhaustive of the expressions used therein, but are merely illustrative of the expression "procure" and "prohibitory law". (vii)The provisions of section 47 of the Travancore Act which by a Notification could have been but were not brought into effect in the present case, must still be deemed to be law in ' force, and since no notification was issued before Ch.

The appellants, who were the reversioners of a Hindu widow, had acquired title by adverse possession against the widow. The widow 's estate was in this case completely extinguished by adverse Possession exercised by the defendants, and she had, in fact, no interest left in her which she could make a surrender of in favour of reversions. The first branch of the appellants ' contention was that as the widow 'S estate was completely extinguished, by adverse posses sion exercised by them she had in fact no interest leaving in her, which she can make a surrendered of in her favour of the reversions and that even though such alienations might not be binding on the reversion _of the reversioners. Held, that the surrender was not an alienation of the widow of her rights in favour Of the reversioner. The reversionary right to challenge it is no part of the estate which is severed from the husband 's property when there is an alienation by the widow, and the reversioner when he takes the estate on surrender takes it subject to the interest already created. If the effect of surrender, as explained above, was to destroy the widow estate in the same way as if she suffered physical or civil death, there is no conceivable reason why the reversioners should not subject to any question of fraud or collusion that might arise, be in a position to recover possession of the properties from (1) Vide Vaidyanatha vs Savithri, I.L.R. Pat. Boys J. in course of his judgment observed: "The doctrine of surrender having been imported into the Hindu law by judicial decisions, it is now well settled that an alienation made by a Hindu wife of her husband 'S property without any justifying necessity or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by reversion against her interest created is to be deemed to be severed from inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widows, the surrender must take it subject only to such prior interest. In the present case no equitable considerations at all arise.

The appellants, a company governed by the (U.P.) Government Industrial Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958 appointed a Receiver in respect of the Cotton Mills Company for a period of six months with various powers specified therein and in particular to seize I lakh of shares of the Polytex Company of the face value of Rs 10 lakhs held by the Cotton Mill Company and to pledge them in favour of the State Government of Uttar Pradesh against a loan for the purpose of meeting the dues payable to the employees of the cotton Mills Company. The requisitionists of the meeting also asked the Polyester Company to treat the said notice as a special notice under section 284 (2) and (5) read with section 190 of the Act for appointment of Sitaram Singhania, Rajaram Jaipuria and R.D. On receipt of the notice, an emergent meeting of the Directors of the company was held on February 23, 1984 to consider the said notices issued under section 169 of the . The Board was informed that a notice had been received at the Registered Office of the Company on 15th February, 1984 from Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. The same was perused and discussed and the following resolutions were passed: "RESOLVED that an Extraordinary General Meeting of the said company pursuant to the requisition received by the Company dated 15th Feb., 1984 under section 170 of the from Swadehi Cotton Mill Co. Ltd. Land Revenue Act, 1901 ( read with Section 5 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Carc Recovery) Rules, 1958, appointing a Receiver for the meeting of its Directors was held pursuant to a notice dated February 11, 1984 issued under Section 169 of U. P. Government Irrigation Undertakings (Recovery) Act 1958 by some of its members. " The Board of Directors of a company shall, on the requisition of such member or members of the companies as is specified in sub section (4), forthwith proceed duty to call an extraordinary general meeting of that company. " On receipt thereof, the Board of directors of the aforesaid Polytex Co. issued a notice under Section 170 of U P. government Electrical Undertakings Act, 1952 appointing Sitaram Singhia and R D.D., a Receiver to call a special general meeting for considering and, if thought fit, to pass with or without modification the following as ordinary resolutions: " REQUISITION NOCE" The Board also asked M/s. Swadeshy Cotton Mills Ltd. (the appellant) to treat its notice as special notice u/s 284 (1) (a) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951 for appointment to vote at a meeting of a Company since it was likely that one or the other member might raise it as an issue at the next meeting. The Board, however, did not call any extraordinary general general meeting and without the support of the shares held by M/S. Swadehy Cotton Mill Ltd. The appellants thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed on the ground that since a Receiver had been appointed by the Collector in respect thereof, he had also been attached, the shares holding by the cotton mills could not be taken into consideration for determining the required qualification to issue the notice under s 169 of Act requisitioning the extraordinary general meetings and that if those shares were omitted from consideration then the shares would not be sufficient to issue it. The High Court held that since the Receiver had already been appointed in respect o the shares in question, he could not take into consideration the required qualifications to issue a notice u. 169 of that Act requisitioning of the extraordinary General meeting and that the requisitionists would not have been eligible to requisition the meeting.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. They instituted a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in possession of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat had no sort of right in the suit property and that the suit lands had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering their possession. The Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High Court, which came to the conclusion that the issues involved in the case were not triable by a civil court by virtue of section 11 read with section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The plaintiffs have preferred this petition under Article 136 of the Constitution praying for leave to prefer an appeal against the decision of the High court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contention that the land in question was shamlat deh confer jurisdiction on the civil court when by virtue section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act the jurisdiction of civil courts to try such suits had been taken away. [835E] 1.2 In the instant case, the Panchayat which had been impleaded as a defendant had raised the plea that the plaintiff had only stated in the plaint that the lands in question belonged to it as shamlat k deh and that he did not belong to the Gram panchayat. The crucial issue which had to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation ) Act,1961 was whether the land was shamil deh or not and whether it belonged to the village Panchayat or not. [861F] 1:3 In the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question is shamlat mallat deh or is not shamlat, the suit had been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the said land belonged to him as shamil k deh. [862G] 1 :4 The High Court found that plaintiff in that case had only mentioned in the Plaint that the property was 'Gali Sheh re aam ' or a throughfare belonging to Gram Panchayat which was being used by the plaintiff as an approach to his house for about 30 years and had prayed for an interim injunction restraining him from interfering with his right. The Gram Panchayat in question had not been impleaded, as a party defendant. [863B] Bhagu & Ors., vs Ram Sarup & Ors. , ; Bhagu and Ors. vs Ram Swarup & Ors.; , ; Ram Sarup and Ors., [1985] Punjab Law Journal Page 366 in which the suit has been held to be maintainable in a civil Court even though the defendant had contended that the Panchayat was entitled to the suit Land. The plaintiff in this case had not claimed that he had the suit 'Gal ' or ' throughfare ' belonging to it, and that it did not belonged to that Gram Panchayat.

The appellant Board had fixed the consumption of electricity for three months. The Electricity Board had to borrow and make payment of interest. This was a condition of supply. The Board had power to demand additional security but the average consumption of three months should be taken as the basis for calculating the amount of such security. The appellant Board did not pay any interest on the security deposit. The respondent Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy and the demand notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Board had no power to impose penal interest at 2% per month for non payment of bills within the stipulated period. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board: (1) The Board has power to recover additional security, but the rate of interest on security deposit cannot be equated with the rate applicable on fixed deposit because the nature and character of a security deposit is basically different from fixed deposit; (2) The clause relating to non payment Of interest was not reasonable. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that there is no legal obligation to pay interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Board in terms of Clause 20(a) & (c) of the General Conditions of Supply. The rate of Interest on security deposited cannot be linked with the rates of interest payable on fixed deposits because the category and character or the security deposited is basically distinct from fixed deposits; (3) The appellant has a right to adjust his tariffs for the purpose of Board 's finance, but this right cannot be denied to him. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumers in trust with the Electricity Board to secure the Board against default in payment of bill. [251F] 1.2 The object of the deposit is to secure prompt payment and is intended for appropriation. [252C] 1:3 The Board entitled to adjust its tariffs to ensure generating a surplus of not less than three per cent even without such specification by the State Government and when the State government specifies a higher surplus, then the Board must ensure generating the higher specified surplus. The condition of Supply requiring a consumption security deposit has a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. [253D] 1 :4 The nature of consumption deposit is such that it represents the moneys of the Electricity Boards. It cannot be doubted that Section 59 requiring the Board to adjust their tariffs for ' the purpose 's finances is to be read along with Section 49 which provides specifically for fixation of tariffs and the manner in which that exercise has to be performed while dealing with any question relating to the revision of tariffs. into force from April 1, 1985 is that the Electricity Act or Schedule VI of the Supply Act that interest must be paid on the securities furnished to the Board. The requirement of consumption security deposited by a consumer in trustwith the Board cannot be said to be unreasonable merely because no interest is paid on it as security deposit by the purchaser. [254F G] 1;5 The nature and nature of use deposit is essentially different from that fixed deposit. It is not possible that if the object of security is to securing payment of arrears, then insistence on cash deposits would be unreasonable because the object could also be served by furnishing of any security and it is said that the consumer was willing to furnish a bank guarantee. In addition, it is urged that the period of consumption for which these security is required should not exceed two months and, therefore, the determination of three month is arbitrary.

The petitioners are working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre of the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They were recruited in four batches in 1965, 1967, 1970 and 1973. The Class I posts in the P & T Department consist of the following posts: 1. Director (Senior Adminstrative Grade) 2. Additional Director (Junior Administrative Grade) 3. Deputy Directors (Senior Class I). The Posts of Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors and S.T.Os Grade I are filled by the following methods: 1010 (a) by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission, (the petitioners belong to this category; (b) by transfer of Group A Field Officers recruited through the P&T Board of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India, (c) by Transfer of Group B Field Officers who are Posts and telegraphs departmental promotees belonging to the Indian Telecommunications Service Group B and (d) by transfers of Group C Field Officers appointed through the union Public Service Commis sioner by written examination followed by an interview, (These officers belong to the P and T Department which is directly under the control of the P. &T. Board of ly Ministry of Communication, Government o f India. The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belonged are not given any Special Pay in these grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is stated that the total number of officers who are thus getting Special Pay is of the order while only about 25 officers who were direct recruits working in the E & T Departments are not give ing any Special pay to the direct recruits also. The petitioners have filed these petitions demanding payment of Special Pay to them also. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1(a) The first question relating to the grant of Special pay requires 1011 to be decided by this Court. It does not mean that persons who are directly recruited and working in tho centre are inferior to those who enter the Centre by transfer. It was interesting to note that the Minister of State for Communications answered the question relating tO non payment of special Pay in the Lok Sabha on March 30, 1982 thus: "Question No. 5864 Wi11 the Minister Of State for Communication answered the ques tion relating to non payment Of Special Pay In the Lok Panchayat on March 31, 1982 thereby: " Question No . 5864Wi11 The Minister of Communications be pleased to state: (c ) whether it is a fact that Special Pay was not given to a few graduate engineers recruited specifically for TRC when the qualifications, functions, duties and responsibilities of these officers in TRC are the same as those of the field officers transferred to TRC and what is the reason for not doing so". [1010 F] Randhir Singh vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to. (b). The Government had virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions duties and responsibility are thesame as between direct recruits and the transferred officials and that the transferred officers have to be paid extra amount by way of Special Re Pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same As the transferred official had to perform in the telecommuni cation Research Centre. Denial of Special Aden sion in the above circumstances to the directing recruits amounts to viola tion of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. Following the decision of this Court in Randhir Singh & Ors. vs Union o India, [Writ Petition Nos. 1309713 176 of 1984 decided today), the question regarding the grant Of Special pay at t0 the same rates to the transferred officer working in that centre with effect from the date on which the transferred Officers have been drawing the Special Pay upto date and to continue to pay it in future also as long as the transferred Officer continues to get it. [1012 F] (c).

The appellant, a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara, was employed as a mamshi in a company governed by the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The respondent framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence and gross negligence of duty insubordination etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry was held on May 15th after receipt of written statement from Nathu. Holding that the charges levelled against him were proved, the employer dismissed the third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965, and the said respondent filed an application under section 78 of the Bombay Act for relief under section 7 8(1) D. The Labour Court after holding an enquiry took the view that the findings of the enquiry officer were perverse, that the order of dismissal was passed by a person not authorised to exercise the power and consequently the Labour Court directed reinstatement of the third Respondent with all back wages. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending inter alia that the third respond ent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application for relief before the Labour court, and prayed that the said order should be set aside on that ground alone. In order to appreciate the scope of the Labour Courts ' jurisdiction under the Act and in particular the attractability of section 78(1D) it is necessary to examine the scheme of the Act as a whole including the provisions relevant for this appeal. The Act suffered numerous amendments from time to time until 1965 when Maharashtra Act 22 of 1965 was passed. The new Act was described as an Act "to extend the Bombay industrial Relations Act 1946 throughout the State of Maharashtra and for that purpose for certain other purposes further lo amend that Act, and to repeal corresponding laws in force in any part of the State". Under section 2 of that Act the BombayIndustrial Relations Act of 1946 as in force immediately before the commencement of the 1965 Act in the Bombay area of the state of Maharashtra was extended to the rest of the States. The Bombay Industrial Disputes Act of 1947 as in operation immediately before its commencement was extended by the President of India, and for certain purposes further to amend that section, and repeal corresponding law in force In any part Of the State. Under section 3(18) an employee desiring a change in respect inter alia of any industrial matter specified in Schedule 11 of which item 6 read "Employment including (i) reinstatement and recruitment" must make an applica tion to the Labour Commissioner. The application was made by an employer intending to effect any change in regard of an order passed by the employer under standing orders which would of necessity include an order of dismiss, discharge, removal, retrenchment, termination of service or suspension as the case may be, and ending on the date on which the Labour Tribunal orders such payment, such sum not exceeding four thousand rupees by way of compensation, regard being had to loss of employment and possibility of getting suitable employment thereafter. Explanation to section 84(1)(d) provides that any employee desiring an change in a respect of an industrial matter enumerated in Schedule II of which Item 6 read with the proviso thereto has to give notice of such intention in the prescribed form to the representative of the employees. Under sub section (2) of section 42 an employee intending to affect any change, in respect Of an order made by the employers under standing order which would be of necessity included an order dismissing, discharge or removal from employment. The scheme of section 7(1), seems to be that a Labour Court is to have power to decide all the disputes covered by paragraph A. As already noted, the Statement of Objects and Reasons (A clause 31 of the Bill which later resulted in Act 22 Of 1965 shows that the underlying dea was to enlarge the powers of the labour court.

The appellants, who were the successors in interest of the lessor company, filed a suit for eviction against the respondents on the ground that they had formed a partnership firm as a result of which a new month to year tenancy was created. The respondents contested the application and raised several points in defence which were rejected by the trial court. The appellants ' revision petition before the Judicial Commissioner was dismissed. The respondent then moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction, inter alia, contending that the appellants ' application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif was not maintain able. The plea was accepted by the High Court and the deci sion of the court below was set aside. The parties led full evidence both oral and documentary. On the disputed issues and after an elaborate trial the learned Munsif accepted the appellants case that they were the heirs and successors of the original lessor and the lessee respectively. He, however modified the decision of the trial Court in so far as the decree had directed that his order would be executed and the respondents would be evicted from the premises on their failure to vacate within the time allowed. The appel lants thereupon moved the High COurt in its revision application contending that they ' application was not maintainable before the civil court, and that the entire proceeding was mis conceived. It was also contended that the application under Section 12 of Act before the Civil Court was not entertain able. On behalf of the respondents it was urged that on the expiry of such a tenancy the only remedy is to file a suit and in any event section 12 is wholly inapplicable in the facts of the case as the respond ents, by their notice, did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. The notice, therefore, was not one under Section12 of the Act at all. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 In view of the circumstances of the present case as discussed below, the proceeding arising out of the appellant 's application before the learned Munsiff should be treated as a suit, and his decision as a decree. It has to be kept in mind that it is the same court before which both a suit under Section 11 and an application under Sec tion 12 are to be filed. But as regards the question of dealing with eviction of tenants under section 11 and extension of period of lease under Section 13, the civil Court is the proper forum. In the present ease, it is not the Civil court, Ranchi which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit or for eviction under Section11 or making an application u/s 12. The question is whether the petition which was filed by the appellants as an applica tion under section12 should be treat ed as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. With the assistance of learned counsel for the par ties, we have gone through the relevant papers in the case and are satisfied that both the parties dealt with every aspect of the matter from their respective angles elaborately and led their full evidence Both oral and conclu sion both oral as documentary and the case was tried by the learned trial court in the same manner as the trial of an eviction suit. The decision of tho learned Munsif is also a detailed one considering every relevant question in the cases. The respond ent 's lost the case once more and moved the high Court but in civil revision application instead of second appeal, presum ably because the Judicial Commis sion after deciding the disputed issue in favour of the appellants instead of confirming the decree of 977 the Munsif directed them to file fresh application under sec tion 12(3) for a formal decree of eviction.

The appellant a registered society filed the suit against the respondent for an immovable property through its then Secretary which was numbered as Suit No. 11 of 1973. The prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as the Secretary of the Society. In support of his claim, he produced certain documents on the basis of which the Trial Court allowed the suit to be withdrawn. According to the case of the appellant, Hari Narain Pandit was not elected as Secretary and had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. Since no notice was given of his application for withdrawal of the suit either to the then Secretary Laxman Das Swami or to the learned advocates Sri Satya Narain Sharma or Sri Shyam Bihari Agarwal, through whom the suit had been instituted, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court. Later, in the next election another Secretary named Jeeva Nand Swami was elected and when he learnt about the fate of the case, an application was filed for recalling the order of withdrawal and restoring the suit which to its file. The request was contested and the trial court rejected the application. The appellant society challenged the order before the High Court by a petition under section 1 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A court has inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it is satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. The principle was correctly discussed in the judg ment in Sadho Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483, pointing out the distinction in cases between fraud practised upon the court and fraud practised on a party. Let us consider the cases in which consent decrees are challenged. If a party makes an application before the Court for setting aside the decree on the ground that he did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the order if it is satis fied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree. However, if the case is of the party challenging the decree is that he was in fact a party to the compromise petition filed in the case but his consent has been procured by fraud, the Court cannot investigate the same in the exercise of its inherent power, and the only remedy to the party is to institute a suit. It was succinctly summed up in the aforementioned case that the factum of the consent can be investigated in summary proceedings, but the reality of the repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to it. However. if the Case of the Party challenging the order is that the he was In fact a Party to the compromises petition filed before the court but his assent has been obtained by fraud fraud, he Court cannot investigation the matter in the exercising of its revisional power, or the only forum to the parties is to institution a suit [237B C] Sadho Shankar Patil and Others v Anant Rai & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.2 In the instant case, the factum that the represen tation can be investiga tion in summary proceeding, but it has declind to exercise its revisional powers on the assumption that it had no jurisdiction to do so. [237D] Sadhho Saran vs Anant Ram Rai and others, AIR 1923 Calcutta 483, referred to In re: Sadho Krishna Saran Rai & Others vs Vayalilakathala Raman vs Vyalil Putu, ; , relied upon. 1.(a) The principle is correctly discussed and applied in the instant cases. If consent decrees were challenged that he Was in fact one party to a compromise petition made to that effect the party has actually consented thereto.

The appellant was charged along with the accused Nos. 2, 3, 5 and 6 with having on or about July II, 1953, transferred by sale 10 High Denomination Bank Notes of the Denomination of Rs. 1,000 each to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi for Rs.1,800 at the rate of Rs 180 per note and thus contravened the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with section 109 Of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was further charged along With the accused No. 2 with having transferred by transfer 10 Highly Denomination bank Notes of Denomination to one V. The trial court convicted him under section 7 read with s.4 thereof and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for six months and to pay a fine of Rs, 200 in default to suffer simple imprisonment for three months. On appeal the High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to one year R. The question for consideration was whether the Ordinance promulgated by the Governor General on January 12, 1946, was in operation on July 11, 1953 when the offence under section7 read with sections 4 and 5 of the Act was committed by the appellant. Held, that the Ordinance in question continued in operation even after April 1, 1946. The law in the State of Jammu and Kashmir with regard to these High Denominomination Bank notes issued before January 13, 1946 was thus brought into line with the law as it obtained in the rest of India. J. J., observed: "The Ordinance in the present case continued in force even after the declaration of emergency having come to an end was made on April 1,, 1946, and was in force right throughout even after that date. The Ordinance in this case continued operation even thereafter after April I, 1946 and was not in operation at all. J J. K. J observed: (i) The Ordinance was in effect in operation only after April 11, 1946; (ii) the Ordinance having been promulgated between June 27, 1940, and April 1. 1946, the date on which the offence was committed was predicated and the adaptations prescribed in the Adaptation of Laws Order 1950, issued under the Constitution of India were made applicable thereto; (iii) the ordinance in question continues in operation till it is repealed; (iv) the law in Jammu and Kahnapur vs The State of Assam ; , followed.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Additional Sessions Judge, on the ground that they had committed murder of a person who was not guilty of murder. The High Court confirmed their convictions. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the sentence imposed against them was neither 'erroneous in principle nor was 'arbitrary or excessive ' or 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion '; and (2) the court had no power to impose death penalty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Court has in Rajendra Prasad 's case held that death penalty is unmerited. [1076C] 2.1 In the instant case, the High Court was justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure being satisfied that there were special reasons within the meaning of section 354(3) of Cr. P.C. and the award of death sentence to the two appellants was neither proper or uncalled for. [1170E] 2:2 The Court is enjoined with a duty to record 'special reasons ' in case the extreme penalty is awarded. But the question whether the death sentence should be awarded or not must, in my view, be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such case. When a sentence of death is passed it is subject to confirmation by the High court under section 366(1) of Criminal procedure 1973 and the accused also has right of appeal to the High Courts under 5. It would, therefore, be manifest that it is neither feasible to define nor legally permissible for this Court to limit or circumscribe the connotation of the expression 'special reason ' occurring in section 354 (3) Cr.P., 1973, nor is it constitutionally or legally permissible to this Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down that on grounds of compassion and humanism the sentence of imprisonment on a conviction for murder under section302, as a rule of universal application, be substituted by a sentence Of imprisonment for life, irrespective of the gravity of the clime as the surrounding circumstances i.e., virtually abolishing the extreme punishment. [1107C E] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar, ; , referred to.

The appellant was compulsorily retired by the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., on 2nd April 1956, and his case was that he had worked to the entire satisfaction of his immediate superior officers and higher authorities and earned a number of certificates highly appreciative of his work. He was confirmed early in 1952 as an Income Tax Officer. The appellant also claimed arrears of salary but he reduced this claim to Rs. 16,561.29. The Commissioner of Incometax, U P., Lucknow, on the basis of a preliminary enquiry held by him, recommended that the appellant should be given a further opportunity to produce nine witnesses in his defence with some documents. On the basis Of a preliminary inquiry conducted by the Deputy Director of Investigation, who was appointed by the commissioner of Income Tax as the Inquiring Officer, the second charge was that the appel lant had made various investments in the name of various members of his family far in excess of and disproportionate to the known sources of his income. The third and last charge gave particulars of thirteen assessment cases in which the appellant was alleged to be either "grossly negligent, careless, inefficient, and/or corrupt in the performance of his duties as Income tax Officer". The appellant 's defence was that a fresh enquiry into the same charges was not permissible under the Departmental rules and was also barred by rules of natural justice. He also pleaded that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by Shri A. Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of income tax, Meerut, by Shri R. N. Srivastava, another Inspecting Assistant Commissioners, who were pursuing the appellant for some unknown reason which he did not find mentioned anywhere. The question whether the appellant ' was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural Justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial. Prejudice to the government servant resulting from an alleged violation of a rule must be proved. The plea that the enquiry was not properly conducted and fully inquired into by officers whose integrity and sense of justice is not challenged, cannot be accepted as correct. A question which could effect the result in a civil suit has to be of such nature that it goes to the root of the jurisdiction and the conduct of the department trial and vitiates the result. It was only after the appellant had his activities had become more than notorious that further enquiry was undertaken and regular charges framed. It would not, by itself, merit a revocation of special leave at this stage after hearing arguments.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that their sales of manga nese ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called M.M.T.C. were complete within the state of Andhra pradesh. The Sales Tax Authorities rejected these contentions holding that there existed a bond between the contracts of sale entered into by the appellants with the M. M.T.,C. and the actual exportation of the goods. The High Court held that these contracts were intrinsically linked and connected and the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of export out of the territory of India. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the contracts between the M/M.M.,T. C. and their foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis indicated that the appel lants ' contract of sale occasioned the export and that the contract of the appe ants with the S.T .C. was integrally connected with the contract entered into between them with M.S.T,C. (2) the appellants were not the last purchaser but the MM. T.C., and (3) the M M.Ms.T C. who was the exporter of goods. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1(a) The contracts between M/s.M/M/T.c. on the one hand and the foreign buyers are two separate and independent con tract of sale. The S. T.,C., entered into direct contract with their foreign buyer. The M.P. Trading Corporation is often the only authorities allowed to export out Of its country. These Corporations enter into direct contracts with their Foreign buyers for export. The directions given by the Corporations to the merchants to place the goods on board the ship are pursuant to the contracts or sale between the merchants and the S .T.D. It has to be appreciated that quite often merchants dealing in goods which are exported out of our country enter into what is called string contracts for purchase of the tipper from the factory or the mines for sale to exporters for sale To fulfil F. O.B contract with a foreign buyer may itself buy the goods F.0.B., Indian port from Indian seller in order to fulfill F.o.B, contract with foreign buyer and this Court in Serajuddin 's case has laid down that the mere mention of F. 0.B price or F.A. delivery in contract between a merchant and the C.T./F.OB. which .exports the goods under a separate contract with the foreign buyer to the latter will not make the two contracts either inte grated or the contract between the merchant and S.S., an F.I.C, an F F.L.B." contract. There cannot be two last purchasers in the sale of same goods within the same State. Similarly there cannot be a two exporters in respect of the same goods. After the decision of the Constitution Bench in B.K. Wadeyar 's Case (supra) the decision in National Tractors case (supra). is no longer good law. In the National Traits case this Court was concerned with the question whether the contracts were integrated contracts in the Course of export or they are different. If they are two different contracts, as they are in the present case, the last purchase within the con tract will pass as it crosses the (1 ) ; 445 ship 's rail. The loading of the said goods is an unconditional appropriation which passes the property. This is not because of any peculiarity of F .O.C B. contracts but because in this type of contract the seller 's duty is to deliver the goods E.O.,B. Indian port From Indian seller to Indian seller In order to fulfil Fo.F.0B.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974. Consequent upon this termination, an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" The respondent management at one stage failed to participate in the proceedings. The reference was heard ex parte and the Labour court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per mensem from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate In the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent inter alia contended that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, the period of probation was extended upto 8th Sept., 1974 and on the expiration of this extended period of Probation, his service was terminated by letters dated 12st October, 1975 with effectfrom 19th Oct. 1974. The Labour Court held that the termination would not constitute retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) read with section 25F of the Industrial Dispute Act. On appeal, the High Court held in favour of the respondent and dismissed the appellant 's writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service of the appel lant was ab initio void and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in service with all consequential benefits, namely back wages in full and other benefits, if any. However, as the Award is to be made by the Labour Appellate Court, it would nonetheless be a retrenchment within section 2 (oo) and in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 25 F, termination was held to be invalid. [532C D] 2.1 The termination was ab legally void and unenforceable and a declara tion is made in that he continued to be In service with full consequential benefits. But there is a catena of decisions which rule that where the termination is illegal especially where there is an ineffective order of retrenchment, there is neither termination nor cessation of service but a declaration follows that the workman concerned continues to remain in service for a period of one year or six months, as he has rendered service for 240 days within a period Of 12 calendar months and indisputably, therefore, his case falls within section 25B(2)(a) and he shall be deemed to bein continuous service for one year for the purpose of Chapter VA. [525E F] 2:2 The termination is ab initio invalid and inoperative. He must, therefore be deemed not in continuous service. If the termination was due to sickness or authorised leave or an accident which is not illegal, a lockout and a cessation of work not due to any fault on the part of the workman are known hazards and there are bound to be interruptions on that account. [435F] 3.1 In industrial employment or for that matter in any service, sickness, authorised leave, an accident, a strike which is neither illegal, nor a lock out and a absence cessation of duty not due by any fault On the part Of the workman, are known diseases and there were bound to have been interruptions.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Commissioner of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. The appointment was on temporary basis and terminable with one month 's notice. On February 5, 1955, the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the settlement officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The Deputy Commissioner by order dt. March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and that in lieu of notice he will get one month pay as required by the Rules. The appellant asked the Deputy Commis sioner to review the order and also submitted a memorial to the Minister for Revenue affairs. Having failed to obtain relief, the appel lant applied to the High Court of Pepsu for a writ under article 226 of the Constitution quashing the order dated March 17. 1965 on the ground inter alia that the order of dismissal from service was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order was at all given. The High Court held that the appellant 's appointment was not in accordance with the terms of employment, and no penalty was imposed upon him, but it set aside the order passed by the Deputy Commi sioners on March 17 and directed the appellant to consider his representation. Held: (1) that the protection of article 31(2) of the Consti tution applies as much to a temporary public servant. By virtue of article 310 of the Con stitution, the petitioner was not liable to be dismissed or removed from service until he had been given reasonable opportunity against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The fact that the holding of an enquiry is not decisive of the question. What is decisive is whether the order is by way of punishment, in the light of the tests laid down in Parshotam Lal Dhingra case and State of Orissa vs Ram Narayan Das ; , referred to. (2)The appellant ' was given no such opportunity and article 311 was therefore not complied with.

The appellant State Government was aggrieved and had filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotions of respondents Nos. 1 to 46 and others as Professors in supersession of their claims of the writ petitioners who contended that they were senior and more qualified for promotion, and that the High court erred in taking a contrary view. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's order No. 643 HTETE dated July 25, 1969 in regard to the appointments of respondents nos. 3 to 46. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) what clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133 requires is that the Commission shall be consulted on the suitability of the candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers; and (ii) on the merits of the candidate for such appointment, promotions promotions or transfer. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government at first framed rules on November 15, 1968, for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. By Notification No. SRO 161 dated March 25,1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professors, which were called the "Jammu and Kashmir Professors of Colleges (Selection) Rules, 1969". The Commission set out the reasons for its decision and finally made its recommendation on merits. The Commission was therefore consulted on tho suitability of candidates for promotion as Professors and the second requirement of clause (B) of subsection (2). [875H; 874A] 2. It is not provided by section 133 that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed all or any of the Candidates, or that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members, so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. No argument to the contrary has in fact been urged for our consideration. Had the Commission de facto abdicated its power in favour of some committee composed of strangers to the Commission the position might have been different.

The petitioner was the Chief Minister of Bihar. The Assembly of Bihar was dissolved by a resolution passed in accordance with the provisions of article 194(3) of the Constitution.
