The petitioner challenged the validity of the said resolutions on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the House of Commons had the privilege of preventing the publication of its proceedings; and (2) that it had the right to prohibit all publication of proceedings a right which the House had possesses with its own history, but never exercised it. Held, that the petitioner was entitled to succeed. The provisions of articles 194(1)(a), (b) and (c) of article 105(3), as amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, do not import into India the law of a foreign country; nor do they either make the existing law subject to the provisions Of any law made by Parliament or declare a particular law to be in force unless modified by Parliament. The power, privileges and immunities of a House of the Legislature of a State and of the members and committees thereof are conferred by the latter part of article 195(3). The powers, privileges, immunities and immunities enjoyed by the House Of Commons of the legislature of a state and of its members and committee thereof are not subject to any law prescribing reasonable restrictions within the ambit of article 19(2) of that Article. Sankari Prasad Singh Deo vs Union of India, ; , referred to. The Legislature has the privilege to prevent the publication or publication of the proceedings of the House or any Committee thereof. It is only when it infringes the fundamental right of a citizen that the law made in respect of the powers, rights privileges and immunity of a member and committees of a house of Commons of Parliament of the United Kingdom has the power or privilege to prohibit the publication thereof. The words "anything done or omitted" in article 194 (3) are wide enough to include all matters which can be said to be done by the Legislature. The word "law" is not defined in the Constitution and it includes any ordinance, regulation, order, notification, rule, regulation or bye law. The expression "law made by a legislature in pursuance of the earlier part of Article 105(2), means an ordinance, ordinance, order etc., which is considered in Sankari Pratap Singh Deo v Union of lndia, ; and the word " law" does not mean any ordinance or regulation. The definition of "law " in article 2(3)(a) includes a ordinance, rule or bye laws made by the legislature. The term "law ' has been defined in section 3(1) of Act 1 of 1951 to mean an ordinance promulgated by the Governor General of India and includes a Ordinance promulgated by him. The said Ordinance is not a law made under article 19 of the Constitu tion and therefore, if the House was of Commons at the commencement of the constitution, i.e., January 26, 1950, it had no privilege to take any action in respect thereof.

The respondents were working as Readers in different faculties in the said College on the date of transfer in the scale of pay Rs.510 860/ whereas the Government scale for Reader was Rs.600 1000/ . On July 30, 1970, the Government prescribed a qualification for appointment as a Reader by a Circular of that date addressed to the Director of Public Instructions (Higher Education) Orissa which appears to supersede the earlier circulars on the subject. The respondents were appointed as Lecturers in Class II temporarily on ad hoc basis for a period of six months with effect from the forenoon of March 9, 1971 or till the appointment was made in consultation with the Orissa Public Service Commission, whichever is earlier; subject to verification of character and antecedents and production of medical fitness certificate. On July 31, 1970 the Government issued a circular superseding the earlier circular on the ground that they were drawing as Reader salary less than Rs. 600/ . The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid circulars. The High Court accepted the Writ Petitions and held that the Respondents were entitled to consideration by the Public Service Commis sion for appointment to posts as Readers under the Government in the manner laid down in the circular of March 23, 1971. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since they had all the requisite qualifications for the appointment as Reader and they were all holding the posts of Reader before the take over, their names were not referred to the Public Services Commission for consideration of their suitability for appointment. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The Respondents are eligible to be referred to. the Public service Commission for the post of Reader. Whether they will be suitable for appointment Readers will be a matter entirely for due and proper consider ment of the Public Serv ices Commission whose recommendations will be considered by the Government In the instant case, the Respondents answering the test of educational qualifications, as well as experience of teach ing in a recognised private college are discriminated amongst the very category of Readers on an irrational and illusory consideration. When a fairly well recognised institution, as in this case run for more than a century, is completely taken over by the Govern ment for management, it is not merely taking over the land and buildings, tables and chairs. It is understandable that the employees had to join the new service under the government, for the first time, and so could be, in that sense, fresh entrants. But to say that the teaching experience of the Readers in the private institution is completely effaced to the extent that they will not be even eligible, on the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government service, for consideration for appointment, as Readers is a seriously issue. [777 E F] 2. The question is entirely different when, as In the present case, it run for less than a decade, is totally taken over over by Govern ment, for management. It was not merely taken over the Land and buildings but also buildings, table and chairs.[777 G H; 778 A B] 3. The employees had ted to join their new service in the Government, for, the first lime, and thereafter so could he, in the sense, new entrants, but could be in that sen iority, fresh recruits. But, to say, that the Teaching experience of Readers in private college is completely imprinted to the effect that they would not be Even eligible, for appointment since Government may not undertake to take over all the employees by maintaining the billabong of a status quo ante.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) of the U.P. State Road Transport Corporation Act, 1948 for plying their vehicles on routes on Khurja Tahsu Chhatari Dabai Rajghat Ramghat route (route for short). The State Transport Authority granted three temporary permits to ply their vehicles. The appellants made applications to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition to the High Court did not meet with success. It was a common ground that in respect of the route a scheme has been prepared and published under section68C of Chapter IV A of the . The route in question is an inter regional route and therefore an application for temporary permit for the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date thereof of publication thereof by the State Government under section 69 C of Chapter V A of Part VI A of that Act has to be made to the state Transport Authority under section 66(1) C. The Corporation applied for only 3 permits. The State Road Authority granted temporary permits on the route. The High Court upheld this view and dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 68 F (1 C ) clearly envisaged a situation where application for a temporary permit is not made under section 67F(1 A) by the Corporation. And there is felt need for providing transport service on the routes in question. [984G] 2. The expression 'any person ' would comprehend any person even other than the Corporation, and one has to read section 68F (1 D) and section 68 E (1 F) harmoniously. If the Corporation applies for temporary licences undoubtedly the State transport Authority cannot grant permit to any one else if the Corporation has applied for all the permits. But section 68 C(1 D), clearly envisaged that a situation when application for an temporary permit was not made by the corporation. And, there is apprehension need for provision of transport service in respect thereof. [986C] 3. The word 'any other person ' in section 68 A means any person who would comprehends any person either even other as the Corporation and one had to read Section 68F( 1 C) and Section 68 E(1 F (A) harmoniously, if the corporation applies for all permits. If it is willing to operate vehicles to the maximum strength undoubtedly the state transport Authority will have to grant permit permit to the Corporation under section 64 F(I A). [986E] 4. The authority under the Act must not ever lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be the service available to the travelling public. While interpreting the provisions of Chapter III A it is undoubtedly true that the Corporation enjoys a preferential treatment in the matter of obtaining permits. [987F G] 5. Section 69 F( 1 D) clearly envisaged the situation where an application is not filed under section 8 C(I C) by tho Corporation. But if the State Road Corporation applies only for 3 temporary permits, once the Corporation made an application to grant such temporary permits it cannot grant to any other person. [98H; 999A] 6.

The appellant, a son of Sarup, filed a suit for declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind his own reversionary rights. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the property inherited by respondent 10 was 'not ancestral property qua the appellant and so it allowed the appeal preferred by respondents 1 to 9 and dismissed the appellant 's suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Under the Hindu law, it is now clear that the only property that can be called ancestral property is property inherited jointly with his father an interest by birth, must be confined to the property descending to the father from his male ancestor in the male line. Sir Shadi Lal, who delivered the judgment of the Board, explained the earlier decision of the Privy Council and held that it was not necessary to express any opinion upon the abstract question whether the property which the daughter 's son inherits from his maternal grandfather is ancestral property or that such property in the hands of a grandson can be given that description. Mahajan J., as he then was, in support of his conclusion that they have overruled the earlier Full Bench decision and proceeded to deal with the appeal on merits. [1107 D E] (ii) The doctrine of stare decisis is not applicable and should present no obstacle in holding that the earlier cases of the Full Bench of the Punjab High Court were not correctly decided. In the present case, however, the question as to whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather was ancestral property could be described as ancestral property. [1108 F] (iii) The decision of this Court in Narotam Chand 's case is wholly unsustainable as a decision on the point of the relevant custom.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum on charges under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them was sitting on the verandah of the hut they were attacked by two other persons with a dagger while the other three held him down. Fortunately, the injury inflicted on Ebrahim Ali did not prove fatal. The jury returned an unanimous verdict of guilt against all the appellants on both charges. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there could be no conviction under section 446 of the Code unless murder has actually been committed. HELD : (i) There can be no doubt that the words "in order to" have been used in section 449 of the Penal Code, but in the two succeeding sections 450, 451 and 457 of the IPC. Section 450 prescribes the punishment for house trespass if it is done "in Order to" the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment. [982 H] (ii) The fact that the murder was not actually committed will not affect the applicability of section 449. [980 D] (iii) There could be a no doubt in the present case that the murders were not actually com pensation under section 147 of the I.P.C. but in some special circumstances as mentioned in section 300 of the Cr. P.C., the punishment prescribed being imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extended to one thousand rupees, or both. Higher punishment is prescribed where house trespass is committed "in" order to 'the committing of an offence punishable under section 450 of the .

The appellant, a Sarswat Brahmin, was the daughter of one of the sons of the last male holder of the properties in suit. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the suit for declaration of title to the lands was maintainable as all the lands in suit were in the possession of tenants, (ii) that there was a custom according to which daughter was excluded from inheritance by the collaterals up to the fourth degree with respect to ancestral as well as self acquired property of the first male holder as laid down in the case of Buta Singh vs Mt. (I) A.I.R. 1913 P.C. 306, and (iii) that under the custom prevailing in the Gurdaspur district a daughter was entitled to succeed to non ancestral property in preference to collaterals even though they were within the fourth degrees. The Subordinate Judge held that the lands were ancestral while the rest of the lands being non ancestral, and that there wag a custom as regards the rights of the daughters to inherit (i), the suit was not maintainable in view of the provisions of the Indian Succession Act relating to succession certificates, (2)that the appellant was a collateral of Gurdial within four degrees, (3) that he was not a collateral or collateral of the deceased at all and (4) that in any case he had fully discharged the onus that was on him by producing in evidence the Riwaj i am of 1913 and consequently the appellant must succeed. The High Court also held that there were no custom whereunder the collateral 's of the father who was the last female holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired properties of her father, and dismissed the cross objections on the following findings: (i). that the appellant had fully discharge the initial onus in two ways, namely (1) by producing the Rwiwaji am of the Gurdasapur district prepared by Mr. Kennaway in 1913 and (2), by adducing evidence showing that the collateralS of one Harnam Singh, who was also a Satesar Brahmin of the Punjab District and indeed a member of this very family of Gurdial succeeded in preference as to his daughter. The appellant contended that in view Of the provisions contained in section 23(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1913, the suit must succeed as all those lands were non ancestral and the respondent had failed to discharge the onus which she could have discharged by adducing additional evidence of particular instances. Held: (1 ) that the High Court was right in holding that the instance relied upon by the appellant is wholly insufficient to discharge his onus that he had been merely producing in proof of the Rawiwaj, i am the truth of which is doubted by the compiler himself in the preface and which stand contradicted by the instances collected and set out in Appendix 'C ' of the same Riwazi am. (2 ) that even if the presumption as to the correctness of the Pwiwaji was weak, the respondent has not cited a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collateral from succession, to the properties left by Harnam Singh even if they were self acquired, might well have been the result, as held by the High court, of some family arrangement. (3 ) that in order to enable the appellant to displace the general custom recorded in Rattigan 's work and to shift the onus to the respondent the appellant should produce a Riwaji i am which is a reliable and trustworthy document. Fateh Bano vs Mt., A. I.R, (1924) P. C. 306; referred to.

The respondent was acting as Managing Agents of several companies registered under the Indian Companies Act. He was also a Director of a number of other companies and had on occasions acted as liquidator of some Com 107 844 panies, as executor or administrator of estates of deceased persons and as trustees of various estates. On 4 7 1949 he applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney marked as exhibit A in the proceedings which he proposed to execute. By that power he empowered Messrs Douglas Chisholm Fairbairn and John James Brims Sutherland jointly and severally to act for him in his individual capacity and also as executor, administrator, trustee, managing agent, liquidator and all other capacities. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Act to the High Court of Calcutta stating his own opinion that the stamp duty was payable on the power for as many respective capacities as the principal executes the power. The Chief Justice with whom Das agreed held that the different capacities of the executant did not constitute distinct matters for purposes of section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 and that the proper duty payable was Rs. Das Gupta, J. agreed, held that in construing the section in the light of that scheme the expression "distinct matter" must be construed as distinct categories. The question whether a power is related to distinct matters is one that will have to be decided on a consideration of the terms of the instrument and the nature and extent of the authority conferred thereby. Held, that when a person executes a power in respect of all the matters in which he could act, it should be held as a matter of law and without regard to the contents of the document to comprise a single matter. The fact however that the donor of the power of Attorney executes it in different capacities is not sufficient in his opinion to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters and thus requiring to be stamped with the aggregate amount of the duties with which separate instruments each comprising or relating to one of such matters would be chargeable under the Act, within the meaning of section5. The words "districtly" are used in the sense of general power of power of an attorney by the donor in favour of the donees constituting the doneers his attorneys to act as for him and in his name and on his behalf. The instrument in question cannot be split up into separate instruments Each comprising or dealing with a distinct matter in so far as the different responsibilities of the donor are concerned. A general power may comprise all acts which can be done by the donee himself, whatever be the capacity or capacities which he enjoys and cannot be divided up into individual acts which the donor is capable of performing whether in his personal capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee or as executoror administrator are also comprised within the instrument. The word "distferent matters" used in section 5 is synonymous with the word "description".

The assessee was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State. In 1948, the Raj Pramukh of this newly formed State instituted the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949. This Ordinance was in force for one year only the assessment year 1949 50. In assessing the profits of the business by the two appellant companies for the year 194950 the Income tax Officer had to proceed in accordance with the provisions of this Ordinance. The assessee 's contention that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words which would have been allowed to him if the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 was in fact in force in the past" as in fact no claim was made or could be made for such allowance, was rejected by the Income Tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Incometax Tribunal took a different view and held that this expression "or which would had been allowed under the Indian income tax Act was in operation in the previous years" did not permit the Income 843 Officer to make any deduction under this bead. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The words "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be applied according to its terms. It was never a law of a Part B State and so depreciation which the assessee availed of under it will not come within the words "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a part B State relating to income tax and super tax. If it does, the depreciation which he availed of tinder the Act has to be deducted in computing the written down value. After careful consideration, we have come to the conclusion that the omission of the word "or" in this paragraph is not by way of ellipsis but a deliberate omission with the intention of including laws which could not be stated to be laws of a whole State and it would be reasonable to think that the words 'any law respecting tax ' would also have been omitted and this part of the paragraph would have read as "all the depreciation actually allow under any law or rules relating to Income tax and Super tax or any law relating thereto. " [228 H] (ii) The expression "any laws relating to taxation on profits" in para 2 of this Removal of difficulties Order must, therefore, be construed in its widest sense so as not to include the depreciation allowed under such laws, even though they were not laws of part B States but of a component State. [228 D] (iii) The word "any Law relating to taxes on profits ' of business ' is also a law relating 'to income tax, and so, depreciation actually permitted under a law pertaining to Income Tax and supertax or tax on profit profits of Business.

The petitioner, a contractor in the State of Karnataka, was awarded contract for construction of a Main Station Building of a Power House at the Raichur Thermal Power Plant at an estimated cost of about Rs. 1.8 crores. The petitioner had also submitted his tender forms for the same. The respondent No. 2 issued a notice inviting tenders for the said works. The peti tioner submitted his bid in the prescribed form and the respondent No 2 issued the tender notice inviting tender. The Respondent No. 3 issued a letter to the petitioner stating that he was willing to accept the tender of M/s. M.C.C., as the M. C.C did not fulfill certain preliminary requirements which, under the Notification Inviting Tenders (N.I.T.), had to be ful filled even before the forms of tender could be supplied to any intending contractor. The contract pertained to the construction of the Main Station building of a power house at the Bellary Thermal Power plant at an estimate cost of Rs.1.8 crore. The Petitioner submitted his tenders in the form of tender dated 3.11989 and the Respondent No 2 also issued a certificate on 4.2.1989 stating that the petitioner had fulfilled the prequalifying requirements set out in para I of the N.I.,T. and that the details called for in para V could be furnished at any time before the final award of the contract. The Respondents No. 1 to 3, who were the tenderers, submitted their tenders on 5.21989 and 6.3.1989 respectively. The respondents No. 4 to 7 issued a notification inviting tender for the works. In response to the said notice, the petitioner submitted his written statement in the negative. The last date for submission of the tender was 11.1 1989. The Court directed the Respondents Nos. 1 and 2 to submit their accounts on or before 30th April, 1989. On 30.4.1989, the Petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification dated 3rd January, 1989 issued by the Respondent Nos. 4 and 7. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that it was only para I that stipulates the pre conditions and that all the documents referred to in the other paras can be supplied at anytime before the contract could be supplies to any person. Hence this special leave petition. Allowing the Special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that there is nothing unfair or arbitrary about the award of contract tO the MCCC. [237E] 1.2 In order to satisfy itself that the requirements of para I(1) and (2) are fulfilled, the K.P.C calls for the certifi cates mentioned in para VI and the fulfilment of the require ment in para l(3) has obviously to be verified by reference to the audited balance sheets called for under clause (a) of para V. It is clear that at least some, if not all, of the documents refer ed to in para IV are intended to verify the fulfilment Of the three prequali tive requirements of Para I. It may not, therefore, be correct to read para I in isolation and treat it as the only condition precedent for the supply of forms of contract. [236F G] 1:3 The delay was only in supplying the details regarding "hollow cement blocks" and to what extent this lacuna effected the conditions in para 1 was for the KP. C to assess. Secondly, whatever may be the interpretation that a court may place on the N .I. T. the way in which the tender documents issued by it has been understood and implemented by the K P.C,.

The appellant was a displaced person from Lahore. She was the owner of a house. The appellant was put in possession of the said agricultural lands in Punjab Khore presumably by way of attornment 1120 of tenants who were in actual cultivating possession of them. Under section 5 A of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, as amended in 1948 and applied to the State of Delhi such a transaction required confirmation by the Custodian. Section 5 B provided that any person aggrieved by an order made under section 38(which corresponds to the previous section 5A of the Act may prefer an appeal in such manner and within such time as may be prescribed to the Custodian General where the original order had been passed by the Assistant Custodian or Additional Custodian was not subject to appeal or revision. The main contention of the appellant was that the application for confirmation which was made by the appellant in 1948, and which remained pending until Act XXXI of 1950 came into force and superseded the earlier legislation in this behalf, had to be disposed of in accordance with sections 5 A and 5 B of the Ordinance. Held, that the order under appeal was one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the Custodian under section 27 of the Central Act. If it was meant to be an open general remand, as the concluding portion of his order seems to indicate, his definite findings on points (1) and (2) which he formulated for himself and the doubt he has expressed in his order about the usefulness of examining afresh the various notifications and directives to which his attention was drawn by the Deputy Custodian would render it difficult for any Custodian on remand to consider any of those matters.

The appellant company was a manufacturer of hardware businesses. Its factory was situated in Bombay and its workmen were getting on well in their business and in their relations with their workmen, and this goodwill manifested itself in ex gratia payments to them of small amounts for a number of years prior to 1965 when trouble began. The claim for bonus for the relevant four years was founded on tradition or custom or condition of service and in that light, the Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. " The appellant company contended that the claim put forward by the appellant before the Tribunal was on the face of it unsustainable on the short ground that what was pleaded was profit based bonus only and, therefore fell squarely within the Bonus Act; that the subject matter of dispute, as referred by the Government, dealt with bonus based on custom or conditions of service. The workmen in their statement had asserted that bonus had been paid for several years and what transpired at the conciliation stages was clear from the letter of the Commissioner of Labour who adverts to the 'usual ' custom and practice of payment of bonus '; that a scrutiny of the accounts of the firms was unnecessary 'since the demand is not based on profits or the financial results of the employers but is based on law ': "The contention of the Sabha that the conditions of services under all these employers should be governed by one standard and one criteria was, not tenable. The Tribunal rejected this contention and held that the demand relating to practice or customs prevailing in establishments before1965 was not such as had to be adjudication and it did not fall within the provisions Of Bonus Act, and that the omission to mention the name of a festival, as a matter of pleading, does not detract from the claim of customary bonus. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the Tribunal 's demand that a sample scrutiny of accounts should be made by the Tribunal is irrelevant in this respect since the demand was not based upon profits or financial results but is founded on custom ': and that it would be subversive of the scheme of the Act to allow an invasion from the flank in that manner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The claim put up by the workmen before the tribunal was, on the facts, unsustainable on this short ground, unsustainable. [616 B] (2) The Tribunal 'has no jurisdiction to try the dispute referred to it. It is true that if the Bonus act deals wholly and solely with profit bonus, it cannot operate as a bar to a different species of claim merely because the word bonus is common to both. It will be seen from the above extract that an additional circumstance has also been insisted upon, in the case of customary or traditional bonus, that the payment must have been at a uniform rate throughout to justify an inference that the payments at such and such rate had become customary and traditional in the particular concern. [613 C D] (3) The letter of law is the body of the law, and the sense and reason of the Law is the soul of the statute '. The story of 'war bonus ', the Full Bench formula and this Court 's view that 'bonus is not a gratuitous payment made by an employer to his workmen nor a deferred wage, and therefore, in later years, such a ground is barred by the general principles of res judicata.

The petitioners who were officiating continuously in the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana for two or three years prior to the appointment of Respondent 3 directly to that service lost their seniority over him by being allotted a date of confirmation which was one day later than the date on which he completed his probationary period. These rules were originally framed by the Governor of Punjab in consultation with the High Court in exercise of the powers conferred on the Governor by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution. On December 31, 1976 the Governor amended Rule 12 by the Haryana First Amendment Rules 1972 providing that seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers, shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmed) and in regard to the rule of seniority, the position as it obtains in the two States is fundamentally different: In Haryana under Rule 12 as amended on December 31. 1976 with retrospective effect from April 9, 1976, seniority was determined by length of ' continuous service on a post irrespective of that date of the confirmation. In Haryana, Rule 12 provided that the seniority of members of service, if direct recruits and promoted officers shall be fixed by the date from which they have satisfactorily completed their probation of to years. On January 31, 1975 the Governor promulgated Punjab Superior Judicial Services (Second Amendment) Rules, 1976 providing that the inter se seniority of direct recruits appointed or promoted officer shall be regulated by the rules framed under the proviso. Rule 12 was amended by clause 6 in the same manner as in Punjab, that is to say, 1038 by providing that 'the seniority of a member of the Service, whether directly direct recruits, or promoted Officers, shall he determined by tho length of the continuous service ' on a Post in the Service irrespective of date of his confirmation. The petitioners who had been officiating continuously continuously in Superior Judicial service of the State as Additional District and Sessions Judges for two/three years prior before the appointment were confirmed in the Higher Judicial Service. These Rules were originally made by the Government of Punjab, in consultation With the High Courts of Punjab & Haryana. Rule 13 provided that seniority shall be reckoned with reference to the dates of confirmation. Rule 14 provided that 'in regard to a direct recruit, the seniority inter se between direct recruits (direct recruits or promotees) shall be the determined by that date. Rule 15 provided for the fixation of inter se Seniority of direct recruitment and promotion of officers in the State. The High Court held that both on principle and logic and in view of the trend of the present authorities it appeared to be plain that the Seniority of the petitioners and Respondent No. 3 therein by reason of the decision of this Court in N. section Rao vs State of Haryana, (supra) was not violative of Article 235 of the constitution and that the High court acted upon the amendment made by Governor of the Punjab on December 1, 1976 in the definition of 'cadre post ' by appointing direct recruits to temporary posts in the Subordinate Judicial Service and that therefore it was not open to the High 943 Court to give an arbitrary date of approval to the promotees. In the meanwhile the Governor revised Rule 12 in the year 1975 providing that "the seniority shall he reckoned with effect from the dates on which vacancies became available to them in the quota of promotees; (b) The petitioners, if they are otherwise fit for confirmation, shall, be confirmed with effect on the dates from which vacancies become available to their promotions in the quotas of promotees and direct recruits as District and Session Judges." In the meantime the Governor superseded that amendment again with effectfrom April 1, 1970 and restored the rule. On September 2, 1977 the Governor again superseded that amended Rule again with retrospective operation from April 1 1970 and restoring the rule to seniority as it existed originally in the 1963 Rules.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, in this appeal filed R.P. No. 1615 of 1984 before the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal contending for promotion from Senior Assistant to Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer, Zonal seniority of Warangal local area comprising of Warnagar, Khammam, Karimnagar and Adila bad is the criteria. The Adilabad division consisting of Adilabad and Karimnagar Districts of the Commercial Taxes Division cannot be treated to be a zone and the divisional seniority prepared by the department is bad in law. It was held by the Tribunal by order dated February 18, 1986 that the zonal seniority is the criterion. Though, for the adminis trative convenience a division consisting o the revenue districts of Adilpur and Karim Nagar may be carved out, for purposes of promotion Zonal seniority has to be maintained. Accordingly, the Tribunal allowed the Representation Petition. The Government of Andhra Pradesh in exercising its power under cl. (5) of Article 371 D annulled that order which had given rise to filing of W.P No. No 3203 of 1989 which was allowed by this Court and remitted to the Tribunal and directed "to examine the legal effect of the Government order in G.O.Ms. No No. 3203 dated January 24, 1981 in accordance with G. O. Ms. No, No. 1503/87 dated April 1, 1982". The Government issued G.0.Ms No. 581 dated April 21, 1987 and directed that "to summon the legal effects of the Govern ment order in the G.Os. No., 3203/89 dated April 18, 1987 in respect of the State of Andhra pradesh empower ing the President, having regard to the requirements of the state as a whole for equitable opportunities and facilities for the people belonging to different parts of the States, in the matter of public employment and in the matters of educa tion, and different provisions may be made for various parts of tho State to make an order in that regard requiring the State Government to so organise it. " No. Para 2(1)(c) inter pretation defines 'local area ' in relation to local cadre thus: "local area" means any local cadre of posts under the State Govern ment organised in pursuance of paragraph 3, or constituted otherwise, for any part of the Sate. " Para 3(1) provides organisation of local cadres: "The State Government shall, within a period of twelve months from the commencement of this Order, organise classes of posts in the civil services of, and classes of civil posts under, the State into different local cadres for different parts Of the State to the extent, and in tho manner, hereinafter provided. No Para 2 (1)(e) inter alia defines ' Local area '. "local cadre" means a local cadre comprising the posts belonging to a category in a Department and located within a specified part of that State. No para 5 declares that "(1) Each district shall be regarded as a local area (i) for direct recruitment to posts in any local Cadre under the state Government comprising all or any of the posts in either department in that district belonging to the category of a lower division clerk or to any other category equivalent to or lower than that of a higher division clerk, (ii) for promotion to the post of Senior Assistants and Assistant Commercial Tax Officers, which are zonal posts common seniority of the Junior Assistants working in all the four revenue districts shall have to be maintain and promotions made in accordance therewith.

The appellant was the manager and Karta of a joint Hindu family. The suit property was mortgaged by the appellant to the respondent Bank for a period of five years. The appellant filed a suit against his son, alleging that he had been subrogated to the position of the Bank. The trial court held that the appellant was not entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants and dismissed the plaintiff 's suit. On appeal by the respondents the High Court held that in spite of the fact that there was no allegation in the plaint that the respondent 's lease had the effect of rendering the security insufficient, the High court went into this question and a calculation of some figures came to the conclusion that the lease of the disputed villages did not in any way render the security of the bank insufficient. It therefore held that as the appellant had in good faith granted the lease for a limited term a fair and reasonable rent, the mortgagee or the purchaser in execution of his decree could not repudiate it specially as the mortgage deed did not prohibit the grant of temporary leases to middlemen or cultivators. The question was whether the appellant 's right to redeem the mortgage was affected by the respondent having no power to lease the mortgaged property. Held: (i) The rule of English common law under which a mortgagor could grant leases is well settled and it is for the lessee if he wants to resist the claim of the mortgagee to establish that the leased property in his favour was granted the usual terms in the ordinary course of management. Such a plea if established and it must not be overlooked that the burden of proof in this matter is upon him would furnish a complete answer to the claim. (ii)The true position has been stated in the following terms by Mukherjee, in Madan Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar, ; , and Balmukund vs Motilal, A.I.R. 1937 P.C. 92, referred to.

Clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the respondent, the respondent is duty bound to appoint an arbitrator. The petitioner sent a notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the Respondent for reference to arbitration. On receipt thereof, the Respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. The learned Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. In appeal, the division bench set aside the order of the learned Single judge and directed the respondent to appoint a arbitrator and on its failure it was open to him to approach the Court for appropriate remedy under section 8 of the Act for appointment. Hence these special leave petitions. Allowing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in allowing the respondent 's prayer to rescind the contract of Arbitration provided in clause 68 of Contract. [362G] 1.2 In view of the clear language of section 5 and 12(2)(b) it is clear that the court has been given power in given circumstances to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed and the arbitration agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked. Thus it could be seen that the Court has the power and jurisdiction under sections5 and 12 to grant Leave to the applicant in exceptional circumstances to revoke the contract. The period of limitation for commencing an arbitration runs from the date on which the cause of action accrued, that is to say, from the day when the claim accrues. [363A B] 1:3 The Court has been conferred power in give circumstances to revocation the authority of the arbitrator 's decision unless the parties have agreed which is not suggested here to exclude that defence. Were it otherwise, a claim for breach of contract containing a reference cause could be brought at any time, it might be 20 or 30 years after the cause for action had arisen, although the legislature has prescribed a limit of three years for the enforcement of such a claim in any application that may be made to the law courts. [365C D] Mustiu and Boyd 's Commercial Arbitration (1982 Edition) under the heading "Hopeless Claim" in Chapter 31 at page 436 it is stated thus: "There is no undoubtedly jurisdiction to interfere by way of injunction to prevent the respondent from being harassed by claim which can never lead to valid award for example in cases where claim is brought in respect of the alleged Arbitration agreement which does not really exist or which has ceased to exist. In these circumstances it is an exceptional case and the courts below have justifiably exercised their discretionary power, and jurisdiction in sections 5 and12(2) (b). [363D E] Musammat vs Mustiyana and Boy d 's commercial Arbitration (82 Edition) at page 435; Pegler vs Railway Executive 1948 Appeal Cases 332 at 338, House of Lords held that just as in the case of actions the claim is not to be brought after the expiration of a specified number of years from thedate on which cause of arbitration accrued, so in the ease of arbitrations, the claim for damages is not, to be put forward after the expiry of a specific number of year period from the dates when the claims accrued. [366E F] Musantiu and Others vs Railway executive 1948 Appeal cases 332 at 337; Pagler vs railway Executive 1948 appeal Cases 332 @ 338, house of Lords, held inapplicable.

The appellants obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of the Act. That property included both Bakasht lands as well as other lands. The Estate mortgaged vested in the State of Bihar on January 1, 1956 as a result of a notification issued under section 3(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. It was contended that the decree could not be executed in view of the provisions of the said Act. Held: (i) The decision of the Full Bench in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh 's case is not correct. The true effect of the decisions of this Court in Sidheswar Prasad 's Case is as explained by Kamla Sahai, J. In that case the whole of the property mortgaged is an estate, there can be no doubt that the procedure prescribed by Chapter IV has to be followed, in order that the amount due to the creditor should be determined by the claims officer and the decision of claims officer or the Board has been made final by the Act; (ii) The words "in the case where the interest of a proprietor or tenure holder is subject to a mortgage or charge" indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under s.3. Therefore in construing section 4(d) it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions Of the Act do not fall within the protection of the section; and again at page 578 "Having regard to the said scheme, it is difficult to confine the application of section 4 (d) only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the estate of the debtor. In fact an execution proceeding to recover the decretal amount from the estate which has already vested in tho State would be incompetent because the said estate no longer belonged to the judgment debtor. "

The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 1023 of 1990 were candidates for the post of Assistant Commissioner, Group 'A ' and who had appeared in Civil Services Main Examination of a subsequent year under the interim orders of the Tribunal for the Civil Services Examinations 1988 or 1989 and have succeeded, are to be given benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the C.S.E. Rules, as amended by Notification No. All those candidates who had been allocat ed to any of the Central Services Group ' A ' or I.P.S., and who have appeared in civil Services Main examination of a later year under interim orders passed by the Tribunal, for Civil Services Examination 1988 or1989 and have failed, are entitled to be considered for appointment to the Indian Police Service (Prelimi nary) Examination held in 1979 and onwards will count as attempts for this purpose. The respondents in Civil Appeals No. 1123 of 1989 who had filed Civil Appeal Nos. 1024 of 1990 and 1074 of 1990 in the High Court, have also filed Civil Application No. 309 of 1989 seeking directions to the respondents that all those candidates should be given benefits of their successful success subject ties subject to provisions of Rules 17 and 17 of C.C.S.(E.S.) Rules, 1987. The Tribunal allowed the applications holding that the proviso to Rule 4 of the Civil Service Examination Rules which insists that a candidate who has already been allocated to the I. P.S./Central Services Group "A" or to a Central Services group 'B ' and whose services have been allocated on the basis of the next Civil Services (Main) Examination, can either join that service or the service to which he has already be allocated on tho basis of his previous C.E., but subject to certain provisions of rule 17, and that the said candidate when allocated to a service subsequently and is appointed to the Service "shall not be eligible to appear again in the Civil services Examination unless he has first resigned from the Service". The High Court also held that the restriction imposed in the second proviso to rule 4 of CSE Rules was in no way ultra vires clause (iii) of Regulation 4 of Regulations, 1955. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the expression "may be allowed to sit at the next civil Service Examination" occurring in Rule 17(iv) of the Code of Civil Procedure is wide enough to include a candidate whose services are allocated to an I.A.S and who has been allocated by the UPSC to the CSCS/Central Services group A 'C ' and that he was permitted to abstain from the probationary Training in order to do so, will become eligible to compete for IAS, IFS, IPS or Central Services Groups 'A" and considered only for those appointments. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The restriction/embargo contained in Rule 4 is not ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution. [46C] 1.2 The restriction imposed by the second Proviso to Rule 6(i) of CSC (E.A.) Rules which is in no manner ultra vires Clause (iiia) of Section 4 of Regulation, 1955 is in any way ultra viola tion clause (iv) a) of Article 14.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by filing a writ petition before the High Court and that application, had been dismissed. The appellant challenged his order of detention on the ground that he was not very much acquainted with him and that he had sought the assistance of a friend at the hearing and for the reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit the request was turned down. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the appellant his case would have been better placed before the Advisory Board, and that, therefore, when the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, the detenu was denied the assistance. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The detaining authority had the assistance and the Deputy Collector of Central excise and a superintendent of Central Excises. In order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer, it does not disentitle him from making a request for the services of a lawyer. [792C D] 2. The rule in A. K. Roy 's case made it clear that the detenu should be allowed the facility of appearing before the Board through a legal practitioner. [789E] 3. The word 'friend ' used there was obviously not intended to carry the meaning of the term in common parlance. One of the meanings of the word 'contribution ', according to the Collins English Dictionary is "an ally in a fight or cause; supporter". The term 'friends ' used in the judgments of this Court was more in this sense than meaning 'a person known well to another and regarded with liking, affection and loyalty. ' A person not being a friend in the normal sense could be picked up for rendering assistance within the frame of the law as settled by this Court. [788E F] 4. The term "friend" used there had been obviously not meant to carry 'the meaning of 'contribing ' according to 'the Collins Law Dictionary is 'an alloy in a right or cause, supporter." [793F G] 5. The words "friends" used therein were obviously not used to carry it the meaning Of the term. One one of the meaning was that person known to another, and regarded by liking. affection andoyalty. [781A B] 6. The expression 'friending ' used therein had been meant to be used in a sense which would include liking and loyalties. [783C D].

The appellants were the owners of certain goods requisitioned by the mills on September 30, 1946. The requisition orders were served on them on September 15, 1946, and they were put in possession on September 10, 1946 respectively. On September 30 the appellants filed a suit for their eviction from the property on the ground that the goods were not delivered to them as required by r. 75 A(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1939, and that the Government which was claiming ownership through the mills was also subject to pucca delivery orders and in view of the usage that pucca delivery Orders were only issued against payment, were passed from hand to hand by endorsement and were sold and dealt with in the market as absolutely representing the goods to which they relate. The suit was dismissed on the grounds (1) that the requisition orders did not apply to the case, because the goods had been requisitioned and acquired were subject to a pucca delivery order and in spite of the use of the said orders the property in the goods passed (see Anglo India Jute Mills Co. vs Omademall ([1946] A.C. 206), referred to. Held, that the notice of acquisition in this case having been admittedly served on the managing agents of the mills it was effected on one of the principal officers of the corporation and 835 would be a good service under 0. XXIX, r. 2(a) of Rules, and as such there was no acquisition following on the service of the notices in this ease. The notice of the decision to acquire was given to the various managing agents on September 20, 1946 and the appellants were not entitled to any relief against the requisition order.

The assessee company was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1963 64 under the provisions of the Companies Sur Profits Act, 1964. The assessee contended that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision, the assessee set apart a sum of Rs. 6,52,000 in its books for the year ending March 31, 1956. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. By the date this appeal was taken up for hearing, another appeal preferred by the assessee relating to the assessment year 1964 65 was also before the Tribunal. That appeal arose under the Companies ( Sur Profits) Act,1964 which replaced the . The Tribunal first disposed of the appeal relating to assessment year 1965 65. In so far as item in question is concerned it held that it was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The High Court answered the same in favour of Revenue and against the assessee following the decision of this Court in Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, , it held: "The distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "In other words the broad distinction between a provision and a reserve is in commercial accountancy fairly well known. Provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and therefore to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand, reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are rep resented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. Provisions are usually shown in the balance sheets by way of deductions from the assets in respect of which they were made whereas general reserves and reserve funds are shown as part of tile proprietor 's interest". (See Spicer & Pegler 's Book keeping and Accounts, 15th Edn. p. 42). " While approving the said statement it was stated in Vazir Sultan: "in other words, the broad difference between the two is that whereas a provision is a charge against the profits to be take into account towards gross receipts against gross receipt in theP.& L. account, a reserve has been in appropriation of profits and the asset or assets bywhich it is represented being retainedto form part ' of the Capital employed in that business". Bearing in mind the aforesaid broad distinction we will indicate how the two concepts are defined and dealt with by the . Applying the said test it must be held that the provision made by the appellant in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under section 23A) was indeed a provision. And not a reserve. The appeal accordingly fails and is dismissed." In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax was made on or before the date relevant to the assess year 1963 64 the said amount cannot be treated as a provision; and that the description given or the Book entries made by it are conclusive. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The question referred to at the instance of Revenue is answered in favour. [111F] Metal Box, which has been followed in Vazazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , relied on. 2. In Metal Box and which has since been followed by this Court it must also be held to be a provision, and not a reserves. [112C] 3. The expression "in the course of business" in section 23(A) is undoubtedly a provision but not a Reserve. The appellant itself called it a provision". It did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve." [111D E] 4. In the circumstances of the case, there must be no doubt that the High Court was right in holding it to be an "provision" and not "a reserve". The appeal therefore fails and dismissed. No costs.

The petitioners in these appeals were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class I) (Engineers ' at places) on a later point of time known as temporary Assistant Officers appointed by the Railway Board pursuant to the authority given by the President of India. The Union Public Service Commission was constituted under the . The appointment authority of the officers was the appointing authority of those officers. There were a host of other factors which distinguished the quality and character of the personnel of the two parallel services as elaborately detailed in Katyani Dayal 's case, including the length of service as a Civil Engineer. While the President was the Appointing Authority of the Engineers, the Railway board was the recruiting authority of these officers as well as the tenure of temporary Assistant Engineers (on a later Point of time), and the minimum educational qualification which was the same for both the services three years experience as a civil Engineer was. additionally required for the aspirants to the I.P.S.C. of Engineers Class 1. This figure in the subsequent years was increased from time to time when in 1975, the figure as increased stood at 25 per year. The net result was that after absorption, 107 officers were residually left unabsorbed in the year 1976 by the time of filing of the connected writ petitions in Katakani Dayals case and they too were finally absorbed in 1979 by what was described as a "blanket order". Before hand on September 17, 1965, the railway Board had taken a decision to the effect that the Officers so absorbed into the Indian Service of engineers would be given weightage in seniority "on the basis of half the total years of continuous service in working posts in Railways prior to their permanent absorption into Class. The then writ petitioners describing themselves as members of the Federation of Temporary Officers Association, Indian Railways joining with them, their President, Vice President and Secretary of the aforesaid Federation as writ petitioners approached this Court by way of a representative capacity to seek relief in their seniority status. The principal claim of the writ petitioners was that officers were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis that they were recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Services Commission, terming it as arbitrary and not permissible under the equality clause in the Constitution. It was contended that the development of law has gone a long way so as to shed the views expressed in Kattani Dayal`s case justifying demolition of the demarcation between the two services made as it was in Katilani Dayal vs Secretary, Home (Police) Department, Government of Bihar & Ors [1988] Supp. 1 SCR 829 and that this Court had struck down the classification of temporary officers separately from the Indian Railways Service of Engi neers into those that were recruited on the same basis of selection by the Union Public Serv ices Commission. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The distinction and the classification between the both services was well marked in Katalani Dayal case claiming the same relief and this time by the Temporary Assistant Officers through a body styled as the Federation Of Directly Appointed Officers (Suppressed) of Indian Railways and a few others, in a representative capacities across which stand arrayed the Union of India and the Railway Boards as respondents. When there has been complete absorption of the Personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be counted from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half of the length service subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprudent now, at this point of lime to dig up old issues.

The Saurashtra State Public Safety Measures (Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1949, was promulgated by the Governor of West Bengal on May 5, 1949. The Act was amended by the Amending Act of 1948 and the effect of which was to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State. Section 11 of the Ordinance provided that "all offences under the Indian Penal Code shall be investigated, inquired into, tried and otherwise dealt with according to the provisions hereinafter contained", and that delegation of such power to the executive Government was beyond the competence of a legislature and was therefore void. The appellant contended that sections 9 and 11 by empowering the State Government to establish a Special Court and to direct it to try under a special procedure such offences as may be notified by the Government in effect authorised the Government to amend section 5 of the Criminal Procedure Code read with the Second Schedule (as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra) were discriminatory in that they infringed article 14 Of the Constitution. Held, that the impugned Act was not violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion inasmuch as it vested in the executive government unregulated official discretion and therefore had to be adjudged unconstitutional. The preamble to the Ordinance of 1948 which is still intact as the later one is only an amending (1) L.R. 476 measure merely refers to the need to provide 'public safety, security of public peace and tranquility in the state. The circumstance that the deviations from normal procedure prescribed in the Ordinance were not so many or vital, as in the Bengal case, does not affect the result, as the defect of absence of a reasonable or rational classification is still there.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 396 I.P.C. and the sentence of imprisonment for life awarded to them by the Sessions Judge, Kanpur in Sessions Trial No. 172 of 1969 in which all 18 accused persons were tried. On the moon lit night of 16/17.2.1968 deceased Mauji Lal (PW 2) and his wife Ram Shree (P.W.8) woke up on hearing some commotion when the miscreants entered the eastern kotha of the house, they were breaking open the northern door P.W 2 raised the wick of lantern, material Exh. P. W. 2,700/ from his house was looted in the night of 17.2 1968 and that in 571 that incident Mauji Lai 's wife (P .W. 2) & brother in law (P.) were injured and P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 about their presence in the eastern wall of the western kothakha when they were attacking her husband and causing injuries to her and carrying away the properties from the house. The deceased Maui Lal 's mother (PW 3) and Ramadhin (A 4) who had seized that lantern has stated in his evidence that it was found hanging on a peg on the eastern side of the eastern Kotha and also while they were attacked by the appellants, ran towards the western wall of northern kothara where P. Ws. 1 to 7 and others were attacking him and causing injury to her husband. The appellants were convicted under section 302 I. P .C. for having committed the murder of Mauji lal 's sister (PW 8) and for having caused injuries to his sister PW 2. The Sessions Judge acquitted all the accused persons but convicted them under section 395 I. A. No. 955/74. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellants under section 397 I. C. P., but reduced the sentence to one of life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) no property out of the properties looted from the houses of the deceased and PW 2 has been recovered from any of the accused and that it is, therefore, not probable that these appellants were seen by P.w. 2; (ii) there must have been sufficient light in the western eastern ketha for P.S.I. to note the presence of the culprits who are stated to have been moving in and out of deceased and P; (iii) no such light was necessary for rejecting the evidence of PW 1 altogether, 7, 8 and 9; (iv) there is no reason whatsoever for not accepting the evidence as of PW 2 who undoubtedly was in the northern ketkha where the main part of the occurrence has taken place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify with the help of lantern which was burning, the appellants who were previously known to her, and (v) there was no reason whatever for not rejecting the prosecution evidence of P. PWs. 1 and 7 and submitted that PW 2 had denied the suggestion that unknown persons came to commit dacoity inside the house and that they had falsely implicated the appellants because she could not recognise the real culprits. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High Court for rejecting their evidence are not convincing. There is no justification whatsoever for rejecting P.M.s. 1 7 and 9. [581F] (2) It is not improbable that PW 7 who had undoubtedly come near the scene of occurrence would have seen any of these appellants in the light of the lantern as well as the moons.

The respondent employer terminated the services of some of its employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. The Labour Court held that section 25F had no application to the effect that the discharge was invalid. A learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for non compliance with section 25 F of the Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the services had been terminated on the grounds of unsuitability and it was not a case of disbanding surplus labour force and, therefore, did not amount to retrenchment. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as 'deemed retrenchment ' for the purposes of notice, compensation etc. [787G] 2.1 In the instant case, the requirements of section 25FFF had not been complied with in these cases. The requirement of section 26F had never been complied. If due weight is given to the words 'the termination by the employer of the service of the workman 'for any reason whatsoever ' are understood to mean what they plainly say, it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of the services Of a workman by an act of the employer. The underlying assumption, of course, is that the undertaking is running as an undertaking and the employer continues as an employer but where either on account of transfer of the undertaking or on account or the closure of the Undertaking the basic assumption disappears, there can be no question of 'ret retrenchment ' within the meaning of the definition contained in section2(oo). [790A B] 2:2 The termination by act of employer even if such termination involved was a consequence of transfer or closing of the undertakings was to be treated as 'retrenchrenchment ' for purposes of notices, compensation and etc. Ltd. vs The Workmen, ; , referred to. 3.1 The expression 'termination of service for any reason whatever ' is understood to include what they really say, It is difficult in this case to escape from the conclusion reached that the word 'retrenched into section 2 (oo) covers every case of termination of services except those which have been embodied in the definition, discharge from employment or termination of servic tion of a probationer would also amount to disboting surplus labour or staff by the employers for any reasons whatsoever. [788B C] 3:2 In the absence of any compelling words to indicate that the intention was even to include a bona fide closure of a whole business, it would be divorcing the expression altogether from its context to give it such a wide meaning as is contended for by learned counsel for the respondents. 'The underlying assumption of course is that 'the undertaking is run as an Undertaking and the employee continues as employer but when either on Account of transfer the undertaking Or on account Of the closure or the closing of his business, the basic premise disappears. There can be a no question to put the clock back or for an anti clockwise operation. Once the conclusion is reached that retrenchment as envisaged in section 3(oo), covers every ease of termination service except those not expressly included in section 25G or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the , such as sections 25FF and 25FF F, it cannot escape the inference that the term 'retrial ' must be understood to have include every terminated of the servicec tion of the workmen. [789E G] 3.3 The expression "termination of Service for any purpose whatsoever" is not defined in the Act but has been used in a wide and ordinary sense.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposed of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act in respect of unconnected or unclaimed goods, and was accordingly registered. The Commercial Tax officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the assessee was not a " dealer". On 6 June 1959 he made an order rejecting the application on the basis that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assesse s 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The assessee applied in revision before the Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes. The Board of Revenue held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assessee and that it was engaged in selling scrap and unserviceable material. The High Court dismissed the revision application on 27 January, 1960. In these appeals by special leave, the question for consideration is whether the assessee Railway in each case is a "business" for the purpose of as sessment under the Act, and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern railway was a "workman" for purposes of the Bengal Reve nue (Sales tax) Act 1941. In the other case, the assessee Eastern Railway dispose of scrap and wasteable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423.

The appellants were convicted of certain offences arising out of the overt acts committed by them. The prosecution case was that the appellants had failed to account for the purchase and sale transactions of securities, in contravention of the manner in which he was to deal with that money. The defence of the appellants was that they had nothing to do with the diversion of the funds of the Insurance Company to the Union Agencies, even though he was a Director of the latter as he never issued instructions regarding the activities of the Union agencies and had no knowledge of the passing of money from the funds. Held, that the prosecution case against the appellants could not be accepted. The appellants were rightly convicted under section 120 read with section 409 I.P.C., and all of them except Vishnu Prasad were also convicted of various offences arising from the overt act committed by the appellants. The circumstances showed that they mentioned Bhagwati Trading Company as that represented the true state of affairs and Chokhani had to inform the Delhi Office of the Bharat Union Agencies about the source of the money he was receiving for the Union Agency to meet its losses. The fact that the securities were being purchased on behalf of the insurance company, in breach of the terms of the contract, did not make any difference as the appellants were not concerned with the transactions and they had no connection with the purchase or sale of securities. The evidence showed that Bhagwati Trading Co., was a director of the appellant 's firm and he was also a Director. The statement of Dalmia that he had borrowed money for the company to pay its losses, from Bhagwati Trading company, was not a case of the securities missing but a case Of the Insurance Companies not getting those securities at all. He also denied the suggestion that Dalmia told him that he would be paid the amount of the short fall of securities and also that he asked him to debit the amount to Asia Udyog Ltd., The prosecution evidence showed the receipt of the amounts from Bhagwati trading Company, but the prosecution evidence was that he did not know what was required to be know by one earring on business for the sale and sale of the shares held by it or could have raised the money on its credit. Held further, that in view of the statement of the Dalmia that the moneys were being paid to the Insurance Co., the Union Bank of India had no information about the diversion. The entries did show the receipt or the amount from Bhagwati Investment Company, and therefore the falsification of the journal vouchers related back to the original diversion of Insurance Company 's moneys to the appellant.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 of 1956 the new State of Bombay which included the territories of the states of Saurashtra and Kutch was formed. The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the former Saurashtra State under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. The newly constituted State of Gujrat found a dearth of experienced officers in the Secretariat transferred them atdiverse times between the years 1961, 1962 and 1963 to the Secretariat and of the Gujarat and 'assigned them duties in connection therewith. Under section 81(1) of the Act it was provided that conditions of service applicable immediately before the appointed day to the case of any person allotted to another State shall not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government. By the proviso to sub section (7) it was further provided that in cases where a person who was allotted to one State could not be absorbed in equivalent posts, he would be deemed to have been allotted to serving in connection With the affairs Of another State and were allotted duties in various districts in Saurashtra and Saurashtra. The officers of the secretariat of the erstwhile Saurashtra and Gujarat were posted in different districts in the former States of Saurashtra, and Kutch. Under s. 81(7) of ' the Act the conditions of services applicable immediately prior to November 1, 1956 were to be varied from their disadvantage except by the previous sanction of the Government. The appellant who was a ministerial officer in the Ministerial branch of the Department moved a petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the government. The High Court held that since the impugned order purported to amalgamate the former and Kutch States personnel with the Gujarat Secretariat Service contrary to the terms of r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules which was mandatory, the orders of transfer to the secretaries which were not made in the process of integration could not operate as absorption under the Allocated Government Servants ' (Absorption, Seniority, Pay & Allowances) Rules, 1957. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The conditions of Service applicable immediately after November 1 1956 were served on the appellants and they were allotted duty in various Districts in Saurashtra,and Kutch. But in the absence of evidence to show that the previous approved of the central Government was obtained, their right to be absorbed into equivalent posts in tho Secretariat could not, therefore, affect the right of the personnel to be appointed in the equivalent posts. [519 E] (ii) The expression "absorption" has not been used in the order but that will not justify an inference that there was no intention to absorb the former or Kutch States and personnel in the secretarial establishment of the Gujrat State Secretariat. [525 F] (iii) Junior Assistants: Appointments shall be made either by nomination on the results of a competitive examination held by the Bombay Public Service Commission, or (b) by promotion from among members of the Lower Division. [511 E] The expression 'absorption ' has not not been defined in the Act but used in its ordinary sense and it is used in relation to the affairs and conduct of the officers concerned. It is a well settled rule of interpretation that where two views are possible, one should be preferred. The first view must be adopted by the Court on a consideration of all relevant facts and circumstances. [500 G] (iv) The second view must also be taken in the light of the broad purpose underlying the proviso. [401 D] (v) The State has the authority to transfer, subject to the Constitution and the rules made under article 309 any public servant to render service which by his training and aptitude he was competent to do.

The petitioners who were dealers in cotton and sell them at a higher rate challenged the constitutional validity of section 5(2)(a) (vi) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The contention was that since the tax was levied, whether on sale or purchase at the very first transaction, the stage was fixed and that the dealer could always claim exemption under section 5 (2)(i) or a refund under section 12 of the Act. HELD: (1) Section 5(1) of Central Sales tax Act, 1957 is not ultra vires the State Legislature. The rate of tax same in every case is from other States or the Union territories any tax to which similar goods manufactured or produced in the State and similar goods imported in the state are subject, so however, as not to discriminate between goods so imported and goods so manufactured or manufactured or sold. [550 E] (2) The levy of tax at one stage either on sale of such goods by the last dealer liable to pay the tax and in the case of purchase tax the stage is purchase by the first dealer liable liable to be paid the tax.
