It is also provided that the turnover of any dealer for any period shall not include his turnover during that period of any sale or purchases of declared goods at any other stage than the stage referred to in sub clause (i). or as the case may be, sub clause(ii) of clause (a). [550 G] (3) The tax cannot be said to be higher in the ease of imported goods. It was not correct to say that a person who is not liable for payment of tax must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claim refund at a later stage. [551 A B] (4) The rate in every ease is from another State or Union territories, any tax which similar sales manufactured or produce in the States are subject so, however, to no discriminate between persons so imported or goods so produced or manufactured.

The appellants, who were the representatives of three original plaintiffs, instituted a suit (being O.S. No. 30 of 1934) in the Court of the District Judge, East Tanjore for enforcement of a mortgage against the present respondent, who was defendant No. 1 and six other persons. The mortgage bond was executed by defendant No 2 for himself and his minor undivided brother, the defendant No, and also as authorised agent on behalf of defendants 3 to 7 who were interested in a joint family business. The suit was contested by all the defendants except defendant No 1 against whom it proceeded ex parte, and there was a preliminary decree passed on May 15,1937, by which a sum of RS. 1,08,098 was directed to be paid by defendant Nos. 2 to 7 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties. The appellants contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to he paid by them under the decree. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the suit was not maintainable because the mortgage was a mortgage debt and indivisible. Arunachalam Pillai vs Seetharam, (1923) L.R. 70 I.A. 222, referred to. The contention of the appellants that the decree in question should not only have stated the amount payable by defendant 1 and that by defendants 2 to7 separately but should have expressly directed ,that on payment Of the amount ordered to be deposited by them together with the payments already made completely wiped off the amount due under the decrees as scaled down by the High court in favour of defendants 2, to 7, was not correct. Arunachalukam Pillai v Seetharam (1924) L R. 70 1 I. A. 222 and Arunachalam Chettiar vs Seethaaswami, (1878) L M.R., Mad. 891, referred.

The City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. The City Civil court was called upon to decide whether the first plaintiff was a tenant of the premises within the meaning of the Act and whether he had lawfully sublet the same to the second and third plaintiffs. The city Civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to try the suit but dismissed the suit on the ground that there bad been no lawful subletting by the first appellant of the Premises to the Second and third appellants as the provisions of section 10 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act No. XIV Of 1947) were not applicable to the City Civil Courts. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the view that the City civil court had no juris diction to entertain a suit in the City of Bombay. Held, that the suit filed by the appellants could not be determined by the City Court. The suit related to possession of the property and the right of the landlord to evict any of the plaintiffs was denied on the grounds that the first respondent was a landlord or a tenant within the definition of the expression "landlord" in section 2(d) of the , and the premises had been lawfully sublet by him to the appellants. The Act specifically provided that nothing contained in sections 28 or 29 shall be deemed to bar a party to a suit, proceeding or appeal mentioned therein, in which a question of title entirely arose out of the . Act or any of its provisions may be determined incidentally. On the other band, in a suit under section 28 the court had to determine all questions relating to recovery of rent or relating to possession and all claims or questions arising out of that Act or of its provi sions. The courts specified in section 28 shall have the jurisdiction to deal with any claim or question arising out Of the Act or anything of its provision, and expressly excluded any other court from having such jurisdiction.

The appellant was a private limited company. On May 26,1955, the respondent transferred his business to the appellant. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba transferred his office to the respondent. The appellant filed a suit for dissolution of its partnership and for an injunction restraining the respondent from appointing him as managing director. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court held that the appointment of the appellant was void in view of section 312 of the . The High Court also took the view that the word "assignment" in the section included "appointment", and so such an appointment would also be void under the section. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent had ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the directors ' meetings, and that the appellant could not be appointed as managing directors by the will of Dadoba. Held: (i) The word "resign" in section 312 is used in two senses, namely, (1) appointment by a director to the office which he previously held but did not hold at the date of the appointment, and (2) appointment made by his will was not an assignment of his office by him for, the old Act contained in section 83B, 340 provisions substantially similar to those contained in sections 255 and 317 of the new Act. The word 'resignatures" in that section is used with reference to appointment by directors. It is legitimate therefore to infer that by using the word 'his ' the Legislature indicated that an appointment by one director to another person under an agreement with the company void unless such assignment was approved by a special resolution of the company. The Act contemplates an appointment of a successor to his office, and it is intended that a certain number of directors would be the chosen representatives of the shareholders. It would follow that the Act contemplates a appointment by the director of another person as director to take his office when made vacant by his resignation or death or the expiry of the term of his Office. The section contemplates an appoint by a directors to the post which he originally held but does not hold in the case of the death of the director, by an appointment made otherwise than by the company in a general meeting, if the articles make provision in this regard. It follows that within the limit as to the number prescribed by the section, a power of appointment of directors can be legitimately conferred by the articles on any person including one who holds the office of a director. It will follow that section was intended to render void a transfer of hisoffice by a Director for, if he had intended only to avoid an appointment from a director of his successor, it would have clearly said so and would not have used the word `assignment '. The rule of construction applied by the High Courts, which enables by raising a presumption, something to be included in the main part of a section by reason of a provision in a proviso to it, has no application to the new section for, here the provision in the proviso has been enacted in the form of an independent section, namely section 313. The words 'assignment of his appointment ' in the present case did not include "appointment" would equally lead to the same conclusion in regard to section 86B. In view of the fact that the power to appoint alternate directors was not given by the old section, it could not have intended to prevent what another section in the same Act made legal. It made an assignment by a partner to another persons under an arrangement with the appellant company void, unless such appointment was approved or disapproved by a Special resolution of a company.

The respondent landlady filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart and were also joined by the respond ent as respondents in the eviction petition on the ground that they had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop to the respondent. The Trial Court held this ground established and passed a decree for eviction as sought by the respondent, holding that the appel lants had unlawfully sub tenants. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. In the appeal before the Appellate Authority under Section 23 of the Act, the appellant contended that the application against the partnership firm was not maintainable without joining its partners as re spondents. It was further submitted that the Code of Civil Procedure was not applicable to the proceedings under the Rent Act either and hence the ratio laid down in the aforesaid decision was directly applicable to it. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellants are before the Court though in a wrong name. In this case no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. [420B] 2.1 The partners of the firm are before Court though, in a proper wrong name, there was no such objec tion at all until the stage were of Special leave and it was certainly not open for the appellants now to raise this contention at this stage at all. This contention must be negatived. [421C] 2:2 In the instant case, no such objections have been raised in the Trial Court or even in the first Appel late Court, it would have been open to him to amend the eviction application and join the partners as resents. [416D] 3:3 The appellants were not before the Trial court or even at the first appellate stage, it was not open open to them to raise the objection at this belated stage and thus delay mattersfor a number Of years. This argument must fail. Although Mr. Nayar wanted us to undertake detailed scrutiny of the evidence and to reappreciate the same, it is not open tO the appellants either to raise these an objection in a very belated stage or thereby delay matter for a period of about 8 years. The contention that there was nothing on record to show that M/S. Adeswar Glass Mart was carried on business at the said premises and that firm was carried for business in that premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business, there is no substance in this contention. There is evidence to show from the evidence that M /s. J.J.J., was carrying on the said business even for a few time during that period. [414E] 3. The respondent landlady has not been able to prove that M.J J. J., was carried out business at that premises and firm was carrying business in it even for several years during which it had ceased lo carry on its business there. Moreover, although a notice was given by the Respondent to the appe lants and M/M. Adarseshwar Glass Judgment of this Court in Chhotelal Pyarelal 's case, relied upon by Mr. Jani, the objection to the main tainability of the petition was raised at the earliest stage and was wrongly negatived by the Trial Judge. In these circumstances, this contention must fail [418F] 3 :4 The appellants have not been unable to prove their tenancy. There was no evidence to indicate that M was carrying out business in them even for few days during which they were not produced.

The Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Act, 1964 was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on urban immovable property and acquisition of such property in excess of the ceiling area and all matters connected therewith or ancillary thereto should be regulated in the State by Parliament by law. Section 10 is the key section which imposes ceiling on holding of land by providing that if the extent of the holding of a person is in excess, of the Ceiling Area, the person shall be liable to surrender the land held in excess. If an individual or a family unit holds land in excess Of the ceiling limit, the excess would have to be surrendered to the State Government. The Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted with effect from 1st January 1975 and it was with reference to this date the surplus holding of the land in the case of a family units consisting of not more than five members shall be an & extent of land equal to one standard holding. It would thus be seen that the Central Act imposes a ceiling on holdings of land situate within these urban agglomeration other than land which is mainly used for the purpose of agriculture and agriculture in this connection includes horticulture, but does not include raising of grass, dairy farming, poultry farming, breeding stock and cultivation or the growing of such plants as may be prescribed by the Rules, and, moreover, in order to fall within the exclusion, the land must be entered in the revenue or land record before the appointed day as for the purposes of agriculture. The lands held by a person in excess were included in the family unit and by reason of section 4 his land whether self acquired or obtained on partition would be liable liable to be clubbed with the land holding held by the other members of the family units not because the partition is invalid but because the land hold by him howsoever acquired was liable to he clubbed together with the lands of others for the limited purpose of application of the ' ceiling area. The land obtained by the divided minor son on partition was liable lo be aggregated with the Land held by other members. The ceiling area in the cases of a Hindu family unit consisting of five or more members, was equivalent to one Standard holding and so also in the ease of a major son. The Explanation requires that the lands held were held by all the members of a Family unit as an undivided minor son and consequently the lands hold by a divided minor sons would have been included in his holding of family unit for the ' purpose of applying the ceiling areas to the family Unit. Both stand on the same footing and a divided major son is as much a member of thefamily unit as a member. The Ceiling area in this case was an extensive one consisting of 5 acres and 6 acres and 7 gunthas respectively. In order to come within the definition of 'vacant land" in section 2(n) (A)(ii), the Explanation requires "that the lands holding held on all the three categories mentioned therein shall be aggregates for the " purpose of computing, the holding", of the Family unit". Both stand together and a division minor son is equivalent to a one standard hold. It will thus be clear that the ceiling in the instant case was not within the legislative competence of the Andhra Pradesh Legislature to provide that the land should be entered into in the Revenue or Land Record before the notified day as provided for by the rules, and therefore, any property which comes to the share of a divided unit would be outside the area of its legislative competence, because it 1156 cannot provide for imposition of Ceiling on urban immoveable property. The contention that merely because an area may possibly in the future be notified as an urban agglomerations under section 2 (n)(A)(iii) of the Central ' Act, the Andhra Act was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competency of the State Legislature, was rejected by this Court.

The workmen who were employed by the appellant company on a regular and proper enquiry in which they had been dismissed from service, applied to the Tribunal for relief under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Tribunal held that all the workmen who turned up on or before October 2, 1953, must be taken back in employment without condition and of the two men who came later, one was ill of typhoid fever and had sufficient reason for reporting himself for duty on October 9, 1953. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the Industrial Tribunal had in each case considered the justification for absence without leave and in view of the circumstance that the men were in custody, the Company was not justified in refusing leave. Held: (i) The Industrial Tribunal having found that the decision of the company to terminate his services was justified, the proper order would have been to give the Company permission to dismiss Chattoraj. (ii) The Tribunal had considered the case of each workman under the four categories mentioned previously and had refused reinstatement to those against whom it found that they were near Burnpur and might have joined earlier, some claimed to come back to their services as of right without any explanations and none of the workmen had done any actual work for the period. The Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, was not a court or Tribunal and in the absence of exceptional or special circumstances or of grave injustice, it could not be justified in interfering with what really was a finding of fact. In September 1953, the dispute was referred to the Fifth Industrial Tribunal which included the case Of Chattorraj there being a suspension order against him. But as the workmen were given continuity of service for the entire period of their absence, they reported for duty and therefore they were not entitled to be taken into service without any condition. The management could not take up the case on merits. If that was the case, then it should have produced the writing which embodied the result of the interview or given sufficient evidence to establish that in each particular case the workmen failed to produce satisfactory evidence of absence. As to Civil Appeal 45 on behalf of the workers in which the prayer for payment of full compensation, it was sufficient to state that no question of principle is involved. The Fifth Industrial Tribals refused to give compensation, for the periods anterior to October 2 1953, on the ground that some of the workman were near Burhanpur and might had joined earlier some claimed claimed to came back to his services as right without anything more than a "more or less indefinite period".

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under Section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Nathawat for the said post. Dr. Urea Kant was appointed as Professor in a department of the Bot any. Dr Shiv Sharma, Dr. Sudhakar Mishra and Dr. T.N. Bhardwaj who were not selected filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challeng ing the appointment of Dr. Uma Kant on the ground that the Selection Committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve list exhausted itself. The Single Judge held that the constitution of the Selection Commit tee was valid but as regards the appointment to Dr.Urea Kant from the reserve List it was held that once the person selected by the Selection Commi sion Committee had joined that post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the person named in the reserve lists could not be appointed against a future vacancy. The Division Bench further held that since once a person selected for the appointment on the post was given appointment and he joins, then selection mad e by the committee is exhausted, and the candidate named in his reserve list could not he appointed against future vacancy, and that once again a selected candidate joined the post then, selection made under the reserve ments list stood exhausted and that the person mentioned in the reserved list could no be appointed. The appointment of Shri Urea was rightly made as the life of the reserve. Allowing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 3(1) of the Act of 1974 lays down that the procedure for the meeting of a selection committee constituted under section 5 shall not be less than five out of which at least two shall be experts, if the selec tion to be made is for the posts of a lecturer or any other post of a teacher equivalent thereto. The quorum required for the meet ing of a Selection Committee for the selection of a professor in BotAny was also adjudged by the selection committee which is constituted for selection of teachers in the university. Thus no fault can be found that the incumbent recommended in the Reserve List by the duly constituted Selection Committee, was not selected for that post of teacher. [421C D] 1.2 The very purpose of preparing a reserve list would be defeated if the view taken by the High court is accepted that once an person selected has joined that office then selection ac quired by the selected committee has joined, that post is filled and some vacancy is caused thereafter a fresh and de novo selection committee 'procedure has to be started because that will be a case of future vacancy after the post had been filled up on the recommendations of the selection Committee. [420D E] 1:3 The very object of preparing the reserve s list would not be defeated, if it is found that there was no violation of section 5 in the Constitution of the Consti tution. [411E F] 1 :4 In the instant case, even the High Courts have arrived to the conclusion that the Committee constituted for the ap pointment of Professor In Bot Any was proper and in accord ance with the provisions of Section 5. The very purposes of preparing reserve list will be defeated. If the view of the High courts is accepted, it would create chaotic situation in the University as all appoint ents so far made from the reserved List will become assail able.

The petitioners were owners of plots of land in areas round about Bombay, commonly known as Greater Bombay. They had all similar but separate grievances with respect to the development plan prepared and published under the Act. In Writ Petition No. 215 of 1966 the petitioner 's complaint was that the list of sites reserved for public purposes was for the first time submitted by the second respondent to the Development Committee on February 8, 1964 showing for the second time that a major portion of the petitioners ' lands were earmarked for recreation centre and for green belt in the development Plan of 'P ' Ward of Greater Bombay and that the order of the Assistant Engineer, Bombay Municipal Corporation rejecting the petitioners proposal for construction of two factory buildings and lavatory blocks should be quashed and a declaration be made that sections 9, 10, 11 12 and 13 of the Act are ultra vires the Constitution of India. The petitioners contended that the reservation and re designation of these lands for recreation centres and green belt was in contravention of section 9 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, as the reservation was temporary though it was not definite. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that sections 4 and 11(3) of the said Act were ultra vires article 19(1)(f) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (i) that the combined operation of sections 4, 5 and 11 (3) would be operative with the result that the acquisition might be delayed for a further period of ten years; (ii) that if the power or discretion had been conferred in a manner which is legal and constitutional, the fact that Parliament could possibly have made more detailed provisions, could not be a ground for invalidating the law. HELD: (1) The local authority must be given a rea sonable time for the purpose and, the legislature thought that a period of 10 years was a sufficient one; section 11(1) empowers the local authority to acquire any land designated in the Development plan for a purpose specified in cls. This provision again is for the benefit of the owner of the land for unless the land is acquired or steps taken in that be. [284 D] (2) The preparation of the tentative plan or the final development plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authorities. The preparation and the final Development Plan were not something what was left by the mind or discretion or discretion. The preparing of the draft development plan in all its stages, it was difficult to envisage what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. [285 E] (3)(a) The State Government must have given a reasonable opportunity to the petitioners before making up its mind to acquire land for a public purpose. It would not be reasonable to place such a restriction on the power of the Local Authority which is out to create better living conditions for millions of people in a vast area. [286 G] (b) The provisions of sections 14, 15 and 16 would again become operative with that result that acquisition might have been delayed for more than 14 years.

The petitioner appeared in person (in W.P. No. 234 of 1968) and section Khanduja, for the Union of India (in C.A. Nos. 1528, 1900 and 2118 of 1968). The petitioner appeared before the Court in person and filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of the award on the ground that there was no territorial dispute as there was a well established boundary running roughly along the northern edge of the Rann of Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps, which needs to be demarcated on the grounds. The petitioner contended that (i) the area in question belonged to the Kutch State and that claim was supported by survey maps, correspondence between the officials of Kutch State, and the British Adminis tration, assertions made in the annual Administration Reports for 75 years before 1947, Statistical abstracts relating to British India, Bombay Administration Reports Gazetteers, Memorandum on Indian States and a number of official publications, and by the Resolution of the Government of Bombay dated 305 February 24, 1914; (ii) the award merely fixes or demarcates the boundary between the State of Gujarat in India and West Pakistan regarding which there were disputes and much friction, and that the area was in different state at different seasons in the year, for part of the year it was water and for the remaining part it was land; (iii) the claim of the petitioner that there is no territorial con stitutional dispute as the area is in different State at different season in the years for part, of the period it is water and that for implementing it amendment of the constitution is involved, and (iv) the compensation awarded by the Tribunal was not adequate. HELD: (i). The territory in this sector is contiguous to and in fact is an extension of the mainland of Sind, and apart from the survey maps there is also no evidence that it is part of Great Rann. [301 D] (ii). The area in this sectors is contiguous. It is not a part of great Rann which has at all material times remained indefinite. There is no evidence of exercise of any such right before or after the occupation of Sind. There being no evidence to show that the inlets were territory over which the Maharao of Kutch exercised sovereign rights and which by merger of the territory became Indian territory, there was an extension Of the main land of Sind and apart therefrom from the Survey maps there was also no material that it was part of this Great Rnann. The claim made by the claimants that in imple menting the award of the International Tribunal an attempt is made to cede any part of tho territory which formed part of its State of Kutch before 1948, or was in de facto occupation and in respect of which sovereign authority was exercised by the Maha Rao of Kutch. [302 C] (iii). The claim of Indian citizens to exercise fundamental rights in respect Of the territory in that sector may be entertained only if it be established that the territory is found to be originally governed by the Bombay Merged Territories Act, 1948. But the claimants ' case was that there will be a cession of Indian territory and the rule earlier laid down by this Court applies if no constitutional amendment is required the.

The mortgagor borrowed Rs. 5,500 from one Rabindra Nath Chakravarty and executed a deed of mortgage whereby he agreed to repay the amount and encum bered his share in Mauzas Bansjora and Simitanr for repayment of the amount borrowed with interest at the rate of Rs. 1/8 per mensem and further agreed that in default of payment, the mortgagee do recover the amount due by sale of his interest in Mauza Bansjuna and Sim Karnrhari. By the mortgagedeed the mortgagor also agreed that the mortgagee did receive the amountdue as royalty from the tenants under mining leases in Mauza Bahaldih in the month of Aswin of the Vikram year and the second in the months of Chaitra. The mortgagor also undertook not to transfer or assign Mauzhatas BansJora and simitanrhari to any person, and had merely assured the mortgagee that he had not assigned the rights in Mauza Bhairandih till the date of mortgage by way of any encumberance to any other person. But that distinction would, for the purpose of ascertaining the true nature of the document, be immaterial, for even in the absence of a covenant not to assign the mortgagor 's interest, so long as the mortgage remained outstanding, the transfer made by the mortgagor of MauzAs Bansjida and Simannrhari would be subject to the mortgage. That may prima facie suggest that those two Mauzos alone were mortgaged but the mortgagor had in the same paragraph agreed that should "any cause of action arise" the mortgagee shall be competent to realise the full amount due to him together with interest and costs by selling Mauz as Bansjuma and Simyanrhari was assigned to strangers many years before those par payments were made. In respect of the mortgage dated August 27, 1922, the Judge held that the claim was within limitation both on account of part payment of principal and interest and upon the cause of actions furnished by the dispossession of the mortgagees in respect of Bahaldh property. The High Court also held that Mauza BahaWih was not given in mortgage to the mortgagees under either of the two mortgagedeeds and dispossession of tho mortgagees from Mauza Baha,ldih by virtue of the sale under the money decree passed against the mortgagor, a cause of Action accrued to the mortgagee to enforce the mortgage and the plaintiff 's suit filed within twelve years from April 14, 1925 was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by the covenants in the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922 a usufructuary mortgage was created on the mortgagor "s interest in Village Bahaldipih" and by the attornment made pursuant to paragraph 7 of the said mortgage, the mortgagor must be deemed to be in possession till the mortgagors interest In Mauza Bahawih by the auction sale which became affective from January 16, 1937, and that the suit to enforce that mortgage was accordingly within limitation. HELD : (i) The right conferred by section 68 is again not a right to enforce a mortgage but a right of sue for the mortgage money on the personal covenant or to claim compensation when the mortgagee is deprived of his security.

The appellants employ as many as 7.000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees to come to the factories from their respective villages, the appellants provided transport which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Alandi or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimpri and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was levied for the transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TodarCo factory at Pimgra and back, and for the Transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to Turi factory, they were charged at the rate of Rs 5 per month. A charge of RS. 2 per month for the transported of employees was levied on transport of staff from Chinvad Village and back and the appellants further averred that these amounts were realised by the appellants only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in supervisory grades. In the course of arguments it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities, there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and Mr. Nariman contended that even if a nominalcharge is realised from the employees that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act, the tax could be levied only on passengers who are carried by a stage carriage which is of the nature of a public services vehicle. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Bombay Motor Vehicles Rules 1959 define 'private service vehicles ' as follows: "Private Service Vehicle ' means any omnibus constructed or adapted to carry more than nine persons excluding the driver and ordinarily used by or on behalf of the owner of such vehicle for the purpose of carrying persons for or in connection with his trade or business, or otherwise than for hire or reward; but does not include a motor vehicle used solely for Police purposes". The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the aforesaid definition. [362G H] 2.1 The term 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules, but that however does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the Bombay Motor Vehicle Rules 1959, it cannot be said that the transport vehicle provided to employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. Thus qua public the employees form a separate class and cannot be so said to be public as contemplated by rule 2(i). [362A B] 2:2 The tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public serv vehicle. It is true that the term 'Public service vehicle" has not yet been defined, either by Act or Rules but that too does not creating any difficulty, because having regards to the preamble of the said Act, it is not necessary for us to go into such meticulous details, because the legal position appears to be clear enough. [363C] 2 :3 The tax can be levied on only passengers who were carried by stage carriage and not on a private service vehicles. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of private company which are given facility not as member of the Public but as held a special Status, namely. the employees in that company.[362D] 2.(i) The word 'public ' has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It could not by any stretch of reasoning be deemed not to include employee of a Private Company who are granted facilities notas members of public but As holding a Special status, viz., the employees, of that Company.

The appellants, who were residents of the locality and had objected to the grant/renewal of a licence for a temporary cinema under the M.P. Cinemas Regulation Rules, 1972, applied for a quasi permanent cinema to respondent No. 3 Prem Narayan son of Ganpatlal Chouksey, proprietor Chitra Talkies, Lalbagh, Burhanpur (M.P.) against which a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution was filed by the appellants. The District Magistrate granted a no objection certificate vide his order dated 10th February 1976 for a period of six months. This licence was renewed upto 30th June 1976 and there was a further renewal up to 30th September 1976. A subsequent application for renewal was turned down by the Distt. Magistrate by his order on 29th June 1977 on the ground that Paras Talkia with permanent cinema licence which was closed, has now been functioning in the locality, and therefore a renewal of the licence for the temporary cinema in the same locality would not be proper. Respondent No. 1 filed an appeal before the State Government which by its order dated 27th December 1977 granted a licence to respondent Prem Narayan, son of the third respondent present appellants under sub section (3) of Section 5 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1974 for a term of six years. This license was renewed up to June 30, 1976 and thereafter there was further renewal upto 30st September 1976 and the same was renewed from time to time. A fresh application for grant of a "no objection certificate" was turned out by the District Magistrate by its Order dated 29th 6 1977 on ground that Para Talkiya with permanent Cinema licence which is closed, had now been running in the area and therefore, a renewal up upto 30 th September 1976 would not he proper. The appellants filed an application for a "No objection certificate". This application was turned aside by the State Govt. by its impugned order dated 29st June 1977. Aggrieved by this order, the appellants preferred a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it on 6th March 1978. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants did not file any objection at that stage "no objections" certificate was granted to the third Respondent. Thereafter, when the second respondent applied for renewal of his licence, the appellant objected to it on the grounds that there was mosque a madrasa and a temple in the vicinity and that the cinema house if permitted would constitute an obstruction and annoyance to the local residents. Inasmuch as those grounds were available to them during the proceedings for considering the grant of "no Objection" certificate, and they did not filed any objection, they cannot now be permitted to plead a right to oppose the grant or a licence. [899B C] 1.2 The appellants had not raised any objection to the granting of a noobjection certificate to the second Respondent but were entitled to be heard. There fore, there is no substance in the grievance that before granting renewal of such licence the State government in the appeal filed by respondent No 3 had not heard them and that such a decision was rendered in violation of the principles of natural justice. [800C] 1:3 The appellants ' objection to grant of no objection Certificate to the fourth Respondent, yet in the Appeal preferred by the third respond ent under sub s (3), of section 5 of Madhya Pradesh Cinema (Regulation of) Rules 1972 relate to the grants of a quasi Permanent cinema licence. When any person desires to erect a cinema meaning thereby a place where an exhibition by means of cinematograph is to be given, he must apply for a no objections certificate in respect of the site where the cinema houses are to be constructed.

The respondent entered into a contract with the appellant for mining iron and manngase ores. The appellant 's offer was accepted by the respondent on September 2, 1957. In November 1957 the respondent wrote to the appellant that the agreement was concluded on September 3, 1957 and that in breach of the contract the respondent failed to apply for and obtain the necessary consent of the central government to the assignment of the mining lease. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant claiming a declaration that they were entitled to remain in possession of the Mining area. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the appellants accepted the offer of September 2 by their plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 and the acceptance was communicated to the respondent before November 6, 1957; and that the acceptance of the offer was communicated before November 1, 1957, and that it was communicated on November 6. The present appeal has been filed after obtaining a certificate under article 133 of the Constitution. It is not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint nor is it usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint through the medium of the Court. In re: Pellatt 's Case, , referred to. Held, that the plaint in the present case was not an acceptance of a tender and the service of a copy thereof along with the writ of summons was a communication of the acceptance. Under the old chancery practice the mere filing of a bill in a suit to enforce specific performance was regarded as sufficient acceptance of 'the respondent 's offers unless the offer had been withdrawn before, the filing of the suit, see Boys vs Ayerst, ; , Fry on Specific Performance, 8th ed. article 306, Pomeroy on Specific performance, 3rd ed., article 306 and Fryon Specific Performance.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K.G Sugar Ltd., (Lauriya). A complaint was registered against them under sub rule (3) of rule 3 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1955 read with section 7 of the Act on the ground that they had failed to pay the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The appellants contended that sub rule 3(3) Of Rule 3 could not have been validly issued under section 3 of Act. According to him the said section 3 cannot be used for controlling the payment of the price, of food crops; it can only deal with foodstuffs; food crops are outside its scope. This contention was negatived by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the regulation of the prices of sugarcane is expressly dealt with by the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 and therefore the power conferred on the Government under section 2(a) could not be challenged as invalid. HELD : (i) The authority altered or amended that law is a competent one. [677 G] (ii) The Authority altered or modified that law was a competent One. The next contention of the appellants was that the Parliament had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture. This argument was again unsustainable in view of Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution which empowers the Parliament to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs. It is not disputed that the Central Government had declared by law that it is expedient in public interest that it should exercise control over foodstuffs. That being so it was well within the competence of Parliament to enact the Act and hence the power confer on the State Government under s 3 of that Act cannot be challenged. [67 D F] Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , followed.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An Order No. CI 58 FMI 69 dated 30th June, 1969 was issued which recited that the Government had on 30th November 1966, issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. The said order stated that the reasons for making the said order of 12th January, 1977 were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th September, 1969 when the order dated 12th June was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concessions constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industrial units requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order of 30th May, 1969. A Single Judge of the Karnataka High Court allowed the writ petitions and granted relief on the ground that the concession granted under the said Order dated 30.6.1969 was being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. The Division Bench dismissed the appeals. In these appeals by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Govern ment of Karnataka that the concessions granted under that order dated 30st June,1969 were being misused, and undue hardship was being enjoyed of the similar. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The Government had, therefore, failed to establish the requisite ground or the basis for which it might be allowed to go on its promise. [948G] 2.1 In order to test the validity of the order granting 30th 6 1969, one has to see the substance of the concession given under the order and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries is by way of refunds of sales Tax paid to the extent provided in the Order, it is clear that in effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of the sales tax/or reduction in the sales Tax liability to the amount stated in the order. In view of this, there is no substance whatever in the contention that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds. [948D E] 2:2 The doctrine ofpromissory Estoppo rises was not attracted in the instant case because, in the facts and circumstances of the case, even on merits the contention raised must be rejected. [947G H] Union of India vs M/s Indo Afghan Agencies Ltd., ; , referred to.

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. A 1 to A 6 were however found guilty for the offence punishable under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C., but convicted them under Section 148 and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A6. The appellants contended that after acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 149 could not be sustained. It was also argued that there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I.p.C.; in any case, apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime. The High Court accepted the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 to the extent it is corroborated by the evidence 6 of PW.3 in so far as the presence and partic ipation of the accused in the attack on the deceased is concerned. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 149 deals with a combina tion of persons who become liable to be punished as sharers in the commission of offences. The non applicability of Section i49 I. p.C is, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants Under Section 7(1) if the evidence discloses commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of them all. PW 1, the wife of the deceased, PW 2, the daughter of the de ceased and there was long standing enmity between the parties. During the last 30 years, there had been murders and rioting between the two factions. The deceased Maddaakhamandas was undergoing life imprisonment for the murder of one of the persons belonging to the group of the said accused. He had come on parole. On the day of occurrence at about 7.00 A.M., when he was passing near the field of A I he was attacked by the accused party. According to the eye witness es, PW 1 and A 3 were armed with spears, A 2, A 4, A 5 and A 6 with knives and A 7 was armed with a stick. All of them way laid the deceased and dragged him into the Tobacco plantation of A1. It is in evidence that the complainant and the accused belonged to opposite factions and there were long standing rivalry between the ac cused and there Was long standing dispute between the con tained parties. The prosecution case from the very beginning was that A 1, to A7, the named persons formed the Unlawful assembly. A 4 was armed alongwith some unidentified person. All the accused undishabilately inflicted injuries on the de ceasei sity with their respective weapons. When the deceased fell down the acused kept on giving him spear, knife and stick blows. The injured was crying for water and when his daughter brought water A 2 caught hold of her and pushed aside. She was also given beating by fists. Thereafter, at the asking of A 2 he gave blows to the deceased on his head. The accused died instantaneously on the spot. Thereafter at the request of PW 1 he went to the Police Station and lodged a complaint. The police registered a case under Section 302 readwith Section 34 I.I.P.,C. against all the accused persons. The assessee was a sub divisional owner of certain properties. The Income Tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500 to tax relying on section 52(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. While Raghvan C.J. agreed substantially with the view taken by Isaac J., the Revenue took a different view and held that in order to bring a case within section 52 sub section (2), it was not necessary that there should be under statement of consideration in respect of the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability of the sub section if the fair market value of the property as on the date of the transferred exceeds the full value of consideration declared by the assessee in respect thereof. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Sub section (1) of section 52 provides that where an assessee transfers a capital asset and in respect Of the transfer two conditions are satisfied ' namely, (a) the transferee is a person directly or indirectly connected with the assessee and (b) the Income tax officer has reason to believe that the transfer was effected with object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains, the fair Market value of such property as is on the day of the transferor 's transfer exceeds the total full value. The provision existing in section 52 of the Act before the amendment (which has now been remembered as sub section 2) enables the computation of capital gains arising on transfer of a capital assets with reference to its fair market Value as on date of its transfer, ignoring the amount of consideration shown by the assesseee, only if the following two conditions were satisfied: (a), the transferee was a person who is directly or directly connected with him and (ii) the income tax officer had reason to belief that the transferred was effected A with the object of avoiding avoidance or reducing the liability. [629 H] 1.2 Sub section 2 of section52 sub section(2), however, provides that the statutory measure for determining the consideration actually received by the assesses and permits the Revenue to take the fairmarket value of capital asset as the full market value as on that date of transfer shall be taken to be the full amount of the consideration declared in respect 'of the transfer. If a capital item is transferred for a consideration below its market value, the difference between the market value and the full price of the considerations received in respect for the transfer would amount to a gift liable to tax under the Gift Tax Act 1958, but if the construction of sub section 1(2)(a) was literally construed as applying even to cases where the fullvalue of the consider ed by the Income 8 Tax officer was correctly declared or disclosed by the asscssee and there is no understatement of the value, it would result in an amount being taxed which has neither accrued to the assessee nor been received by him and which from no view point can be rationally considered as capital gains or any other type of income. [530 H] 2.1 The provision existed at the time when sub section was enacted. It is obvious that if the restrictive condition of difference of 15% or more between the fair price of a transfer and the consideration declare in respect o the transfer is not provided in sub section 3, many marginal cases would, having regard to the possibility of difference in subjective assessment of the fair value, fall within the mischief of that sub section and the statutory measures enacted in that sub s for determining tho consideration actually receive by the assessees would be applicable in all its rigour in such cases.

The appellant was charged with the offence of selling adulterated food. The prosecution case was that the Til seeds sold were unfit for human consumption and thereby committed an offence under section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The two witnesses produced to support this charge were D. P. Tambe and section P. Gaydhani. D.P. Tambbe (P.W. 1), a businessman said that he had gone to "a shop to make purchases", without giving either the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. Under cross examination, he stated that he did not know whether it was a foodgrain shop. He said that when he sold these Til seeds 'o the Food Inspector told him that they were not meant for human use, and that he would be taking "some commodity from the jar" which would be sent for analysis. After this, the appellant who had a grain shop, must have known that the Food inspector could prosecute him if he kept adulterated foodstuffs for sale for human Consumption. If, as the analyst 's report showed, these black Til seeds were full of cocoons, visible to the naked eye, nobody could be expected to purchase them for consumption as food. In order to judge whether the Food Inspectors ' version or the accused 's explanation was more credible, it became necessary to examine the evidence of the only witness produced to corroborate the food Inspector. The appellant denied the presence of D.W., but asserted that he was not aware whether it had been a food Grain shop and that the complainant told him in his examination in chief that the black Tils were only meant for pooja for being burnt like incense or thrown into fire in the course of pooja. The trial court held that the purpose for which the Til plants were kept was quite immaterial, and it was not correct to say they were used only for poojas and not as human food. On appeal by special leave: HELD : (1) It is a matter of common knowledge that black Til seed seeds are not used as food, even though mens rea in the ordinarily understood sense may not be needed to be proved in such cases, yet, the purpose of which articles of food covered by the Act are manufactured, distributed or sold. What is the position in this respect about black Til plants with which we are concerned here? It is true that mens rea is in the ordinary or usual sense of this term is not required for proving an offence defined by section 7 of the hereinafter referred to as 'the Act '. It is enough if an article of adultered food is either manufactured for sale, or stored, or sold or distributed in contravention of any provision of the Act or of any rule made there under. But, the prosecution has to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what Was stored or sold was `food '. The charge was that Til seeds with which the appellant had written on the cash memo when he sell these Til plants 'o were meant, was more probable because it was supported by what the appellant bad written on his cash memo. [330 E G] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to. (2) It cannot be said that this case had been repelled by the mere statement of the Food Officer that they could be used as a food also. Such a statement amounted at least a partial admission that they are used for pojoja and not for human food.[330 E] Bhagwan Dass vs Delhi Admn., ; , followed. (3) It was not necessary to prove that the appellant told him to have only black Tles used for Poojas, and not that it was so widely known a fact that we could take judicial notice of it.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966 on the plea of limita tion. The order of dismissal was communicated to the plaintiff on 19th September, 1960. The plaintiff gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 17.6.1969 asking for a declaration that the order of dismiss ment was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed in the Courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58 of the First Schedule of the . When this appeal came up for hearing before a Division Bench reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in Sita Ram Goel vs The Municipal Board, Kanpur & Ors., ; in support of the contention that the suit was barred by limitation. The Division Bench dismissed the plaintiff 's suit on the ground of limiti tion. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the cause of actions shall be taken to arise not from the dates of the original adverse order but on the date of the appellate order, the suit would be within time. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The cause of provi sions in section 80(1), a person shall be deemed to have availed of all the remedies available to him under the rele vant service rules as to redressal of griev ances, (a) if a final order has been made by the Government or other authority or officer or other competent to pass such order with regard to the appeal preferred or representation made by such person in connection with the grievances; or (b) where no final order had been made, though the remedy has been availed of, a six months ' period from the day on which such appeal was preferred or representa tion is made. The civil court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, therefore, as far as Government serv ants are concerned Article 58 may not be invocable in view of the special limitation. [54D E] 2.1 In every such case only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of proceed ing shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from thedate when the Appeal was filed or representation was made, the right to sue shall first accrued. [55E] 2:2 In the instant case, the claim has been dismissed on the pleas of limitation and our conclusion is that the plaintiff was within time, the judgment of the trial Court, the First 55 Appellate Court and the High Court are set aside and the matter is remitted to the trial court for disposal in accordance with law. [56E] 3:3 In the case of a service dispute that the original order merged in the appellate orders of April 22, 1950, and both the orders in due course merged in that revisional order of April 2, 1950. The operative order is the order passed by the Collec tor, whether it has reversed the original ordi nal or modified it or confirmed it. There, it was held in the case that the decree of the State Government had merged into the order dated May 7, 1949 and both orders in the due course merge in the revisional order. The legal position was not at all referred to or examined.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittoor for his half share in the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father and to this suit he impleaded his father as defendants. His case was that the alienations effected by his father were not binding on him and so his share in all the said properties was not affected by them. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienation did not bind him, upheld all the alienations and dismissed his suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the trial court 's decree in respect of alienations which covered items 2, 10 and 14 in Schedule A as well as item 5 in Schedule B. Held, that the decision of the lower courts was correct. The word "decision" in article 133(1) should mean not a part of the decision but the decision on that part of it. If the judgment or decree of the High court varies the decision in respect thereof it is necessary to consider only that part and enquire whether it is a decree of affirmance or not. There are cases in which more than one decree can be and are passed under the Code of Civil Procedure, for instance, cases where preliminary decrees are passed, but the normal rule is one decree passed in one suit and so it is argued that the appellate decree which confirmed the decision Of the trial Court though on different grounds was in law a decreeof affirmance. If that be so, in deter mining the character of the decree it would be necessary to take the decree as a whole and enquire Whether it is one of affirmation or not; but if that be done, in order to determine the character or nature of the appellate decrees it is essential to consider whether part of that decree should be considered which is proposed to be brought to this Court in appeal. The principle of affirmment on which the provision rests postulates either affirmance, or variation by the appeal court as an act of adjudication and that necessarily means the decision. of the appeal Court on the merits.

The High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of an order of the District Court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act disposing of a revision petition. The High Court possessed exclusive jurisdiction to deal with a revisional order passed by the District Judge under section25, Provincial, Small Causes Courts Act. In 1970, the provisions of section 115, Code of Criminal Procedure read : "115. Revision: The High court may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any court subordinate to such High Court and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such court subordinate appears : (a) to have exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law or (b) to exercise acted in the exercise of its jurisdiction illegally with material irregularity, the High Court may make such order in the case as it deems fit." The amendment made in 1972 added a proviso which declared that in relation to any case decided by a District Judge or Additional District Judge exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes the power of revision under section 24 would vest in the High court. In 1973, the U.P. Amendment Act, 1976 was replaced and the result was that : (i) The High ' Court alone had jurisdiction under Section 115 in a case arising out of an original suit of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above; and 36 (ii) The District Court possessed concurrent jurisdiction under s.115 in cases arising out o.f the original suits of the valuation of Rs 20, 000/ and below, and 36(iii) The Additional District Court had jurisdiction to entertain a revision application under section 5 of the U .P. Act. On the question whether a revisional Order under section 10 of the Provincial Small Causes courts Act is amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Courts under section 114 of the Civil Procedure Code, HELD: 1. The entire sphere of revisional jurisdiction was restored to the High 'Court, no such power being now vested in the District court. [38E] 2. The central principle continues to hold, notwithstanding the amendment effected in section 25 that the hierarchy of remedies enacted in the Provincial Courts Act represents a complete and final order of remedies, and it is not possible to proceed outside the Act to avail of a superior remedy provided by another statute. Bandu Motor Finance (P) Ltd. vs that a revisional power of the district Judge under s 25, U. P.

The respondents were the owners of certain lands belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust , Jaipur for a public purpose namely, for implementation of a development scheme viz. It was not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer Town Planning Department , Jaipur under section 52(2) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for the grant of an appropriate writ , direction or order under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the notification issued under section52 (1). The State Government in its special leave petition have explained that the notification under section 53(1) was not issued till February 8 , 1984 because the Government were primarily thinking of making the land available for construction of residential houses before making provisions for construction or a Three Star Hotel. The respondents contended that they genuinely required the land for starting new businesses in the State to open a branch office at Jaipur and construct residential quarters for their Director and other Senior Executives, but at a later stage they alleged that they wanted to construct a Three star hotel on the said land. Ultimately ,the Special Officer by his order April 9 , 1976 held that the alleged need of the respondents was just a pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was really not needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition on one ground or the other. with these observations, he rejected the prayer of the respondent for release of the land and recommended that the entire land be acquired by the State Government under section 51(1 ) of the Act for the Urban improvement Trust , Jodhpur and forwarded the papers to the Secretary to the State Govt. Town Planning department Rajasthan for issue of the requisite notification under s.52 (2) or his jurisdiction to proceed with the inquiry under section 50 (6) thereof to secure such possession. The State Govern ment in its Special Leave petition have stated that the said notification was duly served on the respondents and they in compliance therewith appeared before the Special officer, Town Planning , Jaipur and filed their reply dated September 8, 1975. In the reply, the respondents while denying the existence of a public pur pose for acquisition of the lands under section 2 52(1), asserted that they needed the said lands to start new businesses and that they were entitled to retain the said property on payment of the prescribed fee for converting the land use from agriculture to hotel business. The Special Officer adjourned the case from time to time and issued several notices to the respondents for personal hearing under section 55(2). Nor did the respondents place any material before the special officer to show that they really needed the notified land for the purpose of expansion of their business activities to the state of Rajasthan. As a result of this , the State Govern ments issued the impugned notification dated February 8, 1984 under s .52 (I) Or the Act and the notified Land vested in the Government free from all encumbrances. The respondent filed an application before the High Court for quashing of the said Notification on the ground that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article226 of the Constitu tion was not maintainable as the cause of action wholly or in part arose within the territorial limits of the Calcutta High Court and therefore the learned Single Judge had no jurisdiction to issue a rule nisi on the petition. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order passed by the learned single Judge of the High court dated March 13 , 1984 issuing a rule on the Petition filed by respondent under article 227 of the Consti tution and the ad interim exparte prohibitory order made by him are set aside and the proceedings before the Calcutta high Court are quashed.

The respondent filed a suit for eviction and for arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation pendent lite and future on the allegation that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises in suit on a monthly rent of Rs. 250 on 7th February, 1972, that the building in question was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2) of the new Rent Act, and that it was covered by the new rent Act. The respondent terminated the tenancy of the appellant. The claim was resisted by the appellant on the ground that the premises was constructed in 1968 and that the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the learned Judge that the new Act had no application to the building was erroneous. The Additional District Judge negatived the defence and decreed the suit for ejectment as also for recovery of arrears of rents and damages. The High Court allowed the appeal in part and set aside the decree of the trial court relating to the recovery of Rs3158 30 as arrears of land revenue for use, occupation pendent parte and future. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the buildings in question had been constructed substantially by funds obtained by the co operative society and the landlord having purchased it through the Society and, consequently, the decision taken by him that the old Act would be applicable to the premises would be erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The building was not ten years old on the date of suit. Then the question arose whether the new section would be attracted if the building completes ten years during the course of litigation. [335B] 1.2 In the instant case, however, the building had become more than ten years ago to be reckoned from the date when their revision petition came to be decided by the High Court and, hence, the question assumes importance in the present case. The trial court, however relying on a recent decision of this Court in Om Prakash Gupta vs Dig Vijendrapal Gupta, ; , held that it is the date on which the building shall be deemed to have been completed on the day of assessment which was 1st October 1971. [340C D] 2.1 In the present ease, however the building has become more ten years ' old to be computed from the dates of completion, the new Section would become applicable. Admittedly the building is not ten year old on that date. Then, the questions assumes importance and in this case it may be argued that the Court had to decide the case on the basis of cause of action that accrued prior to the date Of filing the suit and not on a new cause of actions, but this question need not detain as it is covered by decision of the Supreme Court in Pasupati Venkateswrlu vs Motor & General Traders. [1985] Supp. SCC p. 891; Pasupati Rameshwrarama Rao vs Andhra Pradesh Housing Board, ; and Om Prakash Agarwalla vs Digav Gupta, , referred to.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. After the above works were completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and eventually by an agreement dated February 6, 1948, they were referred to arbitration of one Col. A. W. section Smith. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948 and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The appellant contended that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date, and it was therefore void, that the award passed in proceedings founded thereon was a nullity and that no decree should be passed in terms thereof. Held: (i) The agreement dated January 6,1948, was executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor, and in consequence there was a valid reference to an arbitration. It was not a copy of the Award. What the arbitrator did was to prepare the award in triplicate, sign all of them and send one each to the party and the third to the court. This would be an original instrument, and the words "certified copy" appearing thereon were a mis description and cannot have the effect of altering the true character of the instrument. There is no substance in this contention either. The law was no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated: That was held in The State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., ; , followed. (ii)The words " certified copy" occurring in section 175 (3) are not intended to convey a different meaning and can have the same meaning as used in section 35 of the Stamp Act. The words " Certified copy" appear in the section itself to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person, and when that is established the requirements must be held to be satisfied. In the present case the copy was not produced in court. The copy of it which was sent to the respondents was said to have been seized by the police along with other papers and was not now available. When the third copy was received in Court, the respondents paid the requisite stamp duty under section 35 Of the Stamp .

The respondent, a Superintending Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab, was working as Executive Engineer in the Public Works department in the year 1979. On various dates in that year some complaints were received against him pertaining to the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforesaid orders. In the year 1980 some complaints relating to the purchases of sign Boards were received in the Department against the respondent pertaining to his purchase of the sign boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged on August 27, 1985 against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. In that meantime, the respondent retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The aforesaid First Information Reports were challenged by the respondent in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Criminal Miscellaneous No. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules has been misinterpreted by the High Courts in holding that the said rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said Rule and the High court committed an error of law in taking the view. It is also contended that keeping in view the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule 2, the said Rules cannot be interpreted to be a rule placing an embargo upon prosecution of government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. PG NO 917 PG NO 933 PG NO 930 PG NO 925 The respondents submitted that the view taken by the Punjab High Court was correct and in view of Rule2.2, the First Information report against Kailash Nath and the prosecution as against Mangal Singh Minhas were rightly quashed. In order to appreciate the respective submissions made by learned counsel for the parties with regard to the scope and interpretation of Rule (2), it would be useful to extract the relevant portion of sub rule (b) of Rule 1.2. (3) No such judicial proceedings, if not instituted while the officer was in service, whether before his retirement or during his re employment shall be instituted in respect of a cause of Action which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution. If a rule containing an absolute or general embargo on prosecution of Government servant after his retirement for grave misconduct or negligence during the course of the service does not fall within the purview of laying down conditions of service under Article 309, such a provision cannot in the purported exercise of power under Article 311 be made by either incorporating it in the substantive clause of a rule or in the proviso thereto. In view of what has been said above and keeping in mind the scope for Rule making power under article 309 and the purpose for Rule 2(2), there is no doubt with regard regard to interpretation of the said rules. [917G H; 918A] The question whether the said r.2 can be interpreted as laying down an absolute and general embargo upon Prosecution of a Government servant, if the condition stated therein is satisfied. The embargo on prosecutions spelt out by theHigh Court is not to be found in the main rule 2.3 but in the third proviso to the said clause. It cannot be construed as laying it down an unqualified or general ban on prosecution for government servants if the Conditions stated therein were satisfied.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. 100/each and the issued and paid up capital was 2,500 ordinary and 3.000 preference share shares. The respondent company took over the business conducted by it for Rs. 5,50,0001 paid in the form of 2, 500 ordinary and three,000 preferences fully paid up shares. This company was managed by a firm which after the death of 12 Nageswara Rao Panthuluulu consisted of Ramayamma, widow of Nageswara Rhnamma, Kamakashamma, his daughter, Ramayalaamma 's brother Ramchandra Rao and Kamakhamma ma 's husband Sambu Prasad. Under the Articles of Association of the Company both preference and ordinary shareholders were entitled to vote at the meeting of the respondent company each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings of the Respondent company, the Income tax Officer found that for the three years ending March 31, 1947, March 31. 1948 and March 31 1949 the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on the preference shares and 61 per cent of the amount available for distribution as computed under section 23 A of the Income Tax Act. As it stood at the material time no order could be passed in respect of any company in which the public were substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company was held by the respondent, or by the nominees thereof. The third question which alone is material in these appeals was whether the provisions of section 23A were correctly applied for the two relevant years.
