Held: (i) Where there is no individual member or a group of shareholders acting in concert holding fifty one per cent or more of the voting power, which controls the working of a company, it is from its very nature a company in Which there isno controlling member or group and therefore the public are substantially interested; (ii) where a shareholder holds or a Group of shareholders act in concert hold 50 per cent share or more or of the shares entitled to a fixed rate of dividend have to be ignored. But the Legislature by the Explanation has raised a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares of the companies carrying not less than twenty five per cent Of the voting right are held by persons other than the controlling group, the shares yielding a fixed percentage of the votes power is allotted unconditionally to or is acquired unconditionally by or is beneficially held by public; (iii) Where not less then fifty percent of the shareholders ' voting rights are held in shares entitled lo a fixed dividend carrying not more than twenty per cent. Of the ordinary shares. In assessing whether the share in fact there exists such a control ling interest in the hands of one shareholder or a groups of shareholders as would render the company one in which, the public is substantially interested, is a question to which no attention was paid by the Tribunal. Whether in fact, there exists any such a controlling interest in a group Of persons. so as to bring the case within the third proviso.

The appellants were convicted under sections 7 and 9 of the Essential Supplies Act on two counts. The first appellant was a registered joint stock company, the Seksaria Mills Ltd., which was fined Rs. 10,000 on each of the two counts, that is to say, a total fine of Rs. 20,000 and this was upheld in appeal. The second appellant was the General Manager of the Mills. He was sentenced to two months ' rigorous imprisonment and to a fine of RS. 2,00,000. This has been upheld by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the sale was not on record but was made in the course of the trial; (2) the entry in column 3 was not intended to be confined to quota holders or their agents but means what it says, namely, the person to whom delivery was made, who may be. HELD : The goods did reach the quotaholder in the end, or rather his proper agent, and the record amply bears it out that this godown belonged to Dwarkadas Khetan. [835 D] (1)(a) The entry in Column 3 is not intended only to be restricted to quotaholders but means something more than what it does. It says, viz., the person who to whom the goods were actually delivered. [827 E F] (b) The fact that the goods did come to the conclusion that they had been physically delivered to Dwarkeshwaras Khetan and not taken back to the Mills, is a correct statement of law.

The respondent was a Government college affiliated to the Gujarat University. He was also a resident of Jamnagar. It was alleged that in April 1964, the Physics practical examination for the first year B.Sc. was to be held by the Gujarat university. One of the centres was Surendranagar. Dwivedi had been appointed as an Examiner for Physics practical. He accepted gratification of Rs. 1,000/ . The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of section 161 Indian Penal Code on the ground that he was an officer in the service or pay of the Government or was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of a public duty. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that as regards section 161, Indian Penal code, it is necessary that the person committing that offence must be a public servant and that he should have obtained the money while acting as a public Servant. Dismissing the appeals, HELD : (1) A public officer abusing his position as a Public servant obtains for himself or for any other person valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. So some limitation will have to be put on that word and that limitation is that it takes colour from the preceding words along with which it appears in the clause, that is to say something savouring of dishonest act on his part. [728 B] (2) The use of corrupt or illegal means by other means of the nature mentioned in section 1 65, if it is habitual, is comprised in clause (b) Clause (c) contemplates criminal breach of trust by a public officer. It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. According to the High court such a construction would also keep the offence within the limitation and the object of the Act. [628 C] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to.

The petitioners in each of these applications under Article 32 of the Constitution are a workman engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in Northern Railway. All the writ petitions having been disposed of by a common judgment as questions of law and fact involved therein were similar, and the petitioners have filed this group of writ petitions under Article 226 of the constitution. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed a counter affidavit on behalf of the respondents challenging the claim of the petitioners. According to them five out of forty four petitioners in this group had been directed to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line; five others have refused to go to the open Line for permanent absorption. He further averred that though prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984 project casual labourers were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave etc., they are now entitled to be all the benefits as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. The respondents have filed a Counter affidavit on their behalf and reiterated the stand taken by them in the counter affidavit. It is stated that out of the forty four writ petitioners in the group of Writ Petitions had undergone medical examination and were granted temporary status as Khallasisis. One of them has been directed by the Administration to be absorption against permanent vacancy. The petitioners have also filed a Rejoinder. At the hearing of the applications, counsel for the petitioners as also the learned Additional Solicitor General were given full opportunity of placing their arguments and documents. In addition, they have also furnished written submissions. 141 It is contended on behalf the Administration that out Of forty four Petitioners in this batch of writ Petitions had underwent medical examination, and were denied temporary status because they are project employees and do not belong to the Open line. According ly the Railway Administration was requiring continuous service for purpose of eligibility, learned Additional Advocate General on instructions obtained from the Railway officers present in Court during arguments has clarified that continuity is not insisted upon and though there is break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. The learned Additional Counsel for the respondents has pleaded that the allegation of discrimination does not exist. Disputes arising out of termination of employment and inter se seniority came before this Court in the Writ Petition No. 147 of 1983 (Inderpal Yadav & Ors vs Union of India). This Court changed the existing practice for reckoning seniority and directed that seniority of project casual labour should be combined and prepared departmentwise and category wise and in terms of the directions of this Court, steps have been taken. It has been further contended that by the time these writ petitions were filed, the Railway, Board ' 's order of 1st June, 1984 had not been given but with those directions now holding the field, the ambit of grievances has been very much reduced. The Writ Petitions are disposed of with the directions indicated above without any order for costs.

The Forward Markets Commission, constituted under the Forward Markets Regulation Act 1952, to determine the rates of forward contracts and fix the rates at which such contracts might be closed out a provision whose validity was not challenged in the present proceedings. The Forward Markets Act, 1952, provided that no bye law shall be deemed to have been made by any person unless it has been reserved for the Central Government by a notification in the Official Gazette. Section 12(1) of the Act empowered the Central Govern ment to make bye laws with retrospective effect and section 12(2) provided that where in pursuance of this section, any bye law had been made or amended, the bye laws so made or amend shall be published in the Gazette of India and also in the official Gazette of the State in which the principal office of the recognised association was situate. The appellants who were owners of forward contract entered into contracts with the Forward Marketing Commission under a. (1) whether or not the prices at which the cotton may be bought or sold were at any time controlled under the provisions of the Essential Commodities Act, 1055, if the Textile Commissioner with the concurrence of the Forward markets Commission and after consultation with the Chairman (of the Board), be of opinion that the continuation of trading in certain types of forward Contracts in cotton including that known as "hedge contracts" was likely to result in a situation detrimental to the larger interests of the economy of India, and so informs the Board, the Board shall forthwith cause a notice to be posted on the Notice Board to that effect and on the posting of such notice and notwithstanding anything to be contrary contained in these bye laws or in any hedge or on call contract made subject to these Bye laws, the following provisions shall take effect. On January 21, 1956, the Central Govt. notified a new bye law 52 AA to be substituted in place of the earlier bye law. The said bye law was amended by Act 52AA and the new byelaw 52AA was substituted in its place under the old bye law 53 AA. The appellant challenged the validity of the notification on the grounds (1)(a) that it was beyond the power of the Association to have conferred the power which it purported to do under the amended bye law, and (b) that the Association was in law incapable of conferring that power on the Forward Market Commission or on any other body. Held, that the Central government had no power under section 12 of the , to make a bye law assigning any function to the Commission. The power conferred by section 12 is undoubtedly co extensive with the power to make byelaws for all or any of the matters specified in section 11 and it cannot be said that unless retrospective operation was given to the provisions Of section 12, the objects of the legislation would be defeated or the purposes for which the power was conferred could not be fulfilled. The words "by or under this Act" apply only to the exercise of the powers by the Board. If a rule was not comprehended by the phrase "Under the Act", it would be illogical to hold that it would take in a byelaw.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The following table sets out the amounts of dividend received by it from the Company and the years in respect of which they were received : Year of Year of declaration amount of assessment of dividend 1951 52 1357 B.S. Rs. 37,125/ 1952 53 1358 B. S. Rs Rs. 28, 125/ 1952 54 1359 B. Rs 28,125. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669 for the year 1358B, Rs. 20,469/ for the years 1358 and 1357B for the period 1358, Rs 21,822/ for those years were taxable as dividend and the remaining amount was not taxable since they were declared out of capital gains of the company which comprised salami or premia received by them as consideration for grant of long term leases. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire sum for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but only a part of it being dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Income tax, 1922 was liable to be grosed up. The Tribunal also referred under section 66(1) of ' the Indian Income tax and held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the assessee for the grant of lease of longterm leases after the 31st March, 1948, was not in the hand of the Company receipt of dividend within section 2 (6A). In second appeal, however, the Tribunal held that it was agreed between the parties that the answers in the negative on all the questions were subject to the final decision in appeals filed against the orders made in Income tax References Nos. 131 of 1961 and 3 of 1964 and pending in this Court. The High Court also observed that it could not be said that the distribution of dividend out of profits was taxable as dividends, but as income of the assesse from "other sources" (not being dividend) under section 12 of the Indian Incometax Act, for no such question was referred. In appeals to this Court, HELD : The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the case remanded to the High court for disposal according to law. [35 C] The High Courts have not recorded final answers in respect Of the answers given by the Tribunal. Apart from the technical defect that the High Courts has not recorded finally answer the order, the order is subject to another infirmity.

The respondents, who were engaged in the manufacture of timber, challenged the jurisdiction of the court in C.C. Nos. 145 and 148 of 1988 to quash the complaint holding that Sandal Wood Oil is not 'wood oil ' as defined under Section 2(f) (1) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short the Act '. When proceedings were laid under section 51 (1)(e) of Kerala Forest Rules against the respondents in Special Leave Petition (Crl.) Nos. 27 29 of 1992, they questioned the jurisdiction to the court and contended that Sandrial Wood Oil was not a wood oil as defined in Section 2 (f) of Act. The learned Senior counsel on both sides neatly presented question of law whether "sandlewood oil" is forest produce within the meaning of section 2(1)(f)(i) of 'the Act. When the proceedings were taken under section 50 (1), the jurisdictional question was raised on the premise that Sand Mining Wood Oil being a bye product derived commercially manufacturing process is not wood oil and as such, it cannot be included in its ambit cut pieces in the context and purpose of the Act. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The word wood oil used in the Act will require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [503C] 2.1 In order to attract applicability of the provisions of the statute, it is necessary that the word 'wood ' should receive its colour from its context and connotation. When used in an interpretation clause, it seeks to enlarge the meaning Of the words or pharases that word would be properly applicable, but to enable the word as used in section 2 (j) of tho Act, when there is nothing in the sense or the subject matter to the contrary, to be applied to some things to which it would not ordinarily be applicable. [506D E] 3.2 The expression 'wood Oil ' has been defined in section2(k) of and the word wood ' as used therein will have a meaning to be gathered having regard inter alia to the object and purpose for which the oil is used, the purpose for Which the oil was extracted, the purposes for which it is used and the purpose the Act seeks to serve. The Legislature does not intend to restrict the wordwood oil nor we find any compelling circumstances in the Kerala State and Tamil Nadu, like the Act, do not specifically incorporate Sandalwood oil in the definition of forest produce. It must be noted that there are several types of essential oils in India, the important being Sandal wood oil, agar wood, deodar oil and pine oil apart from oleo resin and wood oil derived from exudation from living trees in the forest area. Sandal timber as observed by the High Court is forest Produce. When use in an interpreting clause, the Legislature seeks to restrict it to the word receiving its ordinary popular and natural sense whenever that word will be properly applied, but in such a manner so as to defeat the principle object and purposes of the enactment. The process by which the Oil is extracted is not decisive as oil may be extracted by natural process of exudition or it may be extraction by subjecting to chemical or mechanical process and Sandaloods (Santalum Album) are cut into pieces. Its heart wood and roots of Sandal trees removed from the forest are used as a raw material at a factory level that too by mechanised process to extract sandalwood oil. The purpose forwhich the oil has been used is not determinative.

The appellant was tried for an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code but were acquitted by the Sessions Judge. The High Court, in appeal, held that the evidence produced by the prosecution was not " free from suspicion and not sufficient to convict them ". Held, that the conviction of the appellant must be set aside. It is well settled that the Supreme Court will not interfere with the findings of the High Court because its conclusions on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the accused differ from that of the trial court. But where the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused was guilty this court would set aside the conviction. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Stephen Seneviratne vs The King, (1923) L.R. 50 I.A. 289, relied on. Emperor vs Sibnath Banerjee, A.I.R., 1936 P.C. 289 and Emperor vs B. N. Banerji, Aher Raja Khima vs The State of Saurastra, ; , referred to. Held further that the High court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons for doing so. Surajpal Singh vs State, (1947) L .R. 45 I. A. 1, approved. Emperor V Sibnath Banerji, (1948) L R. 50 1, disapproved. The judgment of the Rajasthan High Court does not disclose any such reasons justifying interference with the finding of the Sessions Court. It was a well settled principle that the Judicial Committee in Stephen senevirathne vs State of Madhya Pradesh, Aharkha Raja Khimima vs State Of Saurastara, (1949) L L. R. 45 1, considered.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar alone, it has two factories, one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi and have depots at Patna and other towns. The factory at Jamshedpur is an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory at the com missioner of the appellant 's factory at Dhanbad, the appellant made a joint application dated September 7, 1963 to the Government of Bihar for a reference under section 10(2) of the . By a notification dated October 23, 1963, the Government referred five disputes to the Tribunal for adjudication. The statement accompanying the said application signed by the District Manager on behalf of the company and the General Secretary of the said union representing the said workmen contamed inter alia the following information: "I. That the said disputes concerned the workmen employed In the factory 's Factory at Jamshedpur, and (2) that these workmen were represented by the Indoxco Labour Union. " The statement accomping that agreement clearly stated that the disputes agreed to be referred to were between the workmen of that factory and the management of that industry. Even assuming that the Indoco Labour Union validly amended its constitution so as to extend its membership to the company 's other workmen in its other establishments, inasmuch as the disputes referred to the tribunal were only those set out in the said agreement and the said statement and not that of the Indian Oxygen Workers Union was erroneous and cannot be sustained. The Tribunal held that the constitution of thesaid Indox Co Labour Union came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company & Indox co Labour Union does not materially affect the position that the dispute raised by the union is in respect of the employees of the Company wherever they may be stationed". The Tribunal further held that since the said references were made in December 1963 i.,e. after the said purported amendment and the statement signed by them, any award made by the Tribunal in respect thereof must necessarily be confined to the disputes set out therein, the parties to those disputes 'and the parties who had agreed to refer those disputes for adjudication, and that consequently it made no difference that the name of Indox Company Labour Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the agreement and that the said statements and not the Indian oxygen Workers Union were erroneous and could not be sustained, and dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The Tribunal 's conclusion, therefore, that the union 's constitution was duly amended on either January 6 or 21, 1963 or that, therefore the/ndian Oxygen Workers ' Union represented the workmen in the appellant Company 's another establishment, inasmuch, as the dispute referred to it were only these set outin the agreement. [352 B] (2)(a) The contention of the appellants that it cannot be called upon to pay for overtime work anything more than its ordinary rate of wages if the workmen do work beyond 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours a week, is without substance. It is obvious that if the company were asked to pay at the rate equivalent to the ordinary rate Of wages for work done beyond 39 days but not exceed 48 hours work a week would be paying no extra compensation at all for the work done within the agreed hours of wo.rs.

The assessee was dissolved in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm had ceased to carry on business and that it succeeded to the business on April 1, 1943. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) of section 25 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to the family firm was not admissible. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that the assessee was entitled on dissolution of that firm in March 1944 to the benefit under section 25(3), or in the alternative under section 5(4) and to the second succession which took place on April Ist, 1943 after Act 7 of 1939 was brought into force relief under section25(4). The High Court also held that in the absence of other evidence, it could be held that assessee was not entitled to the benefits provided in section 25 (3), nor was it admissible. In appeal by certificate, HELD : The Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act 7 Of 1939 came into force on April 31, 1939. Section 5(3) of the General Clauses Act 10 of 1897 provides that unless the contrary is expressed, a Central Act or Regulation shall be construed as coming into operation immediately on the expiration of March 31, 1948. [653 C] The deed recites that the accounts were settled upto March 31st, 1939 and upto March31, 1939, and it was recited that all the partners had become separate from April 1. 1939. It is then recited that the partners have become separate, would imply that the partnership had continued for the whole or a part of the day on April I, 1939 i.e., the business had continued till the midnight of March31. [643 D] The recitals in the instrument that the account were settled up upto March 30, 1939 are not set out in the document and there is no other evidence in that behalf. But the assessee 's contention that the business of Messrs. Hakam Mal Tani Mal was dissolved on April January 31, 1943, and immediately thereafter the business was started, cannot be accepted. The partnership therefore came into being at the precise point of time at which the Indian income tax (Amendment ) Act 7o 1939 came in force and it could not be said that the asses was not carrying on business at the commencement of the Income tax ( Amendment) Act, 7 Of 1949.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimandhar, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the operation of the permit. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order of the issue of the permits respondents 4 to 13 preferred appeals to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal which dismissed the appeal holding that there was no period of limitation under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the said permit. On April 25, 1967, the Secretary to the Regional transport Authority called upon the appellant to produce the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit, but the appellant produced it on April 27, 1967. Against this order of respondent No. 4 to13 preferred appeals before the State Government Tribunal which allowed the appeal and held that there had been no period Of limitation under Rule 119 of Mysore Motor vehicles Rules, 1945 after a long lapse of time from tho date of grant of permit. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The order granting the permit to the appellant stands restored There will be no order as to costs. V.P.S. Appeal allowed.

The appellant contested the election on the ticket of the Republican Party. He was then a sitting member of Parliament. Among the rival candidates, Prakash Vir Shastri was an independent candidate. The election symbol of Prakash Vir Gandhi was elephant and the election symbol was of Prakashvir Shastri. The appellant challenged the election by means of an Election Petition. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no meeting was held at Hapur Town Hail Maidan on 7 February 1967, and there was no attack on the office of the Stale Party. With regard to the meeting at the Town Hall Maidyan at Hapur, the appellant relied on the oral evidence of PW 18, a newspaper published in the Hindustan 's daily newspaper dated 8 February 1967 and also on exhibit 23 the news report in the newspaper named 'Vir Arjun ' published on 8 February, 1967. The newspaper report in question was not mentioned at all either in Vir Arjun of 8 February1967 or in the Indian Express. The other allegations of the appellant were that respondent Shastri attacked the office by forcibly taking necessary papers and a flag of the Party. The evidence on behalf of the respondent was that the meeting was conducted in support of the candidature of the appel lant 's supporters and supporters. The witnesses on whose testimony the appellant relies did not mention or refer at all to any meeting on behalf o respondent Prakash Vir Sawant on 7 2 1967 at the town Hall M/s. R.P. Singh, who were alleged to have said that voters at Nagola were prevented from voting did not lodge any report about the alleged corrupt practice particularly when it was said to be committed by Prakash Vir Upadhyaya himself. The Court also held that there was rejection of evidence on account of the fact that the appellant 's witnesses belonged to particular castes and sects. The appeal filed by the appellant was dismissed by the High Court. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the publication in the newspapers 'V 'ir Arjun Exhibit 22 gave news from Hapur under the date 7 February,1967, that a meeting was organised by the supporters of the Congress Party and no election meeting was con sidered on 7 6 February 1967; (ii) the news item in the Newspaper 'Vilir Arjun published on 7 Feb. 1967 did not refer to any meetings on behalf or of respondent Prakashvir; (iii) the appellant made communal propaganda against the appellant and also published false statements in relation to the personal character of the appellants, and (iv) the allegations were that on 2 February 1967 an election meeting at Hapur was organised in support thereof. HELD: (i). The publication in question 'Vlir Arjun exhibit 22 is to the effect that differences between Hindus and Harijans were being spread by the leaders of the ruling party meaning thereby the appellant, and if students from Muslim University were brought in by them then students from Ghaziabad would be brought into the field. [897 F] (ii).

The mortgagee decree holder in execution of the final decree for mortgage himself purchase the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. On September 20, 1978, the judgment debtor Ganpat Singh filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. Two other petitions of objections were filed by Chiranji Lal and Mst. Abhey Kanwar. On July 17, 1980, that is, more than one year after the sale was confirmed, the decree holder auction purchaser filed an applica tion under Order 21 Rule 95 of the C.P.C. for setting it aside the auction sale. The said application was opposed by the judgment debtors on the ground that as the application was filed more than two years after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . It was held by the learned District Judge that in view of the provision of Explanation I1 of Section 47 read with Article 136 of the , an application for settingaside the sale could also be made within a period of 12 years from the date on which the sale became absolute. The learned Single Judge dismissed the revisional application of the judgmentdebtor under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code. In appeal, the Division Bench held that after the amendment of Section 21 of the code of Civil Proce dure, an application filed under Order XXII Rule 95 will be governed by Article 136 and that as held by this Court in Chandra Mani 's case (supra) the application for delivery of possession could be made only after the decree was put into execution within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 134, Article 136 stood impliedly repealed by section 47 readwith Article 136. The appeal filed by the appellant against the said order was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of clause (a) of Explanation II to Section 47 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, an applicatio n for setting setting aside sale can also be filed within a prescribed period of twelve years from tho date on Which sale became im pugned. [360F] 1.2 The periods of limitation prescribed by Articles 136 and 134 are for two different purposes, the former being for the execution of a decree. Merely because the auction purchaser will be deemed to be a party in the suit in which the decree has been passed, as provided in clause (b) of explanation II all questions relating to delivery of posses sion of the property shall be deemed t he questions relating lo the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree within the meaning of Section47, an appli cation for setting up aside the re sale may be made under Rules 89, 90 or 91 of Order XXI of the Cr. P.C., cannot be equated with an application seeking the execution o f a decree for possession so as to apply 12 years ' period of Limitation as prescribed under Article 136 by Article 137 of the Limitation Act. [361G H] Chandra Mani vs Shri Chandra Mani & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.3 In view, clause (c) of Section 2 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 will not be applicable to an application made under Order XI Rule 95 or 91. There can be no doubt that when an application is made, the order passed by the executing court either allowing or dismissing the application will be final and effective subject to an appeal that may be filed under the provisions of the Consti tution. [362G H; 361A] Chandra Mohan vs Shri Chander Mani & Anr., ; ; Chandra Mani Mani vs Smt. Abhhey Kanwar, ; , relied on.

The appellant was the candidate of a political party. The first respondent was the election petitioner. In the election, the appellant was declared elected by a margin of 1873 votes over his nearest rival, the first respondent. P 14 and P 15 were the supporters of the Congress I, Kerala Congress, Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) and others on the one hand and the left Democratic Front (LDF). In the said election, P 14 was declared as elected by margin of 1964 votes over the nearest rival. The appellant was also declared elected. The election petition filed in the High Court challenging the election of the appellant to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. 73 was dismissed on the ground that the appellant had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court recorded a finding that the said wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the first res pondent his election agent. It also held that the evidence of P 1 was not sufficient to prove that he had taken the photographs in question on the said days, that it was published in the presence of and under the supervision of the workers of the appel lant 's election agent and hence it attracts all the requirements of Section 100(2) of Act. The appeal by special leave is against the High COurt judgment. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In a libel action it may further be necessary to prove whether those with special knowledge of the extrinsic facts were likely to interpret or understand the words complained of in a defama tory sense, in an election action, it may not be necessary for doing so and all that is necessary is to prove such words. [776F] 1.2 In the instant case, the question whether it was necessary for the election peti tioner to state in the petition the extrinic facts which would connect the person concerned with the libelous statement was not raised and, therefore, was not answered. Since the election Petitioner had proved that the theatre belonged to Chowd hary 's sons and that Chowdhary was the Minister in charge of the Rajasthan Canal, it must be held that he has reasonably calculated that the voters or at any rate the voters in and about the locality where the theatre was being put up, had knowledge of fact that it is being constructed by the Minister or his sons, and that such extrinsicsic facts could not have been unknown to the voters. [767G H] 1:3 In the present case, P 1 has stated generally that it Was the appellant, his agents and his workers who had pasted the wall posters. What is more, in paragraph 84, he had made it clear that he was going to examine witnesses only in connection with the pasting of the poster on the aforesaid one wall and no more. Secondly even with regard to the past ing of the wall poster on a later date and just prior to the filing of the present election petition, he is not sure as to who had done it and with whose knowledge and consent. Nowhere in the Petition it is stated that it has been done with the knowledge and the consent and at the behest of or in the absence of any other evidence, nothing more has to be established to hold the appellant guilty of the corrupt practice within the mischief of Section 116(4). [775A B] 1 :4 In the case of the election petition there is no reference to the election agent in this connection anywhere and the reference to P 1 cannot be construed as a reference to him.

The respondent No. 5 proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay bearing R.S. Nos. 416 (Part) and 417. The land in question had been purchased by the respondent No 5 from its erstwhile owner, Byramji Jeejeebhoy Pvt. Ltd., In 1966 sanctioned Development Plan of Greater Bombay, the said land was shown as a green belt. With a view to developing the disputed land, the respondent Corporation submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of GreaterBombay for the construction of a five Star hotel. The Commissioner of the Municipal corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the Respondent No. 2 submitted a revised development plan. The Municipal Corporation accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the order of the respondent granting sanction of the Plan submitted by the Respondent for the constructions of a hotel on the said plot. Being dissatisfied with the rejection, the appellant filed an appeal before the Minister of State for Urban Development, which was dismissed. The respondent No 2 set aside the order granting sanction submitted by respondent No 4 after hearing the appellants as also the Municipal Commissioner and directed sanctioning of the building plan on certain conditions which will be referred to later in this judgment. Being Aggrieved by the said rejection of respondent No, the appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court which was allowed by the learned Single Judge of the High court. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground has been adequately considered and taken into account by the High Courts. [922D] 2.1 In granting sanction to the plan the respondent Authority in considering an application for permission shall have due regard to the provisions of any draft or final plan or proposal published by means of notice submitted or sanctioned under the Act. It seems that the Municipal Com missioner was not justified in merely relying upon a proposal for the preparation of a revised Development Plan. [936E] Life Insurance Corporation of India and Another vs Municipal Corporation, Greater Bombay & Ors., Writ Petition No. In that case, a development application was rejected by the Municipal Corpo ration on the ground that the property was proposed lo be reserved for public purposes or for recreational ground in the draft revised development plans, apart from those mentioned in section 46. The Respondent No 2 directed sanction of tile plan out of 44,821.49 sq. yds.

The appellant, a manufacturer of textile mill, filed two complaints against the employers under section 28 read with Items l(a), l(b) and 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971. The Industrial Court dismissed the complaints holding that the employer had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of schedule II of Maharashtra Recognition Of Trade Unions & Prevention of Misfair Labour practices Act, 1972. Thereafter, the appellant filed two special civil applications in Bombay High Court under article 226 of the Constitution questioning the correctness of the decision of the Industrial Court. Both the applications were dismissed in limine. The Union thereupon filed these appeals by special leave. 66 At the hearing of the appeals, Mr. Govind Dass, learned counsel for the employers stated that the employers had re opened the industrial units and there was partial resumption of manufacturing process. He further stated that since the old workmen who responded to the advertisement in a local newspaper have already been employed, they will be re inducted in service as resumption work is gradually expanding and that till all the old workman are re inducted into service no new hand will be recruited. An undertaking to that effect by Dr. P. D. Meghani s/o Dharam Chand Meghani has been placed on record and is treated as an integral part of this judgment. In order to be assured that the undertaking is carried out in letter and spirit, it would be directed the Industrial court Maharashtra Bombay to depute its senior ministerial officer to visit the industrial undertakings of the employers and to satisfy itself that the old workers are being re inducted In service and that as resumption of production is gradually expanded, the old employees will be allowed re inducted. There was a statement of law made by the Industrial Courts while rejecting the complaints filed by the appellant union which does not command to us and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the industrial undertaking had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the new hands are being recruited. Allowing the appeals in terms of the undertaking of Dr. M. PD. Meghi as recorded in this judgment, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the closure is brought about malafide and whether it could have been avoided were matters irrelevant and what is to be seen is whether in fact and in effect there is a closure or not. [68C D] 2.1 In examining whether the employer has imposed a lockout or has closed down the industrial activity, the Industrial Tribunal before which the action of the employer is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the time of closure decide and determine whether the closing down of the industrial activities was a consequence of imposing lock out or the owner employer had decided to close down the industry. [69D] 2:2 The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employee at the relevant time of the closing but is not decisive of the matter. To accept the view taken by the industrial Court would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted to closure, bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial process he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device or pretence. Therefore the correct approach ought to be that when it is claimed that the employee is not guilty of imposing a lock Out but has closed the industrial establishment, the industrial court before which tho action of employer is challenged must keep In view all relevant circumstances, at the first instance, before which action of an employer is assailed must keeping in view the relevant circumstance at the stage of closure deciding and determine what the closure was a bonafide one or was a device to determine whether that the closing up of the industry was a result of imposing the lock out.

The assessee company, which was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company, the objects of which are set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. The assessment years in question were 1943 44 to 1948 49 excepting the year 1947 48. According to its petition made in the High Court, the assessee company dealt with its assets as follows: "The petitioner company purchased during the period 1st July, 1925 to 30th June, 1928, shares of the value of Rs. 101/2 lacs. In the year 1930, the petitioner company promoted two companies known as Loyal Mills Ltd., and Hamilton Studios Ltd. and took over all their shares of value of RS. 1010 lacs. The Income Tax authorities accepted the plea of the assessee Company and treated it as a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties and assessed it on that basis. Since that return was submitted the Central Board of Revenue has decided that the company is an Investment Holding Company and accordingly an amended Return of total income under section 22(1) of the Indian Income tax Act is submitted herewith on which the assessment for 1943 44 may be based, as on this particular question the assessee 's company obviously cannot have one status for Excess Profits Tax and another for Income taX. The High Court in reference held that in the case of the appellant company not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case was that it never carried on any business in the purchase or sale of shares, security and immovable property during the assessment year in question. On appeal by certificate, HELD: (i) The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law. To put it differently, the proper construction of statutory language is always a matter of law and therefore the claim of the asses see that the questions should be modified as suggested by the assessee. [73 C D] (ii) The High Courts have in its judgment reached the correct conclusion on what the High court assumed were 'the questions to be decided by it. It is open to the High Courts to examine whether the Tribunal had applied the relevant legal principles correctly or not in reaching, its final conclusion; and in that sense, the scope of enquiry and the extent of the jurisdiction of the High courts in dealing with such points is the same as in dealing With pure questions of law.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On July 27, 1950 the Government issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed or removed from service. The appellant filed his reply and contended that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules 1953 which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953, it was only a Tribunal as provided in Rule 4(1)(a). Held, that the enquiry against the appellant was not one of dismissal or removal from service within article 311 of the Constitution. The order passed by the High Court on January 28, 1954, was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government and such an order was neither one of discharge nor removal from Service within article 310 of the Constitu tion. It was also not correct to say that the appellant had no authority under the rules to suspend a judicial officer pending final order of the Government. The High Court had no jurisdiction under the Rules to suspend the appellant pending final proceedings of the government. The orders passed by it were merely one one of removal from the service and such a dismissal was neither an one of dismiss ment nor removal of any person from service outside article 311 Of the Constitution, and it was not correct in law to say, that it was open to the High Courts to hold an enquiry into the conduct of a judicial Officer pending final adjudication.

The respondent, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Co. was made an executor to the estate of Gannon in British India and appointed the respondent as his attorney to administer the estate in British country. The respondent applied for and obtained in India on August 14, 1946, Letters of Administration "durante absentia" to the Estate of Gannon because he had died before the date on which the fiction of distribution became effective viz. August 14. 1946. The Income tax Officer included dividends deemed to be distributed and after processing the amount under section 18(5) included it in the total income of Anderson and levied tax thereon at the appropriate rate. The estate of the respondent was then transferred to the appellant by virtue of section 211 of the Indian Succession Act, in which he did not take steps to get his name entered in the register of shareholders maintained by the Company and the Income tax officer sought to tax the dividends deemed as distributed and thereafter levied tax on the dividend deemed to have been distributed in the hands of Andsel as administrator of the estate. The sole question in this appeal was whether the Act contains machinery for assessing dividends deemed not to have actually been distributed by virtue Of an order under section 23A in respect of shares held by a shareholder when before the day on which fiction of transmission becomes effective viz., August 14 , 1946, and that the expression "shareholder" in section 23 A of the Income Tax Act, 1922, means a person by whom income tax is payable. Held, (per Hidayatullah, J., dissenting), that the Act does not contain machinery for assessment of income receivable by the estate or of the deceased person, but to a fiction of receipt by a deceased person of income by extending (1) 600 his legal personality. The Legislature not having made any provision generally for assessment and levy of tax in respect thereof, if he had not died" cannot be deemed to had supplied the machinery for taxation of income received by a legal representative to the estates after the expiry of the year in the course of which such person died. It was then contended that even if after the expiration of the period of account receipts which were received by the deceased, the income ceased to be liable to assessment as income of the assessee, they could still be taxed as his income in the income of their legal representative and (2) that where the income was notional as under section 22A the legal personality of the person who died, a different interpretation of the same expression in the context of notional income would be impermissible. The legislature not having enacted any provision expressly for assessment or levy of income accruing by the death of the shareholder in the company, the expression 'assessee ' in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means "a person by which income tax or any other tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he has not died". The Legislature cannot having made a provision generally to assessment of Income receivable by an order tinder section 23(4) for assessment on such receipts on the footing that it is the personal income of a legal repre sentative of the Estate after the death, had been received by such deceased person. It could not be said that they were income which may be deemed by fiction to have beer received by them or his legal representatives after the end of that year. The expression "assessee" in s 2(1) as amended by Act 25 of 1952 with effectfrom April 1 , 1952, meant a person who was by whom Income tax was payable and not a person ' by whom or by whose estate income tax was paid. It is only when the Legislature has failed to set up the procedure to assess such income, the courts cannot supply it.

The appellant was the Ruler of a State merged with Madhya Pradesh. After the passing of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947. Thereafter he entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State of Baster to the Government Of India to be integrated with the Central Provinces and Berar (now the State) in such manner as the Government was of the opinion that fit. The appellant 's petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that article 362 of the Constitu tion was not applicable to him. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the appellant could not be denied his ownership over them. He had given no evidence to establish that the villages in question were not assessed to land revenue but no evidence had been led to this effect. The burden was on the appellant to prove this fact which he never attempted to discharge. It is impossible therefore to accept this contention on behalf of the appellant. The onus was on him to prove that the appel lant as a maufidar had no right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in his villages. The obligation was on his person to prove it which he neither attempted nor discharged. It was impossible therefore, to accept the contention that the burden was upon the appellant for proving this fact. The High Court rightly held that the question whether the villages were assessed to Land Revenue was not correct.

The respondent was transferred to the Shillong Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Eastern Circle, Shillong. He approached the Gauhati Bench of that Tribunal questioning the order of his transfer. He submitted that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the central Government, that his children are studying at Shillong and further that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time ago. He also submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer, and that the transfer was ordered on administrative grounds and is unexceptionable. The Single Member of the Tribunal recorded the following finding: "In view of the above facts and circumstances and findings it is held unhesitatingly that the respondent 's transfer order No. BSI. 80/5/80 Estt. dated 29.1.1991 in respect of applicant S.L.Abbas was malafide and liable to be quashed. The Union of India has preferred this appeal. An order of transfer is an incident of Government Service. Fundamental Rule 11 says that "the whole time of a government servant is at the disposal of the Government which pays him and he may be employed in any manner required by proper authority". Fundemental Rule 15 says that the President may transfer a government Servant from one post to another". That the respondent is liable to transfer anywhere in India is not in dispute. It is not the case of the respondent that order of the transfer is vitiated by mala fides on the part of the authority making the order, though the Tribunal does say so merely because certain guidelines issued by the Central Government are not followed, with which finding we shall deal later. The Administrative Tribunal is not an Appellate Authority sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the Authority competent to transfer. In this case the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order dated of transfer, because the order passed by the Senior Administrative Officer (competent authority) was a former Judge of the High Court and is thus aware of the norms and constraints of the writ jurisdiction.) The Administrative Tribunals are not an appellate Authority sitting over the order. It can substitute its judgment for the that of tho authority competent to transfers. In the instant case, the Tribunal had clearly exceeded the jurisdiction in interfere with the orders dated of the transferred. The order of Tribunal reads as if it were sitting in appeal over the Order of transfer made by the senior Administrative Officer. The respondent attributed"mischief"to his immediate superior who had nothing to do with his transfer." All he says is that he should not be transferred because his wife was working at shillong, his children were studying there and also because his health had suffered a set back some time afterwards. He relied upon certain executive instructions issued by Government in that behalf. Those instructions are in the nature of guidelines. They do not have statutory force. Who should be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide. Unless the order is vitiated, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued on the subject. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer the appropriate Authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees." (emphasis added) The said observations in fact tend to negative the respondents contentions instead of supporting them. The judgment also does not support the respondents ' contention that if such an order is questioned in a court or Tribunal, the Authority is obliged to justify the transfer by adducing the reasons therefor. It does not also say that the Court or the Tribunal can quash the order if any of the administrative instructions/guidelines are not follow, much less can it be charactrised as malafide for that reason. To reiterate, the order also doesnot support the respondent in any way.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them. A7 was charged under Section 302 read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 commit the murder. The second charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A5 and A6 armed with sticks, A3 armed with aruval (bill hook) and A4 armed with vel stick (spear stick), attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. [3E] 2. The intention of the appel lants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P.C., and instead convict them under Section 325, IP. C. read with section 34, IPC. [4F G] 3. Taking in view the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case the 3 offence committed was found on the dead body of Jawahar. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High Court while consid ering the nature, of offence observed as under: "The accused and their associates who be set themselves on Jawahar could never have intended to cause the death Of Jawahar for, if such was their intention, they could have certainly killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing simple and grievous injuries to him. Even with reference to the aspect whether the accused persons could have intended ted to cause such injuries as would be sufficient, in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, it is not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. " Agreeing with the above observations of the High court, this is not possible to give any finding in respect favour of tho prosecution.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents including the respondent firm and its partners to recover a sum of Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs3.00,000 and Rs.80,000 respectively advanced by the Bank to the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. It may be noticed here that the Bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970, which came into force on July 19, 1969. The case of the Bank is that in addition to the hypothecation of the A and Schedule properties made in its favour to secure repayment of the aforesaid amounts of loan, the other partner, the respondent No. 1, had advanced a sum Rs.10,00, 000 and Rs80, 000 respectively by the bank to the Firm under cash Credit account on the 28 11 67 1967,3 4 1968 & 17 2 72 respectively. The Bank was also nationalised on August 7, 1970 under the Andhra Pradesh Agriculturists Relief Act IV of 1938 which came in force from July 19. 1969 under which the appellant Bank was created. In addition to this mortgage, the Bank had also advanced Rs. 10,00 lakhs by way of loan to the respondent Bank. The appellant Bank instituted a suit being O.S. No. 12 of 1979 against the respondent and its partner to recover the amount claimed by it against the bank under cash credits account on or before 28 1167 1967, three 4 1968, 17 21972 and 17 February 1972 respectively, which were decreed in favour of the firm. The High Court held that the appellant bank was entitled to recover only the amount after scaling down of the debt in accordance with the provisions of the Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even assuming that the expression `special Indian law ' means a law enacted by the British Parliament, and that the Banking companies Act is such a law, still the provision of section 4(e) of the would not apply inasmuch as the appellant was not formed in pursuance of any `specialIndian law ', but by or under a `special ' Indian law, that is, the Banking Company Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of section 3(27)(a) of The Banking Companies Act are not applicable to the appellant Banks and, therefore, there is no question of scaling down the debt due to the Bank by the respondents. [966C] 1.2 In view of the definition of `special law ' in section 4 (e) as it stood on the day the Act was passed, the provisions Of the Act will be inapplicable to any debt due from any corporation formed in pursuant of an Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom or any special Indian law or Royal Charter or Letters Patent. The question is whether the Banking company Act by orunder which the appellants Bank was constituted, is a `Special Indian law" or not. It is not disputed that the banking Companies Act is a special law enacted under the Indian Parliament. [964D] 1:3 In view Of section 4 of the , as it stands on the date the Act came into operation, the appellant 's Bank was not, therefore formed or created under any special law. Even assuming that this Bank was formed under the Ordinance VIII of 1969 and not under the banking companies Act, still it must be held that it was created under a special Indian Law, for an ordinance is as much a law as an enactment of Parliament or Legislature. Therefore, it is manifestly clear that the provisions are not inapplicable to the appellants bank and, there was no question to scaling down this debt due by the respondent.

The Central Government fixed ex factory prices of sugar produced in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned notification on two grounds: (i) that the impugned Act was violative of article 19(1)(g), inasmuch as it imposed an unreasonable restriction on the right to trade under article 19 (1) (g); (ii) that even if the ex factory price can be fixed at a later stage or not, the Act requires that prices for the consumer only should be fixed; and (iii) that there was no reasonable safeguard against the abuse of power. Held:(i) The impugned notification merely fixes ex factory rates and is bad as it cannot possibly subserve the purposes of the Act ensuring equitable distribution of the commodity to the consumer at a fair price, and makes sugar available at fair prices. It is well known that the wholesale and retail prices depend upon ex factory Price, in the case of a commodity like sugar. Therefore if fixation of price at the exfactory level is enough to ensure a fair sale for the consumers, there is no reason why the Government should go on also to fix wholesale or retail prices. The impugned Act merely fixes the ex factories prices and is not bad as such it cannot obviously subserve the purpose of the provisions of the . It is clear that the object of the , is to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in essential commodities in the interests of the general public so that the State may not be achieved if retail prices are fixed and that there is a reasonable basis for such clasification factories in other parts of India are left uncontrolled with the result that there can be no discrimination. The object of section 3 (1), is to secure essential commodities for the ' consumer, i.e., the general Public at fair price; but it does not follow from this that this object can only be achieved by fixing the ex industry prices at all stages, the act requires that the price must be fixed for the purchaser, whether it is fixed at an earlier stage or at not. It cannot be said that any further safeguard is necessary in the form of an appeal or otherwise. The fact that there are 97 sugar factories in Punjab and North West Bihar while there are 50 sugar factories, in which there are about 18 sugar factories and there are 100 sugar factories which are left free to sell at any price is not a ground for holding that under section 3(1) and section 3 the Act the Government must not only fix ex factory sale prices but also wholesale and wholesale prices. [133 E F] (ii)(a) The object Of the Act is to ensure fair prices for consumers, i.,e., , the general ' public at fair rates; but there can he little doubt that fixation of ex factory sales prices in these three regions and the contention that there has been discrimination is purely theoretical. In fact there is, however, no distinction between the fixation of prices in the main surplus areas would have the effect of stabilising sugar prices for those areas and the argument that there should be discrimination is merely theoretical, because it fixes ex factories at lower prices than the level at which they were at the end of May 1958, and that any price below them would not even meet the cost of production. [134 E F; 135 A B] (b) The contention that the notification fixing ex factory rate prices was bad as there is discrimination between the two regions and that the factories in the other areas are left unguided with the results that there could be no reasonable basis, for holding it to be unreasonable restriction.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 transferred the dispute between the parties to the Second Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the , and the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. The Fifth Industrial Tribu nal held that there was a rise in the cost of living index and that to neutralise the said rise the employees should get an increase of Rs. 2,000 per annum on the basis of the rise in cost of live index. On appeal by special leave: Held, that in regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date of the agreement is the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class cost of ' living index in the year 1957. The Tribunal had rightly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the ground that it did not relate to the working classes cost of the living index. In regard to matter covered by the second written statement filed by the Company on December 20, 1956 a contention was raised that the award dated June 21, 1951, was not terminated under section 19(6) of the Act and therefore no reference was bad in law. Though it may not be quite relevant, it may be mentioned that even in 1951 when the dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal though a similar contention was open to the Company and indeed was suggested by the Tribunal, it moved the Tribunal to give an award on the merits of the matter. The Company preferred an appeal against that award to the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Calcutta which with some modification confirmed the award of the Tribunal on August 30, 1957.

The appellant was the Matadhipati of Sri Gavi Mutt which is a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The predecessor in office of the appellant filed a suit challenging the scheme on the ground that it contravened the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) and as such, was invalid. The District Judge dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the scheme having been framed as early as 1939 under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act which was valid when it was enacted could not be challenged on the grounds that some of its provisions contravened the appellant 's fundamental rights under article 19. Held, that the impugned orders did not come with in the purview of section 103(d) of the , and were not warranted by the provisions of section 105(a). The scheme was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early at 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over the actual administration of the Mutt and its properties, it was partly because the appellant had continuously challenged the implementation of the scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation. But it is clear that when the scheme was made and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law his property rights had been taken away. The fact that the order was not implemented does not make any difference to this legal position. The provisions of sections 103(a) and (b) clearly bring out the fact that if a scheme governed by section 103 (d) is deemed to have been settled or modified under the provisions Of the latter Act, it has so provided. If it is found that any of the said provisions are inconsistent with the relevant provision of the latter enactment, they must be modified so as to make them consistent with the said pro visions. The scheme of section103(a), and (d), clearly brings out the facts that if the legislature wanted the conti nuance of the action taken under the said Act only if the said action was consistent with, the relevant pro visional provisions of that Act, there is no reason why it should do so.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982 and continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. Although the period of summer vacation during all these years was not approved by the educational authorities, the appellant continued to work as such teacher with repeated spell of 89day appointments and a day break was in between them. Though the period was of summer vacations during all the years, the management of the school had been running from time to time under orders of the managing committee yet his appointment after 1986 had not been approved by educational authorities. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the petitioner was appointed on 12.7.1982 and continued till 18.7 1986 with breaks in between and the petitioner 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. His case, therefore will not come within the preview of the validation Act and, therefore, the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the validate Act does not arise. " The High court rejected the writ petition holding that the appel lant was entitled to be regularised as Hindi Teachers with effectfrom July 121982. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Validation Act covers the field upto December 31, 1984. [994G] 1.2 The State of Orissa will do well to consider the cases of all those who have completed one year or more as ad hoc teachers after December 31. 1984 and come out with a scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise their services. [995C D] 1:3 The State Government is expected to function as a model employer". "We strongly deprecate the policy of the State Government under which `ad hoc ' teachers are denied the salary and allowances or the period Of the summer vacation by resorting to the fictional breaks of the type referred to above. These `adhoc ' teachers shall be paid salary and allowance for the period during of summer as long as they hold the office under this order. Those who are entitled to maternity or medical leave shall also be granted such leave in accordance with the rules. " [995E F] 1 :4 The appellant was initially appointed on July 6, 1982, and continued upto 18.07.1986. He had been working with the approval of the authorities for almost 4 years with short breaks. The managing committee is still utilising his services though there is no approval by the Education Authorities for the periods subsequent to 1986. It is no body 's case that his services were ever terminated on grounds of inefficiency or misconduct. The case of the appellant is, thus fully covered by Section 3 of the validating Act.

The appellant was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly, because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The respondent challenged the election of the respondent in an election petition inter alia on the ground (1) that he had been disqualified from becoming a member; (2) that the allowances paid under rules 3 to 7 were not in addition to the payment of the consolidated monthly allowance under r. 3 only, and (3) that no travelling allowance was to be drawn by a Member if the journey was performed for attending a meeting held within a radius of five miles from his place of residence or he performed the journey in a transport provided at the expense of the Zila Parishads/Panchayat Samiris or any other local authority or Government. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the various questions involved were of considerable importance and should be settled by a larger Bench, referred the petition to a Full Bench. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1 ) the High Court had erred in holding that allowances paid to members of Panchayat Samiti under rules 2 to 7 of the Rules did not convert the office of Chairman of Panchayat Samitis into an office or profit; and (2)(a) the payment was in addition, to the pay of the daily allowance under rule 3 only. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1)(a). The appellant had failed to establish that the allowance payable under rules 1 to 7 was in fact addition to his payment of daily allowance. [427 B] (b) The High court had erred by holding that no evidence had been adduced on behalf 'of the appellant to show that out of the amount received as daily allowance the Chairman would in fact invariably make a saying, it cannot be held that this payment would result in gain so as to make the office an office profit. [445 C] (2). The High Courts were right in holding the allowances payable under r 3 to the appellant.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later, they filed a suit for eviction on a number of grounds including the 972 ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. It was not necessary to refer to other grounds as the sole ground which survived for the decree of eviction relates to the material alterations made in the tenanted premises without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The disputed constructions include a partition wall in a hail converting the same into two portions and tin sheds shown by letters ABHG and CDGH. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the trial Court 's order on the findings that none of the construc tions constituted material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under sec. The High Court set aside that order on two grounds: (a) that the tin shed marked by letters CDG H as well as the parti tion wail made in th e hall converting the said same into one rooms, constituted material alterations as contemplated by the section; and (b) that since the constructions had been made with out permission of the respondent, the tenant was liable for eviction. On a second appeal, a learned Single Judge of the High Court held that temporary construction made by a tenant in the shape of kitchen and bathroom did not constitute material alteration as the constructions were temporary in nature which could be removed at any time without causing any damage to the accommodation. The Division Bench also held that the partition wall constituted 'material alteration '. The appellant came up in appeal by special leave against the judgment of the learned Single judge. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court committed error in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail constituted material additions. [975D] 1.2 In determining the question as to what constructions could materially alter the accommodation was considered. On the facts of that case, there could be no doubt that the tenant had made substantial constructions which changed the form, front and structure of the tenanted shop. The construction of tin shed could not be held to have materially altered the accommodation.[975E] 1:3 In determining whether the constructions are sub stantial in nature and they alter, the form front and structures of the building without destroying its identity. [977F] 2.1 There is no material on record to sustain the findings recorded by t he High Court that the appel lant had construct ed pucca wails on three sides of the tin sheds; instead the Commissioner 's report is contrary to it.[978C D] 2:2 The construction in question even though temporary in character, which could he removed without causing damage to tile building. [978D] 3.1 In determining a question the Court must address itself to the nature, character of the constructions and the extent to which they make changes in the front and t structure of tho building without destroy its identity.[978E] 2 :3 The material alterations contemplate change of substantial nature affecting the form and character of construction.
