Construction of a Chabutra, Almirah, opening a window or closing a verandah by temporary structure or replacing of a damaged roof which may be leaking or placing partition in a room or making similar minor alterations for the convenient use of the accommoda tion do not materially alter 'the building as in spite of such constructions the front & structure of tile building may remain unaffected.

The appellant company filed a suit for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. Hence he set aside the ex parte judgment. The respondent firm filed a revision before the High Court under section 115 of the Code. The High Court allowed the revision, set aside its judgment and upheld the passing of the exparte decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant under the orders of the court had furnished bank guarantee for the decretal amount. It has agreed to continue the same till the disposal of the suit. [1031E] 2. In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the Respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous case that the service of summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the C.P.C. may kindly be perused. [ 1031F] 3. The judgment by the Trial Court setting aside the decree was correct. In any event no error of jurisdiction was committed by it. The order by the trial court setting aside that decree was erroneous. [1002B] 4. The suit shall now proceed to disposal in accordance With the law.

The respondents filed a complaint against the appellant under section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code, for having committed breach of the peace. The Magistrate passed an order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court found that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was an apprehension of breach of peace, therefore, the final Order was bad and the High court accordingly allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate for passing a final order under sub section (1) and thereafter to pass a final Order under sub s.(6) of section 145. The appellant contended before this Court that the final orders of the magistrate were vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of law existed at the time the order was passed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach of a peace and once he records his satisfaction in the preliminary order, he is not required to record a finding again about the existence or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the Magis trate is based. [952G] 2. The enquiry under section145 is limited to the question who was in actual possession on the date of the preliminary Order irrespective of the rights of the parties. The inquiry under section 146 is limited only to the questions whether he was in possession on that date or not. Once he records its satisfaction in an preliminary order the High ' Court cannot go into the sufficiency or otherwise Of the materials placed on the record of which his satisfaction is based, [953G H] 3. It is well settled that under section 144 it is only for the magistrate to be satis fied regarding the validity of a dispute likely to cause a breach or of the disturbance of the order under subsection (5) of Section 145 that he must be satisfied about the exist ings of a particular breach of that peace and Once he record his satisfaction, in the main order, it is not necessary that the breach of ' peace should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show that the dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section(5) Of section 145 Cr. [962A B] Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant, a public company registered under the Indian Companies Act and its Managing Agents are the firm of Messrs K. R. Thyagaraja Chettiar and Co., whose partners are Mr. Thoyagarajaia Chettiar, and his two sons. The appellant contested this position and maintained that the state of affairs disclosed by its accounts was true, that its sales in favour of intermediaries were genuine and that, in fact, little or no profits were made by it in those transactions, that it purchased cotton only from the intermediaries and did pay them the amounts as shown in the accounts. Held, that the question whether the sales entered in the books of the appellant in the names of the intermediaries were bogus was one of mixed law and fact and that their determination was open to review by the courts. The decision in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. (I) L.R. , approved. Commissioner of income tax, Madras vs Ahmedabhai Umarbhai & Co., ; , referred to. Commissioner Of Income tax Bombay vs Ahmadbhai Umarubhai and Co.(1) was not applicable to the present case as the question was one which was actually in issue in the proceedings was a question of law and that the decision in the Com missioner of Income Tax, Bombay City vs Ahmed Bhai Umarbhai (I.L.R , referred only to nonresidents and consequently declined to refer the question ' The correctness of this decision does not appear to have been contested before the High Court, the only point dealt with in the judgment of the learned Judges being as to the correctness of the ratio in which the apportionment was made.

The appellant assessee carried on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager, Shri J.P. Vaish. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish in excess of tiffs amount was not really paid wholly for the purpose of carrying on business. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner reduced the commission payable from Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 37,733 in that year. The assessee took the matter in appeal to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal which held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish, the General manager and that the commission paid was not actually paid wholly or exclusively for the purposes of carrying out business. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the circumstances of the case the amount of Rs., 37, 733 paid to him was an amount laid out wholly and exclusively for tho purpose of the business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. HELD : The question whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or expended wholly or partly for the purpoSe of business, professions or vocation is a question of law. In the present case both the Appellate Tribunal and the Appellate Tribu nal rejected the view of the Incometax Officer that the rate of commission paid by Shri Vaish was not fixed on account of business considerations but there was some collateral reason. But considering the practice in similar business concerns, the Income. Tax Department expressed the view that the rates of 121/2 % commission were reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amount claimed by the asses see. The case of the assessee however is that a higher rate of Commission of 25% was fixed for Shri JP Vaish because the mill was old and dilapidated and it never made profit of even a lakh of rupees in the past and that, the rate Of 25% being fixed in order to create special interest of the General Managers for accomplishment of the task entrusted to him. In this case, neither the High Court nor the Appellate tribunal has applied the proper legal test in this case. [530 H] Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P., ; , referred to.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On January 13, 1954, the management served him with a charge sheet alleging that he had been doing anti union activities inside the factory during the working hours and so was guilty under section 12B(1) of the Standing Orders and Rules of the company. The appellant submitted his reply denying the charge and asking for being excused. On March 7, 1957, the Tribunal made an order fixing December 20, 1956, "for filing compromise or hearing". On January 31, 1957 the parties that was the management and the Union filed a joint petition of compromise settling all points of dispute out of court. Prior to this, on January 12, 1957 when the appellant filed his application for separate representation, this officer, was in charge of the conduct of the proceedings on behalf of the appellant. Neither before the Tribunal nor before the High Court any such plea was taken either in the appellants application before the tribunal or in his application under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution to the High court. The High Court dismissed the application summarily. Held, that the Tribunal committed no error in refusing the appellant 's prayer for representation through representatives of his own choice in preference to Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union. As a last resort, learned counsel for the appellant wanted to urge that the Secretary had no authority to compromise on behalf Of the Union and that the High Courts erred in rejecting the appellant application for a writ. The appeal must accordingly be dismissed.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against two defendants on the allegation that defendant No. 1 was the tenant inchief who had sub let the premises to defendant No 2. The suit was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent. On appeal by defendant No, 2 the District judge set aside the decree for ejectment against defendant No: 2 and confirmed the rest of the decree against defendant Nos. 1 and 2. In view of rr. 3 and 11 of O. XLI, r. 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the appeal abated so far as Kedar Nath was concerned as no application for bringing his legal representatives on record was made within the prescribed time. On October 1, 1956, two applications were filed in the High Court one under section 5 of the Limitation Act for the condonation of delay in filing the application for substitution of the heirs in placec of Kedar Nath and the other under section 6 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The other was the application made on October 1. 1956, for substituting the sons of Kedarnath in place of the deceased appellant as they were his heirs and legal representatives. When the appeals of the appellants other than Kedar Nath came up for hearing on September 1, 1958, a preliminary objection was taken for the, dismissal of the appeal by the surviving appellants. The High Court allowed the appellants time for filing an affidavit stating that the deceased was a member of the joint Hindu family and other relevant facts. A counter affidavit was filed stating that defendant Nos . 2 and 3 formed a joint Hindu Family. The application was on the basis that Kedar Nath, the deceased, and the surviving appellant constituted a joint family. The appellants contended that the surviving respondents were not competent to continue the appeal in view of OXLI r. 3 of O.[ XLI, rr. 4 and 11. Held: (i) The provisions of 0. XLI r. 9 of O., XXII and those of r. 33 of O, O.XXII, r., 33 are of no greater help to the contention of the appellant that their appeal could continue even though the appeal against Kedar Nath had become final. The provision of 0, XLI, R. 33 is not to be reversed or varied with respect to such rights to which the appellant is not found entitled. It empowers the Appellate Court to pass any decree and make any order which ought to have been passed or made in the proceedings before it and thus could have reference only to the nature of the decrees or Order in so far it affects the rights of the parties. When an appeal has been filed by all the plaintiffs, the provisions of O,. XLI, Rule 4 of O . XLI, rule 33 are not of greater help than to the appellants. In fact such an exercise of power will lead to the existence of two contradictory decrees between the heirs of Kedar Kumar and the respondents, one passed by the appellate Court and another to the contrary effect by the Court below which has attained finality consequent on the abatement of the appeals in so much as they are concerned. The defendant cannot be ejected from the premises when he has a right to remain in occupation of the premises on the date of the judgment holding that Kedarnath, one of the persons having a joint interest in letting out the property could not have ejected him. It is immaterial that the modification which the Court will do is one to which exception can or cannot be taken. No question of the provisions Of 0. XLII overriding the provisions contained in r.9 of O XLI, Rules 4 and 5 of O ' XLI, rules 3 and 4 of Order XLI, C.P., was not intended to apply to an appeal which was not a competent appeal against a party under the Code or under the Letters Patent.

The appellant tenant fell back on certain defences grounded on ss.106 and 111 of the TP Act on the score that no notice to quit had been given nor notice of forfeiture as prescribed by those sections. The landlord sought to break through these defences by urging that the lease has expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(a) and no notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 is needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise can be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g). The landlord seeks to breakthrough these defences, by urging: (1) that the leases have expired by lapse of time limit limited thereby unders.111(a), and no notices terminating the lease under section 107 are needed and (2) that forfeiture of tenancy causedby sub letting in contrary to terms of deed of lease can be avail of by him even in absence of notice as envisaged by section 112(g). Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Act which are but a statutory recognition of the rules of justice, equity and good conscience also govern those transfers. If, therefore, it does not whether its present provision, as amended in 1929, has to be treated as a rule of justice equity and fair conscience, undoubtedly the case will have to be decided in accordance with the rule laid down in the section, although in express terms it has not been made applicable to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force. [918C D] 2. The specific principle to which the legislature has now given effect by the amendment to section 111 of (g) did in fact represent a principle of justice. equity and justice are not such a variable commodity, that they change and stand altered on a particular date on the mandate of the legislature and that to leases made between 1882 and 1930 the principle of equity applicable is the one contained in sub section (g), as it stood before 1929, and to leases created after 1st April 1930, the principle underlying the provisions of sections 106 and 111(g) as embodying equity and Good conscience also apply those transfers.[918E F] 3. The law stands today under the Act, notice in writing by the tenant is a condition precedent to a forfeiture and the right of re entry. It cannot be gainsaid that a notice, as envisioned in section 111, not having been given to the lessee in the present case, determination of the demise under section III(g), cannot be claimed by the lessor. [936C D; 919A] 4. The requirement therein is merely statutory and it cannot trace its origin to any rule of equity. The principles of justice are equity and common conscience that a tenant has reasonable notice of termination even though it doesnot expire with the end of the month of a tenancy. It is a fitting finale to this part of the argument that in the High Court arguments proceeded on the footing that the Supreme Court had ruled in Namdeo (supra) that 'there being no requirement in English law of a written notice to the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the ground that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stood determined either by efflux Of time limited by under terms of section 111 or by forfeiture following the breach by the lessee of the express condition regarding sub letting. [948E F; 920A] 5.

The Governor of Assam was satisfied that the appellant, a Superintendent, P.W.D., and Wing against whom more charges had been received was unfit to be retained in public service and that he ought to be dismissed from service. The Governor was also satisfied under sub cl.(c) of the proviso to clause (2) of article 311 of the Constitution that in the interest of the security of the State, it is not expedient to give the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him as stated above. The appellant challenged the validity of the order of dismissal on the grounds (1) that the Governor had no power under sub clause (c) to cl.(2) Of article 311(2) to give him an opportunity of showing cause against his action proposed; and (2). that in any case, the satisfaction of the Governor was recorded in the language in which the provision in article 311 stood prior to its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act 1963. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the Governor did not satisfy the requirements of sub cl. (c), and as the satisfaction required by the amended article 311 (2), that the satisfaction did not extend to the inexpediency of giving P.K. H.ore an opportuni tory opportunity to the appellant to show his cause against action proposed, was too strict and technical and it should be held that in fact, the Governor intended to record his satisfaction on the question of inexpliency of holding the inquiry as required by article 320(3)(c) continued to be in force and applicable. HELD : (1 ) The order passed under sub el. (C) of cl. 2 of article 310 of the Constitu tion does not satisfy this requirement, because, it stands after amendment by Constitution (Sixteenth Amendment). Act 1963, and which was as follows: "311.(2)(c)" No such person as aforesaid shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges and where after such inquiry, the third step to be adopted is that if it is proposed to impose on him any penalty of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank he has to be given a specified reasonable opportunity. [488 E F] (2)(a) The satisfaction under the unamended provision, therefore, that the Government servant must be given an opportunity should have used these words in the sense in which they were used in the Constitution prior to their amendment and in the light of the interpretation placed on those words by this Court in State of U. As a result, the appellant 's satisfaction was recorded by the President in the manner prescribed under article 320 (3)(C) and that the opinion expressed by him was not binding on the Governor. [489 E F; 489 A B] (b) The word "shall" used in sub cl(c) refers to an inquiry in which, the delinquent government servant is to be informed of the charges against him and given a reason for such action. It does not mean that the consultation required by Article 320(2)(C), continues to be effective. [490 E] (3) The Governor had to arrive at his satisfaction as required under article 321(3) (c). The satisfaction of his Governor was not conclusive on the point of inex pediency or irregularity in consultation does not afford him a cause of action in a court of law, vide State of Uttar Pradesh vs Ram Kishan Rohtagi & Ors., ; , referred to.

The Sunni Central Board of Waqfs had to send a copy thereof to each Central Boards, (the Committee) and the Shia Sunni Central Wakf Board and Shia Shia Board and the Sunni Central Sunni Central Boards. The petitioners and through them Shia Community of Mohalla Darwara, Varanasi were complaining against various actions of the respondents including respondents 5 and 6 as representing the Sunni community of village Dosliha in the city of Varanasi and in particular are seeking a declaration that the 9 plots of land bearing plot Nos. 1 to 4 are basing their customary rights to perform the aforesaid religious rites, practices, observances and functions on the said nine plots, and structures on two foundations: (i) Decision 's of Competent civil courts adjudication these rights were in their favor in earlier litigation and (ii) Registration and registration of Shias concerning the plot and structures for performance thereof or their entitlement to the performance of the religious rites practices, practices etc. under section 38 of the aforesaid 1936 Act concluding in favour of Shiadas ' title to the concerned plots or structures thereon or their respective entitlement to perform their religious rites and functions over the plots or structure thereon or they entitlement to performance of their religious duties, practices practices, Observances and observances on certain plots and properties situated in the said Mohalla of Doswara, Police Station Jaitpura (formerly Adampur) in the City of Varanasi, and in the particular are sought a declaration as to the title to those concerned plots and the structures thereon and structures thereto or their claim entitlement to such performance of religious rites etc. The Petitioners and through their Shia sect of MohallaDoshipra were complaining about the various actions taken by them against the respondents (including respondents 5 & 6) as representing Sunni community in the matter of enjoying their religious faith and performance of various religious ceremonies, practices and observance on certain plot and properties situate in the aforesaid Mohalla of Darwara. The assessee company, a limited company, disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10 lakhs but claimed set off of capital loss of Rs 3.17,500 sustained by it during the assessment year 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 and 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the same should be set off against the capital gains in the assess ment year in question. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal by holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim of set off to be admissible had to be notified by the Income Tax Offi cer under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. That having not been done, the claim was not admissible. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the loss claimed for setoff to be allowable had to he notified by an Income Tax officer under Section24(3), and accordingly allowed the assessee 's claim. At the instance of the Revenue four questions were referred for opinion of the High Court. Whether on the facts and in the circum stances of the case, the Income tax Officer 's order for the assessment Year 1957 58 had not merged in the Appellate Assistant Commission 's Order in which the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner had given a clear finding that the losses was notional? If the answer to the above question is in the negative, whether any loss could be said to have been determined for the assess year 195758, which could be carried forward to subsequent years? Whether in view of the provisions of Section 80 of the Income. Tax Act 1961, the loss claim claimed for the asses see 's assessment year was not allowable. The High Court found that both the IncomeTax Officer as also the Appellate Assista tioner had clearly disallowed the assessee"s claim of carry forward and set off loss on the ground that loss had not been determined as required under Section 25(3). Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order for assessment year 1965 66 to which the Act of 1961 applied, it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. For convenience they are extract ed: "Section 74 (1)(a) Where in respect of any assessment year, the net result of the compu tation under the head "capital gains" is a loss such loss shall. subject to the other provisions of this Chapter. be dealt with as follows: "(i) such portion of the net loss as relates to capital assets other than short term capital assets assessable for that assessment year and, if it cannot be so set off, the amount thereof not so set aside shall be carried over to the following assessment yearand so on. However, that no loss shall be carry forward under this section for more than eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessmentyear for which the loss is first computed under the Act or as the case may be. " 1165 (ii) "When, in the course of the assessment of the total income of any assessee, it was not estab lished that a loss of profits or gains has taken place which he is entitled to have set off under the provisions Of this section, the income tax Officer shall notify to the asses sees by order in com pensation the amount of the loss as computed by him for the purposes of this section.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Engineering Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the three units. All the service conditions of the persons working in the three Units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz., Defence Science Services (DOS) and D.S. in which flexible complementing scheme was applicable would also retire at the age of 60 years provided they had been promoted to the grades they were holding at the time of attaining the age Of 58 years within the preced ing five years. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, who held that respondent K.T. Shastry was entitled to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 58 years and was not liable to be retired at the alleged superannuation age. The Tribunal, however, held that the re spondent was not enti tled to be retire at that age of 55 years his superannu al age being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10.2.86 referred to above. It is this decision which is challenged before this Court by the appellants. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation ages of the members of the staff of the Department were increased, it could not be held that he respondent who belonged to another unit, viz DAQAS was entitled ted to the said benefit. There is no dispute that the Govern ment has power to vary the service condition of the member of the services from time to time. The question involved in the appeal is, however not whether the Government has such power. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question is whether the respondent was also entitled to the benefit of the power so exercised in the facts and circum stances of the case. [85D] 1.2 The question whether the Govern ments had such power, is not whether Government has power. The fact that the government has power has to vary it on the basis of the basis on which it has come into existence. [86E] 1:3 In spite of the decision of the Tribunal and even pending this appeal when no stay was granted, the appellant Union of India retired the respondent at the said age of superannuation. The classification made between them further has no rational basis and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown to us by Mr. Subba Rao appearing for the appellants.[86E F] 1 :4 In spite thereof the decision was not implemented, the Appellant Union of india & Ors. vs Union of lndia & Anr., [1985] Suppl. SCR 491; referred to.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election of councillors to the said Municipality was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. The counting of votes took place with regard to Ward No. 25 on June 4, 1967. According to the election petition, the results were published in the Official Gazette on June 15, 1967 and the petition was filed on June 24, 1967, i.e., within time prescribed by the Act. The appellant denied that he was responsible for the publication of any of the impugned pamphlets. It was further alleged that the first publication having taken place on August 21, 1968 the appellant 's name as councillor had been declared in the official Gazette on July 16, 1967; and that the second publication having took place on the 8th June, 1967 the petition filed by him on June 25, 1967 was beyond time. The trial Judge rejected this application holding that the election petitioner was guilty of publication of two pamphlets which cast serious aspersions on his character and conduct and prejudiced him materially in the eyes of the voters as a result whereof he lost the election and that he had thereby prejudicing the voters generally against him and in particular instigating the Muslim voters to vote against him by arousing their religious sentiments. The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The trial judge had jurisdiction to call these two persons as witnesses under the provisions of the Act and that there was no evidence on which the Judge could have come to the conclusion he did and find the appellant guilty of corrupt practice. [975 E] (ii) There is no error apparent on the face of the record before the High Court and consequently the jurisdiction under article 226 of the Constitution could not have been exercised on the facts of the case by the issue of a writ of certiorari. Instead of framing a separate issue with regard thereto to each charge of corrupt practices raised in the petition, it was quite clear that but for the evidence of these two witnesses, it would have been very difficult if not impossible, for the Judge to have come into the conclusion that he did, and find out why there were two Gazette Publications and which was the publication to be taken into account for computation of the period of limitation prescribed by section 21(1) of the Representation of the People Act. [936 C] (iii) The High court had jurisdiction under Article 226 of 'the Constitution to call those two persons, as witnesses, under the provision of the . [976 E] R. In the instant case, if the two persons had not been examined, the Judge might well have decided the issue the other way. But the Act certainly gave him the power to do so and no exception can be taken to the course adopted by the Judge although it must be recorded that his earlier order refusing to issue summonses to them in the first instance when asked to do it on the 21st August was hardly justifiable. [946 D] R, In the present case, there is no merit in this point raised by the appellant. The first point therefore fails. [948 A] (iv) There was no error in the order of the High court and consequently, the jurisdiction tinder article 226 could not be exercised on facts of ' the case.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The validity of this notification was challenged by the petitioner under article 32 of the Constitution on the ground that it was ultra vires. Held, that the Validation Act was not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, for the reason that it operates retrospectively. It was finally urged on behalf of the State that the impugned notification was intra vires and that it is not a law which the State Legislature was competent to enact and it was therefore a nullity. The fact that the 1947 Act permitted the seller who was a registered dealer to collect the sales tax as a tax from the purchaser did not alter the real nature of the tax which, by the express provisions of the law, was cast upon the seller. In the present case the sale sought to be taxed took place between April 1, 1956 and July 31, 1955 whereas the Validation Acts were passed in 1958. It is therefore not a tax on the occasion of sale. P. Sales Tax Act XV of 1948 contemplates a levy of tax in future, that does not affect the competence of the Legislature under entry 52 in List II or List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The circumstance that the 1946 Act, after the amendment, permitted the buyer who was registered dealer, to collect sales tax from purchasers did not do away with the primary liability of the seller to pay the sales Tax. This also makes it clear that the salestax need not be passed on to the purchaser and this fact does not alter its real nature. The State Legislature derives its authority to enact a law, which is either prospective or retrospective. P, 16 Acts, the levy of taxes is annual and the rules contemplate submission of quarterly returns and payment of taxes every quarter on the admitted turnover, and that a conditional legislation under which payment of tax will become enforceable in fururo would be inconsistent with the scheme of the Act and the Rules. The circumstances that the 1941 Act, by force of which the tax became payable came into force in 1958, did not affect its validity as it operates prospectively.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Sessions Court, and the High Court affirmed it in appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. [592 D] 2. In prison treatment must, therefore be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from being deterrent. The insulated years behind the insensitive bars must possess a hospital setting if correction is a social purpose, as Gandhiji often insisted. [593 E] Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative, apart frombeing deterrent. [595 F G] Sunil Kumar Batra vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to. 3. The Special circumstances of the instant case constracted us to re ferred a little more on principle since the restatory approach to sentence has been re quired by the Courts below. The task is not done by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a newlic leaf of normal life. [597 C] 4. The Court must restore the man. A hyper sexed homo sapiens cannot be occupilitated by humiliating or harsh treatment but that is precisely the perversion of unreformed Jail Justice which some criminologists have described as the crime of punishment. This Court has held in Sunil Batra vs Batra, ; and later reiterated that constitutionally viewed, punitive deprivation Of personal freedom should be goalvanised and humaneally restorative apart from be deterrent. In this background, it is not necessary to refere with correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. [598 C D] 5. The appellant is a youth barely 22 with no criminal antecedents save this offence. He has a young wife and a farm to look after. Given correctional courses through meditational therapy and other measures, his erotic aberration may wither away. A man like the appellant has a reasonable prospect of shaping into a balanced person, given propitious social environs, curative and congenial work and techniques of internal stress release or reformatory self expression. In such circumstances, it would be desirable to superadd to the sentence of imprisonment a few directives to ensure that the carceral period reforms reforms the convict. [596 E F] 6. The State Government will defend Indian Womanhood by stamping out voluptuous meat markets by merciless criminal action. [599 C D].

The assessee company maintained its accounts on the mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the Act certain plots of land measuring about 19.17 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the assessee were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5, Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952 published in the Gazette dated January 8, 1953. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the assesse. The assessee was not satisfied with the amount of compensation and preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator 24 Parganas, Calcutta. The Arbitrator made an award on July 29, 1955 whereby he fixed the amount at Rs.30,10,873 on account of the permanent acquisition of the land thus enhancing the original amount of compensa tion by Rs.513,624 on which he directed interest at 5 per cent per annum from January 8. 1953, the date of acquisition to the date when the payment was made till the date the date Of payment. The State Government then appealed to the High Court and during the pendency of the appeal on April 25, 1956 it deposited Rs.7,36,691 which the assessee was permitted to withdraw on May 9, 1956 on furnishing security. On receipt of the amount credited it in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956 the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum Rs. 7,24,914 in the assessee 's business income. This represented the difference between the sum of RS.737,190 payable to it in terms of the award dated July 29. 1956 of the Arbitrator and a sum Of Rs.12,276 out that amount which had already been assessed to tax. The Income Tax officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assesses on the date on the award. On appeal by the assessee before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income tax, two contentions were raised by it. It was urged that in any event the amount did not accrue to the appellant as its income during the relevant previous year ended April 31,1956. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the first contention and held that the compensation received by the assesee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of business carried on by the assesses, and therefore, was a trading receipts of the business carried On by the Assessee. The High Court accepted the other contention and upheld the order of the Appellate Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding that when land was taken over by the Govern ment for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment, no income could accrue to him. It is the amount actually awarded by the Collector or subsequently decreed by the court which accrues to him, and the respective amounts, whether awarded by Collector or the Court accrue on the respective dates on which the award or the decree is passed. Income tax is not levied on a mere right to receive compensation; there must be something tangible, something in the nature of a debt, 395 something in, the nature or of an obligation to pay an ascertained amount. On the date When the Collector awarded the compensation, it is only that amount that amount has accrued or deemed to accrue, whether in fact paid or not.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the respondents on the ground that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. The appellants thereupon appealed to the High Court which held that the decree was not a nullity and was executable. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant respondents that paragraph 1 of the compromise petition was an admission in respect of only the first part, namely, the positive aspect of clause (f) and not of the second part, viz., that the landlord has no other reasonably suitable non residential accommodation of his own in his occupation in the city or town concerned. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The terms of the agreement under consideration in that case clearly showed that the parties were to vacate the premises by 31 12 1970. [882 D] 2. The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree for eviction because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decree under the law. It is too late in the day to contend that the provisions Of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. [888 E] 3. The object of the section is very different from many similar State Statutes. Section 12(1) (f), which provides for summary eviction of tenants, lays down that no decree for the eviction of a tenant from any accommodation can be passed except on one or more of the grounds enumerated in section 12(11). [889 F] 4. The inhibition related to the filing of the suit only. No suit can be filed for eviction except on the one or other of the ground enumerated in Section 12 (1) [883 A B] 5. In sub sections (2) to (11) of section 12 certain conditions have been engrafted to show under what circumstances an order for the ejectment of a tenants cannot be passed in relation to some of the reasons enumerated in sub section (1). Reading the section as a whole and remembering the beneficial object of this Act for the protection of a tenancy based upon public policy, it does not find much difficulty in bringing the section at par with other similar State statutes and holding as a matter of construction that no decrees for the evict of atenant from any premises can be made except on two or more grounds enumerated In sub section. Reading the Section as a part and rememberting the beneficial purpose of the statute for the benefit of a landlord based upon Public Policy, it would appear that the inhibition related only to the filling of the suits only. [878 E F] 6. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23 Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". If on the other hand, the court is satisfied on consideration of the terms of compromise and, if necessary, by considering them in the context of the pleadings and other materials, in that the agreement is lawful, as in any other suit, so in an eviction suit the Court is bound to record the compromise and pass a decree in accordance therewith. Passing a decree on adjudication of the requisite facts on or their admission in a compromise either express or implied, is not different. [864 A B]. 7. The expression "in any other law" has been used in the sense of wide import and it cannot be said that the section applies to eviction cases governed by special statutes.[878 C] 8.

The assessee company was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 69,973/ leaving a distributable balance of Rs, 91,116/ . The Income tax Officer however, again invoked the provisions of section 23A(1) and levied additional super tax @ 4/ per rupee on the surplus of Rs 60,761/ . In appeal, the Asstt. Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he therefore cancelled the orders of the Income tax officer under section 23 A(1). The Tribunal, however, did not declare any dividends for the year in question. In appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the assessee had suffered a capital gain of Rs 12,00,000/ as a result of the depreciation of the value of the shares of Elphinstone Mills Ltd. [864 A] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co. (Pvt.) Ltd., ; , referred to. (ii) The question whether the Directors of a company had acted as prudent businessmen in refraining from declaring any dividend is a matter primarily for the Directors or the director of a Company and deal with the problem with a sympathetic and objective approach. [851 D] Commissioner Of Income tax West Bengal, vs Gangadharshyam Das Gupta, , referred tOere: Whether in a particular year dividend should be declared or not is a question primarily for him Directors of the company. The question is not whether the value or the shares may go up in future but whether the directors were justified in not declaring dividends in view Of the loss suffered.

The appellants filed objections before the Civil Judge, Aligarh. The Civil Judge modified the award and announced by Shri Vikram Singh was accepted. On appeal to the District Judge a preliminary objection was raised that no appeal lay under section 39 of the Act. The District judge overruled the objection and held that the Civil Court was not justified under section 15 of the , in modifying the award merely because he disagreed with the finding. He, therefore, allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Civil judge modifying the Tribunal 's order. On further revision by the appellants before the High Court, a preliminary objections were raised. The High Court held that section 37 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act (U.P.) Act V of 1954) applies only to arbitrations referred to in section 37 and section 39 Of the Act does not apply because the appellants had apparently applied under section 5 of the . In appeal to this Court, HELD: The effect of section 37 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act. Section 37 of U. P. Consolidation Of Holdings Rules 1954, does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15 Of the . Further, the effect of s. 46 and section 47 is that every provision of the excepting sub section(1) Of section 6 sections 7 to 12,36 and 37, apply to arbitration proceedings under the Act.[354B C] Attar Singh vs The State of U P., ; , referred to.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of the superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. In 1974, it was made under section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961. Thereafter in 1988, the corporation passed a resolution for the first time making 75 per cent of the posts of superintending Engineers available to the executive Engineers holding degrees and 25 per cent to the Executive Engineers who were diploma holders. This resolution was also admittedly not a regulation made under the said section 64. But for this resolution, the petitioner who was senior to respondent NO. 2 would have been promoted to the post on 31st October 1990. However, since respondent No.2 was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to that post on that date. It is this promotion which was challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the Special Leave Petition it was contended for the petitioner that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineer on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the posts as Superintending Engineer since they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineers and do the same work. There was also a common seniority of the Executive engineers maintained, hence the classification was discriminatory in nature and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the Special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proposition that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [717G] 1.2 In the absence, of rule, or regulation, the authority could prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this was what was taken till the Year 1988 and was also sought for to be made since 1988. By the impugned Resolution, the respondent corporation was created. Thereafter, in 1988 the Corporation passed a Resolution for the second time making 25 per% of the post posts of Superintending Engineer on 31 10 1990. The promotion which is challenged by respondent No 2 was a Degree holder Junior Engineers and diploma holder Junior Engi cers. The degree holders Junior Engineers Junior Engineers had sought a relief that such a quota be kept. It was while dealing with this relief claimed, that this Court had observed that it could not be don e except by carving out two classes in the same category of junior Engineers. It may be observed that the very Bench which decided Roshan Lal 's case [supra] was thus no authority for the proposition that if direct recruits and promotees are integrated into one cadre they cannot be classified for purposed of promotion on a basis other than that in case before the them the classification classified for purpose of promo tion on a par tional basis other then that they were drawn from different sources. The Court also pointed out that the principle that in State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. Narasing Rao, ; and The Union of India and others vs Dr. S.B. Kholi; , , it was already held that classification on the ground of educational qualification was permissible. [Emphasis supplied]. The Court pointed out in Roshan Lal Tandon vs Union of lndia, ; , relied upon Roshan Lal Kothari vs Union o India, ; relied upon. Roshan Lal Desai & Ors., ; , referred to Roshan Lal Pathak and others etc. vs State of Gujarat and others; , 372 is, therefore, not justified.

The petitioners in the writ petition were advocates practising in this Court. They filed applications under Article 32 of the Constitution for a mandamus to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme Court and the various High Courts of the country and ancili cial orders of directions in regard to the same. The petitions were contested by the Attorney General on the ground that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancies in the superior courts was not a justiciable matter. The petitioners contended that the petition was not maintainable as the filing of the writ petitions was not justiciable matter, and that the filing up of vacancies in superior Courts was not an justiciable matter; that the Court 's jurisdiction and power to issue writs under Article 226 of the Constitu tion were not justiciable matters; that it was the constitutional obligation of the Union to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the subordinate courts and the default, if any, was a matter exclusively within the domain of the constitutional scheme and concern of the concerned constitutional functionaries. Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The primacy of the Chief Justice of India in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. [439C] 1.2 In view of what we have already stated and the assurance held out by the learned Attorney General, it is clear that further monitoring for the time being was not necessary. No. 1303 of 1987 to be placed before the Chief Judge for constituting a Bench of nine Judges to examine the two questions indicated above, namely, the position of the chief Justice of the High Court and that of the view that the fixation of Judge strength is not justiciable should be re considered by a larger bench. Indeed, the Union Government has quite often both before the Parliament and outside have stated that it has, as matter of policy, not made any appointments to the superior judici ary without the name being cleared by the Chief Justices of the States and that it had, as a matter of Policy, not make any appointments or to the subordinate judiciary without the names being cleared. [454D E] 1:3 The primacy is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. There are preponderant and com pelling considerations why the views of the learned Chief Justice Judges of the State States and the Supreme Courts should be afforded a decisive import unless the executive has some material in its possession which may indicate that the appointment is otherwise undesirable. [453F] 1 :4 The primacy, of theChief Justice of lndia in the matter of selection will improve the Quality of selection.[454C D] 2:5 In view Of what we had already stated, and the assurances held out, by the counsel for the AttorneyGeneral, it was clear that re consideration is not necessary to be examined in the view of the fact that by the Amendment the Chief justice of India would become the Chairman of the Commission. [449E] 2.6 The primacy and primacy of 'the position of 'Chief Justice ' of India and the viewthat the fixation is not judi cation should be considered by the larger bench.[454F] 2 :7 The primacy to the Chief Judges of States and their views that the determination of Judge sen iority is not a constitutional obligation for the executive to adopt and apply the standard. [450G] 2 8.1 In view, what we are required to be re examined relate to and arise from the views expressed by the majority opinion touching the very status of 'consultation ' generally and in particu lar with reference to 'Consultation" with Chief Justice.

The respondent was a Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch of the Bank in Banga lore city availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April 4, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by M/s. Shri Manju Travels of Bangalore and claimed reimbursement for the same. The said bill was passed by the Bank on May 15, 1978 but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/S. Shri Manu Travels was a spurious one which indulged in issuing fake travel receipts. Thereupon the respondent was served with a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978 followed by a departmental enquiry. It is not necessary to go into the details in regard to proceedings at the departmental enquiry but it would be sufficient to state that the respondent participat ed in the departmental inquiry till it was completed by the enquiry officer Shri U.B. Menon. 200 Paragraph 9.14 of the Memorandum of Bi parperate Settle ment dated October 19, 1966 empowers the Chief Executive Officer, etc., of he Bank to decide which officer should be empowered to hold an enquiry and take disciplinary action in the case of each office or establishment. Accordingly, Shri U B. Menon, Special Officer was appointed an Enquiry Offi cer under the Chief Execu tive Officer 's Order dated January 9, 1979, which reads as under: "Pursuant to the powers vested in the Executive Director by the Chairman and Managing Director of the bank, as per his office order dated 20th December, 1978, authorising him to appoint Enquiry Officers and Appellate Authorities under the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi parganas Settlement dated 19th October 1966, the undersigned is pleased to appoint Shri UB. Hegde, Special officer to work as an Enquiry Officer to hold and conduct departmental enquiries against the members of the staff governed by the provisions Of the Award and Bi paramom Settlement dated 20nd December,1978 authorising him (i) to appoint enquiry Officers and to pass necessary orders under the provi sions of Chapter19 of the said Bi parirana Settlement dated August 19th 10, 1966; (ii) to pass appropriate orders under t he provisions of chapter 19 of Bi Parsi ty Settlement Settlement dated May 19th Octo ber, 1966. Shri U .B. Shah, Special Offi cial Officer was appoint ed an Enquiry officer under the chief Executive Officer ' s order dated January 14, 1980, which read as under; "Pur pursuant to the Powers vested in him by the chairman and Managing Direc tor of the KG. road Branch of Banga Ltd., as per my office Order dated 20 th December, 1977, the Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure, New Delhi is pleased To appoint Shri M.B." The said Enquiry Officer conducted the departmental exami nation against the respondent and found that the firms of M.S. Manju Travel were a spurious person which indulged into issuing fake travelling receipts. Thereafter, the respondent retired from service on January 31, 1979. Not withstanding his retirement he continued to function as an Enquiring Head Cashier in K. G. Road branch of the appellant Bank. The respondent was then served with the charge sheet on October 12. 1978 followed and a departmental inquiry was held against him. However, during the pendency of the departmental proceedings, he retired from serv ice on January 1, 1979 and gave an opportunity to the respondent to be heard on the question of punishment and thereafter passed the impugned order of discharge on January 14. 1980.

The respondents are owners and are in possession of the building bearing municipal door Nos. 3766 to 3776 situated in the main Chawri Bazar, Delhi. As the building was an old construction and required urgent and extensive repairs, on October 16, 1965, the appellant submitted to the Commissioner of the appellant Corporation under section 336 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (Act LXVI of 1957) for sanction of the plans of a building or the execution of a work unless such a building, or work contravened any of the provisions of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. The Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was residential against proposal of commercial. The Chief Justice held that the Commissioner could decline the sanction only if there was a contravention of sub s.(2) Of section 336, or section 339(2)(a) of the Act. On appeal by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, the High Court confirmed the order of the Chief Justice. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Master Plan prepared under the Delhi Development Act,1957 and the Master plan prepared thereunder showed that the proposed user mentioned by them in the Master plans submitted by the respondents did not conform to bye laws and contravened section 336(2) (a) in respect of land use and section 340(2); (2)(b) the Commissioner had no power under section 337 or section 343 of the Municipal Act to refuse sanction of a Building or work if the building or work or use of the site for building or works would contravene any other law; and (3) the order rejecting the application was justified by the provisions, of cl. The Master Plan had been prepared under section 7 of the Development Act and it had come into operation under section 11 in the area concerned. HELD : (1)(a). Under sub s(2), the Master Plans shall (a), define the various zones into which Delhi may be divided for the purposes of development and indicate the manner in which the land in each zone is proposed to be used; (b) serve as a basic pattern of frame work within which the zonal development plans of the various Zones may be prepared; and, (c) serve, as a Basic pattern of framing work within Which the Zonal Development Plan may be submitted. [175 E F] (2). The Master plan is prepared for the area, before it comes into operation in the Zone, the procedure indicated in section 10 will have to be followed and parties will have been given an opportunity of placing any objections or making any representations or offering any suggestions. So far as the respondents ' lands are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part of the proposed road, mentioned in the master plan and, if that is so, there is no violation of section 14 of the development Act. [176 G H] (3). The Commissioner has to give sanction for the erection of a buildings or execution of work unless the building, work or the use of such site for the building etc. are contravened by any other laws. [177 D E] (4) The Master plans have been prepared and sent to the Central Government for approval. parties and local authorities will have also to be given an opportunities of placing objections or make any representations. So long as there is a proposal regarding the width that a road should have, all use of land adjoining that road is prohibited for an indefinite period, the Master Planning Plan will hold the field. [174 E F; 175 A] (5) The respondents ' land are not within any manner specified in section 336 and, therefore, they are not entitled to the sanction.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No, 2 was charged with having committed offences under sections 120 B, 161, 465 and 466 of the Indian Penal Code and the appellants were tried in the Court of Special Judge at Rewa under the Vindhya Pradesh Criminal Law Amendment (Special Courts) Ordinance LVI of 1949 and the Special judge acquitted both of them. The State took an appeal to the Judicial Commissioner, Rewa. The Judicial Commissioner reversed the order of acquittal passed by the Special Judge and convicted both the appellants of the several offences with which they were charged. The appellants contended that the statements made by the appellant to them were not recorded on the night of 11th April, 1949, but they had appended their signatures to the Panchnama of the numbers of the currency notes actually found in the bedroom of the appellant 's house and that the statement was inadmissible in evidence as it was not recorded under the provisions of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Held, that the appellants could not have by any mischance failed to appreciate that these Government currency notes which were recovered from the top drawer exceeded by far the amount which according to him had left with him by way of balance and the most natural reaction to the recovery of this large sum of money would have been that he would have certainly denied that these moneys were his and he would be surprised at finding that such a large sum was found there. The evidence of these witnesses being thus worthy of credit and the statements given by the appellants being admissible in evidence there is no doubt that the appellant 1 was asked by Shanti Lal Ahuja, the Additional District Magistrate to make the statements to these two witnesses not with a view to avoid the bar of section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or by way Of colourable pretence but by way thereof greater caution particularly having regard to the fact that the accused No. 25,000 tallied with the numbers mentioned in the memo prepared at that time was enough to establish the falsity of the allegation made by him.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the respondent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. He was acquitted by the trial court. The suit was decreed. On appeal, the Additional District Judge dismissed the respondent 's suit on 20.4.1976. This order of dismissal was challenged as illegal in the present suit which was instituted on 6.11.1982. Besides taking several technical objections, the suit was defended on merits as well as on the ground of limita tion. From the judgment of the trial Court it appears that only two questions were pressed by the parties, namely, whether the suit be barred by limitation and whether the order of dis crimination was illegal on the grounds that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. Both the issues were decided by the learned 824 Subordinate Judge against the plaintiff and the suit is accordingly dismissed. The respondent appealed against the decision. It appears that before the Additional Distt. Judge who heard the appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the other accused constable Kahan singh had also filed a separate suit against his dismissal from service which was decreed with an observation that it was open to the competent authorities to pass fresh order of punishment in accordance with law but while no further punishment was awarded to him, the respondent could not be re instated in service for a short time in pursuance of the decision in the suit as the order was of his dismissal had been passed by an authority not compe tent in this regard, and that later he was again dismissed. It was also contended on his behalf that the finding of the Additional Sessions Judge on the question of limitation is patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation was applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. The High Court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. Serious objection has been taken against the observations of the first appellate court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the respondent in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments. After heat ing the learned counsel for the parties it was agreed that the question involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Court in the manner it has been done. The appellants contended that the High court should have called for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. Allowing the appeal of the State, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the question whether serious questions of law are in volved in this case and the High COurt erred in dismissing the second appeal in limine. [825G] 1.2 The question involved was a pure question of law which should not be lightly brusheded by the high Court in its manner it had been done.[825A B] 1:3 In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the High Courts shall permit the plaintiff to file relevant rebutting evidence. [826C D] 1 :4 The operation of the decree of the First Appellate Court shall remain stayed till the final disposal of the second appeals by theHigh Court. The operation and of the decrees of the Ist appellate court shall remain stay till the finally disposal of second appeal by the 1125 High Court.

The appellant company entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee entered into a contract with M/s. Raghunath & Sons (P) Ltd., for 500 bales and 2500 bales of corn sacks: the contract for B Twill was with two parties M/S. Raghunath and Sons ( P) Ltd. for 500 consignments and M/o Mahadeo Ramkumar for 600 bales. The assessee had no godown for keeping the goods and had not handled them. The goods were in the godown of the mills and only the delivery orders addressed to the mills changed hands. The amount realised on sale to M/ s. 98,534/ to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh, ; , D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, ; and D. Wadhwani vs Commissioner Of Income tax (supra) on which the Tribunal 's decision in D.M. Wadhwai vs Commissioner for Income tax was based. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the transaction between the appellant and the respondents could not be called contracts involving actual delivery of possession of the goods concerned. HELD: (i) The definition of speculative transactions in the explanation is not relevant for the purpose of this Explanation. [184 D] (ii) The explanation does not invalidate speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual delivery or physical delivery, and having regard to the mischief which was sought to be averted by the promulgation of the ordinance to prevent persons who dealt in differences only and never intended to take delivery under any circumstances it was held that such a transaction was speculative in the general sense or under the Contract Act. [185 E] (iii) The Explanation does not validate speculative transactions according to Explanation 2 if the actual delivery is of the commodity or the scrips has taken place; on the other hand, a transaction which is otherwise speculative would not be a speculative transaction within the meaning of explanation 2. [186 G] D. Kolla Sreeramurthy vs Commissioner Income tax ; , followed.

The first respondent was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. The appellant filed an Election Petition challenging the rejection of the appellant 's nomination papers on the ground that it was not accompanied by a copy of the nomination paper. The Tribunal decided in favour of the first respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words " sign" and "subscribe" mean both signing, so called, and the placing of a mark is to be treated differently. [488 F] (ii) The word "sign" used in section 33(1) of the Representation of the People Act means "to attest or confirm by adding one 's signature". It is well settled that attestation in the prescribed manner is required in the case of proposers and seconders who are not able to write their names. [490 G] (iii) The requirement of attestation in a prescribed manner was not, therefore, mandatory. [448 B] (iv) The Returning Officer had at the time of scrutiny stage been to see whether the nominations were in order and to hear objections. It is true he was not to reject any nomination paper on the grounds of any technical defect which is not of a substantial character but he cannot remedy the defect. He must leave it as it is. If it is technical and unsubstantial it will not matter. [489 C] (v) The proposer and seconder are not merely signing by way of attesting the candidate 's signatures to the nomination form but are actually putting the man forward as a suitable candidate for election and as a person for whom they are prepared to vouch, also that the candidate "s signature imports more than a mere vouching for the accuracy of the facts entered in the form. [486 E] (vi) The attestation in prescribed manner under section 36 is required if the proposer or seconder as many nomination papers as there are vacancies to be filled. If they are not signed " either in one way or the other, then it is clear that they have not been " subscribed" because " subscribing " imports a "signature" and as the Act sets out the only kinds of "signatures" which it will recognise as II signing", for the purposes of the Act, there is no valid signatures of either of a proposer or a seconder in any one of the four nomination papers.

The appellants, who were employees of the Company, went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to the strike notice given by their registered union called 'the Association of Chemical Workers ' in support of its demand for re instatement of three of the Unions. The company sent a cheque to each one of the appellants for the amount due to him on account of gratuity, leave salary and one month 's salary. On September 7, 1972, the Company issued notices to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the company. The appellants replied that since by not reporting for duty they had confirmed its presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of the respondent Company and had totally abandoned the Company 's service, their names had been struck off. On October 23, 1972 the appellant wrote to the Company returning the cheques sent by the Company and stating therein that it did not wish to revise its earlier decision under which their names have been struck out from the rolls of respondent company. On May 19, 1973, the appellants ' union wrote a letter to the Works Manager of the factory protesting against the action of the appellant in removing them from service and asserting that the said action was by way of victimization for their participation in the strike. The Company sent a letter dated September 7. 1972 stating therein: "I am interested in the service of this company and had neither voluntarily abandoned the service nor did they wish to do so, and that they would report for work the moment the strike is called off by their union." On October 3, 1973 the appellant addressed a letter asking the Company to re instart the appellants from its rolls on the ground that they had abandoned their service. The Works Manager replied that it was not willing to revise the earlier decision. Thereupon the appellants made the aforesaid complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with the result as stated above. On March 30, 1973. the union made a formal demand calling upon the Company for re dis instate ment of its three dismissed leaders and had not only by their letters dated September 21, 1972 and September 26, 1972 but also returned the cheques received from them on account Of their leave salary gratuity etc. The workmen addressed letters to the works Manager of respondent No. 1 company requesting him to report to for duty the moment they were called off for duty. On July 5, 1973 a formal demands calling upon it to re disengage the appellants, and 10 other striking workmen addressed letter to them stating that since "by not reporting duty they have confirmed its presumed presumption that their services were no more interested to be continued in service" of the Respondent Company and requesting the Company that they should report for duties on or after September 18. 1972 failing that their absence will be construed "as voluntary abandonment" of service, and their name would be strike off from their muster rolls. On these demands the appellants sent separate communications to the appellant and 10 Others informing them that since the company 's letter dated 9th September, 1972 had reached them only on September 20, 1972 they were interested in service and had never abandoned the services of the Appellant Company and did not desire to do it, and therefore, they would, report for worked the moment a strike was called off. The appellant replied that the action was illegal and invalid. Three questions arose for consideration in this case namely: (1) what is the true meaning of the expression "abandonment of service"; and (2) whether in the circumstances of the case it could be said that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned their services. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.

The trustees of a public trust mortgaged a house belonging to the trust to one Saheba to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000. An action instituted by the mortgagee against the trustees to enforce the mortgage was compromised and it was decreed that the trustees do pay Rs. 3,910 due under the mortgage by monthly instalments of Rs 100 each and in default of three instalments the entire amount remaining unpaid shall become due and recoverable from the mortgagee property. The trustees applied under 0. 21 r. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale and deposited Rs. 250 being 5 % of the purchase money for payment to the appellant and Rs. 6 for payment of the mortgage amount, claiming that in consideration o the latter amount the mortgagee had agreed to "give to them six months ' for payment Of the mortgage money", and had agree in the meantime to abandon the application for execution. The Subordinate Judge passed an order disposing of the execution application and directed that Rs.250 out of the amount deposit by the trustees be paid over to the appellants. 21 Code of civil Procedure, the executing Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the auction held in execution of the decree. The High Court of Gujarat in exercise of powers under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code set aside that order and remanded the case to the District Court for decision on all points correctly arising out of tho matter. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The Legislature did not intend to put any restriction upon the power of the civil court executing a decree for recovery of money due from the trust, by sale of the property of the trust.
