The learned Judge completely misconceived the nature of a reference made by a Judge or a Bench of Judges to a larger Bench. when it appears to a Single Judge or Division Bench that there are conflicting decisions of the same Court, or there are decisions of other High Courts in India which are strongly persuasive and take a view different from the view which prevails in his or their High Court. or that a question of law of importance arises in the trial of a case, the Judge or the Bench passes an order that the papers be placed before the Chief Justice to enable him to constitute a larger bench to examine the question. [458 D E] (ii) The judgment of the Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court was binding on Raju J., If the learned Judge was of the view that the decision of Bhagwati, J. in Pijare Karimbhai 's case and of Nacleod, C. "It is hardly necessary to emphasise that consideration of judicial propriety and decorum require that if a single Judge hearing a matter is inclined to take the view, that the earlier decisions of that Court, whether of a Division Bench or of a Single judge, needto be re considered, he should not embark upon that enquiry sitting as a single judge, but should refer the matter 'to a Division bench.

The Government of India, by an order dated April 21, 1970, retired him from service under Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules. The Government had also the power under Rule 56(j) to retire a Government servant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying serv ice. The appellant contended that para 620 of the Railway Pension Manual which is identical to Rule 2 (2) was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of Rule 2 of the Pension Rules may also be to weed out unsuitable employees. The object is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 2 gives no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Government. There is no requirement under the rule to act in 'Public Interest '. A valid rule having some lacuna or gap can be supplemented by the execu tive instructions but a statutory rule which is stat utely invalid cannot be validated with the support of executive instructions. The instructions can only supplement and not supplant the rule. [800G H] Union of India & Ors. vs R. Narasimhan, ; , referred to. 1.2 Rule 2046 has no parity with Rule 2.(2)of Pension Rules which is a statutory provision. In any case the point before this Court was neither involved nor raised in Narasimhan 's case and as such cannot be con cerned with the aid of executive instruction. [801C D] Union Of India & others vs R Narasimhan ; , relied on. 1 2. Rule 2045 having been framed under Article 309 of the Constitu tion and being a compendious rule, the railway employees are only gover ed by the said rule and para 620 was void and inoperative. This Court while setting aside the judgment of the High Court held as under: "Thus the areas of operation of Para 620 of Railway Pension manual is different from that of clause (h) and (k) of Rule 2946 of the Rules. Para 620 is in the nature of executive Instructions but is similarly worded as Rule 2.

The assessee firm had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose and had extracted Katechu from October, 1940 to September, 1941. The sales of katechu were effected by M/s Biharilal Balkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The assessee firm did not maintain any books of accounts and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/S BiharilalBalkishan. The assessee Firm had taken the jungle on leased for this purposes and had quoted Katechku from October 1940 to June, 1941 to September 1941. It was alleged that the sales of Katechoo were effect ed from 30th May, 1941 and March, 1943 remained in stock till the last date of the chargeable accounting period namely 31st March, 1944 and no part of it was sold. The Excess Profit Tax Officer did not set off the said deficiency of profits that accrued in respect of the period 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable assessment period from 1st April, 1941, to March 29, 1943. The submission of the assessee was that there was no profits pertaining to the said chargeable accounting periods and therefore the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency of the said two chargeable accounting years which should have been allowed set off. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. In appeal, the Tribunal held that no profits accrued unless sale was effected and, therefore, there was a no merit in the submission made on behalf of the Revenue that during the said three chargeable accounting Period, although there were no sales effected yet profits accrued to the assessee. It also held that there could be no deficiency of profit. The High Court further held that it was not disputed before them that the assessee firm was carrying on the same business from 28th October 1940 and March 1943 remained In stock till 31st3. 1943 and no portion of it had been sold. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf the Revenue: (1) that there were sales effected but profits accrued only unless sale is effected and therefore, the Act itself did not apply to the aforesaid two chargeable account ing periods; (2) that no part or profits could be charged and were in fact not so charged to income tax as no sales were effected and hence the Act was not applicable to the instant case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The chargeable accounting year is the period from September 1939 to 31st 3 1946. In this case, there is a specific provision that profits must be computed under the Excess Profits Tax on the basis of 'accounting period ' and after that the deficiency in profits for that period should be computed on that basis and after set off carried forward to be set off during the chargeable year. [610E] 2. The excess profits tax is attracted in respect Of a business to which the Act applied when the profits during the relevant chargeable accountingperiod exceed the standard profit. Though profit in a composite transaction could be apportioned as between manufacture and sale in the same accounting year, such an apportionment is not permissible when one part of the transaction, i.e., manufacture, fails in one chargeable accounting for the period but where the profits arose during the 'account ing period 'and as such whether the deficiency or the profits arising during the "accounting Period" could be setoff without computation. [613C D] 3. The method of computation under section 7 of the Act must be on the principle of ' Accounting Period ' and before that the deficit in profits is computed on this basis, it is a part of those very profits which is liable to excess profits Tax. [625E F] 4. The accounting period was 1st September 1939 and 31st march 1944. In case of Haji Rahmat Ullah & Co.

The petitioner, a Mechanical Engineering degree was one of the Special Leave Petitioners before this Court. He had to answer the questions in Category I, questions in Civil Engineering and in Category II, questions were in Mechanical Engineering. The petitioners who were qualified in Civil engineering had to answering the questions indicated in Category 1, and those qualified in Mechanical engineering the questions mentioned in Category 11. After the written test and interview, but before a common rank list was prepared by the KPSC as was intened, 8 Writ Petitions were filed in the Kerala High Court by applicants holding Civil Engineering degrees. By these writ petitions the preparation of a common seniority list and also the procedure of the examination and a method of selection were challenged. The learned Single Judge of the Kerala high Court allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare "two lists, namely, one for the Civil Bench and other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". He proceeded: "With respect to it the Service Commission has not yet published the rank list. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Service Commission is directed to prepare two separate seniority lists, one in the Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Cochin University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the K.PSC. On publication of the two lists the Government can request the Service Com missioner to advise the candidates for appointment to these branches on the ground that there were directions to the K PSC to prepare a common list. " The Kerala Public Service Commis sioner & R will implement the above orders forthwith. " It was contended in the Special leave petitions before this court for clarifications and directions, particularly praying that the expression "the common list prepared by Public Service com mission should be deleted. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner will be entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list for claiming the post. [749E] 2. The High Court was right in dismissing the writ appeals, having regard to the developments which have taken place. Accordingly, the special Leave Petitions are dismissed. There is no order as to costs.

The respondent No. 1 filed a suit for accounts from the appellant No. 2, who was a partner of a partnership firm along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The plaintiff respondent No 1 had alleged that he was a partnership business along with the brothers defendant nos. 1 & 2, and that he had been falsely representing before the Income Tax Department inter alia, that a new deed of partnership had been executed on 15.1.1979 to be effective from 1.1 1979 in which the plaintiff has no interest. The Income Tax Officer passed an order on 26th December 1981 on the basis of the false allegations made by the defendants. The appellant challenged the valuation given by the plaintiff as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The trial court dismissed the suit. In appeal, the High Court set aside the valuation and remanded the case to the trial court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that it is manifest that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the respondent in the suit, and he said that the plaintiff had laid claim to a sum of Rs.1,26,796.72 besides another sum over Rs.84,000 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income tax Department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint, and it was, therefore, preposterous on his part to suggest in paragraph 19 of the Plaint that it could be tentatively valued at Rs.50 only. According to the defence case which is challenged as incorrect by the appellant, the plaintiff requested for and was allowed a larger share 'in the well established and reputed business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" and its assets and goodwill as well as the amount lying in the Habib Bank, Karachi Branch solely and absolutely '. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The interpretation put by the learned counsel on the decisions of this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. None of the two cited judgments relied upon by Mr. Chatterjee helps him. It is true that in a suit to recover accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, [1945] ILR XXIV Patna 334, the respondent filed a civil suit praying for accounts and other sum of money over Rs,84,0001. The defendant 's objection to the valuation was rejected by the trial Court "on the ground that the court was powerless to challenge the valuation put by him on the relief claimed in the plaint. " The Full Bench decision in Mata Ram vs Daulat, ILR (1938) Nagpur 589, was sought to be distinguished on the ground of the principle underlying both the clauses (c) and (f) of section 7(iv)(f). The High Court while repelling the argument pointed out that the principle governing both the clause (c), and (F) of Section 7(v)(C) is substantially the same and the Full Bench decisions governed the case. Accordingly it was held that when the valuation putting by the defendant appears to be arbitrary and unreasonable, the court may reject it and leave the plaintiff to correct the valuation or have the suit rejected. Similar was the view of the Patna High Court in suits covered by section 7 (iv)(c) in Salahuddinhyder vs Dhanoolal, [1946] ILR XIV Patna 334 and Shama Pershad Shahi vs Sheopershad Singh XLI, I.C. 95 (Patna). In Attar Singh vs Manohar Singh, ILR , approved.

The respondent assessee in these two matters and the assesses by the other five Special Leave Petitions are certain concerns in M.P. assess able to sales tax (hereinafter referred as the assesses '). All these matters raise common issue. The assesses ' claim for exemption from sales tax for certain periods in question was accepted by the High Court in the case of G.S. Dhall & Flour Mills and, following it, in the other cases. The State Government may, by notification, exempt the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule below who have set up industry in any of the districts of Madhya Pradesh specified in the annexure to this Notification and have commenced production after 1st April 1981 from pay ment of tax under the said Act for the period specified in Column (2), subject to the restrictions and conditions specified in columns (3) of that schedule. 596 Class of dealers Period Restrictions and Conditions subject to which exemption has been granted 1 2 3 1. dealers who Two years The dealer specified in (a) hold a certifi cate from the column (I) shall continue to furnish the pre scribed returns under the Sales Tax Act; and (b) that they should produce, at the time of their assessment, a certifica tion from the Director of Industries certifying that such dealer is eligible to claim exemption and has not opted for in part I of the scheme of deferring the payment of tax. The assessee 's claim was accepted on the ground that the industries run by them are "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption. It was, however, rejected by the State Government on the view that the said industries run under them are 'traditional industry ' which were neither eligible for nor eligible for the exemption. The asses see filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order of rejection of their claim. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the earlier scheme and the exemption now proposed are total ly different in their object and scope and that while the former scheme was intended as an incentive to any one who set up a new industry in the State so that "tra conditional" industries did not get any benefit, the notification presently under consideration was issued with the object of industrialising the backward areas of the State and so it was immaterial what type of industry went in there and whether the industry proposed to be set up was a 'tradition al" one or not. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The terms of the notification are clear and envisage no denial of exemption to traditional indus tries, this question does not survive. However, the S.L.P against the Full Bench was dismissed and two of us having been members of the Bench that dis missed it, we may observe that Sri Salve is perhaps right in saying that it was the content of para 20 and 21 of the Full Court judgment that persuaded this Court to dismiss the S L.P., there against. The Full Bench has there pointed out that even if it could be said that two interpretations of the Notification were equally plausible, the assesses in those cases had set up the industries after the explicit instructions of 12.1. It does seem likely that the State Govern ment had not intended the exemption to be availed of by certain categories of industries. [610E F] 1.2 The words do not carry the State 's case further, for what the Director has to do is to certify that the applicant is entitled to the exemption on the terms and conditions set out in the notification and not on the basis of any further requirements not so set out.

The petitioners in the writ petition were direct recruits to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. The Union of India, the Delhi Administration, the High Court of Delhi and direct recruits were impleaded as respondents to the petitions. Appointment of direct recruits is dealt with by Rule 5(2), according to which, in regard to persons not already in the Delhi Judicial Service, appointment to service shall be made by the Administrator on the recommendation of the High court. In other words, promotees are appointed to temporary posts in the Service while under Rule 17 they are appointed in a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the service. It provides that not withstanding anything contained in the Rules, the Administrator may, in consultation with the High Courts fill substantive vacancies by making temporary appointments thereto from amongst the members of the Delhi judicial Service either constituted as a result of which direct recruits and promotees who are appointed on a regular basis to posts in that Service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in officiating capacity. Rule 17 provides for the appointment of promotees to substantive posts in service, while sub rule (1) of Rule 8 stipulates that seniority of members of Delhi Judicial Services promoted to the service shall he the same as in the High School and the next two vacancies by promotees and so on. The Schedule to the Rules shows that the initial authorised permanent strength of the Haryana Higher Judicial Services was 16 out of which one was to be a District and Sessions Judge and 12 were to be Additional District & Sessions Judges. If the matter were to rest with the proviso, its interpretation would have to be that it does not prescribe a quota for direct recruits : it only enables the appointmentof direct recruits, to substantive post so that they shall not hold more than 1/3rd of the total number of substantive posts In the instant case, the members belonging to the Haryana Judicial Service who were appointed to permanent temporary posts of Additional District and Session Judges on an ad hoc basis or for fortuitous reasons or by way of a stop gap arrangement. constitute a class which is separate and distinct from those who are appointments to posts In strict conformity with the rules of recruitment. It is difficult to appreciate how, in the matter of seniority, any distinction can be made between direct recruits who are recruited to substantive vacancy in the Services on the recommendations of the high Court under Rule 5 (2) and the promotees who were promoted to temporary vacancies in accordance with qualifications laid down under Rule 7(a), namely, by selection and after completion of a minimum ten years judicial service, cannot and should not rank higher than the latter in the list of seniority; if a direct recruit is appointed after a member of the Punjab Judicial Service thus promoted he would rank lower in seniority than the former. The petitioners who were promotees appointed under Rules 16 and 17 to the Higher Judicial service could rank for seniority along with direct recruits only if they are selected by the High COurt as required by those Rules and if they satisfy the requirement laid down in Rule 7 (a) that they must have completed not less than ten years of service in the Punjab judicial Service. Since the rule of `quota and rota ' ceases to apply when appointments are made under Rules16 and 17, the seniority of direct recruit recruits and promotee appointed under those Rules must be determined according to the dates on which direct recruitment were appointed. The respondents who were directly recruited by the Delhi High Court could not claim that they were appointed regularly in accordance With the rules. They were appointed on ad hoc or for casual reasons or on a temporary basis or on fortuitous basis or by reason of a stay order from the High Curt. In the absence of any provision to the contrary, it was not possible to appreciate why, in view of the provisions contained in Rules 16 & 17, such posts should be filled in consultation and that even substantive vacancies could be filled by making regular appointments.

The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in the three years of assessment. In appeals by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income be deleted. The Tribunal referred the following questions to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the appeals. filed by Shri Debi Parlakhan were maintainable in law ? Whether the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner could give a direction in the case of Ambala Flour Mill to the effect that the income should be assessed in the hands of L. Debi Parker after annulling the assessment in the cases of Ambala Rice Mills 3. Whether on the findings of the Income tax officer, Debi ParII and Balkishan Dass Dass Dass carried on the business of the firm with the property of the firms. " The High Court answered the first question in the negative. In appeal to this Court by certificate, HELD: (i) The expression 'any person ' in section 34(3)(b) of the Act indicates the cases where persons other than the appealing assessee might be affected by orders passed by the Appellate Commissioner. Modification or setting aside 'of assessment made on a firm joint Hindu family, association of persons for a particular year may affect the assessment for the said year on a partner or partners of the Firm, member or members of the Hindu Undivided Family (1) ; 394 or the individual, as the case may be. [392 D] Commissioner off Income tax U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, , followed. (ii) The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner had directed that income in the two assessment years be assessed to tax in the ' hands of the family of Debi Parthshad, apparently on the view that Debi Parath was a member of an association of individuals. Since the Appellate Tribunal set aside tho order of the Appellate Assist ant Commissioner directing assessment of "the family of Devi" it had to give directions with regard to the assessment of the income provided the assessment was not barred by the law of Limitation.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of the joint family properties and an account in respect of the Joint Family assets managed by him. The appellant claimed that he had been adopted by Lakshmi Achi in 1922, and that as Subbiah 's son, the appellant claimed to have a share in the joint Hindu family properties, and in the assets of the undivided family and that was the basis on which a claim for partition and accounts was made by the appellant in his suit. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that section 7(v) of the Act was not applicable to the appellant 's claim for division as the appellant had valued his relief in the suit for purposes of jurisdiction and it was on this valuation alone that the appellant could be justly called upon to pay court fees both on the plaint and on the memorandum of appeal. Held, that the decision of the Division Bench of the Madras High Court that the memorandum Of appeal should be taxed for the purposes of court fee under section 7 (iv)(b) of Act is final under the provisions of section 5 of the . The valuation thus made by appellant in respect Of the value of his relief of partition for the payment of court fees must be taken to be the valuation even for the purpose of jurisdiction. The result is that it is the amount at 1035 which the plaintiff has valued the relief sought for the, purposes of Court fee that determines the value for jurisdiction in the Suit and not vice versa. The computation of court Fees in suits falling under section7(iv)(c) depends upon the valuation that the plaintiff makes in respect thereof of his claim. The value for court fees and the value or for jurisdiction must no doubt be the same in such cases; but it is, the value which the defendant seeks to value his claim for the relief of Court fees.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought special leave to appeal against the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1987 declining to sanction the Revised Plans for the construction of "Statesman House" a high rise building on plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road New Delhi of which the first respondent is the lessee. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of the building plans on or before 5th May, 1989. The NDMC assailed the decision by way of a Writ Petition in this Court contending that the plans for the multi storeyed high rise buildings, as proposed by Statesman Ltd., did not provide for a "podium/pedestrian walk way" made mandatory by the Zonal Development Plan for Zone D 1 (viz. Connaught Place Area) approved by the Central Government on 30th April 1966 in No. The structural nature and basis of its calculation of the extent of these "Refuge areas" are dealt with by Bye law 16.4.8 which requires the location of "refuge area ' for a group of floors as specified therein. (vii) The clearance from the Chief Fire Offi cer, Delhi Fire Service envisaged in Bye laws 17.1 is in addition to the requirements of bye laws 16. 4.8.1. The grant of relief in the writ peti tion in the form of a direction to the appellant to sanction plan was not permissible and that, at best, the High Court could have directed the appellant reconsideration the question of according sanction to the plans in the light of the High Courts order. Disposing of the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The clearance by the Chief fire Officer envisaged by Bye laws 16 4. 8.1 (a) and (b) is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the DDA to satisfy itself that the building plan provide for adequate fire safety precaution in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure. The clearance given by the chief Fire Officer, which is expected to involve and follow a technical assessment and evaluation, obliges the NDMC, to give due weight to it but, having regard to the scheme and language of the Bye laws the decision in the NDMC are considered to provide for the safety in a measure better than those envisaged by the bye laws and the Chief Educa tion preferred to accept them. [610E] 1.2 The clearance of the Chief Exu nity envisaged by bye law 17.4 is anadditional condition and cannot be a limitation On the power to satisfy himself that the buildings provide for sufficient fire safety in accordance wit ing its bye law or in better measure, is conclusive and binding on the NDMC. [613C] 1:3 The clearance made from the chief fire Officer contemplated by Bye Law 17.8 is an Additional condition and is not a limitations on the powers of the Delhi Fire Services envisaged by that Bye laws. [514D E] 1 :4 The clearance to the plan in regard to Refuge Area as may be necessary in the context of the specific objectives of bye law 16 4 8.8 are not inflexible and that in appropriate cases, where the plans and designs incorporate fire safety measures which, in judgment of the Court of the Supreme Court, are considered, to provide protection to persons in the event of an out break of fire in a high reduction building, the expression "external wall" must be held to be one which abuts a vacant space to which fighting and rescue equipment can have access and from which rescue operations are feasible.

The joint family business carried on by the brothers was that of a grocery shop, liquor shops, a ration shop, a motor bus service and also money lending under the name of "Sontakke Brothers". The family also Possessed immovable property. Balkrishna Sitaram Sontakke was the eldest of the brothers and was the plaintiff respondent in the present appeal. He will be referred to hereafter as the plain tiff. It is common ground that up to 1944 the brothers were living and messing together and the income from 101 the family business used to be kept with the plaintiff. On June 29, 1945 all the five brothers filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all joint family properties including the accounts of all the businesses. By this compromise it was declared that prior to 1942 all the accounts had been correctly maintained and shown, that the parties had agreed to have arbitrators appointed through Court for examining the accounts from 1942 up to March 31, 1946, and for determining the amount due up to that date. Each of the sons was to get one sixth share in the cash balance as found on March 31. 1946 upon examination of accounts by the arbitrators. The compromise further declared that the plaintiff was to have one sixth fifth share in his motor garage and that defendants 1 and 2 were to pay the price of one sixth per cent to him. One of the brother was a minor and the Court finding the compromise to be for the benefit of the minor accepted it and passed a decree in terms of the compromise on July 25, 1947. The plaintiff thereupon instituted a fresh suit on February 23, 1949 confining his relief to his share of profits and assets of the motor business carried On February 23.49, confining his claim to account up to the 31st March 1946, only implicitly of not explicitly relinquished his claim for the subsequent period. The trial court passed a preliminary decree directing the accounts for the motor cycle business to be taken from March 31 1946 up to April 14, 1945, and directed that the accounts were to be made up to May 31, 1945. In appeal the High Court held that although the motor bus business carried out after the partition had ceased to be a joint family, yet as it was carried on in by some members of a family their position was analogous to that of partner carrying on partnership after dissolution and applying the principle underlying section 37 of the Partnership Act he held that the two brothers carrying on the motorbusiness were liable to account. Accordingly the High court modified the decree of the trial Court by directing that the account for the period April 1, 1946 should be taken up to June 29 1945, up to which date a final decree for payment of the amount found to be due would be made. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the cause of action in the two suits being the same, the suit was barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Code of Civil Procedure and by order II, Rule 2 of the C.P.C., no further question as to the applicability of section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act could possibly arise under the circumstances. Held: (i) The compromise closed once for all the controversy about taking any account of the joint family businesses including the motor shop business after the 31th March 1946 and the plaintiff is bound by the terms of compromise and the consent decree following upon it. [102 D] (ii) The plaintiff 's claim is barred by the provisions of Order II rule 2 (3), C. P.C. as he did not want his brothers to interfere with his exclusive running of the liquor business after March 31; 1946, but there was also another business; that was a kirana shop which was not a very big business.

The respondent entered the service of the Princely State of Mysore in 1935 as Instructor of Tailoring in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, he was absorbed with effect from December 1, 1949 but no order was passed in the case of the respondent despite repeated representations made by the latter. In 1953, the then State of Madras set up the Department for Technical Education and the Polytechnic at Devangere became part of that Department. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the department of Technical Education with effectfrom November 28, 1949, which was the date on which he initially came on deputation. His specific grievance was that in any case, he could not be discriminated against and treated differently from K. N. Chetty who was junior to him in the parent Department and came on his deputation to the Polytechnics establishment subsequently. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960 made these recommendations in favour of the Respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director who was the Unit officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Sri Srinivasa Murthy who was fully qualified as Tailoring Instructor in the Technical Education Department and there was no need to classify the vacancy post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. The case of Sri Srinivasamurthy Chetty is on all fours with that of Sri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty, who was also an Instructor in tailoring and recommended for their absorption with effect From the respective dates of their joining duty, after deputation, in the Institutes. Accordingly K.N. Chetty was absorbed in 1949 by the Director and appointed as Tailores Instructor under the rules then in force, and as his reversion at this distance of time for no fault of his would cause a great hardship to him, the Commission are of the opinion that he may be absorbed as Tailors from the date of his appointment as such as has been ordered in the ease of Sri. K. Rangaswamy Chetty and five others, with effect on November 28. 1949, and that his reversion to his parent department in 1955 56 was not justified. The question for consideration is whether the respondent was entitled to be absorbed or given the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in the service from a particular anterior date, or to be given the same revised pay scale applicable to them borne permanently. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The absorption of K. R. Rangaswami Chetty and 5 others with effect effect from particular anterior dates, was not made in pursuance of any principle of policy or statutory rule but was done as a matter of concession. [259C D] 1.2 In the special circumstances of this case, the High Court was fully justified in granting the relief, it did, to the respondent. The acceptance of the respondents ' contentions in the present case cannot lead to any untoward results such as were apprehended in Rajalakshmiah 's cases. Indeed, it has not been shown that the absorption of the respond ent with effect to past dates was adversely affected even Narayanaswamy Chettiar who was admittedly junior to the Respondent, and was identically situated, was accorded the same treatment. [260E F] K. V. Rangarajan vs State of Tamil Nadu & Ors., ; , referred to.

The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents. The petition was filed on the basis of a letter addressed by one Laxmi Kant Pandey, an Advocate practising in the Court complaining that malpractices indulged were being committed by social organisation and voluntary agency engaged in their work of providing Indian children. It was alleged that the petitioner had been indulging in social organisations, voluntary agencies and voluntary Agencies engaged in various work of imparting Indian children to foreign parent. The petitioner also alleged that he had been making false statements in the petition. The Court appointed a committee for considering the application of the foreigner for adoption. The Committee submitted its report on August 10, 1987. The State Government considered the report and passed an order appointing the foreign parent as guardian of the child with liberty to him to take the child to his own country with a view to its eventual adoption. In the writ petition filed by Laxmi Kant Sharma, the Court directed that the foreign parents should be allowed to take their child to their own country where the procedure for making the adoption in accordance with law of that country can be followed. The order was challenged before this Court on the ground that it violated Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It also alleged inter alia that the adoption of children by foreign parents need not wait until social or child welfare agencies are recognised by the Government as directed in this order, but pending recognition of social or Child welfare agencies for the purpose of inter country adoptions, which interregnum, the court hope, will not last for a period of more than two months, any social or family welfare agency having the care and custody of a child may be permitted to process an application of a foreigner, but barring this departure the rest of the procedure laid down by this Court shall be followed wholly and the principles and norms enunciated by this court in this judgment shall be observed. Allowing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The adoption of Children by foreign parent need not await until social and child welfare agency are recognised under the Government of India Act, 1935. [842C] 1.2 In order to enable such adoption to be made in the country of the foreign father, it would be necessary for the foreign principal to take a child to its own country wherever the procedure is for making adoption in conformity with the law of this country within a period not exceeding two years and as soon as the adoption is effected, it will send two certified copies of the adoption order to the social or the child welfare Agency in India through which the application for guardianship is processed, so that one copy can be filed in court and the other can remain with the social/ child welfare officer processing the application and from the child study report, they would be able to gather information as to who are the biological parents of the children, if the biological parent are known. [ 839D E] 1:3 The recognised social or Children agency sponsoring the application must also undertake while forwarding the application to the Social or child Welfare agency in India, that it will ensure adoption of the Child by the foreigner according to the law in force of that Country within a time not exceeding one year and as expeditiously as possible, preferably within a month from the date of receipt of the application. [ 837E] 2:1 The recognised Social or Children Agency sponsoring the applications of the foreigners must also undertakes while forwarding it to the Indian family in order to enabling the Indian child to decide whether they would take the children in adopt adoption.

The appellant company employed workmen numbering over 5000. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year amounts to Rs. 1,05,32,880. Its accounting year is from 1st April to 31st March of the succeeding year. For the accounting year 1964 65, the Company declared and paid bonus at 20% to all employes in accordance with the provisions of the . The Central Government by order dated June 23, 1967 referred for adjudication to the National Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, the following dispute " What should be the quantum of bonus payable to the workmen of the Indian Cable Company Limited for the accounting years 1965 66, 1966 66 and to a Tribunal, the workmen received the bonus at 108 the rate of 13.51% offered by the Company. The Central Govern ment referred for adjudica tion to the Industrial Tribunal Calcutta, which held that for the purpose of calculating the available surplus, the Tribunal before calculating the notional direct tax deducted the bonus payable for the year in question and directed the payment of the balance 6.49% within the period mentioned 109 in the Award. One aspect which has to be acted is that (in calculating the surplus, it should have been set on for the next year, namely, 1965 66; and disallowed the deduction from gross profits of the sum of Rs. 21,06,576. The Tribunal took notice of the fact that the Income tax Authorities did not object to deduct the provision made by the company for payment of bonus for the said accounting year. On this reasoning the Tribunal added back to the gross profits as per the profit and loss account the provision for payment Of bonus was considered for the first time by this Court in Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. vs Their Workmen, ; , The Union concerned, which was respondent in the appeal, to support the decision of the Tribunal on a method of computation regarding bonus which was not adopted by the Tribunal and also on ground which had not been taken notice of by the tribunal. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The payment of compensation to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the appellant company on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income Tax Act. [750E F] 1.2 In view of the decision in Indian Oxygen Ltd. etc. vs their Workmen, , this Court permitted the Union concerned which was Respondent in the Appeal, to substantiate the Award of the Industrial Tribu nal directing reinstatement of the employee on grounds which were not accepted by the Tribu lates. [749B] 1:3 The Tribunal was justified in disallowing this claim of the Unions. The last item relates to the claim made by Unions that after distribution of bonus at 15% for the years 1964 65 there must have been a surplus and it should be set on, for the subsequent year, viz., 1965 66. This assertion made on behalf of the Union was controverted by the respondent on the grounds that there was no surplus left after paying, the maximum 20% bonus for, the accounting period in question.

The appellant, a Deputy Commercial Tax officer in 1953, was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28, 1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d). His Service Book showed that he had an excellent record of service. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The several promotions gained by him react his good record of Service. But there was one dark spot. In 1969 when he was working as Commercial Tax officers it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner that the charges should be dropped. The Government accepted the report of the Full Board and dropped the charges making the following order on 29 11 1974: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. Out of eleven allegations levelled against him seven were not substantiated in the enquiry made by the Director of Vigilance & Anti Corruption Department. The Board of Revenue (CT) was requested to frame charges straightaway as for a major penalty against Thiru D. Ramaswami on the basis of allegations levelled in his explanation and sent its report thereon. The Full Board considered that all the charges framed against Thiru C. Ramaswami in consequence of the detailed enquiry conducted by the Vigilance Department cannot be pursued and proved. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of November 29, 1974 contending that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant will be reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules. He is entitled to his costs. P.B.R. Appeal allowed. G. O. Ms. No. 1112 dated September 19, 1975, Commercial Taxes Religious Endowments Department, Government of Tamil Nadu is quashed. The order of the High court is set aside. The appeal is allowed. [80G] 1.2 In the face of the promotion of the appel lant just a few months earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is impossible to sustain the order. of the Government retiring the appellant from service. The learned Counsel for the appellant relied on the decisions in Swami Saran Saksena vs State of U.P., ; , Union of India etc. vs M.E. Reddy & Anr., [1971] 1 S.C.R, referred to.

The appellants who were the owners of certain routes filed objections to the schemes and thereafter there was a hearing of these objections by the Transport Minister under section 68 D(2) on the 11th January, 1963. The Transport Minister of the State passed an order in which the routes were to be nationalised and the choice of the Western part of Kurnool for being taken up in the first instance was made by them alone. The appellants challenged the validity of these Schemes before the High Court. The High Court held that there was no proof that the Transport Department had acted merely as the tool of the Chief Minister in order to carry out his behest and it was not necessary to give a short resume of the history of nationalised transport in Andhra Pradesh as well as certain events in Andhra pradesh. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Regional Transport Authority which is specifically mentioned in section 68 F(1) is empowered to issue the permit to the transport undertaking "notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter IV" and that the section rendered the provisions of Rule 141 of the Motor Vehicles Rules inapplicable to cases covered by section 68F(1). [368 C] (ii) The scheme framed under Ch. IV is not invalid because it does not contain any provision for the grant of a permit by the Regional Transport Authorities. It merely contains an express provision that the permits granted to the Transport Undertaking shall be subject to the conditions mentioned in Ch. No doubt, in a State where there is no Regional Transport authority at all [368 D] (iii) The order in the present case was passed on January 27, 1964 and the appellants were not allowed to ply their buses on the routes under the respective permits granted by them as they were not required by section 69 C of the Act.

The appellant, a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, having its registered place of business at Calcutta, claimed exemption under two heads, namely, (i) under section 5(2)(a)(ii) thereof Rs. 1,33,730 6; and (ii) under s.5(2) (a)(iii) thereof the appellant in order to claim exemption thereunder had to furnish a declaration forms duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. The Commercial Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that the particulars furnished by the appellant did not contain any particulars as required under section 6(2). On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the furnishing of the declaration forms was a condition for claiming exemption thereunder and that the failure to furnish the same within the prescribed time amounted to denial of the exemption. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the order of the Commercial Tax officer was dismissed by the High Court on the view that the requirement of section 5 (2)(b) of the Act in effect exempts a specified turnover from taxable turnover all sales to a registered dealer of goods of the class or classes specified in the certificate of registration of the dealer as being intended for the purposes mentioned therein. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: The substantive part of section 6 (2) of Bengal Finance(Sales Tax ) Act, 1940, which provides for exemption in respect of certain sales to registered dealers of specified classes of goods, is self evident. While they are obviously intended to give exemption to a dealer in respect Of sales to unregistered dealers of certain specified classes or classes of specified goods, it seeks also to prevent fraud and collusion in an attempt to evade tax. In the nature of things, in view of several transactions that may be entered into between dealers. it will well nigh be impossible for the taxing authorities to ascertain in each case whether a dealer has sold the specified goods to another for the purpose mentioned in the section. Therefore, presumably to achieve the twofold object namely prevention of fraud and ' facilitating administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a statement in the manner prescribed under the section and r. 27A says that it shall be furnished on demand that is to say it fixes the time when the form is to be furnished. This reconciles the provisions of r.27A with those of s. 5 (1) (ii). While they were obviously intended for giving exemption to dealers in respect o sales to registration dealers of other specified classes, it sought also to avoid fraud and/ collusion in a attempt to evading tax. [633 H] The object of section 4(2), (a) (iii) is self clear. While the words "on demand" are used in the proviso to the said sub clause, they are not intended to be used as a directory provision to subserve the substantive provision in a reasonable way. If so construed, a dealer is not precluded in a case where the proviso cannot be strictly complied with from producing other relevant evidence to prove that the sales to the registered dealers were for the ' purposes mentioned in section. [534 C D] The expression "ondemand" only fixes the point of time when it the declaration form forms are to be produced; otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with the section.[635 B] State of Orissa vs M.A. Ltd., ; , referred to.

The petitioner, who was detained under trial prisoners in the State of Bihar, was released on bail by the Sessions Court. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the constitutional validity of section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and also the constitutional obligation of the State to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trial to the accused. The High Court directed that the State should furnish to this Court the dates on which these under trial prisoner were remanded to judicial custody from time to time by the Magistrates, so that we can satisfy itself in regard to compliance with the proviso to section 167 (2). Allowing the writ petition and directing the State Government to furnish particulars to this court in an affidavit to be filed within two weeks from today, whether the under trial convicts whose names were set out in the chart filed by Mrs. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the requirement of the proviso was complied with in their case. Dismissing the writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of section 169(2), as it stood at the relevant time, was complied w.e.f. the date from which each of them was in jail after making a broad division into two categories viz., minor offences and major offences but this direction had not yet been carried out by the State. [529C D] 2. The right to free legal services is, therefore, clearly an essential ingredient of 'reasonable, fair and just procedure guaranteed by Article 21. This is a constitutional right of every accused person who is unable to engage a lawyer and secure legal services on account of reasons such as poverty, indigence or incommunicado situation and the State is under a mandate to provide a lawyer to an accused person if the circumstances of the case and the needs of justice so required, provided of course the accused person does not object to the provision of such lawyer. [540D E] Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India, ; , followed. The power of this Court in protection of the constitutional rights is of the widest amplitude and it is the constitutional duty of the Court as guardian of the fundamental rights of the people, as a sentinel on the qui vive, to enforce the fundamental right of the accused to speedy trial by issuing the necessary directions to the State which may include taking of positive action, such as augmenting and strengthening the investigative machinery setting up new courts, building new court houses, providing more staff and equipment to the courts, appointment of additional judges and other measures calculated to ensure speedy trials. The Court in the last mentioned case asserted that it "has the duty of fashioning a decree that will require defendants to eliminate the conditions and practices at Parchman here in above found to be violative of the United State 's constitution" and in discharge of this duty gave various directions for improvement of the conditions of those confined in the state Penitentiary. The powers of this court are of the greatest amplitude and we do not see why this Court should not adopt a similar activist approach and issue to the States directions which may involve taking of negative action with a view to securing enforcement of the rights to speedy trials.[540F G] 3. It is now well settled that as a result of the decision of this Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi v Union of lndia, [1978] 1 SCR 621, the right of one charged with crime to counsel may not be deemed fundamental and essential to fair trial in some countries, but is in ours. These, of course would be the most difficult difficult to anticipate. The rights of one accused charged with offence to counsel might not be considered fundamental and necessary for this purpose has to be done by the Court.

The appellant landlord gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The notice was for one year as required by section 34 (2 A), and the tenancy was to terminate from after March 31, 1953. The landlord therefore made an application on April 7, 1953, under section 29(2) of that Act for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. In the meantime an amendment was made to the Act by the insertion of sub section (2A) to section 34 by the Amending Act No. XXXIII of 1952 which came into force on January 12, 1953 and certain further restrictions were placed on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy of a protected tenant. The Mamlatdar rejected the application of the appellant. On appeal the Revenue Tribunal held that as the tenancy had (1) terminated and the right to obtain possession had accrued to the landlord after the coming into force of the Amending act, the Amending Acts applied and therefore the landlord was entitled to possession. It further held that the Amending acts would apply to all proceedings where the period of notice had expired after the Amending came into effect and that what the Amending Legislation did was that it imposed a new limitation on the tight of the landlords to obtain Possession and if the landlord failed to satisfy the court at the date when the tenancy expired and he became entitled to Possession that he was so entitled in law as it then stood, he could not claim relief from the Court. The High Court also held that section 34 did not apply to the present proceedings. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the view taken by the High Court is correct and sub section(2 A) would apply only where notices might have been given but where the tenancy has not actually terminated before the coming in force of Amending Act. The restriction by sub section 2A is on the rights to terminate tenancy and this restriction would come into play on the day on which the landlord 's right to terminate that tenancy is perfected, namely, the day when the tenant terminates in consequence of the notice given to terminate it. A notice under section34(1), is merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the employer to terminate his tenancy and no further proceedings may be taken by him in consequence thereof. It is only when the period Of notice has expired and the tenant has terminated that the landlord acquires a vested right to obtaining possession, of the lands. Therefore, for the application under section 28(2), it is the date on which, the right is to terminate, but not the date of termination.

The petitioners, who were evacuees and the houses of one Khadim Ali, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of January 10, 1952, on the ground that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held: (i) The petitioners ' interest in the house could not have vested in the Custodian without due notice to him, and there was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting Zafar Ali 's right in the properties. [749 B] (ii) The orders of January 1, 1952 were without jurisdiction so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. It was also not disputed that no notice had been issued to the petitioners under section 7 of the Act. They could not maintain this petition. [700 C D] (iii) The order of December 10, 1953, was without jurisdiction inasmuch as the petitioners were concerned, their interest could not in any way be affected by the order made under section 6 of the , and therefore the petitioners had no longer any claim to them. [ 702 B] In the result, the petition must fail. (iv) The petitioner 's interest in houses, therefore, could not vest in the custodian without due notices to him. [ 703 E F] (v) The acts of the custodian in so far that they deprive them of their properties cannot be sustained. It is well established and not disputed, that no property of any person can be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 8 of the . [748 C D].

The assessee company had two Departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool and (2) for weaving of yarn. The second Department which carried on the operations of spinning of cotton yarn from imported wool tops was started some time in 1952. One of the departments was known as M/s. Panipat Woollen & General Mills Co. Ltd., Kharar while the other was known M/S. Navin Woollen Mills, Kharar, while the others were known as R/s Navin W Silk Mills, Mohali, and M/ s. Navin woollen Mills. It is said that the assessee Company was running at a constant loss as a result of which in 1952 the assessee company decided to instal a plant for manufacture of worsted yarn from import wool to dealers by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The plant went into production in September 1952 and it was started sometime in the year 1952. Weaving operations were how ever carried on in both these Departments. One Department was known called M/ S Pani Pat Woollen Mill, Kharharar while M/ss. Navin & Woollen mills, Kharwar, were started some times in the years 1952. The assessee Company appointed M/o. Navin and Woollen Woollen and General Mills Ltd., as the sole selling agents for the worsted yeast yarn on payment of 2% commission. The Plant went into the production in October 1955. The Income tax Officer accepted the plea of the assessee and held that the payments were a permissible deduction as it was incurred for the purpose of the asses see 's trade in order to facilitate the business ' of the assesses. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In further appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that there was an express provision in the agreement dated October 20, 1955 by which the agents agreed to share losses which were a provision peculiar to the present transaction and was not at all covered by any authority cited before the Tribunal or the High Court, that itself was proof positive of the fact that the transaction amounted to a joint venture with a view to division of profits; and that it was not necessary for the assessee to prove that the payment made to the agents were not expenses incurred for that purpose. The High Court also held that in the absence of any express provision, the payments in question amounted to an expenditure which was laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business profession or vocation. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 In order to fall within section 10(2)(xv) of the Act the deduction claimed must amount to an expense which was incurred by the assessee wholly and solely for the pur pose of thebusiness. [200D] 1.2 The test merely means that the Court will place itself in the position of a businessman and find out whether the expenses incurred could be said to have been laid out for the ' purpose of ' sharing or dividing the profits ascertained in a particular manner. Woollen Manufacturers vs Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., ; , referred to. 1.3 The test is merely means, that the court will place himself in the situation of a person and findout whether the expenditure incurred could he said to be laid out wholly and partly for the Purpose of ' shared or dividing profits ascertained In a particular case, it means on the facts and circumstances found by the Tribunal and not on the fact and circumstances as may be found by that the High court. [201E F] Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay vs Poona Electric Supply Co.

The assessee, a company, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn. It had its factory at Ernakulam. The assessee claimed that it had been withdrawing moneys from the company and in the belief that those amounts were liable to be treated as "dividend" under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee and determined a sum of Rs. 1,000 representing the current profits. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but on further appeal, the Tribunal referred the following question to the High Court: "Whether, on the facts and in circumstances of this case, the Income Tax Officer was right in holding that Rs. 18,950 constituted accumulated profits for the purpose of section 2 (6A) of Income Tax, Act, 1961 ?" The High Court answered the first question in favour of the Revenue and against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The expression "accumulated profits" in section 2 of the Act cannot take in current profits, but it does not mean that the profits must in the first place be accumulated in queueinc tion to the profits being current. [950 F] 1.2 In the instant case, there are cases where it has been held that there is an absolute bar against a non applicant seeking a reference of questions of law on a reference application made by the other party. The statement of the case is drawn up on the basis of the application made to by the applicant, who in that application must specify the questions of the law which he desires to be referred to the Tribunal. He may, in appropriate cases, be permitted by the Appellate Tribunal, to raise further questions of fact at the hearing of the reference application. But in every case, it is only the party applying for a reference who is entitled to specify the question of law which should be referred. [951 G H] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs M. Murugappan & Ors., ; , Commissioner of Incometax, Madras V. G. Sankaran, the Madras High Court has reiterated that the expression " Accumulated profit" in that clause must mean profits which had accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the accounting years In a recent case, Commissioner of income Tax, Madras II vs G. Satyanarayanan & Ors. , Commissioner for Income tax Madras vs K. Some attention has been given to the distinction between the two categories in Commissioner of lncome Tax, West Bengal vs A. In the present case, however, the question whether the provision of Rs 11,000 for tax and Rs. 6,900 for dividend can be taken into account when computing the accumulated profits as on March 31, 1958 is not relate to the question, whether accumulated profits can take in Current profits.
