The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the suits out of which the present appeals arose were instituted by him to recover possession of various plots of land in the occupation of the defendants or in the alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. The respondents contested the suits and pleaded that the lands were not Mal lands comprised within Mouza Nala forming part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, that their income was taken into account in fixing the revenue payable by the estate, that they had been granted as Lakheraj to their predecessors in title long prior to the permanent settlement, that neither the Maharaja nor the plaintiff claiming under him had any title to them, and that the entry in the record of rights in 1931 was correct. The trial court decreed the suits but on appeal the District Judge held that the documents put forward by the defendants as containing assertions by them that they held under a Lakheaj grant were not shown to relate to the suit lands, that the relationship subsisting between the parties was one of landlord and tenant, that as there had been no determination of tenancy, no decree in ejectment could be passed but that the plaintiff was entitled to fair rent. On appeal the High Court held that on the materials on record the Courts below were right in presuming a lost grant in favour of the respondents, and therefore the entry must be taken as properly made. Held: (i) The courts below have held that there is no proof that the defendants claimed to hold under a rent free grant to the knowledge of the plaintiff prior to 1931, and, that what all has been established by them is non payment of rent for a considerable length of time, but it has not been established precisely for how long. In the light of these principles, it has now to be seen whether on the facts found a lost granting could be presumed in favour Of the defendants. The finding is as already stated that they were in possession without payment of rents for a certain period of time. That would clearly be beyond the powers of a Mahant and no presumption of a lost Grant could be made in respect thereto.

The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of agricultural land. The respondent contended that the land which was the subject matter of the contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 ( 'Tenancy Act ') for short). The intending purchaser, the appellant, was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act, section 63 of the Tenancy Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and, therefore, as the agreement was contrary to the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the said Tenancy Act, the same cannot be specifically enforced. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not a ' agriculturist within meaning of section 63, and that the agreement for sale was contrary lo the provisions Of the Bombay Act. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decide or deal with any question which arises under the Tenancy Acts and which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by any competent authority is ousted. In this appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if the court does not take note of Ext 78 an issue on the pleadings would arise whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist and in view of the provisions under section 70 (a) of the Mamlatdar alone would have exclusive jurisdiction under the Bombay Rent Act to decide the same, prima facie on a contention being raised by the defendant an issue may arise which the Civil court would not be competent to try and the legislature stepped in to avoid the conflict of jurisdiction by introducing section 85A making it obligatory upon the civil Court to refer such an issue to the competent authority under the landlord Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of a civil court to settle decided or dealwith any question arising under the tenancy law is totally ousted. Therefore, it an issue arises in a civil Court whether a person is an agricultural agriculturist within tho meaning of Tenancy Act and if section 85 A imposes an obligation on the civil court not only to arrogate jurisdiction to itself to decide that issue if it arises before it in a Civil suit. However, by an express provision contained in Section 85A the jurisdiction to settle , decided or dealing with any issue which is require to be settle, decided, or dealt by the competent authorities is ousted, and therefore, it is made obligatory for the civil courts not only not to artigate jurisdiction but also to refer the same to the Mamlatdar and on the reference being answered back, to dispose of the suit in accordance with the decision recorded by the Competent authority on the relevant issue. [595B C] 2. The High Court was right in holding that if an issue is required in a properly constituted civil suit which the civil suit court is competent to entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of Tenancy Acts, then notwithstanding the fact that it arises in an incidental manner in a suit, it would have to be referred to the Competent Authority under the Land Revenue Act. [596D] 3. The legislature has expressly ousted the jurisdiction by enacting section 85B making it incumbent upon the Civil Courts not only for not to charogate Jurisdiction to itself, decide and deal with the same. This Court first affirmed that whatever may have been the position before Act XIII of 1956, the legislature has unequivocally expressed an intention that even in a case properly constituted Civil suit cognizable by the Civil Judge, it will have no jurisdiction to try an issue was rising in the suit, if the issue is required to be decided or disposed of by the Mamlatdar or other competent authority.

The assessee is a heavy engineer manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the new industrial undertakings were formed by reconstruction of the business already in existence. The Tribunal accepted the claim for exemption under section 15C of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. According to the Tribunal both the Steel Foundry and the Jute Mill Division of the assessee were new industrial undertaking. According t he Tribunal the existing business of the asses see was a manufacturing boilers. It held that even though the manufactured products of the new Industrial undertakings were mostly used in the assessee 's other business of manu facturing boilers, wagons, etc., the element of profit was there and the extent of the same could be ascertained as the assessee was maintaining separate books of account. The controversy centres round the true construction of section 15 C(2)(i) of the Act and in particu lar with regard to the scope and ambit of the expression therein, namely, the reconstruction of business already existing in existence; that the Cement Foundry & the Jute Mills Division was formed by the reconstruction company 's business already there in existence, namely the business of heavy engineering. The High Court held that though the manufacturing products of new industrial con trary to the conclusion reached by the Tribunal were old industrial undertakings mostly used for the assessee and since the articles produced in these two supplemental undertakings help in producing the identical article which has been the end product of the assesses 's main business, section 15B(2) (i) cannot come to aid of the appellant. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The question whether the new undertaking connotes expansion of the existing industrial undertaking of the appel lant but whether it is all the same a new and identifiable undertaking separate and distinct from the existing manufacturing business. [776E] 2.1 In order that the old industrial undertaking can be said to be not formed out of the already existing business, there must be a new emergence of a physically separate industrial unit which may exist on its own as a viable unit. It is clear that the principal business of assessee is heavy engineering in the course of which it manufactures boilers, trucks etc. If an industrial undertaking produce certain machines or parts which are, by themselves, identi fiable units being marketable commodities and the undertakings can be carried on separately without complete absorption and losing their identity in the old business, they are not to be treated as being formed by con struction of the old busi ness. [771C D] 2:2 The principal business is heavy Engineering in the Course of which the assessee manufactures boilers. wagons etc., If an Industrial undertaking produce some machines or part which are by themselves identiable units Being marketable commodities, and the Undertaking can be carry on separately with complete absorption & losing their identification in the new business, it cannot be anything but a new & separate industrial undertaking to qualify for appropri at exemption under s 15C. [761E] Commissioner of Income tax vs Gangs Sugar Corpora tion Ltd., ; , followed.

The inam lands were granted to the appellants by Hindu kings for performance of services connected therewith. The inams were confirmed by the British Government. For over 80 years, the inams were in the enjoyment of alienees from inamdars. By an order passed on April 10, 1947 under section 44 B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, the Revenue Divisional Officer resumed the inam lands and regranted them to the temple. On October 17, 1947, this order was confirmed by his order dated April 10. The Revenue Divisional officer and the District Collector held that the inams comprised both melwaram and kudiwaram rights in the land. The orders were passed on notice to the alienees. The alienees instituted a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Madurai under the proviso to section 44B(2)(d)(ii) asking for a decree declaring that the inam grants consisted of the melwarm only. The suit was withdrawn to the court of the District judge and registered as O.S. No. 3 of 1954 and declared that the order resuming the inam land was illegal and a nullity. The High Court dismissed the suit with respect to all the inams except the Dasi inam. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The inam title deeds, the entries in the Inam fair register prepared at the time of the confirmation of the inams by the Inams Commissioner in 1863 and the contemporaneous statement made by the inamdars are of the same pattern in respect of all the inam. The statements exhibit B 4 show that in fasli 1272 corresponding to 1862 63, Veerabadra Mudali, Periasami Chetty Naidu, Mudaliar Chettiar Mudali andappa Mudali. The plaintiffs claimed title to the lands under a grant from the inamdar before 1861. The only direct evidence as to how Kunjanna Ayyar came into possession of the suit lands is furnished by exhibit A 2, a statement made on August 14, 1868. The District Collector was held that alienation was within the purview of section 44(2) (a)(i). [545 B] (ii) There is no period of limitation prescribed for the initiation of proceedings under section44 B(2). The section gave a new statutory right of resumption of the inam where there has been an alienation of the Inam either before or after 1934. The object of section 43 B was to define and enlarge the grounds on which the inams could be resumed and to devise a proper procedure for the resumption. [546 C] (iii) There can be no doubt that section 44 A(2), (a) (i). allows a resumption of an inam wherethere has been, an alienation either before Or after 1934, but the object of s 44 B wasto define and to enlarge the ground on which inams could he resumed and also devise a properly for the regrant. The first ground is that the holder of the, inam had made an alienation. The inam lands in the present case were not personal inams. They were inams granted to office holders as remuneration for services to be rendered by them in connection with the temple.[546 D] (iv) There was no period Of limitation prescribed under section 43B(1).

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. By virtue of the power conferred on it by that Act the Municipality used to levy and collect house tax 127 at the rate of 7% of their gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The appellant Corporation challenged the validity of the said tax on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the basis of gross annual rent less 10%. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant Corporation that the appellant had not been given a proper opportunity before imposing the tax on its gross annual rental value and that the tax imposed on the appellant by section 2(c) could only apply if the tax was assessed in the manner consistent with the provisions of section 73, that is, if it was assessed on net and not the gross annual lease value after deducting 10% of the gross income. HELD: The appellant had been given notice to show cause why the tax should not be levied on the gross monthly letting value. The assessment list prepared for 1952 53 showed that the amount shown in that list were conclusive evidence of the valuation and the amount of tax assessed thereon and entitled the Corporation to collect the tax assessed on it. [131 E] In order to prevent such a result the legislature has provided by sub section 2 of section 79 that where a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year, the provisions Of sections 75 and 76 shall be applicable as if a new assessment list had been completed at the commencement of that particular official year. The list so adopted was therefore in force.

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. Thomas at Medical. The Memorandum of Association empowered the Company to manufacture and deal in acids, alkalis and other chemicals. The assessee company carried on its business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. Thereafter, the profits from the business became less and less due to War conditions, and the assessee company started to manufacture plywood chests for tea, paints and lemon grass oil. These were contemplated by cl. (3) of the Memorandum of association. On May 9, 1943, the assessee Company entered into an agreement with one Rao Sahib Natesa Iyer for the sale of the lands, buildings, plant and machinery of its match factory for Rs. 5, 75,000. It was agreed that the price would not include manufactured goods, chemicals and other raw materials or any other asset not shown in the agreement of sale. The Income tax Officer took up the position that the match manufacturing had been stopped, and that business had been wound up, and there thus only an appreciation of the capital assets and not a business profit which was liable to assessment. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. On appeal by the Department, the Tribunal held that by the sale no business was done, and therefore the excess represented a capital appreciation and not trading profit. The High Court also held that the sale could not be regarded as a realisation sale after the company was wound up but had the characteristics of a trading sale. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that : (1) the transaction of sale of raw materials along with the business, including machinery, plant, premises and premises was a revenue sale, and whether in the facts and circumstances of the case, the sum of Rs. 1,15,254has been rightly charged to income tax; and (2) the decision that the sales were not in the ordinary course of trade but were part of the realisation of the trading stock and winding up of the business rather than a trading profit was liable for assessment. HELD : (i) The transaction was not during the carrying on of the assessee 's business, because the sheep may be regarded to be the capital with which the wool, which is sold, is produced or the sheep with the wool on them may be treated as the stock in trade. Such a question, fortunately, does not arise in the present case, which can be decided on the narrow ground whether the business was being wound up and the sale, a realisation sales, or whether trading was going on in spite of the winding up, so as to attract tax on profits made. [966 F G] (ii) The fact that the clause in the Memorandum gave power to the Company, to Bell chemicals cannot be used in this connection because the evidence clearly showed that cl was never used and the two sales of chemicals through the years were too petty in themselves to afford evidence of a continued or sustained trading In chemicals. [963 F] Doughty Salmond, who delivered the judgment of Court, observed that there is a difficulty in deciding cases of a business which involve breeding of sheep for the purpose of selling wool This is quite true, because, the sheep might be regarded not as determining what it was that his acts amount to; and the real thing that has to be decided here is what were the acts done in connection with this business and whether they amount to a trading which would cause the profits that accrued to be profits arising from a trade or business. [964 G] Doorty vs Coughty, , referred to.
